BIO 102 
 
     Prof SG Jonathan 
 
      Viruses 
A virus Viruses may be defined as acellular organisms whose genomes consist of nucleic 
acid, and which obligatory replicate inside host cells using host metabolic machinery and 
ribosomes to form a pool of components which assemble into particles called VIRIONS, 
which serve to protect the genome and to transfer it to other cells. When infected by a 
virus, a host cell is forced to produce many thousands of identical copies of the original 
virus. Unlike most living things, viruses do not have cells that divide; new viruses are 
assembled in the infected host cell. But unlike still simpler infectious agents, viruses 
contain genes, which gives them the ability to mutate and evolve. Over 5,000 species of 
viruses have been discovered yet 
 
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites characterized by a simple structure of 
genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), and sometimes a 
lipid envelope. They lack metabolic machinery, requiring a host cell's resources for 
replication and assembly, and exhibit both living traits like genetic variation and 
reproduction within a host, and non-living traits like inactivity outside a host and lack 
of cellular structure. Viruses are extremely small, can infect all types of life, and have 
various shapes and sizes. 
A virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent (small parasite) that cannot reproduce by 
itself. All viruses are obligatory replicates only inside the living cells of an organism. 
Also viruses can infect all types of life forms, from animals and plants to 
microorganisms, including bacteria and archaea. When infected by a virus, a host cell 
is forced to produce many thousands of identical copies of the original virus.. 
 
Most viruses have either RNA or DNA as their genetic material. The nucleic acid 
may be single- or double-stranded of genetic material. The entire infectious 
virus particle, called a virion, consists of the nucleic acid and an outer shell of 
protein. The simplest viruses contain only enough RNA or DNA to encode four 
proteins. The most complex can encode 100 – 200 proteins. 
 
Viral infections can cause disease in humans, animals and even plants. Antibiotics 
have no effect on viruses, but antiviral drugs have been developed to treat life-
threatening infections. Vaccines that produce lifelong immunity can prevent some 
viral infections. 
Viruses reproduce rapidly because they have only a few genes compared to humans who 
have 20,000–25,000. For example, influenza virus has only eight genes and rotavirus has 
eleven. These genes encode structural proteins that form the virus particle, or non-
structural proteins, that are only found in cells infected by the virus. 

 
Size of Viruses 
A small virus has a diameter of about 20 nm. Parvovirus. A large virus has a diameter of 
up to 400 nm. Poxviruses. Viruses are among the smallest infectious agents, and most of 
them can only 
 
Shape of Viruses: - 
Viruses vary in shape from the simple helical and icosahedral to more complex 
structures. A virus consists of two or three parts: genome and capsid or genome, 
capsid and envelope 
 
Characteristics of viruses: 
1.  Acellular: 
Viruses are not made of cells and lack cellular structures such as a cell membrane,

acid, and which obligatory replicate inside host cells using host metabolic machinery and 
ribosomes to form a pool of components which assemble into particles called VIRIONS, 
which serve to protect the genome and to transfer it to other cells. When infected by a 
virus, a host cell is forced to produce many thousands of identical copies of the original 
virus. Unlike most living things, viruses do not have cells that divide; new viruses are 
assembled in the infected host cell. But unlike still simpler infectious agents, viruses 
contain genes, which gives them the ability to mutate and evolve. Over 5,000 species of 
viruses have been discovered yet 
 
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites characterized by a simple structure of 
genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), and sometimes a 
lipid envelope. They lack metabolic machinery, requiring a host cell's resources for 
replication and assembly, and exhibit both living traits like genetic variation and 
reproduction within a host, and non-living traits like inactivity outside a host and lack 
of cellular structure. Viruses are extremely small, can infect all types of life, and have 
various shapes and sizes. 
A virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent (small parasite) that cannot reproduce by 
itself. All viruses are obligatory replicates only inside the living cells of an organism. 
Also viruses can infect all types of life forms, from animals and plants to

is forced to produce many thousands of identical copies of the original virus..

NATURE OF LIVING ORGANISM
What are living organisms?
These are organisms characterized by performance of certain life processes such as Movement, Respiration, Nutrition, Irritability, Growth, Excretion, Reproduction Intractability and Aging.  Non living things may
be able to perform one or more to these process, for instance, a machine can move, it is only living
organism that can perform all of the activities.
Plant nutrition, Elements and their function
Plant nutrition is the study of the chemical elements that are necessary for plant growth. There are
several principles that apply to plant nutrition. Some elements are directly involved in plant metabolism. Metabolism is the life sustaining chemical activity, i.e. The series of processes by which food is converted into the energy and products needed to sustain life.
A nutrient that is able to limit plant growth according to Liebig's law of the minimum, is
considered an essential plant nutrient and if the plant can not complete its full life cycle without
it. Macronutrients are Elements that when are  present at low levels may cause deficiency symptoms, and toxicity is possible at levels thatare too high. Further, deficiency of one element may present as symptoms of toxicity from anotherelement, and vice-versa.
Micronutrients (trace levels) These are elements that are vital to plant growth but are only
required in minute amounts, very much like vitamins in human diets
Plants uptake essential elements from the soil through their roots and from the air (mainly
consisting of nitrogen and oxygen) through their leaves. Nutrient uptake in the soil is
achieved by cation exchange, wherein root hairs pump hydrogen ions (H+) into the soil
through proton pumps. These hydrogen ions displace cations attached to negatively charged
soil particles so that the cations are available for uptake by the root. In the leaves, stomata
open to take in carbon dioxide and expel oxygen. The carbon dioxide molecules are used as
the carbon source in photosynthesis
Functions of nutrients
Carbon
Carbon forms the backbone of many plants biomolecules, including starches and cellulose. Carbon is
fixed through photosynthesis from the carbon dioxide in the air and is a part of the carbohydrates
that store energy in the plant.
Hydrogen
Hydrogen also is necessary for building sugars and building the plant. It is obtained almost entirely from water.
Oxygen
Oxygen is necessary for cellular respiration. Cellular respiration is the process of generating energy rich
adenosine triphosphate (ATP) via the consumption of sugars made in photosynthesis. Oxygengas is produced as a by-product from this reaction.
Phosphorus
 As a component of ATP, phosphorus is needed for the conversion of light energy to chemical energy (ATP) during photosynthesis. Phosphorus can also be used to modify the activity of various enzymes by phosphorylation, and can be used for cell signalling. Since ATP can be used for the biosynthesis of many plant biomolecules, phosphorus is important for plant growth and flower/seed formation.
Potassium
Potassium regulates the opening and closing of the stoma by a potassium ion pump. Since stomataare important in water regulation, potassium reduces water loss from the leaves and increases drought tolerance. Potassium deficiency may cause necrosis or interveinal chlorosis.
Nitrogen
Nitrogen is an essential component of all proteins. Nitrogen deficiency most often results in stunted growth.
Sulphur
Sulphur is a structural component of some amino acids and vitamins, and is essential in themanufacturing of chloroplasts.
Silicon
Silicon is deposited in cell walls and contributes to its mechanical properties including rigidity andelasticity
Calcium
Calcium regulates transport of other nutrients into the plant and is also involved in the activation of
certain plant enzymes. Calcium deficiency results in stunting.

Magnesium is an important part of chlorophyll, a critical plant pigment important in photosynthe

RESPIRATION IN PLANTS
The breakdown of complex molecules to yield energy takes place in the cytoplasm and in the mitochondria (also only in eukaryotes). The breaking of the C-C bonds of complex compounds through oxidation within the cells, leading to release of considerable amount of energy is called respiration. The compounds that are oxidised during this process are known as respiratory substrates. Usually carbohydrates are oxidised to release energy, but proteins, fats and even organic acids can be used as respiratory substances in some plants, under certain conditions. During oxidation within a cell, all the energy contained in respiratory substrates is not released free into the cell, or in a single step. It is released in a series of slow step-wise reactions controlled by enzymes, and it is trapped as chemical energy in the form of ATP. Hence, it is important to understand that the energy released by oxidation in respiration is not (or rather cannot be) used directly but is used to synthesize ATP, which is broken down whenever (and wherever) energy needs to be utilized. Hence, ATP acts as the energy currency of the cell. This energy trapped in ATP is utilized in various energy-requiring processes of the organisms, and the carbon skeleton produced during respiration is used as precursors for biosynthesis of other molecules in the cell. Plants, unlike animals, have no specialized organs for gaseous exchange but they have stomata and lenticels for this purpose. 
C6H12O6 + 6O2                   6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy
If this energy is to be useful to the cell, it should be able to utilize it to synthesize other molecules that the cell requires. The strategy that the plant cell uses is to catabolize the glucose molecule in such a way that not all the liberated energy goes out as heat. The key is to oxidize glucose not in one step but in several small steps enabling some steps to be just large enough such that the energy released can be coupled to ATP synthesis. During the process of respiration, oxygen is utilized, and carbon dioxide, water and energy are released as products. The combustion reaction requires oxygen. But some cells live where oxygen may or may not be available. Even among present-day living organisms, we know of several that are adapted to anaerobic conditions. Some of these organisms are
facultative anaerobes, while in others the requirement for anaerobic condition is obligate. In any case, all living organisms retain the enzymatic machinery to partially oxidize glucose without the help of oxygen. This breakdown of glucose to pyruvic acid is called glycolysis. 
GLYCOLYSIS
The term glycolysis has originated from the Greek words, glycos for sugar, and lysis for splitting. The scheme of glycolysis was given by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof, and J. Parnas, and is often referred to as the EMP pathway. In anaerobic organisms, it is the only process in respiration. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and is present in all living organisms. In this process, glucose undergoes partial oxidation to form two molecules of pyruvic acid . In plants, this glucose is derived from sucrose, which is the end product of photosynthesis, or from storage carbohydrates. Sucrose is converted into glucose and fructose by the enzyme, invertase, and these two monosaccharides readily enter the glycolytic pathway. Glucose and fructose are phosphorylated to give rise to glucose-6- phosphate by the activity of the enzyme hexokinase. This phosphorylated form of glucose then isomerises to produce fructose-6- phosphate. Subsequent steps of metabolism of glucose and fructose are same. In glycolysis, a chain of ten reactions, under the control of different enzymes, takes place to produce pyruvate from glucose. DR. ADEOLA A. ONI

--- SLIDE ---

OUTLINE
Briefs on physiology to include:
Nutrition;
Respiration;
Circulatory systems; 
Excretion;
Reproduction; 
Growth and Development in Animals

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
Living cells require a consistent flow of nutrients to sustain their metabolic needs.

As a result, most animals spend considerable time and energy in acquiring and digesting food.

The ingested food is used primarily by the animal’s body cells to produce Adenosine Tri-Phosphate (ATP), the main energy currency which the cells use to carry out all their metabolic activities. 

In addition, it also provides raw materials such as amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals necessary for growth, maintenance and repair of the body tissues, as well as for reproduction and regulation of body processes. 

Nutrition in animals encompasses all the processes involved in assimilation and utilization of food for energy, growth, maintenance and reproduction.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
The structurally complex food substances of animals are broken down into simple absorbable units by enzymes in a process known as digestion. 

Digestion in animals evolved from intracellular to extracellular digestion. In intracellular digestion, it is only food items small enough to be internalized by the cells that can be digested. 

As a result, intracellular digestion is limited to only few lower animal groups. These include:

Protozoans – Unicellular organisms that ingest tiny food particles and digest them inside food vacuoles.

Sponges (Phylum: Porifera) multicellular animals that use specialized cells to engulf food particles from the water and digest them inside the cells.
In extracellular digestion, larger quantities of food can be broken down and stored.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
Extracellular digestion
An animal’s digestive tract is mainly a hollow sac or tube with an entrance (mouth) and an exit (anus).

Even though this tube, i.e. the digestive tract lies within an animal’s body, the openings at both ends (mouth and anus) are in contact with the outside world and so the digestive tube or gut can therefore be thought of as being continuous with the external environment.

Until the nutrients in food conducted down this tube are broken down into simpler units and absorbed across the walls of the tube into the body cells, they are not considered as “inside” the body, hence the term “extracellular” digestion because food breakdown occurs outside the body cells within the gut.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
Evolution of the digestive tract in animals
The first digestive systems probably evolved as an in-folding of the epidermis into an interior sac (such as those found in Cnidarians), allowing the animal to capture much larger quantities of food.

The sac later fused with the opposite end of the body to form a complex tube known as the gut with an entrance (the mouth) and an exit (the anus).

Cells lining this digestive tube could evolve specialized functions: 
some could be specialized and compartmentalized for acidic digestion (e.g. the parietal or oxyntic cells in mammals, birds and lower vertebrates); 
others for alkaline digestion (e.g. intestinal epithelial cells), some for receiving and storing food (e.g. the crop) and others for processing wastes.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
The gut in most animals can be divided into the foregut, mid-gut and the hind gut. 

Some animals like hydra, jellyfish, sea anemones and flatworms carry out both intracellular and extracellular digestion. 

Most invertebrates like annelids and arthropods, and all vertebrates practice extracellular digestion.

22. 4  Evolution in Action: Measuring 
Natural Selection in Populations Today 
 The theory of evolution by natural selection is testable, meaning 
biologists can test the validity of each of Darwin’s postulates. 
Indeed, researchers have documented heritable variation and 
differential reproductive 
success in a wide array of 
natural populations. 
 This section summa-
rizes two examples of evo-
lution by natural selection 
being observed in nature. 
Hundreds of other case studies are available, involving a wide 
variety of traits and organisms. Let’s start by exploring the evolu-
tion of drug resistance, one of the great challenges of our time. 
 Case Study 1: How Did  Mycobacterium 
tuberculosis Become Resistant to Antibiotics? 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the bacterium that causes the infec-
tious disease  tuberculosis , or  TB , has long been a scourge of hu-
mankind. It usually infects the lungs and causes fever, coughing, 
sweats, weight loss, and often death. In Europe and the United 
States, TB was once as great a public health issue as cancer is 
now. It receded in importance during the early 1900s, though, 
for two reasons: 
1.  Advances in nutrition made people better able to fight off 
most  M. tuberculosis infections quickly. 
2.  The development of antibiotics allowed physicians to stop 
infections. 
 In the last few decades, however, rates of  M. tuberculosis infec-
tion have surged in all countries and age groups. In 2022, the 
World Health Organization identified TB as the second leading 
infectious killer after COVID-19. Physicians are particularly 
alarmed because the strains of  M. tuberculosis responsible for the 
increase are largely or completely resistant to antibiotics that 
were once extremely effective. 
 How and why did the evolution of drug resistance occur? The 
case of a single patient—a young man who lived in Baltimore—
illustrates what is happening all over the world. 
A Patient History  The story begins when the man was admitted 
to the hospital with fever and coughing. Chest X-rays, followed 
by bacterial cultures of fluid coughed up from the lungs, showed 
that he had an active TB infection. He was given several antibiot-
ics for 6 weeks, followed by twice-weekly doses of the antibiotic 
rifampin for an additional 33 weeks. Ten months after therapy 
started, bacterial cultures from the patient’s chest fluid indicated 
no  M. tuberculosis cells. His chest X-rays were also normal. The 
antibiotics seemed to have cleared the infection. 
 Just two months after the TB tests proved normal, however, 
the young man was readmitted to the hospital with a fever, severe 
cough, and labored breathing. Despite being treated with a vari-
ety of antibiotics, including rifampin, he died of respiratory

among individuals in a population is essential for evolution to

because it is populations that change over time. To come up with

EXTRACTION OF METALS
The process of extracting metal ores buried deep underground is called mining. The metal ores are found in the earth’s crust in varying abundance. The extraction of metals from ores is what allows us to use the minerals in the ground. The ores are very different from the finished metals that we see in buildings and bridges. Ores consist of the desired metal compound and the impurities and earthly substances called gangue. The extraction of metals and their isolation occurs over a few major steps:
1

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION OF METALS
Extraction of metals and the reactivity series:
The most reactive metals are at the top of the series
The tendency to become oxidised is thus linked to how reactive a metal is and therefore its position on the reactivity series
Metals higher up are therefore less resistant to oxidation than the metals placed lower down which are more resistant to oxidation
The position of the metal on the reactivity series determines the method of extraction
2

--- SLIDE ---

REACTIVITY SERIES OF METALS
3

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION OF METALS
Concentration of Ore –  the ore is separated from earthy impurities.
Isolation of metal from concentrated Ore – Here the ore is converted to its oxide form and then reduced. The steps involved are either calcination or roasting and then heating with a reducing agent.
Purification of the metal – Here the metal is purified for practical purposes.
4

--- SLIDE ---

Metals extraction method table
5

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION FLOW CHAT
6

--- SLIDE ---

7

--- SLIDE ---

The extraction method depends on the position of a metal in the reactivity series
Higher placed metals (above carbon) have to be extracted using electrolysis as they are too reactive and cannot be reduced by carbon
Lower placed metals can be extracted by heating with carbon which reduces them
8

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in the extraction of metals from their ores.
Concentration of Ores
The very first step, which is the concentration of ore, involves the removal of gangue particles that can be achieved using gravity separation, froth floatation, magnetic separation, and leaching processes.
9

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION OF METALS
The gravity separation method is used when gangue particles are lighter than the ore. This method is generally used for the concentration of oxides and carbonate ores. The method involves the passing of crushed ore particles through a stream of water during which the lighter gangue particles are washed away.
10

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in the extraction of metals from their ores.
The froth floatation method is used to remove gangue particles from sulfide ores. In this method, the crushed ore and water are added to a tank in which a frother, such as pine oil, is added and then air is blown under pressure to create the froth. The gangue particles will be wetted by water and the metal comes up with the froth.
11

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in the extraction of metals from their ores.
The magnetic separation method is used when either metal or gangue particles have magnetic properties. In this method, the crushed ore is passed over conveyor belts with magnetic rollers.
The leaching method is used to concentrate ores of aluminium, silver, and gold, etc. In this method, the crushed ore is treated with a solvent that dissolves the ore leaving behind the impurities.
12

--- SLIDE ---

Metal Extraction Processes
Roasting and Calcination
Roasting is the heating of concentrated metal ore in presence of air. It is mainly done for metal sulfide ores to convert them into their respective oxides. For example, cinnabar is a sulfide ore of mercury with the chemical formula of HgS. When the ore is heated in presence of air, it is first converted into mercuric oxide and then upon further heating, liquid mercury is formed:

CHE 176 – ORGANIC CHEMISTRY I 

PROF. O O. SONIBARE 
OFFICE: F104, CHEMISTRY DEPT. 

LECTURE OUTLINE  
Basic concept of organic chemistry – definition and 
importance of organic chemistry,  atom and molecular 
orbitals including bonding, unique nature of carbon and 
hybridization  
 
Determination of molecular composition and structure of 
organic compounds 
 
Functional group classes of organic compounds and 
nomenclature 
 
Reaction mechanism and Kinetics  
 
Organic reactions- types and factors affecting them. 
 
  

DEFINITION OF ORGANIC CHEMISTRY  
What is Chemistry? 
Chemistry is the branch of physical science that deals with 
the study of composition, properties and reactions of 
substances. 
 
What is Organic Chemistry? 
Branch of chemistry that deals with carbon compounds. 
This branch of chemistry is very important because of the 
large numbers of organic compounds and their 
occurrences and applications.  

IMPORTANCE OF ORGANIC CHEMISTRY 
Most of the substances we use in our daily life are organic 
in nature:  
   (a) The food types that sustain human body are  made up of  
        organic compounds, e.g. carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils,  
        vitamins etc. 
    (b) the clothes we wear (wool and cotton- cellulose) 
    (c) the commodities we use (wood- cellulose, plastic- polymer  
          of hydrocarbons) 
    (d) the source of primary energy (petroleum, natural gas, coal) 
     (e) The medicine we take  
    (f) In agriculture (fertilizers and agrochemicals) 
 

UNIQUE NATURE OF CARBON  
What makes carbon special? Why is a whole field of 
organic chemistry dedicated to carbon? 
Carbon is very unique due to many reasons: 
 
1. Tetravalent nature: Due to its tetravalent nature, 
carbon always form covalent bonds by sharing 
electrons with one, two, three or four carbon atoms or 
atoms of other elements or group of atoms. Carbon 
can form single, double or triple bonds with other 
atoms because of its bonding ability.  

 
  

2. Catenation: The tetra-covalency of carbon atom 
allows it to combine easily with other carbon to 
form stable chain like structure.  
 
Catenation: Catenation is the ability of an element 
to form chains and rings in which its atoms are 
bonded to one another i.e. ability to exhibit self–
linkage. 
 

3. Formation of strong C-C covalent bonds: The 
single bond formed between the carbon atoms is strong. 
This results in the formation of stable compounds. 
Carbon atoms also form stable bonds with other atoms 
e.g. H, Cl, Br, O etc. 
 
 3. Formation of C-C multiple bonds: Due to its small 
size, the C-atom can also form multiple bonds. This 
gives rise to a variety in the carbon compounds.  
 
4. Hybridisation:  Formation of hybrid orbitals allows 
carbon to form double and triple bonds. 
 

ATOMS, ATOMIC AND MOLECULAR ORBITALS – 
Refer to your CHE 156 Note 

HYBRIDISATION OF ORBITALS IN CARBON 
Hybridization simply means mixing 
 
Hybridization of orbitals involves mixing of atomic 
orbitals to form new identical orbitals known as 
hybrid orbitals.  
 
These hybrid orbitals are subsequently used in 
bonding to give more stable compounds. 
 

 
3 types of Hybridization exist in carbon:  
 
sp3, sp2 and sp  
 
All the three types involve mixing of s and p 
orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals. 

sp3 HYBRIDIZATION IN CARBON  
Atomic Number of Carbon = 6   
Electronic configuration of Carbon in ground state =  
   1s2 2s2 2p2 [2p1
x 2p1y 2pz], thus implying that valency of    
   carbon should be 2.  
However, carbon exhibits a valency of 4 i.e. its tetravalent.        
WHY IS THIS SO? 
One electron is promoted from the 2s orbital to the vacant 2pz 
orbital giving rise to four (4) unpaired electrons viz - the new 
electronic configuration of carbon = 1s2 2s1 2p1
x 2p1
y 2p1
z 
1s electrons are considered to be core electrons and are not 
available for bonding. 

Furthermore, there is mixing between the 2s orbital and 
the three 2p orbitals to form four (4) new sp3 hybrid 
orbita

ALKANAMINES
• Alkanamines belong to the amines group and are
organic molecules containing only carbon (C),
hydrogen (H) and nitrogen (N) atoms.
• Primary alkanamines occur when one hydrogen
atom in ammonia is replaced by a carbon chain (R-
NH2). Amines are derivatives of ammonia, NH3, in
which carbon chains replace hydrogen atoms. They
contain the functional group NH2, known as amine
(or amino) joined by single covalent bond. They
have unshared electron pair on nitrogen atom.

CLASSIFICATION
•They are classified based on the number of alkyl or aryl 
groups attached to nitrogen as 
•Primary Amines: The amine is primary amine when an alkyl 
or Aryl group replaces one of three hydrogen atoms. primary 
amine (RNH2) e.g CH3NH2 – Methyl Amine
•Secondary Amines: It is a secondary amine when the alkyl 
or aryl group replaces two hydrogen atoms. secondary amine 
(R2NH) e.g. CH3NHCH3 – Dimethyl Amine
•Tertiary Amines: The amine is a tertiary amine when total 
three hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl group.
Normally, secondary or tertiary amines form a cyclic structure. 
Tertiary amine (R3N) e.g

• Quaternary ammonium salt (R4N+X-). They 
have the general formula CnH2n+3N. A further 
classification include imines (Schiff bases), 
R2C-NH, R2C=NR and aromatic nitrogen bases

N
N..

Alkanamine is more basic than ammonia because of electron releasing 
tendency of alkyl group. The alkyl group shows +1 effect which 
increases the electron density at N atom in alkyl amine which makes it 
more basic than ammonia. 

NOMENCLATURE 
The alkanamine has three parts using the systematic IUPAC name (alkan 
– n -  amine). The name of the parent hydrocarbon (alkan) without the 
“e” ending (prefix or stem), a number which tells us the location of the 
NH2 group –n- (an infix) and last part of the name, amine (a suffix).
For example CH3NH2- methylamine (methanamine), CH3CH2NH2 – 
ethylamine (ethanamine) and C6H5NH2 - aniline (benzenamine, 
arylamine, a primary aromatic  amine)
Secondary and tertiary amines, having two or more similar groups are 
named by adding the prefix ‘di’ or ‘tri’ before the name of the alkyl 
group. For example:

Preparation of Amines
•Reduction of Nitro compounds
Reduction of nitro compounds is done by passing hydrogen gas 
through finely divided nickel, palladium, or platinum, nitro 
compounds are converted to amines. Reduction using iron scrap 
and hydrochloric acid is preferable because the FeCl2 produced 
during the reaction is hydrolyzed, releasing hydrochloric acid.
•Reduction of Amides
Amines are formed when amides are reduced with lithium aluminium 
hydride.

•Reduction of Nitriles
This reaction is utilized for the synthesis of amines with one more carbon 
atom than the beginning amine. Primary amines are formed when nitriles 
are reduced with lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4) or catalytically 
hydrogenated. 
•Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
Phthalimide is treated with ethanolic potassium hydroxide to give 
potassium salts of phthalimide. When this is heated with alkyl halide and 
then alkaline hydrolyzed, primary amine is formed. 

•Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction
Amide is reacted with bromine in an aqueous or ethanolic sodium 
hydroxide solution. An alkyl or aryl group migrates from the amide’s 
carbonyl carbon to the nitrogen atom during this degradation reaction. 
The amine thus generated contains one less carbon than the amide. A 
primary amine is produced.
Alkylation
Alkylation of 1o amine generates 2o amine, 3o amine and finally the
quaternary salts.

Acylation
Acylation is the reaction with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters. These
occur by nucleophilic substitution reactions. The reaction is proceeded by 
the replacement of hydrogen atom of –NH2 or >N–H group by the acyl
group (RCOX).
Tertiary (3o) amine cannot be acylated because there is no Hydrogen 
bonded to nitrogen.
Benzoylation
Here, methenamine reacts with benzoyl chloride. The products are 
hydrochloric acid and N Methylbenzamide.

Fullerenes

Allotropy
Allotropy is the phenomenon in which an element
exists in multiple forms with different structures and
properties. The different forms arise from the different
ways in which the atoms are bonded together and as
such they may vary in chemical and physical properties.
Allotropes are also called polymorphs.

History of Carbon
Carbon is denoted by the letter ‘C’ and it is the number 6 element in
the periodic table. It is the 4th most common element, found
everywhere and unarguably one of the most abundant and most
important in life.
In the study of climate change, carbon is often generally referred to as
carbon dioxide which is the primary greenhouse gas being emitted by
humans.

Allotropes of Carbon
• Carbon is a unique element that exhibits allotropy with three well-
known allotropes: graphite, diamond, and graphene. In recent years, 
a fourth allotrope of carbon has been discovered, known as Fullerene.

Structure of Fullerenes
The bonding in fullerenes is predominantly covalent, with each carbon
atom forming four bonds. The carbon atoms in a fullerene are arranged
in a way that maximizes the number of delocalized pi electrons, which
contributes to the molecule's stability. These pi electrons are
responsible for many of the unique properties of fullerenes, including
their ability to act as electron acceptors in organic solar cells.

WORD CLASSES: Open and Closed Classes 
1. Question: What are open and closed word classes? 
   Answer: Open word classes are categories of words that frequently accept new additions, such 
as nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs. Closed word classes, on the other hand, rarely change 
and typically do not accept new words, including pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, and 
determiners. 
2. Question: Why are nouns considered part of an open class? 
   Answer: Nouns are part of an open class because new nouns are regularly created or borrowed 
from other languages, especially with the introduction of new objects, concepts, or technologies 
(e.g., “internet,” “smartphone,” “emoji”). 
3. Question: How do verbs demonstrate the nature of open word classes? 
   Answer: Verbs are considered an open class because they often expand to include new actions 
or states, particularly as new activities or cultural trends develop (e.g., “Google,” “tweet,” 
“stream”). 
4. Question: Can adjectives be categorized as an open class? Explain with examples. 
  Answer:Yes, adjectives are an open class because new adjectives are continuously added to the 
language to describe emerging qualities or states, often derived from nouns or verbs (e.g., “eco-
friendly,” “trendy,” “digital”). 
5. Question: How do adverbs reflect the characteristics of an open class? 
 Answer: Adverbs are part of an open class because new adverbs can be formed, often by 
modifying adjectives or by adding the suffix “-ly” to them (e.g., “quickly,” “digitally,” 
“sustainably”). 
6. Question: What makes pronouns a closed word class? 
Answer: Pronouns are considered a closed class because the set of pronouns in a language is fixed 
and rarely changes. They serve specific grammatical functions and do not typically expand with 
new words (e.g., “he,” “she,” “it,” “they”). 
7. Question: Why are prepositions categorized as a closed class? 

  Answer:  Prepositions are part of a closed class because the set of prepositions is stable and does 
not often accept new members. They are essential for indicating relationships between words (e.g., 
“in,” “on,” “under”). 
8. Question: How do conjunctions reflect the characteristics of a closed class? 
 Answer: Conjunctions are a closed class because the number of conjunctions in a language is 
limited and rarely expands. They are vital for connecting words, phrases, or clauses (e.g., “and,” 
“but,” “although”). 
9. Question: What role do determiners play, and why are they a closed class? 
 Answer: Determiners, such as articles (“the,” “a”), demonstratives (“this,” “that”), and quantifiers 
(“some,” “many”), are a closed class because the set of determiners is finite and does not frequently 
accept new words. They are crucial in specifying the reference of a noun. 
10. Question: How do interjections fit into the classification of word classes, and are they open 
or closed? 
   Answer: Interjections are words or phrases that express strong emotions or reactions (e.g., 
“wow,” “ouch,” “oops”). They are typically part of a closed class because the set of interjections 
is relatively stable, though occasionally new ones can emerge in informal speech. 
PHRASES:  
1. Question: What is a phrase in grammar? 
  Answer: A phrase is a group of words that work together to function as a single unit within a 
sentence. Unlike a clause, a phrase does not contain both a subject and a verb, so it cannot stand 
alone as a complete sentence. 
2. Question: How does a noun phrase function in a sentence? 
   Answer: A noun phrase consists of a noun and any modifiers (such as adjectives, determiners, 
or prepositional phrases) that add information about the noun. It functions as the subject, object, 
or complement in a sentence (e.g., “The tall man,” “a bunch of flowers”).

CHAPTER FOURTEEN
Socio-Political and Cultural Development in Nigeria since 1993 
Adam Oluwafemi Akewula
Introduction
Nigeria’s socio-political and cultural landscape has undergone significant transformation since the early 1990s, particularly following its transition from prolonged military rule to democratic governance. The journey toward democratic consolidation was neither linear nor devoid of setbacks. After years of authoritarian regimes marked by political repression, economic instability, and curtailed civil liberties, the late 20th century witnessed growing domestic and international pressure for democratic reforms (Diamond, 1999). The eventual shift to civilian rule in 1999 ushered in a new era, but the roots of this transformation can be traced back to the political turbulence of 1993.
The year 1993 stands as a watershed moment in Nigeria’s political history. The annulment of the June 12, 1993, presidential election which was widely regarded as the most credible in the country’s history significantly triggered nationwide protests, galvanised pro-democracy movements, and heightened political consciousness among Nigerians (Ojo, 2000). This event exposed the fragility of Nigeria’s political institutions under military dominance while simultaneously fostering a robust civic demand for participatory governance. The political awakening that followed laid the groundwork for the eventual transition to democracy six years later. This chapter intends to explore Nigeria’s socio-political and cultural development from 1993 to the present, with particular attention to political transitions, governance reforms, civil society activism, cultural expressions and socio-economic shifts. By focusing on this period, the chapter aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of how Nigeria’s post-military era has shaped national identity, democratic practices and socio-cultural resilience. 
Political Development (1993–Present)
The June 12, 1993 Crisis and Its Legacy
The June 12, 1993, presidential election is widely regarded as a turning point in Nigeria’s political history. Conducted under the military regime of General Ibrahim Babangida, the election was praised both domestically and internationally for its transparency, competitiveness and peaceful conduct (Suberu, 1997). Businessman and philanthropist Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale popularly known as (MKO) Abiola, representing the Social Democratic Party (SDP), emerged as the apparent winner. His victory was seen as a unifying mandate across ethnic and regional divides, offering hope for national cohesion (Omoruyi, 1999).
However, the military annulled the election results on June 23, 1993, citing alleged electoral irregularities, a move that triggered widespread outrage and political instability. For many Nigerians, the annulment represented a betrayal of democratic aspirations and the subversion of the people’s will. Abiola’s subsequent declaration of himself as the rightful president in 1994 and his eventual arrest marked the beginning of a prolonged political crisis (Ojo, 2000). The annulment catalysed a surge in democratic activism and the strengthening of civil society organisations. Groups such as the Campaign for Democracy (CD) and the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) emerged as formidable forces, mobilising mass protests, organising strikes and using international advocacy to pressure the military regime (Adebanwi, 2004). The media also played a crucial role, often operating underground to evade state censorship while amplifying the voices of pro-democracy leaders.
Political Transition from Military to Civilian Rule
The political transition from military to civilian rule in Nigeria between 1993 and 1999 was a turbulent but pivotal period that redefined the nation’s governance structure. CHAPTER FIFTEEN
GENDER AND NIGERIAN CULTURES
Francesca C. Ukpokolo
Introduction 
This chapters focuses on gender practices in the contemporary Nigerian society. We will come to understand some gender practices in some societies in Nigeria prior to colonial contact, and how colonialism changed the position of women in what later became Nigeria. We need to note that the place of men and women in society is as varied as the cultures of Nigerian societies. As culture is dynamic, so also is the cultural expectations of how men and women ought to behave in society. There are more than 250 ethnic nationalities in Nigeria. This diversity is reflected in the people’s expectations of how women and men ought to behave. For an accurate understanding of the place of men and women in the contemporary Nigerian society, there is the need to take into account the historical paths of Nigeria, and how these shaped and continues to shape the peoples’ cultures, including gender practices. Against this understanding, this chapter focuses on gendered realities of the peoples of the Nigeria, and how these have altered and continued to alter in the face intercultural contacts and globalisation. This falls within the discipline of Gender Studies.
Gender studies as a field of study gained increasing attention in the past five decades. It is, in fact, an offshoot of women studies of the 1970s. This period was marked not only statements from government representatives and feminist activists about the importance of women in every sector of the society but also by determined efforts on the part of advocacy groups to achieve improvement in women’s education, economic situation, political participation, and subsequently social status. Increasingly, discussions by and about women played important role in the political debates of the era. What informs this move is that first, research findings indicated women’s invisibility in the events that made history (see for example Basden, 1938; Ottenberg,1962), among others). Secondly, official records suggested that women’ voices were systematically left out. This situation implies that the story of the development of human society has been told largely through the male perspectives. These raised the questions: Were women inactive in the events that made history prior to the European occupation of African continent? Were women a subjugated group, chattels of their husbands, who lacked participation in decision-making in their various societies prior to colonial contact as claimed in the literature on Africa written by Western scholars? What informs the invisibility of women in historical constructions or the marginalization of women’s roles in history? These are some of the basic questions that these studies try to tackle and in the process project women’s perspective. The reason for this has been put at the foot of colonialism with its Victorian male ideology, which subjugated women. Victorian male ideology holds that women’s role is at the domestic space, that is in the home.
Despite the achievement of women’s studies of the 1970s, scholars are of the opinion that for a better understanding of gender relations, the study of men and women needs be carried out rather than ‘men’ or ‘women’. This has given birth to Gender Studies. Gender Studies, as a field of study, gained attention in the 1980s in the field of sociology, anthropology, psychology, philosophy and the natural sciences. This period witnessed the focus of interest, no longer on women alone but gender, that is men and women. Gender Studies brings to limelight how the differences between males and females transform into access to resources, knowledge and power between the sexes.

CITIZENSHIP AND CIVIC RESPONSIBILITIES IN NIGERIA
Rasheed Oyewole OLANIYI
Introduction
The idea of citizenship and the duties that come with it are essential for the growth and survival
of any democratic society. In Nigeria, a country with a complicated mix of ethnic groups and a
history of changing politics after colonialism, the discussion about citizenship has taken on its
own historical, legal, and social-political forms. Citizenship means more than just being a legal
member of a nation-state; it also means being involved in the civic life of your society. Marshall
(1950) famously said that citizenship includes civil, political, and social rights. These rights must
be matched by duties that include, following the law, paying taxes, voting and others. He claims
that civil rights include freedoms like liberty and justice, political rights include the right to vote
and to be voted for, and social rights include the right to access welfare and social services that
are necessary for human dignity and full participation in society. Citizenship is also an important
idea in political theory and democratic government. It describes the legal, political, and social
ties between people and the state. It means more than just a legal position as it is a changing and
growing system that sets out the rights, duties, and identity of people in a political society.
In Nigeria, these rights and duties are often affected by concepts like history, religion, and
economic disparity. The Nigerian Constitution lays forth the rules for citizenship and the
responsibilities that come with it, such as following the law, paying taxes, voting in elections,
and being loyal to the state (Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999). However, as scholars like
Osaghae (1994) and Ekeh (1975) have postulated, the post-colonial Nigerian state is shaped by
what Ekeh called a "two publics" dichotomy. This means that citizens often see a difference

2
between their civic duties to the state and their duties to their ethnic or communal groups. This
dualism has major effects for national unity, democratic accountability, and civic engagement.
Nwankwo (1992) says that civic education is important for fostering democratic values since a
well-informed population is necessary for the growth of a responsible and involved society. Also,
as Suberu (2001) and Adejumobi (2002) have opined that, it is even harder to create a strong
feeling of national citizenship in Nigeria because of political corruption, election malpractice,
and ethnic marginalization. These problems with the system often make people, especially young
people, apathetic and disillusioned. They may feel like they are not part of the democratic
process. This chapter examines how the definition of citizenship has evolved over time in
Nigeria, the laws and social norms that define civic duties, and the social and political elements
that affect civic involvement. It looks closely at how people in Nigeria understand and carry out
their duties, and what this means for democracy and national progress.
The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria defines and regulates citizenship. It also mentions the different
ways that people might attain or use it. Citizenship by birth is the most prevalent type. It is based
on where you were born and your lineage, following a modified version of the jus sanguinis
principle. This means that people who were born in Nigeria to Nigerian parents or grandparents
are citizens by birth. You can also get citizenship by registering, especially if you are a foreign

Culture in Centralised States
Taariqa-Rahamat A. Ilupeju, PhD.
Department of History
University of Ibadan

--- SLIDE ---

Culture
Culture is the way a group of people who share the same identity, space and experience make meaning of their existence. 
Culture, according to Asiwaju (1997), is that which gives order and meaning to the linguistic, social, political, economic, aesthetic, religious, and philosophical modes and organisation of a people, nation or ethnic group. 
The Nigerian government (1997) defines culture as the totality of the way of life evolved by a people in their attempts to meet the challenge of living in their environment.

--- SLIDE ---

Centralised State
Centralised states are well-organised groups with a centralised government. 
Most centralised states practised the monarchical system of government. 
The centralised states are the kingdoms in Nigeria that existed before the 1800s. 
The institutions of the state embodied a nation's national heritage. The tradition of origin narrates and symbolises how the reigning monarch's ancestors got to occupy their abode.

--- SLIDE ---

political units
The political unit in a centralised state is headed by a paramount ruler usually the king. 
The term king in Hausaland was Sarkin, in Kanem-Borno meant Mai, in Oyo was Alaafin, in Benin wass Oba, in Ife was Ooni, in Itsekiri meant Olu. 
The paramount ruler was assisted by a council of chiefs who helped in the political and economic administration of the state. 
The kingdom developed into a city-state with a well-organised market. A large centralised kingdom maintained its control over its neighbour with a well-trained large army that helped protect its border and fight following the command of the ruler to expand its territories.

--- SLIDE ---

Southern Region
The kingdoms in the southern region include the Ife, Oyo Kingdom, the Benin Kingdom, and the Itsekiri Kingdom.

--- SLIDE ---

ife
Ruler was the Ooni
The first tradition of origin is centred around a historical character called Obatala and his loss of power to Oduduwa. 
Legend has it that Eledumare handed the power of creation to Obatala, but before he completed his task, he got drunk, and Oduduwa took over the task and created the earth. The tradition stated that Eledumare sent Obatala and along with sixteen Oye (Irumole) with five pieces of iron, a piece of white cloth with a lump of earth and a cockerel to make land on the vast water on earth. Before Obatala could complete the task, he got drunk with palm wine (emu) and dozed off. While asleep, an individual named Oduduwa seized his paraphernalia and led the oye to complete the task.
The second tradition is centred on Oduduwa, who migrated to Ife from the East and established a well-structured political order that was inherited by his son, Okanbi, and later, his grandson, Oranmiyan, set out to expand his influence by establishing many kingdoms.

--- SLIDE ---

IFE HERITAGE AND ARTS
Ife has many historical sites which include the site where the Opa Oranmiyan stands. Many excavations have continued to take place in Ife for research purposes. The group Arts found in Ife are studied as Ife Arts that showcases its rich bronze and brass culture.

--- SLIDE ---

oyo
Ruler was Alaafin
Oranyan (Oranmiyan) is said to be the founder of Oyo. He established the kingdom after he ended his intermission in Benin. However, when he got to the area, it was occupied by the Ibaripa. His military expertise was respected, and the king of Borgu pointed to him the location where he established his capital, known as Oyo Ajaka, and then to Oko.

text_snippet:
Evolution of Nigeria as a Political Unit
and the Rise of Political Parties in Nigeria
1851 – 1999
University of Ibadan 
(CST-112)

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
This chapter examines how Nigeria emerged as a single political unit through British conquest, administration, and eventual amalgamation in 1914. It also traces the development of political parties from the colonial period to the Fourth Republic, showing how historical, economic, and social factors shaped Nigeria’s political evolution.

--- SLIDE ---

British Conquest and Early Control (1851–1897)
- 1851: British naval forces attacked and conquered Lagos.
- 1861: Treaty of Cession, Lagos annexed to Britain.
- 1885: Britain proclaimed Protectorate over Niger districts (Berlin Conference).
- 1886: Royal Niger Company granted charter.
- 1892–1894: Conquest of Ijebu and Yorubaland.
- 1897: Punitive Expedition against Benin, city destroyed, Oba exiled.

--- SLIDE ---

Colonial Expansion and Resistance (1899–1914)
- 1899: Royal Niger Company’s charter revoked.
- 1900: Protectorate of Northern Nigeria created, Lugard as High Commissioner.
- 1902–1903: Kano and Sokoto captured, Sultan Attahiru II killed (1903).
- 1906: Lagos merged with Southern Nigeria Protectorate.
- 1912–1914: Lugard appointed governor of North and South, leading to amalgamation.
- 1 January 1914: Amalgamation of Nigeria as one political unit.

--- SLIDE ---

Early Nationalism and Political Parties (1922–1944)
- 1922: Clifford Constitution introduced elective representation.
- 1923: Herbert Macaulay founded NNDP.
- 1934: Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM) emerged.
- 1944: National Council of Nigeria and Cameroons (NCNC) formed under Macaulay and Azikiwe.

--- SLIDE ---

Rise of Regional Parties (1945–1959)
- 1947: NCNC delegation opposed Richards Constitution.
- 1950: Obafemi Awolowo founded Action Group (AG).
- 1949: Northern People’s Congress (NPC) formed, led by Ahmadu Bello.
- 1950: Aminu Kano founded NEPU.
- 1954: Lyttleton Constitution entrenched regionalism.
- NPC, AG, NCNC dominated politics to independence in 1960.

--- SLIDE ---

First Republic and Collapse (1960–1966)
- 1960: Independence with NPC, NCNC, AG as key parties.
- 1962: Action Group crisis and regional violence.
- 1964–65: Elections marred by fraud and division.
- 15 January 1966: Military coup, parties banned.

--- SLIDE ---

Second Republic and Military Rule (1979–1993)
- 1979–83: Second Republic with NPN, UPN, NPP, GNPP, PRP.
- 1983: Military coup ended Second Republic.
- 1985: Babangida took power, created two-party system (SDP & NRC).
- 12 June 1993: Presidential election annulled, despite Abiola’s victory.

--- SLIDE ---

Abacha Era and Transition (1993–1999)
- 1996: Five state-sponsored parties created, all supported Abacha.
- 8 June 1998: Abacha died, Abdulsalami Abubakar took over.
- 1998–99: PDP, AD, APP registered by INEC under Justice Akpata.
- 29 May 1999: Fourth Republic inaugurated with Olusegun Obasanjo as president.

--- SLIDE ---

Summary of the Study
The chapter begins by outlining the British conquest of different regions at different times, noting that Lagos was annexed in 1861, Yorubaland was subdued in the 1890s, and the Sokoto Caliphate fell in 1903. Economic interests, military superiority, internal rivalries, and missionary activities all contributed to the British establishing control. Amalgamation in 1914 was driven largely by financial motives, merging the wealthier South with the less viable North.

The second part focuses on political parties, starting with the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP) in 1922, followed by the Nigerian Youth Movement and the NCNC. It highlights the ethnic and regional bases of the major parties—NCNC, AG, and NPC—and their role in the politics of the First Republic, which ended with the 1966 military coup.         INDIGENOUS EDUCATION IN NIGERIA
Introduction
This chapter examined indigenous education in Nigeria and the 
relationship between  culture and environment. It also examined how the environment has influenced the culture in Nigeria and finally the two 
concepts were also defined in the chapter
Indigenous Education in Nigeria
Every society in the world, no matter how small or large, has its own way of transmitting its cultural heritage from one generation to another. The objectives and methods of transmitting the societal culture vary from one society to another. In the context of traditional education generally, an educated man in Nigeria is “a warrior, a hunter, a nobleman, and a man of character”. Anyone who combined the latter feature with a specific skill was considered to be a well-educated and well-integrated citizen of Nigeria (Fafunwa 1974). According to Fafunwa, functionalism was the main guiding principle of Nigerian education, and that education is a means to an end and not an end in itself. It has been observed that traditional education is holistic in nature, and it helps in the realization of the Nigerian culture, among other things. Perhaps, it may be regarded as a branch of Nigerian culture. Traditional education may be regarded as the Nigerian way of imparting their culture into the younger ones in such a way that their culture will not go into an extinction. Traditional education generally begins at home, where the parents become the child's first teachers. The first child's lesson is teaching about his environment as well as the culture of his society, including numbers and numeracy. Specifically, Nigerian education is geared towards social responsibility, job orientation, and political participation, as well as spiritual and moral values. There is a proverb in Nigeria that "a child is not intelligent, and his parents do not want him to die; what will eventually kill a child who is not intelligent?" This means that traditional education goes beyond  acquisition of reading and writing skills. In the pre-literate period of Nigerian society, people who were knowledgeable in their vocations,  societal ethics and were indeed repositories of the culture of their societies were considered educated. In other words, Nigerian traditional education prepares the younger ones for adulthood life in addition to preparing them to become useful members of their society.
A critical examination will reveal that the content and methods of traditional education are interwoven, as they are not divided into separate compartments as we have in formal education. It is true that Nigerian  education was not formalized, including its curriculum, but according to Babarinde (2016), it can still be compared with the western form of education. For instance, it involves parents as first teachers, and this perhaps is comparable with the primary level of formal system of education. According to him, the neighborhood education is the secondary level; the community education may be compared with the higher level, while the last stage of Nigerian traditional education is the one that is received from the secret societies, which is designed for initiation, and this is another form of higher education. It should, however, be noted that most of the features of Nigerian traditional education in the past are still in existence today despite the importation of the foreign culture into Nigeria specifically.
Objectives of Traditional Education
It is a fact that every level of education has its own specific objectives which it aims at achieving. Consequently, traditional education has its own objectives. Seven of these have been identified by Fafunwa (1974).They are:

(2) To develop character;
(3) To inculcate respect for elders and those in positions of authority;

Nigerian Indigenous Trade and Market System
Before colonial economic structures were imposed, societies organised the production, exchange, and distribution of goods and services within locally defined norms and values. These economic, social, and cultural frameworks are embodied in the concept of indigenous trade and market systems.

--- SLIDE ---

Historical Context and Global Perspective
From the barter-driven marketplaces of ancient Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean to the regulated bazaar economies of Asia to the decentralised trading posts of the Americas, market systems have long been recognised as essential to the development of human societies in a global historical context.
Ancient Mesopotamia
Barter-driven marketplaces established foundational trading principles
Asian Bazaars
Regulated economies with sophisticated commercial structures
American Trading Posts
Decentralised networks connecting diverse communities

--- SLIDE ---

Pre-Colonial Nigerian Market Systems (Up to 1897)
Indigenous market systems thrived in West Africa long before colonial encroachment, particularly in the Nigerian region. They were based on redistribution, reciprocity, and market exchange, and they supported intergenerational economies of skill transfer and self-reliance.
Yoruba Markets (Oja)
Urban centres like Ibadan grew around thriving market economies whose regulations combined market offices and customary law. Market days were cyclical and connected to four to eight-day customary weeks.
Igbo Trading Networks
Four-day periodic market logic (Eke, Orie, Afo, and Nkwo) organised dispersed producers into predictable meeting points for exchange and social reproduction.
Hausa-Fulani Commerce
Permanent urban bazaars in caravan towns like Kano and Zaria were interconnected with long-distance kola and caravan networks across the Sahara.

--- SLIDE ---

Market Structures and Economic Organisation
Marketplaces coordinated trade, allocated risk, controlled credit, and ingrained business principles into kinship and ritual norms. Market structures operated as layered systems including regional fairs, local daily stalls, periodic rural markets, and long-distance redistribution nodes.
1
Long-Distance Trade
Trans-Saharan and regional networks
2
Regional Fairs
Major trading centers and seasonal gatherings
3
Periodic Markets
Four to eight-day cycles across communities
4
Local Daily Stalls
Neighborhood commerce and basic goods

--- SLIDE ---

Women's Leadership in Market Systems
Market leadership offices like the Iyaloja and the Iyalode institutionalised female authority over market regulation, dispute settlement, and collective price norms, making women not incidental participants but principal organisers of local and long-distance trade networks.
Iyaloja System
Female market heads governed central market squares, combining civic negotiation, ceremonies, and commodity retail. They arranged communal savings plans, controlled pricing, and coordinated large purchases.
Market regulation and dispute resolution
Credit and savings coordination
Political representation for traders
Economic Impact
Women's organisational structures, including market associations, rotating credit groups, and female chieftaincies, were essential institutional pillars of community self-reliance and economic stability.
Revolving savings associations (Esusu/Ajo)
Retail network control
Political influence over authorities

Skill Acquisition and Apprenticeship Systems
Precolonial Nigerian market systems were complex socioeconomic institutions where skill acquisition took place through apprenticeship in crafts and trades, such as blacksmithing, weaving, pottery, leatherwork, and other artisanal vocations, rather than in formal schools.

Nigeria Under Colonial Rule By
Rasheed Oyewole OLANIYI

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
This study examines the interplay of factors that led to the conquest of Nigeria by the British, the strategies for the conquest of Nigeria, the resistance movements to colonial conquest, how the country was administered and factors that informed the choice of the methods of the colonial administration of the area. It also examines the features of the colonial economy, the colonial infrastructure, and social and constitutional development. 
Nigeria's encounter with Europe was part of the larger story of European exploration. This interaction was marked by trade (including slave and commodity trade), conflict, religious missions, cultural exchange and influence, exploration and cartography, as well as economic exploitation.
From the 15th century, European powers, led by the Iberians (Portuguese and Spainish), began maritime explorations along the Niger area.

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction Cont
These early expeditions were motivated by a desire to find direct trade routes to Africa and access Africa’s gold, ivory, and spices. As a result of this, the Portuguese established trading posts and forts, initiating the trans-Atlantic slave trade, which profoundly shaped African societies for centuries. 
 By the 19th century, European powers moved from trade and diplomacy to outright political control. This started with the conquest of Lagos in 1851 and subsequently, the Yoruba hinterland.
In an attempt to conquer Lagos,  Consul Beecroft accused king  Kosoko,the then King of Lagos, of engaging in the slave trade and because of this he was deposed and by  1861, Lagos was ceded to the British and formally became a British colony. 
Also, between 1887 and 1897, British imperial forces expanded their control over the Niger Delta, Benin, and parts of Igboland.
By 1906, British forces completed the military conquest of the northern territories,as a result of  the operations of the Royal Niger Company in the region thereby bringing the entire region under colonial control. 
All these culminated in the loss of political autonomy and the ultimate colonization of Nigeria by the British; and the imposition of British rule in Nigeria.

--- SLIDE ---

Reasons for the Colonial Conquest of Nigeria
The conquest of Nigeria was spurred by a combination of economic, strategic, political, and socio-religious reasons. These reasons were interwoven and evolved as British interests in the region expanded.
	Economically:
The Industrial Revolution in Europe had transformed the nature of production from manual labour to mechanized mass production. This means that tasks which would have taken months to complete using manual labour were accomplished in seconds by machines. As a result, there was an increased demand for raw materials such as palm oil, cotton, rubber, and mineral resources that were abundant in Nigeria.
Britain needed new markets for its manufactured goods, and Nigeria’s large population offered a promising solution
Also, the desire to control trade routes by the British made them want to eliminate African middlemen and European competitors, thereby gaining a total control of the flow of goods in and out of the region.

--- SLIDE ---

Reasons for the Colonial Conquest of Nigeria Cont
Politically:
It was an attempt to partly outpace European rivals, especially France and Germany, as they never wanted rival powers to gain a foothold in Nigeria.
	Religious reasons 
The British believed they had a duty to "civilize" the indigenous people through Christianity, Western education, and European cultural values. They viewed and described the indigenous people as hordes of largely naked savages, among other derogatory terms. Therefore, they had a duty to “civilized these barbarians and establish law and order. DEVELOPMENT IN NIGERIA

INTRODUCTION 
• Scholars and policymakers have contended that development cannot be fully achieved 
or sustained in the absence of social justice and this is because social justice  
encompasses fair, inclusive, and equitable treatment of all individuals and groups 
within a society. 
• Even if states globally can boast of economic growth and infrastructural indices, yet it 
remain deeply fractured due to instability thus the population are marginalised or 
excluded from the developmental process.

INTRODUCTION 
• Social justice discourse is of significant importance to the Nigerian state. Nigeria is a culturally 
and ethnically diverse state which comprises over 250 ethnic groups with varying languages, 
religions, and historical traditions. 
• Prior to the advent of colonial rule, various ethnic groups, although largely autonomous, 
maintained relations within the context of inter-group dynamics – ( the changing processes, 
behaviors, and relationships between different social groups, including aspects like 
stereotyping, competition, and conflict.) The advent of British colonialism and the eventual 
amalgamation of 1914, which merged these entities into a single political unit, have been 
described as the bedrock of Nigeria’s problems with nation-building. 

INTRODUCTION 
• Nigeria has been described as a ‘house Lugard built,’ meaning the 
amalgamation was not driven by the desire to forge a unified nation-state, 
but for administrative efficiency and economic exploitation. 
• However, since the attainment of independence, social injustice has been an 
inherent feature of post-colonial states, bordering issues of growth, politics, 
development, and sustainable livelihood.

INTRODUCTION 
• Post-independence Nigeria has been marred by repeated episodes of socio-economic and 
political instability, ethnic agitation, and civil conflict, including a brutal civil war between 1967 
and 1970, military coups and counter-coups, insurgencies in the Niger Delta and the northeast. 
These crises are not solely political; they are rooted in structural injustices that have consistently 
excluded certain regions and populations from full participation in the nation’s development. Social 
justice is not an abstract aspiration but a practical necessity for national survival and progress. 
• The concept of social justice encompasses the principle of equality in the distribution of material 
resources, including income, the protection of fundamental human rights, and access to power and 
resources.

be analysed from four major perspectives.
1. Social justice is the bedrock for the design and arrangement of basic and 
necessary institutions in a modern society and the bedrock, rules and order are the 
guiding principles of societal relations that prevents vulnerability. 
2. Social justice is important in creating and improving societal efficiency. In the     
process of harnessing social potential, developing human resources, and 
establishing rules of equal opportunities and wealth distribution, social justice plays 
an indispensable role in places.

Social justice is also necessary for a society to bring about safe operation. Social 
justice is only the medium through which various classes of society can engage in 
meaningful interaction and integration.

Development under social justice should be people-oriented. Here, people refer to the

DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND IMPLEMENTATION IN NIGERIA, 1970-1999
Mutiat T. Oladejo

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
As nations and international organisations looked for methodical ways to direct economic growth and social transformation, particularly during decolonisation, the concept of development policy changed around the world in the years following World War II (Chete, Adeoti, Ajakaiye, & Olorunfemi, 2016). As nations and international organisations looked for methodical ways to direct economic growth and social transformation, particularly during decolonisation, the concept of development policy changed around the world in the years following World War II (Chete, Adeoti, Ajakaiye, & Olorunfemi, 2016). 
 Following independence, African countries adopted these frameworks to demonstrate economic independence and promote unified nationhood; Nigeria, recovering from the devastation of the 1967-1970 Civil War, immediately gave organised planning top priority with its Second National Development Plan (1970-1974), signalling a significant change towards economic revitalisation, national integration, and reconstruction (Onitiri, 1971; Ikeanyibe, 2009). 
The Third (1975-1980) and Fourth (1981-1985) national plans that followed each other reflected changing goals and difficulties. Despite improvements in industry and construction, the Third Plan's efforts to diversify and provide universal primary education only allocated a small portion of its budget to agriculture, which led to a decline in output (Ibietan et al., 2013). The Fourth, supported by high oil earnings, prioritised infrastructure expenditures and export promotion, but it eventually failed because of unstable oil prices and financial limitations (Ibietan et al., 2013; Falola et al., 2008).

--- SLIDE ---

These initiatives demonstrated the desire for long-term development planning and the persistent inadequacies in converting rhetoric into action. The Nigerian government also implemented programmatic campaigns for agriculture and rural development within this larger policy framework. For example, Operation Feed the Nation (OFN) was initiated in May 1976 to combat the reliance on food imports and revitalise agriculture by encouraging urban residents, students, and civil service cadres to engage in farming activities with the help of subsidies, extension services, and credit schemes (Arua, 1982; SCIRP, 2019). However, despite its sincere rhetoric, OFN faced implementation flaws, a propagandistic focus that was more appealing to elites than to farmers at the grassroots level (Bamisaye, 1985; Ufahamu Journal, 2019).
 Nigerian development policymaking spans from from the middle to late 20th century into a comprehensive historical narrative. In addition to shedding light on the cyclical patterns of planning and policymaking, this kind of investigation provides essential insights for modern governance, especially about stakeholder participation, institutional longevity, and strategic coherence in development planning.

--- SLIDE ---

The Political Economy of Nigerian Development Planning, 1970-1999
Amid an unparalleled petroleum windfall that reshaped both its fiscal capacity and its development imagination, Nigeria's post-civil war state entered the 1970s with the goal of reconstruction, national healing, and rapid modernisation (Falola & Heaton, 2008, pp. 214-219).

Even though the new abundance concealed structural flaws in production and distribution, the 1973-1974 quadrupling of global oil prices gave the federal military government unprecedented revenues and sparked an increase in the state's role in planning, investment, and social provisioning (Falola & Heaton, 2008, pp. 218-221).

Static and Current Electricity. Electric Charge
▶Electricity (E) is a phenomenon due to stationary or
moving charges; static or current E, electro-statics or
-dynamics, resp.
▶Electric charge is a physical property of matter which is
either positive or negative. Electrically neutral means no
net charge.
▶Unlike (or opposite) charges (e.g., a positive charge and
a negative charge) attract while like charges (e.g., two
positive charges or two negative charges) repel.
▶The charge of a macroscopic object/matter is its net
charge, which is always a very small fraction (typically
≤10−12) of its total positive or negative charge. Such
object is made up of a large number1 (∼1023) of
atoms/mole; each atom is a “point” object with
internal structure (see Fig. on slide 7).
1Number= NρV /Wm, where N, ρ, V , Wm are the avogadro number
(6.022 × 1023 atoms/mole), density, volume, and the molecular weight
of the object, respectively.

Learning Outcomes
At the end of the course, students should be able to:
1. describe and quantitatively analyse the behaviour of vibrating systems and wave energy;
2. explain the propagation and properties of waves in sound and light;
3. identify and apply the wave equations; and
4. explain geometrical optics and principles of optical instruments.
Course Contents

instruments. Wave nature of light. Dispersion. Huygens’s principle (interference and 
diffraction).

OPTICS
Optics is the study of Light. By light we mean the visible part of the 
electromagnetic spectrum.
Early scientists were curious to study light because without it human 
sense of vision cannot be stimulated.
OPTICS

Vocabulary
•Image: That which is formed when light is 
reflected or refracted.
•Real Image: –
•It is made from “real” light rays that converge at 
a point.
•Can be projected unto a screen because light 
actually passes through the point where the 
image appears.
•Always  inverted.

Vocabulary
•Virtual Image–
•“Not Real” because it cannot be 
projected on a screen
•It is formed from virtual rays.
•Normal: An imaginary line that is 
perpendicular to the reflecting 
surface.

Reflection of light from a smooth plane surface
• Laws of Reflection
• The incident and 
reflected rays lie in the 
same plane with the 
normal.
• The angle of incidence 
equals the angle of 
reflection.
• θi = θr

Image formation.
• When scattered light from an 
object falls on a plane smooth 
surface such as a mirror, the light 
is reflected, resulting in image 
formation
• The image is located behind the 
mirror.
• Image properties:
i) virtual
ii) Erect
iii) Same size as the object
iv) Same distance from the reflecting 
surface as the object.
v) Laterally inverted

Virtual Images in Plane Mirrors
Since light energy doesn't flow from the 
image, the image is "virtual".

• Diffuse Reflection
• Light incident upon a 
rough surface
• Laws of reflection still 
hold; Normals are not 
parallel.
• Specular Reflection
• Mirror like reflection
• All Normals are parallel

Deviation of Light by a Plane-Mirror
The total angle between the straight-line path of 
the incident ray and the reflected ray is twice the 
glancing angle 
This is called the deviation of the light. It is a  
measure of the angle through which the light has 
strayed from its initial straight-line path.
