C-ZOO 101-Mammalian Body
Circulatory System:Heart, Blood
Motunrayo Coker
2024/2025 Session

Mammalian Heart 
• The heart is a complex muscle 
that pumps blood 
• The three divisions of the 
circulatory system
• Systemic circulation-heart to body
• Pulmonary circulation-heart to 
lungs
• Coronary circulation- within heart
• The heart is composed of three 
layers; 
• The epicardium (outer layer)
• Pericardium-surrounds and 
protects the heart
• The myocardium (middle layer 
and bulk of heart wall)
• The endocardium(inner wall)
2

Structure of the heart –Atria and ventricles
• The heart muscle is asymmetrical
• In humans, the heart is divided into four 
chambers: 
• Two atria- receives blood into the heart
• Two ventricles- pumps blood out of the heart
• One atrium and one ventricle are on the right 
side
• One atrium and one ventricle are on the left 
side. 
• The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood 
• Superior vena cava-the jugular vein that 
comes from the brain and from the veins that 
come from the arms, 
• Inferior vena cava- veins that come from 
the lower organs and the legs.
• The coronary sinus which drains from the 
heart itself
3

Structure of the heart –Atria and ventricles
• Deoxygenated blood then passes to the 
right ventricle 
• The right ventricle pumps the blood 
through the pulmonary arteries, to the 
lungs for re-oxygenation
• The left atrium then receives the oxygen-
rich blood from the lungs via the 
pulmonary veins
• The left ventricle is where the oxygen 
rich blood is pumped out through the 
aorta ( major artery of the body) to the 
organs and muscles of the body. 
4

Structure of the heart –valves
• Valves are flaps that open and 
close to monitor the direction of 
blood flow in the heart
• Atrioventricular valve/ tricuspid 
valve
• Right atrium and right 
ventricle
• Mitral/bicuspid valve
• Left atrium and left ventricle
• Pulmonic valve
• Right ventricle to the lungs
• Aortic semilunar valve
• Left ventricle and aorta
5

Divisions of the circulatory system
• The pulmonary (heart and 
lungs) 
• The systemic (heart to other 
parts of the body)
• The coronary (vessels that 
serve the heart)
• The right side of the heart is 
not as thick as the left side 
which must have enough 
pressure to pump blood all the 
way to the  legs.
6

Blood vessels-Arteries 
• The wall of an artery consists of three layers
• Innermost layer-tunica intima(squamous 
epithelium )
• Middle layer- tunica media (smooth muscle - 
thickest layer)
• Outermost layer-tunica externa (connective 
tissue with varying amounts of elastic and 
collagenous fibres)
• Arteries carry blood away from the heart
• Pulmonary arteries transport blood that is low 
in oxygen from the right ventricle to the lungs
• Systemic arteries transport oxygen rich blood 
from the left ventricle to the body tissues. 
• Blood is pumped from the ventricles into large 
arteries that branch into smaller arteries that 
results in arterioles
• The arterioles play a key role in regulating blood 
flow into the capillaries
7

Blood vessels-Veins 
• The walls of veins have the same three layers 
as the arteries
• There is less smooth muscle and connective tissue
• Walls of veins are thinner than those of arteries
• Blood in the veins has less pressure than in the 
arteries
• Veins carry blood toward the heart
• After blood passes through the capillaries
• It enters the smallest veins, called venules
• It flows into progressively larger  veins until it 
reaches the heart
• Pulmonary veins transport oxygen rich blood from 
the lungs to the left atrium of the heart
• Systemic veins transport blood from the body 
tissue to the right atrium of the heart
8

Blood vessels-capillaries 
• The smallest and most numerous of the 
blood vessels
• Form the connection between the vessels that 
carry blood away from the heart (arteries) and 
the vessels that return blood to the heart (veins)
• The primary function of capillaries is the 
exchange of materials between the blood 
and tiss

Motunrayo Coker
2024/2025 Session
C-ZOO 101-Mammalian Body
Excretory System: Kidney, Homeostasis

Excretory system
• The excretory system is a vital biological system that 
removes excess and waste products from the body to 
maintain homeostasis
• Most of these products are used and broken-down 
components of metabolism
• They leave the body as urine, sweat
• While there is a specific set of organs generally referred 
to as the excretory system, 
• There are several auxiliary organs that play roles in 
other major body systems that help in the excretory 
system’s function 
• Excretory system refers to those organs that are used 
strictly for elimination and excretion
• The focus of discussion of the excretory system is 
mainly the urinary/renal system
• kidneys, ureters, bladder, and  urethra
2

Mammalian Kidney
• Located in the lower back
• The kidneys lie retroperitoneally (behind the 
peritoneum) in the abdomen, either side of the vertebral 
column.
• They extend from T12 to L3 
• The right kidney is slightly lower due to the presence of 
the liver.
• The adrenal glands are located on top of the kidneys
• The kidney is protected by lower rib cage and spine, fat, 
muscles of the back, renal capsule - layer of fibrous tissue 
that surrounds the kidney
• Kidney receives blood from renal artery (unfiltered)
• Blood  leaves the kidneys to the posterior vena cava 
through the renal vein (filtered)
• Urine is produced from the received blood
• Urine drains through the ureters and carries it to the 
urinary bladder
• From the bladder, urine is passed out of the body 
through the urethra
3

Internal structure of the kidney
• A frontal section through the kidney 
reveals:
• an outer region called the renal cortex
• an inner region called the renal medulla 
• In the medulla, 5-8 renal pyramids are 
separated by connective tissue renal 
columns
• Each pyramid creates urine and 
terminates into a renal papilla.
• Each renal papilla drains into a collecting 
pool called a minor calyx
• Several minor calyces connect to form a 
major calyx
• All major calyces connect to the single 
renal pelvis which connects to the ureter.
4

Blood supply to the kidney
• The kidneys are well vascularized and receive about 25 
percent of the cardiac output at rest
• Blood enters the kidney via the paired renal arteries 
that form directly from the aorta
• In the kidney, each renal artery divides into segmental 
arteries that branches to form interlobar arteries that 
pass through the renal columns to reach the cortex 
• The interlobar arteries, branch into arcuate arteries, 
cortical radiate arteries, and then into afferent arterioles
• The afferent arterioles deliver blood into the glomerulus 
which is a component of the nephron
• Once the nephrons have filtered the blood,
• Renal veins return blood directly to the inferior vena 
cava
• A portal system is formed when the blood flows from the 
glomerulus to the efferent arteriole through a second 
capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries surrounding 
the proximal and distal convoluted tubules and the loop 
of Henle. 
5

Nephrons
• They  are the “functional units” of the 
kidney
• Glomerulus as the filtering hub
• a network of small blood vessels, which 
are enclosed in a sac called Bowman's 
capsule
• They cleanse the blood of toxins and 
balance the constituents of the 
circulation to homeostatic set points
• The nephrons function to:
• Control blood pressure (via production of 
renin)
• Red blood cell production (via the 
hormone erythropoetin)
• Calcium absorption (via conversion of 
calcidiol into calcitriol, the active form of 
vitamin D).
6

Nephrons (cont’d)
• The two types of nephrons
• Juxtamedullary nephrons (15%)
• A glomerulus near the junction of 
the cortex and medulla with loops of 
Henle that penetrate deep into the 
medulla
• Cortical nephrons (85%)
• A glomerulus located nearer to the 
outer parts of the cortex and their 
loops of Henle are short
7

Nephrons (cont’d)
• Each nephron cons

C-ZOO 101-Mammalian Body
Gas exchange/Respiratory System
Motunrayo Coker
2024/2025 Session

Respiratory System
• The respiratory system is the system in animals 
that enables breathing, bringing oxygen into the 
body and expelling carbon dioxide
• Respiration is the sequence of events that results in 
the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide 
between the atmosphere and the body cells
• Every 3 to 5 seconds, nerve impulses stimulate the 
breathing process
• Which leads to an exchange of gases between the 
lungs and the blood (external respiration)
• The exchange of gases between the blood and tissue 
cells is internal respiration
• cells utilize the oxygen for cellular 
metabolism/respiration
2

Mechanism of Breathing (Pulmonary Ventilation)
• It is the process of air flowing into the 
lungs during inspiration (inhalation) 
and out of the lungs during expiration 
(exhalation). 
• The air moves through the passages 
because of pressure gradients that are 
produced by contraction of the 
diaphragm and thoracic muscles.
• Air flows because of pressure 
differences between the atmosphere 
and the gases inside the lungs
• Atmospheric pressure
• Intraalveolar (intrapulmonary) pressure
• Intrapleural pressure (within the pleural 
cavity)
3
Pleura are the two thin membranes that line each lung 
and the inside of the chest cavity creating a space 
between them.

Inhalation and Exhalation
• Inhalation is the process of taking air into the 
lungs
• It is the active phase of ventilation (because it is the 
result of muscle contraction)
• During inspiration:
• The diaphragm contracts 
• The thoracic cavity increases in volume
• This decreases the intraalveolar pressure so air 
flows into the lungs
• Exhalation is the process of letting air out of the 
lungs
• During expiration:
• The diaphragm relaxes
• The thoracic cavity reduces in volume
• The intraalveolar pressure decreases so air is 
pushed out of the lungs
4

Conducting Passages
• The respiratory conducting passages are divided 
into the upper respiratory tract and the lower 
respiratory tract. 
• The upper respiratory tract includes the nose, 
pharynx (throat), and larynx (voice box). 
• The lower respiratory tract consists of the 
trachea (windpipe), bronchial tree, and lungs. 
• These tracts open to the outside and are lined 
with mucous membranes. 
• In some regions:
• The membrane has hairs that help filter the air
• Other regions may have cilia to propel mucus(nasal 
cavity, trachea, and bronchi)
5

Nose and Nasal Cavities
• The nose consists of bone and cartilage
• Two small nasal bones and extensions of the 
maxillae form the bridge of the nose, which is 
the bony portion
• The remainder of the framework is cartilage 
• Air enters the nasal cavity from the outside 
through the nostrils 
• The openings from the nasal cavity into the 
pharynx are the internal nares. 
• Paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities within 
bones (the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and 
sphenoid ) that surround the nasal cavity and 
open into it
• Their functions include:
• Reducing the weight of the skull
• Humidifying and warming inhaled air
• Providing resonance for the voice
• Buffering against facial trauma
6

Pharynx (throat)
• The pharynx is a passageway that extends from the 
base of the skull to the level of the sixth cervical 
vertebra
• It serves both the respiratory and digestive systems
• The nasal cavity-Air
• The oral cavity -Air, food, and water. 
• It opens into the larynx and esophagus. 
• The pharynx is divided into three regions according 
to location: 
• The nasopharynx- posterior to the nasal cavity and 
extends inferiorly to the uvula
• The oropharynx- posterior to the oral cavity
• The laryngopharynx (hypopharynx)- extends from the 
hyoid bone down to the lower margin of the larynx
• The upper part of the pharynx lets only air pass 
through
• The lower parts permit air, foods, and fluids to pass
7

Larynx (Voicebox/Glottis)
• The larynx is the passageway for air between the pha

text_snippet:
C-ZOO 101-Mammalian Body
Nervous and Chemical Coordination
Motunrayo Coker
2024/2025 Session

Coordination
• Coordination is the process enabling organisms to regulate 
activities and maintain internal balance
• Coordination allows organisms to respond effectively to 
environmental changes ensuring survival
• The nervous system and the endocrine system both ensure the 
body maintains homeostasis and proper physiological function
• The nervous system provides rapid electrical communication for 
immediate responses
• The endocrine system uses hormones (slower-acting ) for long-term 
physiological regulation 
2

3
NERVOUS SYTEM

Introduction to the Nervous Sytem
• The nervous system is the major controlling, 
regulatory, and communicating system in the 
body
• It is the center of all mental activity including 
thought, learning, and memory
• Together with the endocrine system, the 
nervous system is responsible for regulating 
and maintaining homeostasis.
• Through its receptors, the nervous system 
keeps us in touch with our environment 
(external and internal)
• The nervous system is composed of : 
• Brain
• spinal cord
• nerves
4

Activities of the Nervous system
•
Activities of the nervous system can be grouped together as three general overlapping 
functions:
•
Sensory input
•
Integration
•
Motor output
•
Millions of sensory receptors detect stimuli
•
External-temperature, light, and sound 
•
Internal-variations in pressure, pH, carbon dioxide concentration, levels of 
various electrolytes
•
All this gathered information is called sensory input.
•
Sensory input is converted into electrical signals called nerve impulses that are 
transmitted to the brain
•
The signals are brought together:
•
 To create sensations
•
To produce thoughts/add to memory
•
Decisions are made each moment based on the sensory input
•
 Integration is the processing and interpretation of the sensory input
•
The nervous system responds by sending signals 
•
Muscles -to contract
•
Glands- to produce secretions
•
Muscles and glands are called effectors because they cause an effect in response to 
directions from the nervous system

Divisions of the Nervous System
• The nervous system is divided into two subdivisions:
• The central nervous system (CNS)
• The peripheral nervous system (PNS)
The Central Nervous System
• The brain and spinal cord are the organs of the central nervous system
• Located in the dorsal body cavity and are encased in bone for 
protection
• The brain is in the cranial vault
• The spinal cord is in the vertebral canal of the vertebral column
• Though considered to be two separate organs, the brain and spinal cord 
are continuous at the foramen magnum.
The Peripheral Nervous System
• The organs of the peripheral nervous system are the nerves and ganglia
• Nerves are bundles of nerve fibers
• Ganglia are collections, or small knots, of nerve cell bodies outside the 
CNS.
• The peripheral nervous system is further subdivided into:
• Afferent (sensory) - transmits impulses from peripheral organs to the 
CNS. 
• Efferent (motor) - transmits impulses from the CNS out to the 
peripheral organs to cause an effect or action.
6

Central Nervous System (CNS)
• The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord
• The brain is surrounded by the cranium and the spinal cord is 
protected by the vertebrae. 
• The brain is continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen 
magnum
• The CNS is surrounded by connective tissue membranes called 
meninges, and by cerebrospinal fluid
• There are three layers of meninges around the brain and spinal

strands that attach it to the innermost layer)
• The innermost layer- pia mater   (thin, delicate membrane) is 
tightly bound to the surface of the brain and spinal cord and 
cannot be dissected away without damaging the surface.

--- SLIDE ---

Anatomy
Anatomy 
the study of the structure of living organisms
in animals, it involves examining bones, muscles, organs, and tissues
 provides a framework for understanding how the body is organised

--- SLIDE ---

Physiology
Physiology 
the study of the functions and processes of living organisms
 Focuses on how organs and systems work individually and together
Explains how animals maintain life and adapt to their environment – adaptation to mode of life

--- SLIDE ---

Studying Anatomy and Physiology
Essential for biological sciences: human medicine, veterinary medicine, zoology, and animal science
Helps in understanding animal health, disease, and treatment
Provides insights into growth, reproduction, and adaptation of organisms

--- SLIDE ---

Levels of Structural Organization
Different levels of organization
Cells – basic unit of life
Tissues – groups of similar cells
Organs – structures with specific functions
Systems – organs working together
Organism – complete living animal

--- SLIDE ---

Major Animal Systems
Skeletal System – support and protection
Muscular System – movement
Digestive System – nutrient processing
Circulatory System – transport of substances
Respiratory System – gas exchange
Nervous System – control and coordination
Reproductive System – continuation of species
While anatomy focuses on structure, physiology is centered on function
 Both fields are interdependent.
Understanding them is key for animal science, medicine, and care

--- SLIDE ---

Mammalian Skin
Mammalian skin and its modifications distinguish mammals from other groups

Being an interface between an animal and its environment, the skin is strongly molded by the animal’s way of life  

Generally, the skin is thicker in mammals than on other classes of vertebrates

--- SLIDE ---

Skin structure and function
The integument or skin is the largest organ of the body, making up 16% of body weight, with a surface area of 1.8m2. 

It has several functions, the most important being to form a physical barrier to the environment, allowing and limiting the inward and outward passage of water, electrolytes and various substances while providing protection against micro-organisms, ultraviolet radiation, toxic agents and mechanical insults.

--- SLIDE ---

There are three structural layers to the skin: the epidermis, the dermis and subcutis. Hair, nails, sebaceous, sweat and apocrine glands are regarded as derivatives of skin.

The skin is a dynamic organ in a constant state of change, as cells of the outer layers are continuously shed and replaced by inner cells moving up to the surface.

 Although structurally, consistent throughout the body, the skin varies in thickness according to anatomical site and age of the individual.

--- SLIDE ---

A cross section of the mammalian skin.

--- SLIDE ---

Cross-section of the skin.

--- SLIDE ---

Layers of the skin

--- SLIDE ---

Skin anatomy
Epidermis - outer layer, serving as the physical and chemical barrier between the interior body and exterior environment.

Dermis - deeper layer providing the structural support of the skin, below which is a loose connective tissue layer, the subcutis or hypodermis which is an important depot of fat.

--- SLIDE ---

Epidermis: The epidermis is stratified squamous epithelium. The main cells of the epidermis are the keratinocytes, which synthesize the protein keratin.

Protein bridges called desmosomes connect the keratinocytes, which are in a constant state of transition from the deeper layers to the superficial layer.

The four separate layers of the epidermis are formed by the differing stages of keratin maturation.

Layers of the epidermis.

--- SLIDE ---

Digestive System and Nutrition
For all organisms, 
a basic requirement of energy to maintain a highly ordered/complex structure 
energy known as Chemical Bond Energy is released by transforming complex compounds acquired from the environment into simpler ones 

Almost all animals are heterotrophic organisms because they depend on already synthesized organic compounds of plants and other animals to obtain the materials they need for 
growth, maintenance and reproduction

food of animals (the complex tissue of other organisms) is too bulky to be absorbed directly by cells and must be broken down/digested into soluble molecules small enough to be utilized. Ingestion of foods/their simplification by digestion are initial steps in nutrition. Foods reduced by digestion to soluble molecular form are absorbed into the circulatory system and transported to the body tissues They are then assimilated into the structure of cells/oxidized (by oxygen transported by blood to the tissues) or burned to yield energy and heat 
Food not used immediately, is stored for future use 
wastes produced by oxidation are excreted 
food products unsuitable for digestion are egested in the form of faeces

--- SLIDE ---

Animals are divided into 4 broad categories based on dietary habits:
Herbivorous animals- feed mainly on plant life. 
Carnivorous animals - feed mainly on herbivores and other carnivores
Omnivorous animals – feed on both plants and animals
Saprophagous animals – feed on decaying organic matter

Various methods have evolved for procuring and manipulating solid food and adaptations are based on the food of the animal 
True mastication (the chewing of food) as opposed to tearing or crushing is found only in mammals
Mammals have 4 different types of teeth, each adapted for specific functions
Incisors- with simple crowns and sharp edges. Designed for biting, cutting and stripping.
Canines- with long conical crowns for piercing, seizing and tearing.
Premolars and molars- large bodies and variable cusp arrangement for grinding and crushing

--- SLIDE ---

This basic pattern is highly modified in animals with specialized food habits 
For e.g herbivores have suppressed canines but well-developed molars with enamel ridges for grinding and the well-developed self sharpening incisors of rodents throughout life are constantly worn away by gnawing to keep pace with growth. An elephant’s tusk have become so highly modified (upper incisor used for defense, attack and rooting; male wild boar has modified canines used as weapons) that they are no longer useful for biting or chewing food

The primitive teeth formula for most mammals expresses the number of each tooth type in one half of the upper and lower jaw
I=3/3; C = 1/1; PM = 4/4; M = 3/3 = 44 e.g Order Insecta, some carnivores, some omnivores
Most mammals grow 2 sets of teeth (reptiles replace teeth continuously). These are:
A temporary set- deciduous or milk teeth
Permanent set

Teeth types in mammals

Teeth types in mammals

--- SLIDE ---

Only incisors, canines and premolars are deciduous. Molars are never replaced and the single permanent set must last a lifetime

mechanical and chemical breakdown of organic foods into 
molecular subunits for absorption. Although food solids consist of CHO, proteins, and fats (the very components that make up the body of the consumer) they must first be reduced to their simplest molecular units and dissolved before they can be assimilated 

The evolution of the alimentary system in mammals allowed for extracellular digestion of large food masses because certain cells lining the lumen (cavity) of the alimentary canal specialize in forming various digestive secretions while others function largely/entirely in absorption

ANIMAL SYSTEMATICS
• Systematics is the science of classifying organisms and determining 
their evolutionary relationships.
• It is the scientific study of animal diversity and the evolutionary 
relationships among them.
• Systematics use data ranging from fossils, anatomy, molecules and 
genes to infer evolutionary relationships
• Systematics categorizes animals into hierarchical groups based on 
synapomorphies (shared derived characters), genetics and 
evolutionary history, often visualized through phylogenetic trees.

• Systematics focuses on how different animal groups are related 
through common ancestry
• Systematists proposed that classification should be based entirely on 
evolutionary relationships. In such systems, names are assigned only 
to groups that include a common ancestors (monophyletic taxa)

• Traditional methods of classification is based on physical and 
morphological characteristics
• While in modern method of classification genetic and molecular 
data are the most frequently used tools to establish evolutionary 
connections
• Animal systematics has 3 goals:
• To identify all species of animals
• To evaluate evolutionary relationships among animal 
species
• To produce a taxonomy that groups animal species in a 
hierarchy of taxonomic groups

Hierarchical Classification
• Beyond naming organisms, Linnaeus also grouped organisms into 
hierarchy of increasing inclusive categories.
• Animals are grouped into hierarchical categories like Kingdom, 
Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, and Species 
• Taxonomic groups are traditionally ranked to denote increasing 
inclusiveness
• Species that appear to be closely related are grouped into the same 
genus (Leopard: Panthera pardus, Lion: P. Leo, Tiger: P. tigris, Jaguar: 
P. onca)

• Related genera are placed in the same family; families into 
orders; orders into classes, classes into phyla and phyla into 
kingdom and kingdoms into domain.
• These ranks can be subdivided to signify taxa intermediate 
between them e.g. Subkingdom, subphylum, suborder etc. 
• The named group at any level of hierarchy is called taxon
• Felidae is a taxon at family level; while mammalia is a taxon 
at the class level
• Taxa broader than the genus are not italicized but capitalized

Hierarchical Classification
Species placed in groups within more 
inclusive groups.
Castor canadensis

Linking classification and phylogeny
• The evolutionary history of a group  of organisms can be represented 
in a branching diagram called phylogenetic tree. 
• All classification scheme are artificial attempt to impose order.
• Once the organisms are assigned to taxonomic categories, it becomes 
possible to consider the evolutionary relationship among and within 
those categories.
• Traits shared due to common ancestry are used to classify organisms 
into groups that reflect their evolutionary history

Connection between classification and phylogeny



ZOOGEOGRAPHY
• Geographical distribution of animals also called 
zoogeography is the natural arrangement of animal species 
across the earth’s surface, influenced by physical geography, 
climate and geological history.
• Animals are distributed in different patterns, including:
• Cosmopolitan: Species are found in many parts of the world, 
often due to their ability to adapt to various environments or 
because they were spread by humans. Examples include the 
house mouse or the pigeon.

• Endemic: Species are unique to a specific location and are 
not found anywhere else naturally. Island chains like the 
Galapagos are known for having many endemic species, such 
as the Galapagos tortoise.
• Disjunct: A species or group of related species is found in 
two or more geographically separated areas. This often 
occurs when a once-continuous population becomes split by 
geological events, climate change, or other factors

• Alfred Russel Wallace in 1876 proposed that the Earth could 
be divided into distinct regions based on their unique animal 
life.

KINGDOM ANIMALIA
Shared General Characteristics
• Heterotrophy
• Multicellularity
• No cell walls
• Active movement
• Most animals reproduce sexually 
• The cells of all animals except sponges are organized into 
structural and functional units called tissues 

Features used in Animal Classification
• When organisms are classified into groups, it is making a 
hypothesis about the extent to which the group share 
DNA.
• Morphological features such as symmetry, tissues,
type of body cavity, sequence of embryonic development, 
and segmentation can show levels of relatedness because 
these traits are based on the genetic material.
• Groups of individuals are more closely related if they 
share very similar morphological and DNA sequences with 
each other than individuals in other groups with vastly 
different structures or sequences.

Body symmetry (Asymmetric, Radiata, Bilateria)
• Asymmetrical animals are irregular and have no ordered 
pattern to their gross morphology.
• In radial symmetry the animal parts are arranged in such a way
that any longitudinal plane passing through the central axis 
divides the organism into halves that are approximate mirror 
images.
• In bilateral symmetry, the animal body has right and left halves 
that are mirror images of each other. 

Asymmetrical



• Sagittal plane defines these halves 
• A bilaterally symmetrical body has, in addition to left and right halves, 
dorsal and ventral portions, which are divided by the frontal plane, 
and anterior and posterior ends, which are divided by  the transverse 
plane 
• Bilateral symmetry is highly correlated with cephalization, which is 
the concentration of nervous and sensory tissues and organs at one 
end of the animal resulting in distinct anterior and posterior ends.

Germ Layers and Body Cavities 
• Cells are organized into layers derived from two embryonic 
tissue layers and Diploblastic organization is the simplest 
tissue-level organization.
• Ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis, the outer layer of the 
body wall.
• Endoderm gives rise to the gastrodermis, the tissue that lines 
the gut cavity.

Diploblastic organization

• Triploblastic animals are organized into several subgroups 
based on the presence or absence of a body cavity:
• Triploblastic Acoelomate; Mesodermal cells completely fill 
the blastocoel, leaving a gut cavity as the only body cavity
• Triploblastic Pseudocoelomate; mesodermal cells line the 
outer edge of the blastocoel, leaving two body cavities: a 
persistent blastocoel, now called pseudocoelom, and a gut 
cavity.
• A pseudocoelom is a space that develops between the 
mesoderm and endoderm.


• In Triploblastic Eucoelomate the coelom develops entirely 
within mesoderm. 
• Triploblastic Eucoelomate body plan is formed either by 
schizocoely or enterocoely
• In the schizocoelous plan (protostomes) mesodermal cells fill 
the blastocoel, forming a solid band of tissue around the gut 
cavity. Then cells simply move apart from one another to 
create an expanding coelomic cavity within the mass of 
mesodermal cells 

• In enterocoelous plan, found in the deuterostomes, the 
central portion of the gut lining, which form the mesoderm 
begin to grow outward as pouches, expanding into the 
blastocoel .
• The expanding pouch move outward and enclose a space 
that becomes the coelomic cavity or coelom. 
• Within bilaterians, protostomes develop the mouth prior to 
the anus; deuterostomes develop the mouth after the anus 
has formed

group.

postembryonic stages
• Earliest phylogenetic split within taxon Bilateria separates 
Deuterostomia from Protostomia

• The two taxa differ in the fate of the embryonic blastopore, 
which becomes the anus in Deuterostomia and the mouth in 
Protostomia

CNIDARIA

• The phylum takes its name from cells 
cnidocytes, which contain organelles (cnidae) 
characteristic of the phylum. 
• The most common type of cnida is the 
nematocyst
• Cnidaria are widespread in marine habitats, and 
a few inhabit freshwater. 
• There are no terrestrial species. 
• Cnidarians sometimes live symbiotically with 
other animals, often as commensals on the shell 
or other surface of their host. 
• Certain hydroids and sea anemones commonly 
live on snail shells inhabited by hermit crabs, 
providing the crabs some protection from 
predators.

• Algal cells frequently live as mutuals in the 
tissues of cnidarians, notably in some 
freshwater hydras and in reef-building corals.
• The presence of the algae in reef-building corals 
limits the occurrence of coral reefs to relatively 
shallow, clear water where there is sufficient 
light for the photosynthetic requirements of the 
algae.

• DIAGNISTIC FEATURES
• Radially symmetrical which allows food capturing 
from all sides. However, there may be 
modifications.
• They are diploblastic; the epidermis and 
gastrodermis are separated by jelly-like mesoglea
ectoderm—and lack organs
• There is a single gastrovascular cavity that opens 
only through the mouth. There is no anus.

• There is no head, brain and CNS. It has a simple 
interconnecting nerve cell which form nerve net. 
Statocysts and oceli are usually the only sensory 
structure.
• The skeleton may be horny or calcerous, internal or 
external or continuous.
• There is no special structures for respiration, 
excretion and transport system (except sea water 
channels in some large jelly fish.
• Extracellular digestion in gastrovascular cavity and 
intracellular digestion in gastrodermal cells.
• Extensible tentacles usually encircle mouth or oral 
region

• Sexual reproduction by gametes in all medusae and 
some polyps; monoecious or dioecious
• Despite having no reproductive, circulatory, digestive, or 
excretory systems, cnidarians reproduce, exchange gas, 
capture and digest prey, and distribute the resulting 
organic molecules to all their cells. 
• The gastrovascular space may serve as a hydrostatic 
skeleton by providing a rigid structure against which 
muscles can operate, and it also gives the animal shape.
• Possession of a unique stinging or adhesive structure 
called cnidae which resides in a cell called cnidocyte. 
The most common cnidae are called nematocyst.


• All cnidarian forms fit into one of two morphological types 
(dimorphism): a polyp, or hydroid form, which is adapted 
to a sedentary or sessile life, and a medusa, or jellyfish 
form, which is adapted for a floating or free-swimming 
existence
• Existing either as a solitary or colonial sessile polyp or

History of Animal Diversity
• Neoproterozoic Era (1 billion–542 million years ago)
Although molecular data indicates a much earlier origin of animals, the oldest 
generally accepted animal fossils are only 575 million years old.
These fossils are known as the Ediacara fauna, named for the Ediacara Hills of 
Australia.
Ediacara fauna consist primarily of cnidarians, but soft-bodied mollusks were 
also present, and numerous fossilized burrows and tracks indicate the 
presence of worms.

Paleozoic Era (542–251 million years ago)
• Animals underwent considerable diversification between 542–525 million years ago, during
the Cambrian period of the Paleozoic Era.
• During this period, known as the Cambrian explosion, about half of extant animal phyla
arose.
• Fossils of Cambrian animals include the first animals with hard, mineralized skeletons.
• The new predator-prey relationships that emerged in the Cambrian may have generated
diversity through natural selection.
• Predators acquired adaptations that helped them catch prey.
• Prey acquired adaptations that helped them resist predation.
• A rise of atmospheric oxygen preceded the Cambrian explosion.
• More oxygen may have provided opportunities for animals with higher metabolic rates and
larger body sizes.
• In the Silurian and Devonian periods, animal diversity continued to increase, punctuated by
episodes of mass extinction.
• Vertebrates (fishes) became the top predators of marine food webs.
• By 460 million years ago, arthropods began to adapt to terrestrial habitats.
• Vertebrates moved to land about 360 million years ago and diversified into many lineages.
• Two of these survive today: amphibians and amniotes

Goals of gastrulation
• Bring endoderm cells to the inside of the embryo
• Allow ectoderm cells to coat the outside of the embryo
• Position mesoderm cells in between the other two germ
cells
Gastrulation

• Gastrulation literally means ‘formation of a gut’.
• The spherical blastula is now converted into a more complex shape and forms a
second germ layer.
• Methods of gastrulation vary among animal species but generally one side of blastula
bends inwards in a process known as In-pushing or Intruding or Invagination.
• During this invagination, the cells frequently at the VP e.g. Amphioxus.
• Or it begin to roll inwards forming a depression or sac within the blastocoel, this
continues to enlarge until it subsequently results in the formation of two-layered, cup-
shaped gastrula (coelogastrula).
• The two germ layers are: an outer layer of cells surrounding the blastocoel called
Ectoderm and an inner layer lining the gut, called Endoderm
• Then the cavity within the blastocoel gradually becomes obliterated and is replaced by
a new cavity, called Archenteron (Greek archae, old + enteron, gut) or a Gastrocoel
(Greek gaster, stomach + koilos, cavity).

• It is otherwise known as the ‘primitive gut’ as this later contributes
to formation of the gut cavity.
• The opening of the archenteron to the exterior where invagination
occurred is known as the Blastopore (Greek blastos, germ + poros,
hole).
• Stereoblastulae
that

from

cleavage

• The archenteron forms secondarily as a space within developed
endoderm.
• Gastrulation by involution occurs when the cells at the edge of the
cytoplasmic disc of a discoblastula divide rapidly and grow beneath
the disc, thus forming a two-layered gastrula with ectoderm on the
surface and endoderm below.
• In amphibians with mesolecithal eggs, gastrulation occurs around
the VP whereas this process takes place on top of the VP in reptiles
and birds with telolecithal eggs since yolk mass constitutes an
obstruction to the process

of

leave

mesenchyme
cells.

of

ZOO 102: ANIMAL DIVERSITY

--- SLIDE ---

Overview: Diversity of animal forms, structures, and functions

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
Animal diversity is defined as the wide range of different kinds of animals on earth
Encompasses the variations in their forms, structures and functions, genetic composition etc
Who are the Animals?
Very diverse with some common characteristics
Most are capable of locomotion
Heterotrophs
Multicellular eukaryotes
Cells are specialized - for various functions
Most have muscular tissues and nervous systems 
Most reproduce sexually
Haploid gametes form zygote (a totipotent stem cell)
that cleaves (divides)
In embryogenesis, a ball of cells, morula differentiates into 
another ball of more numerous cells, blastula, undergoes
gastrulation (infolding of cells making germ layers)
Processes of embryogenesis

--- SLIDE ---

Stem Cells
Are cells that can divide into multiple kinds of others cells
Are formed and differentiated during early embryonic development
Types
Stems cells ae categorised based on their potency (diversity of cell types they can become as they differentiate)
Totipotent Stem Cells (TSC): can differentiate into all cell types in an organism, plus the extra-embryonic tissues (like the placenta), forming entire, complete organism
Pluripotent Stem Cells (PSC): can divide into most, or all cell types in an organisms, but cannot develop into extraembryonic tissue and an entire organism
Multipotent Stem Cells (PSC): can self-renew and differentiate into limited range of specialised cell types within a particular tissues 
Role in diversity
TSC allows for creation of a new, entire organism laying the foundation for future cell and tissue diversity
PSC are crucial for building different tissues and organs, contributing to complexity and variation
Stem Cells: types and examples

--- SLIDE ---

Diversity in forms and functions
Animals have different forms and functions, which form the basis of their classification and relate to their evolutionary advancement and complexity

Level of organisation
Body symmetry/ Body plan
Cephalisation

Coelom formation
Blastospore’s fate

Multicellularity:
Cellular level

Body Symmetry
Balanced arrangement, of animals’ body parts OR correspondence of body parts on opposite sides of a dividing line or distributed around a central point or axis
Types of symmetry
Asymmetry: no symmetry
Radial symmetry: body parts arranged around 
	a central axis, with top and bottom, and oral 
	and aboral but without left and right sides
Bilaterial symmetry: equal arrangementof parts 
	about a vertical plane resulting in two mirror 
	images, with head (anterior) and tail (posterior), 
	front (dorsal) and back (ventral), and right and 
	left sides
Types of Symmetry

--- SLIDE ---

Cephalisation
Formation of anterior and posterior ends, characteristic of bilaterial symmetry fosters the tendency for cephalisation

Cephalisation is the tendency of the sensory organs and nervous tissues of animals to become concentrated at the anterior end of the body to form a distinct head

Bilateral symmetry and hence, cephalisation first appeared in the platyhelminthes

Cephalisation is an adaptive feature that allow central control of the entire organism, and a step towards the evolution of the brain
Cephalisation in Platyhelminthes

EMBRYONIC LAYERS
Cells first evolved from two embryonic layers
Ectoderm – outer cell layer
Endoderm – inner cell layer
Hence, diploblastic – two germ layers (Cnidaria)
Third germ layer (mesoderm) first appeared in Platyhelminthes
Hence, triploblastic – three germ layers
Triploblastic allows for the formation of complex tissues and organs such as muscles, bone

Agnathans (jawless fishes)
Specimens provided: Genus – Petromyzon (dissected adult)
                                Ammocoete larva, i.e. the larval stage of a lamprey - Petromyzon
Classification:
Kingdom: Animalia
Phylum: Chordata (have a notochord – a characteristic feature of chordates)
Subphylum: Vertebrata (have a backbone or vertebral column, even though the vertebrae are rudimentary
Infra-phylum: Agnatha (jawless vertebrates)

Order: Petromyzontiformes
Family: Petromyzontidae
Subfamily: Petromyzontinae

Common name: Sea Lamprey

--- SLIDE ---

General features of Agnathans
The body is slender and eel-like
They lack jaws 
Their skeleton is fibrous and made up of cartilage rather than bone (a similarity they share with the cartilaginous fishes – Chondrichthyes, the difference with this group is that cartilaginous fishes have jaws)
They lack scales 
They have dorsal fins but no paired fins or appendages
They have pore-like gill openings
They have sucker like oral disc and a tongue with well developed keratinized (i.e. contains keratin, a strong natural protein) teeth
Sexes are separate and there is a long larval stage known as Ammocoete larva.

The Cambridge Dictionary of Sociology
Providing an authoritative and comprehensive overview of the classical and the
contemporary, this volume is an indispensable guide to the vibrant and
expanding field of sociology. Featuring over 600 entries, from concise definitions
to discursive essays, written by leading international academics, the Dictionary
offers a truly global perspective, examining both American and European trad-
itions and approaches. Entries cover schools, theories, theorists, and debates,
with substantial articles on all key topics in the field. While recognizing the
richness of historical sociological traditions, the Dictionary also looks forward to
new and evolving influences such as cultural change, genetics, globalization,
information technologies, new wars, and terrorism. Most entries incorporate
references for further reading, and a cross-referencing system enables easy
access to related areas. This Dictionary is an invaluable reference work for
students and academics alike and will help to define the field of sociology in
years to come.
B R Y A N S. T U R N E R is Professor of Sociology in the Asia Research Institute at the
National University of Singapore, where he leads the research team for the
Religion and Globalisation cluster. Prior to this, he was Professor of Sociology
in the Faculty of Social and Political Sciences at the University of Cambridge.
Professor Turner is the author of The New Medical Sociology (2004) and Society and
Culture: Principles of Scarcity and Solidarity (with Chris Rojek, 2001), and is the
founding editor of the Journal of Classical Sociology (with John O’Neill), Body &
Society (with Mike Featherstone), and Citizenship Studies. He is currently writing a
three-volume study on the sociology of religion for Cambridge University Press.

GEO 101: Introduction to Physical Geography
Module 1 (Lecture 1)
Prof. Ibidun O. Adelekan
Department of Geography 
University of Ibadan
29th January 2026

The Discipline of Geography
Geography consists of two 
main sub-fields of knowledge 
with similar methodology. 
▪Physical Geography
▪Human Geography

Physical Geography
Physical geography is the 
branch of geography which deals 
with the processes and patterns 
in the natural environment. 
It deals with the natural features 
of the earth's surface (those not 
caused or affected by humans) 
that have distribution or differ in 
kind from other phenomenon 
e.g. climate, landforms, 
vegetation, soil, and water forms.  

Natural Environment
• Atmosphere
• Hydrosphere
• Biosphere
• Geosphere/Lithosphere

Phenomena studied in 
Physical Geography
• Landforms
• Rocks and minerals
• Soils
• Plants
• Animals
• Water
• Rivers and other water bodies
• Oceans
• Climate and weather

Sub-disciplines of Physical Geography
Climatology and Meteorology (Earth’s atmosphere)
Biogeography (animal and plant life)
Geomorpology (physical landscape)
Pedology (soils)
Hydrology (all forms of water)

Scope of Physical Geography
Combining these two items, we can now suggest that physical geography studies the 
spatial patterns of weather and climate, soils, vegetation, animals, water in all its 
forms, and landforms. 
In addition, we identified some of the key elements studied by physical geographers. 
We have learned that physical geography examines and investigates natural phenomena 
spatially.

Module 1 Lecture 2
Prof. Ibidun O. Adelekan
Department of Geography 
University of Ibadan
5th February 2026

Scope of Physical Geography
Combining these two items, we can now suggest that physical geography studies the 
spatial patterns of weather and climate, soils, vegetation, animals, water in all its 
forms, and landforms. 
In addition, we identified some of the key elements studied by physical geographers. 
We have learned that physical geography examines and investigates natural phenomena 
spatially. 

Scope of Physical Geography -II
The scope of physical 
geography is much 
broader than the 
simple spatial study 
of nature. 
It also involves the 
investigation of how 
humans are 
influencing nature.

• This sub-field of geography is known as the Human-Land 
Tradition. 
This area of geography has seen very keen interest and growth in the 
last few decades because of the acceleration of human induced 
environmental degradation.
• Humans are a force affecting the objects of physical geographic 
study. If the physical geographer excludes those physical features 
affected by man or tries to ignore the role of humans in the earth-
system, he/she is left with little to study or results which do not 
conform to the realities. 

The Development of Physical Geography
• The period from 1850 to 1950
➢Uniformitarianism 
➢Evolution - Charles Darwin’s Origin of Species (1859)
➢Exploration and Survey 
➢Conservation (George Perkins Marsh - 1864)
• After 1950
➢The Quantitative Revolution 
➢The study of Human/Land Relationships

Course Outline

Introduction
The soil layer supports the world’s natural vegetation, land animals, 
and its human population through agriculture. 
➢How is soil formed? 
➢What are the major types of world soils, and where are they found? 
➢What impact will global change have on agriculture? 
➢These are some of the questions we will answer in this module.

Soil Nature
➢Soil is the uppermost layer of the land surface 
that plants use and depend on for nutrients, water, 
and physical support. 
➢Soils can vary greatly from continent to 
continent, from region to region, and even from 
field to field. 
➢This is because they are influenced by factors 
and processes that can vary widely from place to 
place.
➢Vegetation, climate, time, and parent material are 
important factors in soil development

Soil Nature
➢Soil is a complex mixture of solids, liquids, and gases. 
➢Solid matter includes both mineral and organic matter. 
➢Watery solutions and; 
➢Atmospheric gases are also found in soils.

Soil Horizon and Profile
➢Soil horizons are distinctive layers found in soils that differ in 
physical or chemical composition, organic content, or structure. 
➢The soil profile refers to the 
display of horizons on a 
cross section through the soil
➢Soil profile is the display of 
soil horizons on the face 
of a freshly cut vertical exposure 
through the soil.
➢It describes the layered 
structure of a particular soil.

➢Colour is the most obvious feature of a soil
➢Soil colour is usually determined by soil 
forming processes and varies widely.
➢ Some colour relationships are quite simple.
➢For example, western-Nigeria soils are black 
or dark brown in color because they contain 
many humus particles. 
➢And the red soils of the Southeast are 
created by the presence of iron-containing 
oxides. 
➢In some areas, soil colour is inherited from 
the mineral parent material, but, more 
generally, the color is generated during soil 
formation. 
Properties of Soil – Soil Colour

Properties of Soil -  Soil Texture
➢Soil texture refers to the proportions of sand, silt, and 
clay found in a soil. 
➢Sandy soils → drain quickly
➢Clay soils → hold more water
➢Loamy soils → balanced and ideal for agriculture
➢Why is soil texture important?
➢ Soil texture determines the ability of the soil to hold 
water. Coarse- textured (sandy) soils have many small 
passages between touching mineral grains that quickly 
conduct water through to deeper layers. But soils of fine 
particles have far smaller passages and spaces, so 
water will penetrate down more slowly and will tend to 
be held in the upper layers.

Properties of Soil – Soil 
Colloids
➢Soil colloids are particles smaller than one ten 
thousandth of a millimeter (0.0001 mm, 0.000,004 
in.). 
➢Like other soil particles, some colloids are 
mineral, whereas others are organic. Mineral 
colloids are usually very fine clay particles. 
➢They have a thin, plate-like shape that reflect 
their layered chemical crystal structure. 
➢The surfaces of colloids attract base ions, which 
plants use as nutrients.
➢Soil colloids are important because their 
surfaces attract soil nutrients, dissolved in soil 
water. 

Properties of Soil – Soil pH
➢This is the Level of acidity or alkalinity.
➢ It Controls nutrient availability and heavy metal mobility.
➢Soil acidity varies widely. 
➢Soils of cool, moist regions are generally acid, while soils of arid climates are 
alkaline. 
➢Acid soils are often low in base ions.

Properties of Soil – Soil Structure
Soil structure refers to the way in which soil grains are clumped together into larger 
masses, called peds.

C-GEO 101 (Introduction to Physical Geography)
Module 2 - THE EARTH
Dr. R. O. Obateru

12 February 2026

Content Outline
➢Introduction
➢Brief History of the Universe and the Earth
➢The Planetary and Solar System
➢The Earth as a Planet
➢The Structure of the Earth
➢Types of Rocks and Landforms
➢Weathering
➢Mass Wasting
2

Introduction
• The Earth is a unique planet within 
the solar system and the home of 
human life. 
• In Physical Geography, the Earth is 
studied not only as a planet in 
space but also as a dynamic 
system where internal and 
external forces interact to shape 
the natural environment. 
3

Brief History of the 
Universe & the Earth
➢The Universe originated about 13.8 billion 
years ago with the Big Bang, a massive 
expansion of space, energy, and matter. 
➢As the Universe expanded and cooled, 
galaxies, stars, and planetary systems 
gradually formed. 
➢Our solar system developed about 4.6 
billion years ago from a rotating nebula of 
gas and dust. 
➢The Earth formed through accretion, later 
cooling to develop a crust, oceans, 
atmosphere, and conditions suitable for 
life.
4

The Planetary System & the Solar System
➢A planetary system is a general 
term for any collection of stars, 
planets, and other celestial 
bodies bound by gravity, 
whereas the solar system is the 
specific name for our local 
system (the Sun and its 
planets). 
➢Every solar system is a 
planetary system, but only ours 
is called "solar" because it is 
named after the star Sol. 
5

The Solar System
The Earth is part of a larger system known as 
the solar system, which consists of the Sun and 
all celestial bodies that revolve around it under 
the influence of gravity. Understanding the 
solar and planetary systems provides a broader 
spatial context for studying the Earth in 
Physical Geography.
The Solar System
➢The Sun is the centre of the solar system and 
the primary source of heat and energy.
➢The solar system includes eight planets, their 
moons, asteroids, comets, and meteoroids.

elliptical orbits.

Inner (Terrestrial) Planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth and 
Mars)
✓Composed mainly of rock and metal.

2.
Outer (Giant) Planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and 
Neptune)
✓Mostly gaseous or icy in composition.

The Earth’s Position in the Solar System:

suitable for life.

zone.

climate, and many surface processes studied in Physical

The Earth as a Planet
The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only known 
planet that supports life. It belongs to a group of planets called 
the terrestrial or rocky planets.
Main Characteristics of the Earth as a Planet
➢Shape: The Earth is approximately spherical but slightly 
flattened at the poles, a shape known as an oblate spheroid.
➢Size: It has a mean radius of about 6,371 km.
➢Rotation: The Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, 
resulting in day and night.
➢Revolution: The Earth revolves around the Sun once every 
365¼ days, leading to the seasons.
➢Axial Tilt: The Earth is tilted at about 23½°, which is 
responsible for seasonal variations.
➢Gravitational Force: Gravity holds the atmosphere, oceans, 
and all objects on the Earth’s surface.

components that shape the natural environment. These 
components include the solid Earth (lithosphere), the atmosphere, 
the hydrosphere, and the biosphere. The interaction among these 
systems explains how landscapes are formed, modified, and 
continuously reshaped over time.

Physical geography is the study of the processes that shape the Earth's surface, the animals and 
plants that inhabit it, and the spatial patterns they exhibit. Self-identified in the mid- to late 
1800s, physical geographers and in particular geomorphologists dominated the discipline of 
geography to the late 1930s. 
Physical geography (also known as physiography) is one of the three main branches 
of geography.[1][2][3][4][5] Physical geography is the branch of natural science which deals with 
the 
processes 
and 
patterns 
in 
the natural 
environment such 
as 
the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere. This focus is in contrast with the 
branch of human geography, which focuses on the built environment, and technical geography, 
which focuses on using, studying, and creating tools to obtain, analyze, interpret, and 
understand spatial information.[4][5][6] The three branches have significant overlap, however. 
 
Physical geography can be divided into several branches or related fields, as follows: 
• 
Geomorphology[7][8] is concerned with understanding the surface of the Earth and 
the processes by which it is shaped, both at the present as well as in the past. 
Geomorphology as a field has several sub-fields that deal with the 
specific landforms of 
various 
environments 
e.g. desert geomorphology 
and fluvial geomorphology; however, these sub-fields are united by the core 
processes which cause them, mainly tectonic or climatic processes. 
Geomorphology seeks to understand landform history and dynamics, and predict 
future changes through a combination of field observation, physical experiment, 
and numerical modeling (Geomorphometry). Early studies in geomorphology are 
the foundation for pedology, one of two main branches of soil science. 
Meander formation. 
• 
Hydrology[7][8] is predominantly concerned with the amounts and quality of water 
moving and accumulating on the land surface and in the soils and rocks near the 
surface and is typified by the hydrological cycle. Thus the field encompasses water 
in rivers, lakes, aquifers and to an extent glaciers, in which the field examines the 
process and dynamics involved in these bodies of water. Hydrology has historically 
had an important connection with engineering and has thus developed a largely 
quantitative method in its research; however, it does have an earth science side that 
embraces the systems approach. Similar to most fields of physical geography it has 
sub-fields that examine the specific bodies of water or their interaction with other 
spheres e.g. limnology and ecohydrology. 

• 
Glaciology is the study of glaciers and ice sheets, or more commonly 
the cryosphere or ice and phenomena that involve ice. Glaciology groups the latter 
(ice sheets) as continental glaciers and the former (glaciers) as alpine glaciers. 
Although research in the areas is similar to research undertaken into both the 
dynamics of ice sheets and glaciers, the former tends to be concerned with the 
interaction of ice sheets with the present climate and the latter with the impact of 
glaciers on the landscape. Glaciology also has a vast array of sub-fields examining 
the factors and processes involved in ice sheets and glaciers e.g. snow hydrology 
and glacial geology. 
•

The energy systems in the environment: atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, 
and lithosphere 
The Earth's environment is a complex system of interconnected spheres: the atmosphere, 
biosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere. Energy flows and transformations within and between 
these spheres drive virtually all natural processes, from weather patterns to geological activity 
and the sustenance of life. 
Here's a breakdown of the energy systems within each sphere and how they interact: 
1. Atmosphere (Air): 
 
Energy Source: Primarily solar radiation. 
 
Energy Absorption & Transfer: 
o The atmosphere absorbs a portion of incoming solar radiation, particularly by 
gases like water vapor, carbon dioxide, and ozone. 
o This absorbed energy heats the atmosphere. 
o Radiation: Heat is radiated back into space, but greenhouse gases trap some of 
this infrared radiation, leading to the natural greenhouse effect that warms the 
planet. 
o Convection: Uneven heating of the Earth's surface and the atmosphere creates 
temperature differences, leading to air movement (wind) and the transfer of heat 
through convection. This drives weather patterns and distributes heat globally. 
o Latent Heat: Water vapor carries latent heat (energy absorbed during 
evaporation). When water vapor condenses to form clouds and precipitation, this 
latent heat is released into the atmosphere, further influencing weather and 
climate. 
2. Biosphere (Life): 
 
Energy Source: Primarily solar energy, captured through photosynthesis. 
 
Energy Absorption & Transfer: 
o Photosynthesis: Green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy from 
the sun into chemical energy (sugars). This is the foundation of most food webs. 
o Chemical Energy: The chemical energy stored in organic compounds is 
transferred through consumption (e.g., animals eating plants, predators eating 
prey). 
o Respiration: Organisms release energy for their metabolic processes through 
cellular respiration, often releasing heat as a byproduct. 
o Decomposition: Decomposers break down dead organic matter, releasing stored 
energy and nutrients back into the environment. 
3. Hydrosphere (Water): 
 
Energy Source: Solar energy, and to a lesser extent, geothermal energy. 
 
Energy Absorption & Transfer: 

2 
 
o Absorption of Solar Radiation: Oceans and other water bodies absorb a 
significant amount of solar energy, which heats the water. Water has a high 
specific heat, meaning it can store a lot of heat. 
o Evaporation & Condensation: Solar energy drives evaporation, transforming 
liquid water into water vapor and transferring latent heat into the atmosphere. 
Condensation releases this heat. This is a crucial component of the water cycle. 
o Ocean Currents: Temperature and salinity differences, driven by solar heating 
and wind, create ocean currents that redistribute heat around the globe, 
influencing regional climates. 
o Phase Changes: The energy involved in melting ice (absorption of heat) and 
freezing water (release of heat) plays a significant role in Earth's energy balance, 
particularly in polar regions. 
4. Lithosphere (Earth's Crust): 
 
Energy Source: Primarily geothermal energy from the Earth's interior (radioactive decay 
and residual heat from planetary formation), and solar energy at the surface. 
 
Energy Absorption & Transfer: 
o Geothermal Heat: Heat from the Earth's core and mantle rises to the surface 
through conduction and convection within the mantle. This energy drives plate 
tectonics, volcanic activity, and hot springs. 
o Solar Absorption: The Earth's surface (land) absorbs solar radiation, which 
warms the ground. 
o Conduction: Heat is transferred through direct contact within the lithosphere. 
o Radiation: The Earth's surface radiates heat back into the atmosphere. 
o Chemical Energy: Energy is stored in fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) within 
the lithosphere, formed from ancient organic matter that trapped solar energy over

We all live in clusters of houses. You may call it

unporlant criterion it is not a universal
crilerion since many villages in densely

At one time, people living in villages

Ecosystem as environmental concept  
The ecosystem is a fundamental concept in environmental science, representing the 
interconnectedness of living organisms and their non-living environment. Here's a breakdown of 
what it entails: 
Definition: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (biotic components) interacting 
with each other and with their non-living physical and chemical environment (abiotic 
components) in a particular area. These interactions create a stable, self-sustaining unit where 
energy flows and nutrients cycle. 
Key Components: 
1. Biotic Components (Living): These include all living organisms within the ecosystem, 
categorized by their roles in energy flow: 
o Producers (Autotrophs): Organisms, primarily plants and some microorganisms, 
that produce their own food through photosynthesis using sunlight or 
chemosynthesis. They form the base of the food chain. 
o Consumers (Heterotrophs): Organisms that obtain energy by feeding on other 
organisms. They are further classified into:  
 
Primary Consumers (Herbivores): Eat producers (e.g., rabbits eating 
grass). 
 
Secondary Consumers (Carnivores/Omnivores): Eat primary 
consumers (e.g., snakes eating rabbits). 
 
Tertiary Consumers (Carnivores/Omnivores): Eat secondary 
consumers (e.g., hawks eating snakes). 
o Decomposers (Saprotrophs): Organisms like bacteria and fungi that break down 
dead organic matter from producers and consumers, returning essential nutrients 
to the soil and water for use by producers. 
2. Abiotic Components (Non-living): These are the physical and chemical factors that 
influence the living organisms. They include: 
o Sunlight: The primary energy source for most ecosystems. 
o Water: Essential for all life processes. 
o Temperature: Influences metabolic rates and species distribution. 
o Soil: Provides nutrients, water, and support for plants. 
o Air/Atmosphere: Contains gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide vital for 
respiration and photosynthesis. 
o Minerals/Nutrients: Inorganic substances necessary for growth and 
development. 
o Climate: Long-term weather patterns. 
o Topography: The physical features of the land. 
Key Interactions and Processes: 

 
Energy Flow: Energy typically enters an ecosystem as solar energy, is captured by 
producers, and then flows unidirectionally through various trophic levels (food chains 
and food webs). A significant amount of energy is lost as heat at each transfer. 
 
Nutrient Cycling (Biogeochemical Cycles): Unlike energy, matter (nutrients like 
carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water) is recycled within an ecosystem. Decomposers 
play a crucial role in breaking down organic matter and returning inorganic nutrients to 
the environment, making them available again for producers. 
 
Interdependence: All components of an ecosystem are interdependent. Changes in one 
part of the system can have cascading effects on other parts. 
Significance in Environmental Science: 
The ecosystem concept is central to environmental science because: 
 
Holistic Understanding: It allows scientists to study nature as a complex, integrated 
system rather than isolated parts. 
 
Impact Assessment: It helps in understanding how human activities (e.g., pollution, 
deforestation, climate change) impact the intricate balance of natural systems. 
 
Conservation and Management: It provides a framework for developing strategies for 
biodiversity conservation, resource management, and ecosystem restoration. 
 
Predictive Power: By understanding ecosystem dynamics, scientists can better predict 
the consequences of environmental changes. 
 
Scale: Ecosystems can vary greatly in size, from a small puddle to a vast ocean, but the 
fundamental principles of interaction, energy flow, and nutrient cycling apply across all 
scales.

INTRODUCTION: THE CITY
A.
URBAN CONTEXT
1. Overview of Nigeria: Economic and 
Social Trends in the 20th Century 
During the colonial period (end of the 19th century –
1960), the Nigerian economy depended mainly on agri-
cultural exports and on proceeds from the mining indus-
try. Small-holder peasant farmers were responsible for
the production of cocoa, coffee, rubber and timber in the
Western Region, palm produce in the Eastern Region
and cotton, groundnut, hides and skins in the Northern
Region. The major minerals were tin and columbite from
the central plateau and from the Eastern Highlands. In
the decade after independence, Nigeria pursued a
deliberate policy of import-substitution industrialisation,
which led to the establishment of many light industries,
such as food processing, textiles and fabrication of
metal and plastic wares. These were financed by
revenue derived from exports of agricultural products.
During this period, the Gross National Product grew at
a rate of about 3.2 per cent per annum. 
In 1973, with the sudden increase in oil prices, the
government had a huge cash flow to invest in infrastruc-
ture development and to greatly improve social serv-
ices. The main thrust of development plans in the 1970s
was on education, transport, water supply and urban
infrastructure on the one hand, and on rapid industriali-
sation on the other hand. The latter required large
investments in vehicle assembly plants and oil refining
and petrochemicals. Thus, real wages increased in non-

Ibadan, Nigeria

the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) fell from 60 percent
in the 1960s to 31 percent by the early 1980s.
Agricultural production declined because of inexpen-
sive imports and heavy demand for construction labour
encouraged the migration of farm workers to towns and
cities. 
From being a major agricultural net exporter in the
1960s and largely self-sufficient in food, Nigeria
became a net importer of agricultural commodities.
When oil revenues fell in 1982, the economy was left
with an unsustainable import and capital-intensive
production structure; and the national budget was dras-
tically reduced by almost 100 per cent between 1980
and 1982. At the same time, the federal government
continued borrowing externally, accumulating a huge
foreign debt. A sizeable proportion of earnings (about
50 per cent in 1985) was spent on debt servicing The
price of oil fell dramatically in 1986 and the government
was forced to abolish import licences, to devalue the
naira and to eliminate the marketing boards. 
The Structural Adjustment Programmes (SAP) intro-
duced in 1986 advocated an overall cut in government
expenditure on social services, including health and
education. Devaluation and real inflation reduced real
incomes and increased the unemployment rate.

Nigeria is one of the few countries in
Africa which had many large pre-industrial
cities before the colonial period. The
largest concentration of such towns was in
the south-western zone, which is by far the
most urbanised area of its size in sub-
Saharan Africa (NISER 1997: 10). One of
the major factors which explain the devel-
opment of pre-colonial urbanisation in this
area was the continuous internecine war

find refuge in walled cities. Among the 36
towns in the area, six towns had popula-

the mid 19th century (Coquery-Vidrovitch,

General Introduction 
This course, Vegetation Studies, will introduce you to the study of 
vegetation both in the field and classroom. It begins by introducing you to 
the nature of vegetation and the plant community. Thereafter, it considers 
theoretical viewpoints on the nature of vegetation before discussing 
methods of sampling vegetation in the field giving some detailed treatment 
of measures of vegetation structure and floristic composition. An attempt 
was made to emphasize some geographic aspects of vegetation science, 
particularly, vegetation mapping and vegetation environment relationships. 
Vegetation is dynamic over time, vegetation succession, is also given a 
major emphasis, highlighting basic concepts of succession, the climax and 
community stability. 
 
Finally, the vegetation of Nigeria was considered with emphasis on 
regional disparities in vegetation types. This is with the view of not only 
familiarizing the student with the vegetation of his country but also to 
emphasize the fact that vegetation study, as with other sub-fields of 
geography, has a regional component.  
 

 
 
6

or

types,

characterization and an analysis of how they relate to one another in space 
and to the physical environment which exerts a marked control on the 
structure and composition of vegetation. We shall also examine theoretical 
ideas or concepts about the nature of vegetation and its development over 
space and time.

                 GEO 418: ECOLOGY OF NATURAL RESOURCES 
 INTRODUCTION 
A resource is the total means available for economic and political development, such as mineral 
wealth, labor force, and armaments. The total means available to a company for increasing 
production or profit, including plant, labor, and raw material; assets. A resource can also be seen 
as an economic or productive factor required to accomplish an activity, or as means to undertake 
an enterprise and achieve desired outcome. Three most basic resources are land, labor, and 
capital; other resources include energy, entrepreneurship, information, expertise, management, 
and time. 
 Natural resources occur naturally within environments that exist relatively undisturbed by 
mankind, in a natural form. A natural resource is often characterized by amounts of biodiversity 
and biodiversity existent in various ecosystems. Natural resources are derived from the 
environment. Many of them are essential for our survival while others are used for satisfying our 
wants. Natural resources may be further classified in different ways. Natural resources are 
materials and components (something that can be used) that can be found within the 
environment. Every man-made product is composed of natural resources (at its fundamental 
level). A natural resource may exist as a separate entity such as fresh water, and air, as well as a 
living organism such as a fish, or it may exist in an alternate form which must be processed to 
obtain the resource such as metal ores, oil, and most forms of energy. 
Natural resources are naturally occurring substances that are considered valuable in their 
relatively unmodified (natural) form. A natural resource’s value rests in the amount of the 
material available and the demand for it. The latter is determined by its usefulness to production. 
A commodity is generally considered a natural resource when the primary activities associated 
with it are extraction and purification, as opposed to creation. Thus, mining, petroleum 
extraction, fishing, hunting, and forestry are generally considered natural-resource industries, 

2 
 
while agriculture is not. The term was introduced to a broad audience by E.F. Schumacher in his 
1970s book Small is Beautiful.

There are various methods of categorizing natural resources, these include source of origin, stage 
of human use, and by their renewability, these classifications are described below. On the basis 
of origin, resources may be divided into: 
• 
Biotic – Biotic resources are obtained from the biosphere (living and organic material), 
such as forests, animals, birds, and fish and the materials that can be obtained from them. 
Fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum are also included in this category because they are 
formed from decayed organic matter. 
• 
Abiotic – Abiotic resources are those that come from non-living, non-organic material. 
Examples of Abiotic resources include land, fresh water, air and heavy metals including 
ores such as gold, iron, copper, silver,etc. 
Considering their stage of development, natural resources may be referred to in the following 
ways: 
Potential Resources – Potential resources are those that exist in a region and may be used in the 
future. For example, petroleum may exist in many parts of India, having sedimentary rocks but 
until the time it is actually drilled out and put into use, it remains a potential resource. 
• 
Actual Resources – Actual resources are those that have been surveyed, their quantity and 
quality determined and are being used in present times. The development of an actual 
resource, such as wood processing depends upon the technology available and the cost 
involved. 
•

A. 
Nature and scope of Transport Geography 
1. Transport geography is a sub-discipline of geography concerned about movements of 
freight, people and information. It seeks to link spatial constraints and attributes with the origin, 
the destination, the extent, the nature and the purpose of movements. Transport geography, as a 
discipline, emerged from economic geography in the second half of the twentieth century. 
Traditionally, transportation has been an important factor behind the economic representations 
of the geographic space, namely in terms of the location of economic activities and the 
monetary costs of distance. The growing mobility of passengers and freight justified the 
emergence of transport geography as a specialized field of investigation. In the 1960s, transport 
costs were recognized as key factors in location theories and transport geography began to rely 
increasingly on quantitative methods, particularly over network and spatial interactions analysis. 
However, from the 1970s globalization challenged the centrality of transportation in many 
geographical and regional development investigations. As a result, transportation became under-
represented in economic geography in the 1970s and 1980s, even if mobility of people and 
freight and low transport costs were considered as important factors behind the globalization of 
trade and production. Since the 1990s, transport geography has received renewed attention, 
especially because the issues of mobility, production and distribution are interrelated in a 
complex geographical setting. It is now recognized that transportation is a system that considers 

2 
 
the complex relationships between its core elements. These core elements are networks, nodes 
and demand. Transport geography must be systematic as one element of the transport system is 
linked with numerous others; transport systems are complex. 
 
An approach to transportation thus involves several fields where some are at the core 
of transport geography while others are more peripheral. However, three central concepts to 
transport systems can be identified: 
• 
Transportation nodes. Transportation primarily links locations, often characterized as 
nodes. They serve as access points to a distribution system or as transshipment / 
intermediary locations within a transport network. This function is mainly serviced by 
transport terminals where flows originate, end or are being transshipped from one mode 
to the other. Transport geography must consider its places of convergence and 
transshipment.  
• 
Transportation networks. Considers the spatial structure and organization of transport 
infrastructures and terminals. Transport geography must include in its investigation the 
infrastructures supporting and shaping movements.  
• 
Transportation demand. Considers the demand for transport services as well as the 
modes used to support movements. Once this demand is realized, it becomes an 
interaction which flows through a transport network. Transport geography must evaluate 
the factors affecting its derived demand function.  
 
The analysis of these concepts relies on methodologies often developed by other 
disciplines such as economics, mathematics, planning and demography. Each provides a 
different dimension to transport geography. For instance, the spatial structure of transportation 

3 
 
networks can be analyzed with graph theory, which was initially developed for mathematics. 
Further, many models developed for the analysis of movements, such as the gravity model, 
was borrowed from physical sciences. Multidisciplinarity is consequently an important 
attribute of transport geography, as in geography in general.

The study of Politics. What is Politics?
 
Definitions and Conceptions
 
What is Politics?
 
To understand the meaning of politics, it is imperative that we are aware
of it's etymology. Politics is derived from the greek word πολιτικά, which
translates directly to Politiká, which means affairs of the city.
Although politics is difficult to define, it is easy to recognize. To some
extent with the word ‘politics’ we can consider current usage and decide
our own meaning, making our own definition wide or narrow according to
our taste or purposes. From our discussion so far politics is obviously a
universal activity. The conflict of different interests, people or groups of
people who want different things be it power, money, liberty etc- face the
potential or reality of conflict when such things are in short supply.
As politics is a broad and multifaceted concept, we have three
approaches to its definition. They are the Stipulative, Concept-based and
Operationalized. But we'll focus only on the Stipulative approach, which,
according to the lecturer is also the semantic definition of politics
• Stipulative approach; This appeals to authorities that have defined
politics in the past;
Aristotle defined Politics in his Magnum Opus (His most accomplished
work) "Politics" as the essence of social essence, he viewed man as a

essence in relation with others. He believed that whenever two people are
interacting socially, they are invariably (always) involved in politics. The
criticism to this being that it is too inclusive, i.e, it is too broad, and tends to
view every person as a politician.
Karl Marx defined politics as the confrontation or struggle for power
