text_snippet:
Approaches to the Study of Politics
 
•
•
•
Introduction
We discussed the behavioural revolution and scientific quest in the
last module.
The main aim of this module is to help you identify and discuss
various approaches to the study of politics.
Four main approaches that dominate the study of politics before and
after the Second World War will be explained.
 

Four Main Approaches
•
i.
ii.
iii.
iv.
Since the emergence of Political Science as a separate discipline,
there are four major approaches identified to be useful in the study
of politics.  These are:
Normative-philosophical approach,
Descriptive-institutional approach,
Scientific-behavioural approach, and
Eclectic/post-behavioural approach.
 

Traditional Approaches
•
•
•
•
It cannot be emphasized too strongly that traditionalism is a collection of approaches
lumped together today mainly because of a common enemy, behaviouralism.
Perhaps the three most important approaches are the historical, legalistic and
institutional.
From the 19th century beginnings, U.S. political science was looked upon by many of
its practitioners as primarily an historical discipline.
“History is past politics and politics is present history”

Normative Philosophical Approach
 
•
•
•
•
•
Traditionally, the study of politics was dominated by philosophical reflections on universal
political values that were regarded as essential to the just state and the good state.
Among the questions that attracted the attention of such great traditional philosophers as
Plato, Aristotle Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau were:  What is justice? What
should be the proper role of the state?  What reciprocal obligation exists between the state
and its citizens?  What interpretation and importance should be attached to such political
values as justice, natural rights, freedom and obedience?
In short, they were preoccupied with “what ought to be” or normative questions.
Thus, the application of the philosophical approach in political science usually leads to a
focus on the great ideas, values and doctrine of politics.
The normative philosophical approach is the oldest and the least scientific approach to the
study of politics and it has been taken over although not completely displaced by newer or
more contemporary approaches.
 
 

Descriptive Institutional Approach
 
•
•
•
•
The strongest legacy that philosophy, history and law have bequeathed to the study of
politics is in the field of descriptive and institutional approaches.
This approach emerged to strengthen the weakness of normative philosophical approach.
The institutional approach to political inquiry focuses on the formal structures and
agencies of government.
It originally focused on the evolution and operation of legislatures, executives and
judiciaries. As the approach developed however, the list is extended to include political
parties, constitutions, bureaucracies, interest groups and other institutions which are
more or less permanently engaged in politics.
 

Descriptive Institutional Approach
•
•
In the descriptive institutional approach, the emphasis is on facts rather than
values. In other words, the approach seeks to provide factual and historical
answers to such questions as
What are the historical sources of parliamentary supremacy over the
monarchy?
What are the procedures followed when a bill becomes law?
By what electoral arrangement are rulers or representatives chosen?
What are the relative merits and demerits of rigid and flexible constitutions?
The approach has been criticised for the neglect of the informal aspects of
politics, norms, beliefs, values, attitudes, personality and the processes.
 

The Scientific Behavioural Approach
 
•
•
•
•
Beginning in the 1950s, strictly speaking, some Political Scientists started to concentrate their
attentions on actual human behaviour as opposed to thoughts and feelings.
They borrowed the natural scientists’ methods and accumulated statistics from elections, public opinion
surveys and so on.

Arenas of Politics I: Types of Political System
 •
•
i.
ii.
iii.
iv.
v.
vi.
vii.
It is possible to classify political systems or polities into three main groups namely: Liberal
democratic polity, socialist democratic polity, autocratic polity.
Liberal Democratic Polities
These polities share the following important features:
Political Participation: Participation in politics is widespread and open.
Limited Government Intervention: The political sphere is relatively small.
Civil Rule: Rule is by civilian, a large number of who are directly and periodically accountable
to the adult population at large or to a substantial proportion of it.
Respect for the Rule of Law: There is widespread agreement and respect for the procedure
for competition or rules of the political game.
Presence of Autonomous Pressure Groups: Pressure groups enjoy considerable autonomy
(independence) and are able to operate to influence governmental decisions.
Civil Liberties: Civil liberties such as freedom of speech, association and religious belief are
recognized and entrenched in the system
Institutional Autonomy: A system of check and balances exists in relation to operation of the
structure of government and there is also a formal attempt at the separation of powers.
 

Examples of Liberal Polities
•
•
Liberal democratic polities are found all over
the world but are particularly prominent in
North America and Western Europe.
The political systems of Britain, France, The
United States of America, and Germany and
so on are all examples of established liberal
democratic polities.
 

Social Democratic Polities
 
•
i.
ii.
iii.
iv.
v.
Social democratic polities are more popularly known as totalitarian polities.  They
include China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea, Former Soviet Union, and most countries
of Eastern Europe. The major features of socialist democratic polities include:
Adoption of Socialist Ideology:
Monopolization of Political Power: Political power is monopolized by a single
mass party, which is hierarchically organized and led by a dedicated group of
party functionaries.
Promotion of Social Rights: There is a great emphasis on social rights than civil
liberty.  Citizens in socialist democratic polities have the right to work, rest,
leisure and maintenance at old age or cases of sickness or disability.
Limited Governmental Authority: The scope of government authority is not
limited but it is total.
Lack of Institutional Autonomy: There is no equivalent of the liberal principle of
separation of powers under socialist democratic polities.

Autocratic Polities
 
•
•
•
•
This category of political system is very heterogeneous and it seems
to contain that political system that cannot be included in the liberal
democratic or socialist democratic category.
The varieties of the regimes that can be included in this category
include the traditional or historical oligarchies in many Arab countries,
the military oligarchies in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, the defunct
racial supremacist regime in South Africa and the defunct colonial
oligarchies in many part of the third world.
However, while autocratic polities differ in their level of
authoritarianism and modernization they share certain common
condition.
Most of those polities are also relatively backward economically or in
per capita income when compared with the socialist and liberal
democratic countries.  All of these polities are either colonized or
subjected to cheap diplomatic and economic penetration by the
western power.

The major characteristics of autocratic
polities include:
 
i.
ii.
iii.
iv.
v.
Absence of Coherent Ideology: There is an absence of a strongly
articulated and coherent ideology.
Weakly Institutionalized Political Authority:  In other words, political
institutions lack autonomy, complexity, adaptability and coherence.
Widespread Use of Violence:  Might is right and political repression is not
uncommon.  The political dominance prevalent in it is usually depends
on the use of force

POLITICAL CULTURE AND POLITICAL 
SOCIALIZATION
• Under Arena of Politics 1, we discussed political systems or polities 
and categorized them into three main groups namely, Liberal 
Democratic, Socialist Democratic and Autocratic Polities. 
• Although two political systems may look similar in most respect; 
culturally, a careful investigation will show that they are distinct. 
• In other words, one of those things that distinguish one political 
system from the other is political culture. 
• In this study session, you will be exposed first and foremost to the 
meaning, elements and types of political culture.
• After, the meaning, agents and analytical framework of political 
socialization will be discussed.

What is Political Culture?
• Political culture is part of the larger culture of a society. It is just one aspect of 
the total way of life of a given people. 
• It is a differentiated, part of generic culture, a sub-culture influenced by the 
general culture. 
• Each society imparts its norms and values (culture) to its people and the people 
in turn have distinct notions about how the political system is supposed to work 
and about what the government may do to them. 
• These values, beliefs, and symbols are the political culture of a particular 
society. 
• Political culture focuses attention, however, on that part of a culture which 
bears relevance to politics. 
• The political culture of a nation is usually affected by its history, economy, 
religion and social pattern. 

Definitions
Robert Dahl defined Political culture as a significant factor explaining different
patterns of political opposition.
Gabriel Almond and Sydney Verba, considered a political culture as Political
orientations, attitudes towards the political system and its various parts and the
attitudes towards the role of self in the system.
Lucian Pye defines a nation's political culture as "the set of attitudes, beliefs and
sentiments which give order and meaning to a political process and which provides the
underlying assumptions and rules that govern behaviour in the political system.”
Andrew Heywood sees political culture as “pattern of orientations to political objects
such as parties, government, the constitution expressed in beliefs, symbols and
values.”
It may also be defined as “the set of attitudes, beliefs and sentiments which give
order and meaning to a political process and which provides the underlining
assumptions and rules that govern the behaviour in the political system.

Almond and Powell’s three orientations of 
political culture
a.Cognitive Orientation towards the system, that is, the
recognition of the political objects and beliefs.
b.Affective Orientation:
That is the feeling of attachment,
involvement or rejection of political objects and symbols.
c.Evaluative
Orientation:
That
is
the application of
judgements and opinions of political objects and events.
• A nation's political culture, hence, involves the political style,
values, norms, emotions, beliefs and symbolic attachment
that are dominant among a population.

Robert Dahl’s salient elements of Political culture  
i. Orientations of problem-solving; whether they are
pragmatic or rationalistic.
ii.Orientation to collective action: whether they are
cooperative or non-cooperative.
iii.Orientation to the political system: whether they
are allegiant or alienated and
iv.Orientations to other people: whether they are
trustful or mistrustful.

Almond and Powell’s key elements of what 
constitutes a nation’s political culture
i. The degree of social trusts or mistrust which prevails in society.
ii. The general attitude of tolerance and inter-personal cooperation
permeating political relations among people.
iii.Attachment and loyalty of citizens to the national political system.
iv.People’s attitudes towards authority – degree of public recognition of
what constitute the legitimate authority.

text_snippet:
POLITICAL PARTICIPATION AND
REPRESENTATION
•
•
•
Meaning of Political Participation
Political participation could be defined as consisting of those level activities
by private citizens which are more or less directly aimed at influencing the
selection of government personnel and/or the action they take.
Simply put, it is involvement of private citizens in political activities.
Effective political socialization affects in positive terms the future political
participation.
 

What Political Participation entails?
1.
2.
3.
4.
5.
6.
It is concerned with influencing the composition and conduct, or personnel and policies, of government.
It is not limited to voting at elections but includes many other ways in which citizens try to influence government decisions.
Since political participation is often defined to include the activities of private citizens only, government and party
officials are described as objects not source of political participation.
Illegal and often violent forms of participation such as riots and assassinations are treated as abnormal as only legal
forms of participation are recognized.
Participation is often regarded as a desirable or positive process.  It has been seen as civic duty, as a sign of political
health, as the best method of ensuring that one’s private interests are not neglected and as requisite in a democracy.
Finally, political participation is a concrete activity of behaviour, and not simply a psychological orientation or disposition.
 

Forms and Levels of Political Participation
 
•
•
•
Political participation can take a wide variety of forms and can occur at various levels.
It entails costs in time, energy and resources. By implication, the amount of resources
that individuals are able and willing to sacrifice is likely to determine the form or
level of their participation.
Lester Malbraith in his book ‘Political Participation ’ published in1965 has made a very
useful classification of levels of political participation. He distinguishes between
political participation at the Spectator-level, the Transition level and the Gladiatorial
level.
 

Spectator-Level of Participation
 
•
•
These are the activities in which people involve themselves at the spectator level of participation:
(a) Voting at election;
(b) Initiating a public discussion;
(c) attempting to influence another into voting in a certain way; and
(d) wearing a political party badge or displaying party stickers.
Activities listed above entail relatively little costs in time, energy and resources and many people
participate at this level.
Apathetic are those who do not want to involve themselves in politics at all, and are almost totally
unconscious of the political world around them.

Transitional-Level of participation
 
•
•
•
Activities at the transitional level include:
(a) Attending a political meeting or rally,
(b) making some monetary contribution to a campaign or political course and
(c) contacting a public official or political leader.
Activities at this level require more costs in time and financial resources than those at
the spectator level. For example, only 7 and 9% of United States citizens participate at
this level.
Activities at this level are referred to as transitional because of the general tendency
for participants at the level either to descend to spectator level or ascend to
gladiatorial activities.
 

The Gladiatorial-Level of participation
 
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
With regard to gladiatorial level of participation, activities involved include the followings:
a.  Holding a public or party office;
b. being a candidate for office;
c. soliciting or appealing for party funds;
d. attending a caucus or strategy meeting; and
e. contributing time or other resources in a campaign.
At this level activities are not only the most expensive, but also the most effective form of political
participation.
Not surprisingly, only about 1 -3% of the population is usually able to participate in politics at the
gladiatorial level.

Arenas of Politics II: Civil Society, State, Governance, and
Global Politics
 
•
•
•
In our last lecture, we discussed participants in politics and the concept of
representation. Today, we will discuss the arenas where political actors operate
and participate in political activities. The first arena of politics is the Civil
society.
Civil Society is a phrase that is much bandied about in media and by politicians
but if you were to stop and ask a casual passer-by what is meant by “civil society”
it is unlikely many people could give an in-depth answer.
According to the World Bank: “Civil society ... refers to a wide array of
organizations: community groups, non-governmental organizations [NGOs],
labour unions, indigenous groups, charitable organizations, faith-based
organizations, professional associations, and foundations.”
 

Civil Society
•
•
The term became popular in political and economic discussions in the 1980s,
when it started to be identified with non-state movements that were defying
authoritarian regimes, especially in central and eastern Europe and Latin
America.
When mobilized, civil society - sometimes called the “third sector” (after
government and commerce) - has the power to influence the actions of
elected policy-makers and businesses. But the nature of civil society - what it
is and what it does - is evolving, in response to both technological
developments and more nuanced changes within societies.
 

The Significance of Civil Society
• According to Klaus Schwab,
“NGOs, labour leaders, faith-based organizations, religious
leaders and other civil society representatives play a critical
and diverse set of roles in societal development. In the last two
decades these roles have shifted as the external environment
for civil society has changed
.”
 

Civil society’s roles
•
•
•
•
•
•
holding institutions to account and promoting transparency;
raising awareness of societal issues;
delivering services to meet education, health, food and security needs;
implementing disaster management, preparedness and emergency
response;
bringing expert knowledge and experience to shape policy and strategy;
giving power to the marginalized; and
encouraging citizen engagement.
 

The State
•
•
•
•
•
•
The concept of state denotes political organization of society, or the body politics, or,
more narrowly, the institutions of government.
The state is a form of human association distinguished from other social groups
by its purpose, the establishment of order and security;
its methods, the laws and their enforcement;
its territory, the area of jurisdiction or geographic boundaries; and
finally by its sovereignty.

The state
•
•
The state consists, most broadly, of the agreement of the individuals on the
means whereby disputes are settled in the form of laws.
In such countries as the United States, Australia, Nigeria, Mexico,
and Brazil, the term state  (or a cognate) also refers to sub –national
political units that are not sovereign themselves but subject to the authority
of the larger state, or federal union.
 

The State and the Civil society
•
•
•
•
•
For liberals, the state is a necessary evil that serves civil society, and which is
accountable to citizens through political representation.
The state’s functions are primarily to maintain internal social order and to protect
civil society from external threats to its security.
The state is often portrayed by liberals as a neutral arbiter between conflicting
interests. It is not dominated by any section of society, but instead pursues policies
that maximize individual liberty.
Although some liberals allow for a more developed state role in such areas as
welfare provision, all liberals prioritize a clear separation between state and civil
society.
This is contrasted with totalitarian regimes, such as Nazi Germany or the USSR,
where the division between state and civil society is dissolved and the state,
representing a sectional interest, suppresses alternative sites of power.

Classification Of Systems/Forms of Modern Government
Many political thinkers and theorists have made numerous attempts to present the best model or typology for classifying systems or forms of government. 
The earliest and most famous classification of governments was the typology developed by Aristotle in the fourth century (Roskin etal.2008: 48). 
The classification was based on two criteria – how many people ruled a society (who rules) and whether they acted in the public interest or in their own interest? (in whose interest?).

--- SLIDE ---

Criteria for Classification
Major criteria for classification of government include:
Size of the ruling class and degree of public involvement
Patterns of power sharing and distribution
Institutional structure and relationship among the major organs of government 
State ideological thrust among others.

--- SLIDE ---

Size of the Ruling Class and Degree of Public Involvement
Aristotle in his book, The Politics, classified the forms of government into six using the size of the ruling authority and the extent to which the people are involved or their interest promoted. 
Who Governs       Legitimate Forms		Degenerate or Corrupt Forms
		   (Rule in the interest of All)	(Rule in the interest of selves or few)
   One		 	Monarchy				Tyranny
  A few		Aristocracy				Oligarchy
 Many			Polity					Democracy

--- SLIDE ---

MONARCHY VS TYRANNY
A monarchy is government of one person ruling in the interest of all. It is the rule by a king or queen. There are two forms of monarchical system of government, namely absolute monarchy and constitution or limited monarchy. Monarchy is practiced in Jordan, England, Morocco and most traditional African societies.  
Meanwhile monarchy can degenerate into tyranny, which is the corrupt form, under which the single ruler exercises power for the benefit of self. The governments under Idi Amin of Uganda, Sani Abacha of Nigeria, Mobutu Sese Seko of former Zaire, Mommar Ghadafi of Libya were dictatorial or tyrannical.

--- SLIDE ---

ARISTOCRACY VS OLIGARCHY
Aristocracy which originated from the Greek word ‘Aristos’ means government of the best. It is a good form of government according to Aristotle because it involves several persons ruling in the interest of all. In practice, it is a government of the rich who use their wealth for the common good of the people or community. 
However, this legitimate rule by an elite can decay into oligarchy, the corrupt form, in which several persons rule in the interest of themselves. It is a form of government in which a few powerful and privileged people rule for their selfish interests.

--- SLIDE ---

POLITY VS DEMOCRACY
Polity is another word for constitutional democracy. Aristotle saw this as the rule of many in the interests of all and the best form of government. All citizens have a voice in selecting leaders and framing the laws, but formal constitutional procedures protect rights. 
According to Aristotle, polity can degenerate into democracy, which he defined as the rule of many in the interests of themselves, the worst form of government. It is significant to point out at this juncture that democracy is in contemporary world the most desirable form of government. The status that democracy now assumed is different from what it originally was.

--- SLIDE ---

Akindele et.al Classification using the same criteria
Using the Aristotle’s criterion of classification, Akindele and others identify Monarchy, Aristocracy and Democracy as the ‘legitimate form of government’ and Tyranny, Oligarchy and Mobocracy as their degenerates or corrupt form of government respectively. 
Mobocracy is defined as rule or domination by a mob or ‘the mob that rules.

--- SLIDE ---

Patterns of Power Sharing and Distribution
In this sense, governments are classified on the basis of extent to which governmental powers are decentralized or centralized. 
Using the varying degree of centralization and decentralization, we have three forms of government

Study session 1: THE CONCEPT OF GOVERNMENT
Introduction
Government is central to the study of politics
The State is abstract but operates through government
Government gives practical meaning to state authority
No political system can function without government
Example: Nigeria as a state expresses authority through its government (President, National Assembly, Courts).

--- SLIDE ---

Common Understanding of Government
Many laymen see government as:
A small group of leaders
Those in power at a given time
This view is limited and misleading
For example, seeing government only as “the President and Ministers” ignores courts and legislatures.

--- SLIDE ---

Why the Concept of Government Matters
Government affects every member of society
Decisions on: Laws, Policies, Resource distribution
Aristotle: Man is a political animal
Self-Interest and Government
Humans pursue personal goals and interests
Government policies affect: Income, Security, Freedom
Citizens naturally care about governance
Example: Fuel subsidy removal affects transport workers, students, traders, and businesses.

--- SLIDE ---

Political Participation and Government Performance
Government performance depends on:
Political awareness
Citizen participation
Passive citizens weaken accountability
Active citizens strengthen democracy

--- SLIDE ---

Government Defined
Government is the organization that governs a political unit. It can be defined as a process, institution, persons, and discipline.
Found in all modern political systems
Five Usages of Government 
(1) Government as a process (2) Government as an institution (3) Government as people (4) Government as a system (5) Government as a field of study

--- SLIDE ---

Government as a Process & Government as an Institution
As a Process: Refers to the art of governing, Making and implementing policies and Exercising authority and control
Examples: Government policies, Laws, Development programmes
 As an institution: Refers to government as part of the state structure
Exists within a political territory
Examples: Nigerian Government, American Government, Chinese Government

--- SLIDE ---

Government as People & Government as a System or Method
Government as people:  Refers to those holding governing offices
Leaders change, but government continues
Examples: Obama’s government, Buhari’s government, Tinubu’s government
Government as a System or Method: The manner by which a society is governed. 
Examples: Presidential government, Parliamentary government, Military government, Colonial government

--- SLIDE ---

Government as a Discipline
Government as a subject of academic study
Examines institutions, processes, and outcomes of government. 
Examples: Department of Government, University of Essex and Department of Government & Public Administration, IMSU

--- SLIDE ---

Government as Activities
Authoritative decision-making, Binding rules and regulations, Conflict resolution and Allocation of resources
Government activities include:
Legislature – law making
Executive – law enforcement
Judiciary – law interpretation

--- SLIDE ---

Government as Persons
Office holders empowered by law:
President, Ministers
Legislators
Judges
Supported by civil/public service

--- SLIDE ---

Government as Institutions
Executive institutions
Legislative institutions
Judicial institutions
Created to maintain order and justice
Functions of the Three Arms
Legislature: Makes laws 
Executive: Enforces laws
Judiciary: Interprets laws and resolves disputes

--- SLIDE ---

Origin of Government
No specific theory of government origin
Explained through theories of the state
Government may exist without a state
State cannot function without government
Early Human Societies
Early societies were: Small, Simple, Non-hierarchical
No formal government needed initially

--- SLIDE ---

Emergence of Government
Society became complex due to: Population growth, Resource competition and Unequal power relations
Need for authority to regulate affairs
Government

POS103: DISCUSSION FORUM
TOPIC
 Life in a Society Where Government Is Not Well Organized

--- SLIDE ---

How will life be in a place where government is not well organized?

--- SLIDE ---

An Organized Government
An organized government is one in which 
authority is clearly structured 
roles and responsibilities are well-defined
decisions follow established procedures
laws are applied consistently and 
public services are delivered systematically.

--- SLIDE ---

Comparison
Well Organized Government
When government is well organized there will be:
clear chain of command
 law-based decisions
 functional institutions
 accountability mechanisms
political stability and
development.
Poorly Organized Government
When government is poorly organized, there will be:
no clear authority
overlapping responsibilities
Decisions made by force or favouritism
Services fail or are duplicated and 
Citizens lose trust

--- SLIDE ---

Consequences of poorly organized or outright dysfunctional government
Breakdown of Law and Order: When the state cannot protect lives and property, individuals become their own security providers.
Collapse of Public Service Delivery: This leads to widening inequality, as only the wealthy can afford private alternatives.
Economic Chaos and Widespread Poverty: Economic life becomes unstable and unpredictable.

--- SLIDE ---

Consequences of poorly organized……
Weak Justice System and Human Rights Abuse: Citizens losing faith in the rule of law and Justice becomes a privilege of the powerful rather than a right of all.
Political Instability and Loss of Legitimacy: The state gradually loses legitimacy in the eyes of the people.
Social Fragmentation and Moral Decay: The idea of a common national identity weakens.

--- SLIDE ---

Illustrative Scenarios and Questions
Scenario 1: A Day Without Effective Security
In a town where government security agencies barely function, residents avoid going out at night. Armed groups collect “security levies” from households. When a robbery occurs, victims do not report to the police because they know nothing will happen. Community members organize vigilante groups, sometimes leading to wrongful killings. 
Question: What risks does this pose to innocent citizens?

--- SLIDE ---

Scenario 2
Healthcare in Disarray: 
A pregnant woman arrives at a public hospital only to find no doctor on duty, no electricity, and no essential drugs. Nurses demand informal payments. She is forced to seek help from an unlicensed clinic, risking her life and that of her child. 
Question: Who suffers the most in such systems?

--- SLIDE ---

Scenario 3
Education Without Direction:
Schools open irregularly because teachers are unpaid. Curriculum guidelines are unclear, and examination bodies operate inconsistently. Parents who can afford it send their children abroad or to expensive private schools, while others withdraw their children entirely. 
Question: What are the long-term consequences of this for national development?

--- SLIDE ---

Scenario 4
Business in an Unregulated Economy: 
A small business owner faces multiple illegal taxes from different agencies claiming authority. There is no clear regulatory framework. After repeated harassment, the business closes, increasing unemployment in the community. 
Question: What happens to economic growth in such a society?

--- SLIDE ---

Scenario5:
Justice Delayed, Justice Denied: 
A land dispute drags on for years due to missing files, corrupt court officials, and contradictory rulings from different authorities. Frustrated, one party resorts to violence, triggering communal conflict. 
Question: Can peace exist without an effective legal system?

--- SLIDE ---

Study Session 3: Basic Components, Roles and Modes of Establishing Government
The Significance of Government
Government is man’s unending collective adventure
It exists to overcome human limitations in:
Wisdom, Strength, Morality, Material resources
Government matters because society cannot function without it
Government is Necessary Because:
Human desires expand faster than available resources
New challenges constantly emerge
Social order requires coordination and authority
Government provides structure, direction, and stability

--- SLIDE ---

Government as the decision-making and enforcing agency of the state
It converts individual or group desires into: Binding laws and Socially accepted behaviour
Government acts within a defined territory (the state).
Government decisions may relate to:
Moral issues (e.g., abortion, divorce)
Religious matters (e.g., state support for religion)
Economic concerns (e.g., monopoly control, unemployment)
Social welfare and security

--- SLIDE ---

Government operates through:
Politics & Administration
The Political Process Involves Origin of social will, Development of public opinion, and Mobilization of popular support and leads to accepted laws or conventions as well as requires public sacrifices (time, money, compliance)
The Administrative Process is the application of political decisions and the use of Personnel, Procedures and Institutions. It provides services and enforces duties.
Administration is subordinate to politics

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Components of Government
Government has three core components: Decision-making authority, Monopoly of legitimate force and Legitimacy
1. Government makes collective decisions on: Social goals, Economic strategies and Security and welfare. For example, policies to reduce crime, poverty, and corruption in Nigeria.
2. Government has monopoly over legitimate use of force. 
Force ensures compliance when persuasion fails and Enforcement applies to laws, court judgments and public order.
3. Citizens accept government authority as rightful. By implication, obedience is given voluntarily. It should be noted that government authority differs from other social institutions.

--- SLIDE ---

Roles of Government
Government exists to organize society, maintain order, and promote collective well-being.
Its roles arise where private individuals or markets alone cannot effectively solve problems.
According to Michael Laver, government roles arise from: Contract, Collective action and Social welfare needs.
Major Roles of Government
Contract enforcement
Solving collective action problems
Promoting social well-being and welfare

--- SLIDE ---

Contract Enforcement
Many social and economic interactions involve agreements (contracts).
In small or close communities, trust may replace formal enforcement.
In large, complex societies:
People often interact with strangers.
Temptation for dishonesty increases.
Government ensures contracts are honoured through laws, courts, and sanctions.

--- SLIDE ---

Contract enforcement
Contract enforcement matters because it encourages business transactions and investment. 
It reduces fraud, cheating, and exploitation and creates predictability and stability in economic relations.  
Without enforcement: 
Trust declines. 
Trade shrinks and 
economic development slows.

--- SLIDE ---

Collective Action Role of Government
Collective action problems arise when a project benefits everyone but individuals won’t contribute.
Key features: 
Private actions can produce public costs or benefits.
Individuals avoid personal cost even if society benefits.
Social costs rise while social benefits fall.
Government intervenes by: 
Coordinating efforts, Providing public goods  and Regulating harmful activities.

--- SLIDE ---

Social Welfare and Redistribution
Government promotes social well-being and equity.
Sometimes requires helping disadvantaged groups through redistribution.
Without government intervention:
Wealthy groups may resist redistribution.
Ine

A. How democratic elections are conducted B. The structure and functions of governmental institutions C. The political system of a society. D. The establishment of political system of a state.
2. A political philosopher argues that government is necessary because humans, left without authority, would exist in a condition of insecurity and fear, leading individuals to surrender their freedoms to a sovereign power. This view most closely reflects:
A. The Divine Right Theory B. The Force Theory C. The Social Contract Theory (Hobbesian view) D. The Evolutionary Theory
3. A government that combines democratic elections with strict control over political opposition is best classified as:
A. Liberal democracy B. Totalitarian government C. Authoritarian regime D. Confederal democracy

A. A sovereign institution with permanent existence B. An abstract legal entity C. A concrete set of institutions exercising authority D. A voluntary association

Organization of Government
From birth to death, there has been an existence of government.
Government is one of the key concepts of politics. A state is an abstract
entity. A state always has a government. The three main structures of
government are executive, legislature, and judiciary. At the end of the
course, you should be able to
1. Explain the meaning and usage of government as well as how
modern-day governments are structured and organized.
2. Highlight the basic components, functions, and roles of government.
3. Classify major types/forms of government and how it is structured
with examples of government.
4. Analyze the qualities of good leaders and governments.
5. Discuss the influence of other political organizations' (political
parties, civil societies, and pressure groups) operations.
 

Understanding the Concept of
Government
UNDERSTANDING THE CONCEPT OF GOVERNMENT
 
Key to understanding the concept of Government is grasping the 5
usages and identifiable meanings of Government. These are;
 
Government as the activities, art or process of governing; Exercising
a measure of control over others for example through policies, laws or
programmes.
Government as an institution of the state; E.g The Nigerian
government, the American government, e.t.c.
As a set of persons charged with the duty of governing; For example,
Biden, Tinubu, e.t.c
 
The manner, method or system with which a state is governed; E.g
Parliamentary system of government (a.k.a Cabinet system)
 
And finally, as an academic discipline.
 
These meanings and usages will be explained further in this lecture.

NIGERIAN CONSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENT
C-POS 105
Dr. D. Godwin

--- SLIDE ---

CONSTITUTION AND CONSTITUTIONALISM – A CONCEPTUAL CLARIFICATION
LECTURE 1

--- SLIDE ---

Learning Objectives
Define the term "Constitution" using various scholarly perspectives.
Explain the concept of "Constitutionalism."
Identify the primary sources of constitutional rules.
Discuss the essential functions of a constitution in a modern state.

--- SLIDE ---

The whole system of government of a country; the collection of rules which establish and regulate the government
What is a Constitution?

--- SLIDE ---

The supreme law of the land (the "Grundnorm"). Any law inconsistent with it is null and void.
What is a Constitution?

--- SLIDE ---

A "Social Contract" between the governed and the governors.
What is a Constitution?

--- SLIDE ---

Constitution performs these major functions: 

 It defines the power of government; 
it also defines the basic organs of government;
 it sets limits to the power of government.
What is a Constitution?

--- SLIDE ---

It protects democracy by separating state powers into three: the legislature, the executive and the judiciary
What is a Constitution?

--- SLIDE ---

In a Nutshell

--- SLIDE ---

Refers to governance according to the law; the idea that government power is limited, not absolute.
The Concept of 
Constitutionalism

--- SLIDE ---

The Rule of Law: No one is above the law, including the leaders.
Core Principles of 
Constitutionalism

--- SLIDE ---

Protection of Rights: Safeguarding fundamental human rights from state infringement.
Core Principles of 
Constitutionalism

--- SLIDE ---

Accountability: Ensuring those in power are answerable to the citizens.
Core Principles of 
Constitutionalism

--- SLIDE ---

Note

--- SLIDE ---

Establishes State Organs: Creates the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary.
Functions of Constitution

--- SLIDE ---

Allocates Power: Defines the specific duties and limits of each organ.
Functions of Constitution

--- SLIDE ---

Protects the Citizenry: Outlines the fundamental rights of individuals.
Functions of Constitution

--- SLIDE ---

Promotes Stability: Provides a predictable framework for resolving political conflicts and leadership succession.
Functions of Constitution

--- SLIDE ---

Sources of Constitutional Rules
Organic Laws
Specific statutes passed by the parliament.

--- SLIDE ---

Sources of Constitutional Rules
Judicial Precedents
"Judge-made laws" or court interpretations.

--- SLIDE ---

Sources of Constitutional Rules
Customs & Conventions
Unwritten traditions that become binding over time.

--- SLIDE ---

Sources of Constitutional Rules
Intellectual Works
Ideas from philosophers like Locke, Montesquieu, and Dicey.

--- SLIDE ---

Sources of Constitutional Rules
Past Experiences
Historical events and previous constitutions (e.g., Nigeria’s 1963, 1979 versions).

--- SLIDE ---

Summary
The Constitution is the "Lifeblood" of the state.

--- SLIDE ---

Summary
​Constitutionalism ensures that the Constitution is used for the common good through the Rule of Law.

--- SLIDE ---

Summary
Understanding these concepts is the first step in analyzing Nigeria’s specific constitutional journey.

--- SLIDE ---

Discussion Questions
Can a country have a constitution without practicing constitutionalism? Give examples.

--- SLIDE ---

Discussion Questions
Why is the "Rule of Law" considered the bedrock of constitutionalism?

--- SLIDE ---

Discussion Questions
Which source of the constitution do you think is most influential in Nigeria today?

--- SLIDE ---

Types, Forms, and Variants of Constitutions.

Nigerian Constitutional Development
Dr. D. Godwin
Department of Political Science

--- SLIDE ---

Types, Forms, and Variants of Constitutions
Dr. D. Godwin
Department of Political Science
Lecture Two

--- SLIDE ---

Learning Objectives
By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:

Distinguish between Written and Unwritten constitutions.
Understand the difference between Rigid and Flexible constitutions.
Identify variants of constitutions such as Federal, Unitary, and Confederal.
Classify constitutions based on their observance in practice (Normative, Nominal, and Semantic).

--- SLIDE ---

Forms of Constitutions

--- SLIDE ---

Forms of Constitutions
A single document codified at a specific time.
Example: Nigeria (1999 Constitution), USA.

--- SLIDE ---

Forms of Constitutions
​Not found in a single document; consists of customs, conventions, and judicial precedents.

Example: Great Britain, New Zealand.

--- SLIDE ---

No constitution is entirely written or entirely unwritten; both types rely on some level of convention or formal law.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Requires a special, difficult procedure for amendment.
​Often found in Federal systems to protect the interests of component units.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Can be amended easily through the same process as ordinary laws.
​Typically found in Unitary states.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
These constitutions vary by institutional  structure

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Shares power between a central government and component units (States/Regions). 
Example: Nigeria, Canada and India

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Concentrates all governmental powers in a single central authority.
Example: Britain, France and Gambia

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
A union of sovereign states where the central authority is subordinate to the component units.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
These constitutions are classified based on observance in practice.

The Karl Loewenstein Classification

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Effectively followed by both the rulers and the ruled; it is "live" and functional.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Exists formally but is not fully operational due to socio-economic or political realities.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Constitutions
Used merely to formalize and legitimize the existing power of a ruler or a group.

--- SLIDE ---

FEATURES OF A TYPICAL CONSTITUTION

--- SLIDE ---

An introductory statement of intent.

--- SLIDE ---

Establishing the Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary.

--- SLIDE ---

Outlining the liberties of the citizens

--- SLIDE ---

The procedure for changing the document.

--- SLIDE ---

The choice between Rigid/Flexible or Federal/Unitary often depends on a country’s history, size, and diversity.
Summary

--- SLIDE ---

Nigeria operates a Written, Rigid, and Federal constitution to manage its diverse ethnic and regional interests.
Summary

--- SLIDE ---

Why is a rigid constitution considered most suitable for a federal state like Nigeria?
Discussion Questions

--- SLIDE ---

Can a constitution be "Written" but still be "Flexible"?
Discussion Questions

--- SLIDE ---

Based on our current political climate, would you classify the 1999 Constitution as Normative or Nominal?
Discussion Questions

THEMES IN TRADITIONAL AFRICAN POLITICAL THOUGHT
	The history of the pre-colonial independence is rich with examples of political and economic sophistication. Although some of these political system degenerated into authoritarianism and economic stagnation, others embodied the full blossoming of democratic practices and economic expansion. The vast majority of political systems fell between these two extremes. A clear understanding of Africa’s multifaceted past is an essential building block in understanding the challenges confronted by African leaders as they lead their countries into the twenty-first century.
	Essentially, a rich mosaic of political systems existed during the pre-colonial independence era. One of the most difficult forms of African political organization for westerners to understand is what anthropologists refer to as a Segmented Political System. The term “segmented” refers to a decentralized system marked by the diffusion of political power. Segmented political systems lacked a centralized state and a recognized political authority capable of enforcing a preferred set of policies throughout a territory.
	There are five specific types of segmented political systems.
Band organization
Classical segmented system
Universalistic segmented system
Ritually stratified segmented system
Autonomous village system
1.	Band Organization: The most decentralized types of segmented political system in pre-colonial Africa was the band organization. Sharing the same language, customs, and cultural history, the population was divided into small hunter-gatherer groups that ranged in size from several dozen people during times of plenty, to ten to twelve individuals during periods of economic hardship. The hunter-gatherer groups were principally comprised of members of an extended family and did not have any form of centralized political authority. Even political authority at the level of the band was neither formally structured nor permanently emboded in one person. Decisions were the result of a face-to-face decision-making process in which all adults’ males took part. E.g. San people of Namibia & Bostwana.
2.	Classical Segmented System: This system differed from the band organization principally in terms of the size and scope of the distinctive groups which comprised the common nation. Individual groups based on kinship, often referred to as “clans” could number in the tens or hundreds of thousands and were capable of tracing their common lineage back thousands of years to a specific founding members. The size of the clan ensured that more formal terms of leadership, often a group of leaders or committee of elders, emerged to manage clan affairs, although no central authority ever evolved. Classical segmented systems typically fostered competition and conflict between extended clan families, especially in nomadic environments when drought and famine diminished already scarce water and food resources.
	The Somali ethnic group constituted an excellent example of the classical segmented system.
3.	Universalistic Segmented System: This constituted a slightly more centralized version of the classical segmented system. Despite the continued lack of any central authority, the members of various clan families were more closely unified by the existence of age sets. Age set status applied regardless of the clan into which one was born, and allowed for a more systematic organization of the social, economic, and political affairs of the nation as a whole.
	In an age set system based on five years blocks of time, for example, a new age-set was created every five years. Everyone born during that period would constitute a member of the group. These age-sets predetermined an individual’s assumption of various responsibilities within society, ranging from militarily defending the nation through the attainment of warrior status, or entering the ranks of senior political  leader or senior elder. FOREWORD
This publication provides an updated version of the 1999 Constitution of 
the Federal Republic of Nigeria with the first, second and third alterations 
of 2010, the fourth alteration of 2017 as well as the recent fifth alteration 
of 2023. It was inspired by the absence of a single document that 
incorporates all the alterations to the Constitution, considering that the 
country is replete with different versions, making it difficult to use. This 
Constitution document aims to provide a comprehensive Constitution 
that is accessible to lawyers, academics, researchers and the public. 
In compiling this document, PLAC has meticulously delved into the 
archives researching into the original works of National Assembly’s 
Constitution Alteration efforts since the 6th Assembly. PLAC has also dug 
up the original first print of the 1999 Constitution from the government 
printers and gazettes to achieve a comprehensive and up to date copy 
of the Nigerian Constitution. 
Since 2010, PLAC has worked closely with the National Assembly to 
provide technical support for the work of the legislature in Constitution 
review.
Given PLAC’s work and engagement with the National Assembly, 
State Houses of Assembly and the executive arm of government, on 
Constitution Review and other law reform issues, PLAC is very well 
placed to produce a reliable and updated Constitution of the Federal 
Republic of Nigeria.

CHAPTER ONE 
LAW IN SOCIAL CONTEXT 
Abiola Sanni 
 
1.0 INTRODUCTION 
 
1.0.1 Definition of Legal Method 
The phrase 'legal method' is made up of two words -'legal' and 'method.' The word "method," in 
ordinary parlance, means a way of doing something or the quality of being well planned and 
organized.1 The word "legal," which is an adjective, connotes something connected with the 
law.2Law operates in a society based on certain methods, that is, in accordance with certain 
processes, which must be properly understood for law to be put to best uses as an instrument of 
social control. Legal method can therefore be defined as an attempt to explain or analyse the 
technique of 'thinking like a lawyer.3In other words, it is learning to study the use and 
construction of legal rules, with a view to gaining insight into how law is planned and organized 
to achieve its objectives in a society.  
 
This task, like most tasks, is not as easy as it may seems. This is mainly because everyone 
approaches the subject of legal analysis from different perspectives based on their background 
and experiences. In that type of situation, the existence of multiplicity of approaches is 
inevitable. However, there are some areas of agreement or consensus in virtually all the legal 
analysis.  
According to a writer:  
"We cannot see the world as it is because we face it in a 'contaminated' vein. Namely our 
conceptual scheme (or a certain interpretation of it) and our biological constitution 
condition certain perspectives of the world and not others. When we face legal orders and 
legal method, we are placed in a kind of second world that is not possible without the 
first. Nevertheless, this normative world, let us say second world, has some special 
features, inter alia, the primacy of practical reason over theoretical reason ...”4 
This chapter examines the different perspectives and the areas of convergence of jurists and 
authors on the definition, evolution, functions and objectives of law in the society.  
                                                            
1 A.S. Hornby, Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary, Oxford University Press, United Kingdom., 6th ed., 2000, 
p.740.  
2Ibid, p.673 
3 A. Holland & J.S. Webb, Learning Legal Rules, Blackstone Press Ltd., London, 1991, p. xi.  
4 S. Urbina, Legal Method and the Rille of Law, Kluwer Law International, United States, 2002, p. ix.  
 

1.0.2 Nature and Importance of Legal Method  
When a fresh law undergraduate reads through a legal document, textbook, statute or case law, 
he or she may initially be perplexed by some legal terminologies, principles and rules of law that 
pervade the work. Holland and Webb captured the initial feelings of such a student in the preface 
to their book thus:  
"If you are new to studying law as an undergraduate or postgraduate student, the chances 
are that you are finding it (or will find it) a distinctly different experience from any 
previous education you have had, if not disconcerting one!" 5 
Such an experience should not discourage any student. The study of law may be fairly compared 
to the study of a foreign language. It proceeds in an orderly fashion, one step at a time. When 
studying a language, the student must first master the alphabets, then proceed to acquire a 
rudimentary vocabulary. Combining the vocabulary with the basic rules of grammar, the students 
learn to express thoughts in the foreign language. Similarly, in the law school setting, the student

CHAPTER TWELVE
CITIZENSHIP AND CIVIC RESPONSIBILITIES IN NIGERIA
Rasheed Oyewole OLANIYI
Introduction
The idea of citizenship and the duties that come with it are essential for the growth and survival
of any democratic society. In Nigeria, a country with a complicated mix of ethnic groups and a
history of changing politics after colonialism, the discussion about citizenship has taken on its
own historical, legal, and social-political forms. Citizenship means more than just being a legal
member of a nation-state; it also means being involved in the civic life of your society. Marshall
(1950) famously said that citizenship includes civil, political, and social rights. These rights must
be matched by duties that include, following the law, paying taxes, voting and others. He claims
that civil rights include freedoms like liberty and justice, political rights include the right to vote
and to be voted for, and social rights include the right to access welfare and social services that
are necessary for human dignity and full participation in society. Citizenship is also an important
idea in political theory and democratic government. It describes the legal, political, and social
ties between people and the state. It means more than just a legal position as it is a changing and
growing system that sets out the rights, duties, and identity of people in a political society.
In Nigeria, these rights and duties are often affected by concepts like history, religion, and
economic disparity. The Nigerian Constitution lays forth the rules for citizenship and the
responsibilities that come with it, such as following the law, paying taxes, voting in elections,
and being loyal to the state (Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999). However, as scholars like
Osaghae (1994) and Ekeh (1975) have postulated, the post-colonial Nigerian state is shaped by
what Ekeh called a "two publics" dichotomy. This means that citizens often see a difference

2
between their civic duties to the state and their duties to their ethnic or communal groups. This
dualism has major effects for national unity, democratic accountability, and civic engagement.
Nwankwo (1992) says that civic education is important for fostering democratic values since a
well-informed population is necessary for the growth of a responsible and involved society. Also,
as Suberu (2001) and Adejumobi (2002) have opined that, it is even harder to create a strong
feeling of national citizenship in Nigeria because of political corruption, election malpractice,
and ethnic marginalization. These problems with the system often make people, especially young
people, apathetic and disillusioned. They may feel like they are not part of the democratic
process. This chapter examines how the definition of citizenship has evolved over time in
Nigeria, the laws and social norms that define civic duties, and the social and political elements
that affect civic involvement. It looks closely at how people in Nigeria understand and carry out
their duties, and what this means for democracy and national progress.
The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria defines and regulates citizenship. It also mentions the different
ways that people might attain or use it. Citizenship by birth is the most prevalent type. It is based
on where you were born and your lineage, following a modified version of the jus sanguinis
principle. This means that people who were born in Nigeria to Nigerian parents or grandparents
are citizens by birth. You can also get citizenship by registering, especially if you are a foreign
woman married to a Nigerian man or a person of Nigerian origin who was born outside of
Nigeria and wants to be recognized. Naturalization is another way for foreigners to become
citizens of Nigeria. To attain this, they must have lived in Nigeria for a specified amount of time
and satisfied certain requirements. Kymlicka and Norman say that this process shows the liberal

Citizenship
POS114

--- SLIDE ---

Who is a citizen?
A citizen is a member of a political community who enjoys the rights and assumes the duties of membership.
Rights of citizens (1999 Constitution, S33-46)
Duties may include: obedience to law, payment of taxes, respect national symbols, defending the country, respect for people’s rights, upholding the constitution, respect for judicial decisions, etc.

--- SLIDE ---

What is citizenship?
Three dimensions of citizenship:
Citizenship as a Legal status, defined by civil, political and social rights. Here, the citizen is the legal person free to act according to the law and having the right to claim the law's protection.
Citizenship as a political agent. Participating in political process and institution.
Citizenship as membership of a political community that distinguish a member from non-members.

--- SLIDE ---

Model of citizenship: Republican and Liberal
Republican model is rooted in the writings of Aristotle, Machiavelli, and Rousseau and can be found in Athenian democracy, Republican Rome, Italian city-states, etc.
Based on the idea of civic self rule. Aristotle ideas of citizen as one capable of ruling and being ruled in turn.
To Aristotle, citizens are “those who share in the holding of office”.
To Rousseau, citizens are those who come together to make law through general will. Contributing to the formulating the law through general will makes citizens free and law legitimate.
Citizenship involves active participation in deliberation and decision making. This separate citizens from subjects. Citizen is a political agent.

--- SLIDE ---

Liberal model: traced to Roman empire. Extension of citizenships to conquered people due to the expansion of the empire.
Citizenship entails enjoying the protection of the law and not partaking in law formulation or execution. Citizenship becomes a legal status (occasional identity).
This type of citizenship is inclusive and infinitely extensible.
Rooted in Liberal tradition from the 17th century. Citizens as legal status. And involves political liberty that protects people’s liberty from others and the authority excesses. But limited to private associations not public/political domain.

--- SLIDE ---

Distinctions: Republican (R) and Liberal (L) models
R = political office; L= legal status.
R= political agent; L= consumed by private matters, little time for active participation. 
L = Instead, entrust the role of law making to representatives. Most popular model in most modern democracies.

The ideal of republican citizen may be impracticable in modern day. 
People’s political impact is nil or minimal. They will rather focus on other activities: economic, social or familial. Politics is not central but one of many things he does.

--- SLIDE ---

The two models are not really opposite but complementary.
Political liberty is required for individual liberty.
Security provided by the state must be secured, even from the state itself.
Passive enjoyment of citizen right must protected by active citizenship.
Active citizenship is required regularly.

also I believe,—“That government is best which governs not at 
all;” and when men are prepared for it, that will be the kind of 
government which they will have. Government is at best but an 
expedient; but most governments are usually, and all governments 
are sometimes, inexpedient. The objections which have been 
brought against a standing army, and they are many and weighty, 
and deserve to prevail, may also at last be brought against a 
standing government. The standing army is only an arm of the 
standing government. The government itself, which is only the 
mode which the people have chosen to execute their will, is 
equally liable to be abused and perverted before the people can act 
through it. Witness the present Mexican war, the work of 
comparatively a few individuals using the standing government as 
their tool; for, in the outset, the people would not have consented 
to this measure.  
This American government,—what is it but a tradition, 
though a recent one, endeavoring to transmit itself unimpaired to 
posterity, but each instant losing some of its integrity? It has not 
the vitality and force of a single living man; for a single man can 
bend it to his will. It is a sort of wooden gun to the people 
themselves; and, if ever they should use it in earnest as a real one 
against each other, it will surely split. But it is not the less 
necessary for this; for the people must have some complicated 
machinery or other, and hear its din, to satisfy that idea of 

CIVIL  DISOBEDIENCE 
4
government which they have. Governments show thus how 
successfully men can be imposed on, even impose on themselves, 
for their own advantage. It is excellent, we must all allow; yet this 
government never of itself furthered any enterprise, but by the 
alacrity with which it got out of its way. It does not keep the 
country free. It does not settle the West. It does not educate. The 
character inherent in the American people has done all that has 
been accomplished; and it would have done somewhat more, if the 
government had not sometimes got in its way. For government is 
an expedient by which men would fain succeed in letting one 
another alone; and, as has been said, when it is most expedient, the 
governed are most let alone by it. Trade and commerce, if they 
were not made of India rubber, would never manage to bounce 
over the obstacles which legislators are continually putting in their 
way; and, if one were to judge these men wholly by the effects of 
their actions, and not partly by their intentions, they would deserve 
to be classed and punished with those mischievous persons who 
put obstructions on the railroads.  
But, to speak practically and as a citizen, unlike those who 
call themselves no-government men, I ask for, not at once no 
government, but at once a better government. Let every man make 
known what kind of government would command his respect, and 
that will be one step toward obtaining it.

Perspectives on the Origin of the StateByE. Remi Aiyede

--- SLIDE ---

Where Did Politics Come From?
Many have asked this same question. Aristotle himself (the first student of government) had many thoughts about this.
Of all of the ideas four stand out
Evolutionary Theory (Naturalistic)
Force Theory
Divine Right Theory
Social Contract theory

--- SLIDE ---

Theories of Government
Evolution Theory-
Parental rule transforms into tribal rule where the strongest naturally become leaders.
Force Theory-
Base on conquest and subjugation. Weaker groups are forced to submit to stronger ones.
Divine Rights Theory-
God selects the rulers usually absolute monarchy. 
Faith in an interpersonal God is required
We give up our right to ourselves exact retribution for crimes in return for impartial justice backed by overwhelming force. We retain the right to life and liberty, and gain the right to just, impartial protection of our property .
Social Contract-

--- SLIDE ---

Evolutionary theory
State is a result of natural evolution. It is an end product of many factors—biological, economic, cultural, military (force), kinship, religion, political consciousness.

State evolved out of human needs– Aristotle says man is a political animal and his potential can only be realized within a state. Man outside a state is not a man but a beast or a god.

This theory maintains that the state evolved over time starting with the primitive family.

One person in the family was determined to be the leader of the family. Over decades, the family became a clan and a clan became a tribe. The state was then identified when the tribe settled in a designated area and claimed it as their own. Native African extended families are an example of primitive families that formed as tribes and selected a chief or a king to be the leader of this family.
Some scholars believe the state evolved out of the family
From there an extended family could have included hundreds of people.
Then the village
The city-state or Polis
- Aristotle, Aquinas

--- SLIDE ---

Force theory
Claims
Most will not admit it, but it seems that it’s human nature to fight and control others not like us or for resources we don’t have.
It’s through this that some scholars believe that the state was born of force, as the powerful conquered the weak state is the outcome of the process of aggressive exploitation of the weaker by the stronger. 
the state originated due to force exerted by the strong over the weak. The idea contained in the statement is that 'war begat the king'. 
When all the people of a area were brought under control of one person or group, the state was born. –Hume, Oppenheim, Jenks-Bernhardy and Trietschke
Examples: Mongol Empire, Roman Empire, USA, Post colonial African states
Criticism
Force indeed has played an important part in the origin and development of the state. Some of the greatest empires of today have been established through blood and iron.
The theory of force unduly emphasis the principle of the survival of the fittest. It is dangerous to employ such a principle in the internal existence of the state. This theory justifies despotism. It is opposed to the idea of freedom. The spiritual and moral values have absolutely no place in life.

--- SLIDE ---

Divine right theory
Claims
Founded on three claims:
state is established by God’s ordinance
Ruler are divinely ordained
Rulers are only accountable to God
In many of the earliest civilizations the people believed that their rulers were chosen by God or the Gods (e.g., Early Hebrew)
In fact, creation of modern Israel garner support on the basis on fulfilling a (divine) prophesy (e.g., the second coming of Christ).
Depending on the civilization the ruler may be descended from the gods or a god himself or herself (In Yoruba land, Kings are refer to igbakeji osha)
the state is established by God(s), who rule(s) the state directly or indirectly through someone regarded as an agent.

Political Obligation and Lockean Contract Theory
16
Abstract
In John Locke’s Second Treatise of Government, he presents his notion of social contract theory: 
individuals come together, leave the state of perfect freedom, and consent to give up certain rights to 
the State so the State can protect its members. He grounds duties and obligations to the government 
on the basis of consent. Because one consents to the State, either tacitly or expressly, one has 
consented to taking on political obligations owed to the State. Locke also notes that individuals can 
withdraw consent and leave the State. This paper challenges the view that political obligation can 
exist under Locke’s social contract theory. This paper first provides background for the argument 
by explaining Locke’s position. Then, it examines what consent actually is, ultimately coming to 
the conclusion that tacit and hypothetical consent are not true forms of consent and cannot justify 
political obligation, leaving only express consent. Finally, using Isaiah Berlin’s notions of coercion 
and positive and negative freedoms, this paper looks at whether the current political system allows 
one to exit the State, leading to the conclusion that if individuals are coerced into consenting to the 
State, that consent cannot justify political obligation.
Introduction
For social contract theorists, political obligations stem from a group of people consenting, 
at least initially, to give up certain rights to the government. This requires that individuals are 
free from coercion in order to actually consent. Locke specifically allows for individuals to either 
expressly or tacitly consent to government in order to ground that political obligation. Throughout 
this paper, I will argue that consent is a faulty basis for political obligation under Locke’s social 
contract theory. First, I will argue that tacit consent cannot be a solid grounding for political 
obligations. Then I will argue that express consent can no longer justify political obligation because 
there is not a legitimate right to exit in the current geopolitical climate. Individuals cannot consent 
to government because there is not an ability to not consent. In other words, there is no choice other 
than to consent to a government, which is a form of coercion. Ultimately, I come to the conclusion 
that there can no longer be legitimate political obligation under Locke’s notion of social contract.
Locke’s Position
In Locke’s Second Treatise of Government, he puts forth his own version of the social 
contract theory. Within his position, he believes that people begin in a state of nature which is a 
state of perfect freedom and equality. In the state of nature, every person is free to do anything

The Concept of the State: Definition, Features, and Functions
The concept of the state is a fundamental and crucial aspect of political science and governance. It refers to a centralized political organization that exercises authority over a defined territory and its inhabitants. The state is a complex and multifaceted institution that plays a pivotal role in establishing and maintaining order, providing services, and representing the collective interests of its citizens. This essay will explore the definition, features, and functions of the state, while also distinguishing it from the concept of a nation.
At its core, the state can be defined as a political entity characterized by its territorial boundaries, sovereignty, and the presence of a governing authority. Territorial boundaries are essential as they demarcate the physical extent over which the state holds jurisdiction. Sovereignty refers to the supreme power and authority that the state possesses within its territory, allowing it to make and enforce laws, maintain order, and conduct relations with other states. The governing authority represents the institutional framework responsible for managing the affairs of the state and implementing its policies.
Several key features distinguish the state from other forms of political organization. First, the state possesses a monopoly over the legitimate use of force within its territory. This means that it has the exclusive right to enforce laws and maintain internal order through its police and military forces. Second, the state possesses a legal and administrative apparatus that governs and regulates various aspects of public and private life, such as law enforcement, taxation, public services, and justice systems. Third, the state has the power to negotiate and enter into international relations, representing its citizens' interests in the global arena.
The state performs a variety of functions that are vital for the well-being and stability of a society. These functions can be broadly categorized into three main areas: providing order and security, fostering economic development, and promoting social welfare. Firstly, the state ensures order and security by maintaining law and order, protecting citizens from external threats, and resolving conflicts. This includes maintaining a robust legal system, upholding property rights, and defending national sovereignty. Secondly, the state plays a crucial role in fostering economic development by formulating and implementing policies that stimulate growth, regulate markets, and provide essential infrastructure. It can promote trade, investment, and innovation to create a conducive environment for economic activities. Finally, the state assumes responsibility for social welfare, which involves providing public goods and services such as healthcare, education, social security, and infrastructure that benefit the entire population.
While the terms "nation" and "state" are often used interchangeably, they represent distinct concepts. A nation refers to a group of people who share a common identity, including a common language, culture, history, and often a sense of belonging and shared aspirations. It is primarily based on subjective factors that bind people together. On the other hand, the state is a political entity characterized by its institutional framework, authority, and territorial boundaries. While a state can be composed of multiple nations, such as in the case of multinational states, there are also numerous examples of nations existing without their own state, known as stateless nations.

What is the Universal Declaration on Human Rights?
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Universal Declaration) is an international document that states basic rights and fundamental freedoms to which all human beings are entitled.
When was the Universal Declaration created?
The Universal Declaration was adopted by the General Assembly of the United Nations on 10 December 1948. Motivated by the experiences of the preceding world wars, the Universal Declaration was the first time that countries agreed on a comprehensive statement of inalienable human rights.
Australia played an important role in the development of the Universal Declaration.
What does the Universal Declaration say?
The Universal Declaration begins by recognising that ‘the inherent dignity of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world’.
It declares that human rights are universal – to be enjoyed by all people, no matter who they are or where they live.
The Universal Declaration includes civil and political rights, like the right to life, liberty, free speech and privacy. It also includes economic, social and cultural rights, like the right to social security, health and education.
Is the Universal Declaration legally binding?
The Universal Declaration is not a treaty, so it does not directly create legal obligations for countries.
However, it is an expression of the fundamental values which are shared by all members of the international community. And it has had a profound influence on the development of international human rights law. Some argue that because countries have consistently invoked the Declaration for more than sixty years, it has become binding as a part of customary international law.
Further, the Universal Declaration has given rise to a range of other international agreements which are legally binding on the countries that ratify them. These include
the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and
the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR).
Other binding agreements which expand on the rights contained in the Universal Declaration include: 
the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination 1965
the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women 1979
the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment 1984
the Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989
the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2006
The international bill of rights 
After the end of World War II a series of conventions and declarations began to articulate universal human rights. 
A convention (sometimes called a covenant) is a binding treaty, coming into force upon ratification by a certain number of States. Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provides that: ‘Every treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed by them in good faith’.
A declaration is not legally binding but carries moral weight because it is adopted by the international community.
The United Nations was established, partly to continue the work of the dissolved League of Nations, in response to proposals for the creation of a new world body to monitor relations between States. 
The United Nations is an international organisation representing the body of States, established according to the United Nations Charter in 1945.  One of the purposes of the United Nations is to promote and encourage respect for human rights through international co-operation.  
There are currently one hundred and ninety two member States. Each has one vote in the United Nation’s parliament, the General Assembly [http://www.un.org/ga/].
What is known as the International Bill of Human Rights is made up of:
Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) 
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966)
