Introduction 
 
This course introduces students to the fundamental approaches and issues in 
Nigeria's political and constitutional development from 1945. It begins by providing 
the historical context for the emergence of Nigeria as a single political entity, 
examining how its diverse peoples and geographical features have shaped its 
evolution. Key themes explored include federalism and the separation of powers; 
public finance, with particular attention to the recurring challenge of revenue 
allocation; the emergence and role of the military in governance; civil war; civil 
society and the struggle for democracy; elections and the party system; and the 
persistent challenge of leadership for national development. 
 
Objectives 
 
Learning Outcomes 
On completion of this course, the student should be able to:  
1. describe the historical background to the emergence of the modern Nigerian 
state under colonial rule  
2. examine the various theoretical approaches to the study of government and 
politics in Nigeria. 
3. Analyse nationalism and the struggle for independence from the second world 
war culminating in the First Republic. 
4. Analyse the politics of the First Republic and salient issues that led to its collapse 
5. Explain the role of the military in governance and its venture into power (including 
the descent into civil war) 
6. Examine the struggle for democracy and the role of civil society. 
7. Explain the challenges of federalism and the management of diversity in 
Nigeria. 
8. Examine the institutions and reform of governance in the Fourth Republic. 
Delivery Strategies 
 
POS 412 requires active student participation in the lecture sessions to ensure a 
meaningful learning experience. This will be aided when students make it a point 
of duty to read relevant texts before each session.  Additional requirements for the 
course will include an appraisal paper and a final examination. 

 
2 
 
This course will integrate lectures, class discussions, class debates, role play, 
student symposia, assigned readings, oral and written presentation of 
assignments, library research/reviews, teamwork and small group presentations, 
and other activities. All the activities will aid you in attaining the major learning 
objectives of this course. This combination will allow each person to draw on his 
or her own experiences and talents to help themselves and others in the course to 
become competent in the course concepts and skills. 
 
You are expected to come to class prepared to participate in scheduled activities. 
You will be encouraged to share experiences, knowledge, talents, and skills which 
are related to the course.  
 
Course Assignments and Grading 
 
The final grade will be determined by the number of points you accumulate during 
the semester. You can accumulate points by participating in class activities, and 
by completing oral and written assignments in a timely fashion. Preparation for 
class attendance is an essential component of participation, since you must be 
prepared to contribute to the class. Participation also consists of reading the 
assigned material before class, contributing relevant comments to class 
discussions, participating in the team case study analysis and presentation,

POS 211: Political Analysis
Upon Completion of this course, you are expected to:    
define what politics entails and explain what counts as political action. 
Have knowledge of major conceptual and analytical debates in Politics.
develop skill of recognizing and asking relevant political questions and be able to think critically, analyse texts and structure essays in the field of Politics
apply the knowledge and skill acquired in analyzing political issues, actions, events, behavior and processes.

--- SLIDE ---

What is Politics?
Although politics is difficult to define, it is easy to recognize. 
To some extent with the word ‘politics’ we can consider current usage and decide our own meaning, making our own definition wide or narrow according to our taste or purposes.
 Politics is obviously a universal activity and it is exciting because people disagree. They disagree about:
 How they should live. 
Who should get what? 
How should power and other resources be distributed? 
How should collective decisions be made? 
How much influence should each person have? and so on.

--- SLIDE ---

Attempts to define Politics
For Aristotle, this made politics the ‘master science’, that is, nothing less than the activity through which human beings attempt to improve their lives and create good society. 
Politics is, above all, a social activity. 
It is always a dialogue never a monologue.
The conflict of different interests, people or groups of people who want different things be it power, money, liberty etc- face the potential or reality of conflict when such things are in short supply. 
Politics begins when interests clash.

--- SLIDE ---

Politics at Micro and Macro levels
At the micro level we use a variety of techniques to get our own way: persuasion, rational argument, irrational strategies, threats, entreaties, bribes, manipulation anything we think will work. 
At the macro level, democratic states establish complex procedures for the management of such conflicts codified in the form of written constitutions (except in Britain).

--- SLIDE ---

Political Order
However, the political order is essentially peaceful. 
But if violence is involved on a widespread scale e.g. war between sovereign states; it would be fair to say that politics has been abandoned for other means. 
I must point out to you here that, political order within a state is ensured through the implicit threat of force which a state’s control of the police and army provides. 
So while political activity is peaceful for most of the time in most countries, the threat of violence or its reality are both integral parts of the political process

--- SLIDE ---

Definition of Politics
There are several definitions of politics because political scientists do not agree on a common definition. 
1. Politics involves the struggle among actors pursuing conflicting desires on public issues. (Vernon van Dyke).
2. Politics is the authoritative allocation of values (David Easton).
3. Politics is about determination of who gets what when and how (Harrold Lasswell)
4. Politics is the essence of social existence because where two or more men interact; they invariably involved themselves in politics. (Aristotle)

--- SLIDE ---

Limitations
The first definition points to the nature of political activities, as they take place in the “public realm”, i.e. that part of society in which issues affect virtually all members. But the definition does not tell us the outcome of the struggle among political actors. 
This is where the second definition is useful. It tells us that politics is directed at decision-making. The definition fails to tell us who are the authorities, what are the allocated values?. It is too abstract.
The third definition emphasizes the notion of power, which is one of the central concepts of politics. Let me inform you that power related issues occur everywhere in the family, associations, state and inter – state levels. This definition is too broad.

Meaning and Classification of Political Systems
Political System: A political system refers to the set of formal legal institutions that constitute a “government” or a state. 
More broadly defined, the political system is seen as a set of “processes of interaction” or as a subsystem of the social system interacting with other nonpolitical subsystems, such as the economic system. 
The most important type of political system in the modern world is the nation-state. The world today is divided territorially into more than 190 countries, in each of which a national government claims to exercise sovereignty—or the power of final authority—and seeks to compel obedience to its will by its citizens.
However, if a political system is defined as any stable pattern of interrelations which involves power and authority, meaning that a political system is not narrowed down to countries alone, we certainly have millions of political systems in the world.

--- SLIDE ---

Typologies/Classification of Political Systems
A typology is a proposed way of classifying the subject matter in which we are interested. 
It is an analytical construct which seeks to present a simplified view of actual situations. 
For example, we can classify political systems based on the criteria of how many actually rule, the types of authority prevalent, as well as the degree of popular participation.

--- SLIDE ---

Advantages of Classification Scheme/Typology
It helps to simplify our data and organize it because of the outburst of data in political science. 
Classification scheme by sorting any given universe into comparable cases provide a framework for meaningful comparative analysis to begin.
By preparing ground for meaningful comparison, it makes a general problem of prediction and explanation more manageable.
    It helps a lot in developing theory.
The basic logic that guides classification is either / or that is an item or case must be either here or there.

--- SLIDE ---

Criteria for Classification/Typology
Carl Hempel’s logical requirement of classification is useful here. Any classification scheme or typology according to him must meet these necessary criteria.
Mutual or Joint Exhaustiveness: Classification scheme must exhaust all classification properties of that phenomenon under consideration. 
Mutual or Joint Exclusiveness: The categories must be mutually exclusive.  In other words they must be independent and must exclude elements in other categories. An element of a category must not belong to two or more categories (it is either / or).
Relevance: The criteria used for classification must be relevant to the particular subject under examination. In other words, its categories (or types) should be appropriate for the purpose of the research in which they are used. 
Uniformity: The criteria used must be uniformed. These criteria must be consistently used. 
Parsimony: Categories must be economical or parsimonious. In other words, a three categories classification scheme is preferred to a six categories classification scheme.

--- SLIDE ---

Examples of Typologies of Political System
The formulation of typologies of political systems is almost as old as political science itself, as political scientists have always been interested in classification of political system.
 Aristotle’s Six fold Classificatory scheme or Typology
Number of citizens entitled to rule 	Rulers rule in the interest of 
 
One        ALL			THEMSELVES

One    Monarch (Kingship)		Tyranny
Few   Aristocracy 		               Oligarchy
Many  Polity 			Democracy

Modes of Political Analysis
The Orientations of Political Analysis 
In every situation in which you find yourself, you invariably ask certain basic questions. 
What is the state of things? 
How has it come to be the way it is? Is it good or could it be better? 
How can you act to arrive at the desirable state of things (for yourself, your wife, your children, your professional association, your country and so on?). 
Underlying all of these questions is another one which most of us often take for granted: What do you mean by the key terms you use?

--- SLIDE ---

Political analysis can accordingly be categorized into 
semantic analysis (by which you seek clarification of subject); 
normative analysis (by which you seek to assess or “judge” policies and situations based on certain norms); 
empirical analysis (by which you seek to discover causes and establish relationships among the elements you are considering); and 
policy analysis (by which you look for that solution among possible solutions).

--- SLIDE ---

SEMANTIC ANALYSIS
In semantic analysis or what is called conceptual analysis, we try to clarify the meaning of the key terms or concepts that we use. There are two ways of going about semantic analysis.
Nominal definition: a term or concept can be defined by appealing to an authority whose definition is widely accepted, or by relying on definitions offered in standard English or “technical” dictionaries such as Oxford English dictionary, Britannica, Wikipedia etc. 
Operationalization of concepts: in the case of very nebulous concepts like democracy, freedom, or equality which are often coloured by ideological considerations, we can devise certain “objective” indices according to which they can be defined, and insist that they mean exactly what we want them to mean. 
Operationalized concepts are referred to as variables that are measurable and quantifiable.

--- SLIDE ---

NORMATIVE ANALYSIS
Normative analysis involves questions of what ought to be, rather than what is. 
What ought to be is determined by the values we have, whether these are divine, natural laws, or are purely subjective.

--- SLIDE ---

EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
The point is that in empirical analysis, the concern is with what is. 
When you ask the question, what causes destitution; you are asking an empirical question based on what is
In essence, empirical analysis and conclusions reflect the implications of (the) empirical evidence rather than (the analyst’s) personal values, preferences, or presuppositions.”

--- SLIDE ---

POLICY ANALYSIS
Policy analysis involves the search for policies or courses of action which will take us from the present state to that which we desire. 
In other words, policies are solutions which we think will bring desired and satisfactory results. 
Certainly, in any unsatisfactory situation, there would be more than one possible solution.

--- SLIDE ---

How the Modes are related
Although each orientation of analysis emphasizes a particular focus, the four modes of analysis are not mutually exclusive i.e. none is independent of the others. 
Normative analysis requires prior empirical knowledge: to know what ought to be, we require to know what is.
Policy analysis makes use of both empirical and normative analysis because, in a sense, it attempts to bridge the gap between what is and what ought to be. 
Furthermore, normative assumptions provide us the criteria for evaluating polices. 
Underlying all analysis is, of course semantic analysis, without which few analyses can be made.

POS 211 LECTURE NOTES 2016/17 
TOPIC 1: The Essence or Significance of Politics 
Politics and Man  
Many times, you discuss politics without consciously setting out to do so. As a father or mother, 
farmer, teacher, passenger in a commuter bus, indeed, in most roles you play, you are constantly 
drawn into talking politics. 
In each of these instances, what you are doing is discussing politics, expressing that part of 
you which makes you an integral part of society. This is so because you are a political 
animal, as Aristotle, one of the founding fathers of political science, wrote a long time ago. 
The implications of this are two. First, that politics is the essence of social existence because 
our interactions with others in the society invariably involve politics. Except one prefers to 
live in isolation which only very few men would do, no one can avoid politics. Second, that 
every man is a “politician”. This could appear strange. You probably believe that politicians 
are those who belong to political parties, contest elections and canvass for vote, in short, 
those who are directly involved in politics. True indeed, these are the “conspicuous”

The major work of political scientists is political analysis. Political 
analysis entails systematically studying political problems, issues, 
decisions, policies or situations by organizing the available information 
into elements or categories and then relating these to one another. The aim 
of analysis is to explain and predict political occurrences – why things 
happen the way they do, why people behave the way the do, and under 
what conditions such events and enables us to understand the political 
world in which we live. It is very important because if we do not 
understand our political lives, we cannot hope to solve our problems.

I will introduce you to the elements of political analysis. I have three main 
objectives in doing so. First, I want you to become familiar with some of 
the basic concepts we use in political science. Second, I want you to 
develop the skill of recognizing and asking relevant political questions. 
Finally, I want you to learn how to apply the knowledge and skill you will 
acquire in analyzing political issues, events, behaviour and processes. In 
summary, I expect that at the end of this course, you will become an 
“expert” Political Analyst in your own right because, political analysis is 
best done by experts.

political analysis, types of political systems, participants in politics, and

SCIENTIFIC METHODS AND THE STUDY OF POLITICS
An Outline of Scientific Method 
I shall begin by presenting in broad outline, the basic procedure of the scientific method. A simple outline involves:
Making explicit (in a clearer form), in advance, your assumptions and expectations about what you are studying; 
Making explicit, in advance, the rules and/or guidelines by which you will proceed in your study. You do not change the rules of a football game at half-time. 
Making careful observations of the phenomena in which you are interested, with a view to discovering the elements of the study and the regularities (consistent patterns of behaviour of occurrence) which may exist. 
Seeking, through one or more explicit frames of reference (theories, perspective) to map out the relationships among the things you have observed; 
Seeking to explain the relationships you identify. 
Making verifiable (testable) predictions based on your explanations and 
Reporting fully and clearly, your conclusions in such a way that another Scientist could, if he wished, repeat the study by making similar observations. 
Conceptualization of Major Terms
Generalizations: These are statements which describe general conditions or properties of the things we are interested in. They are usually stated in law like terms which are testable. An example of a generalization is; most women are not interested in politics. Notice that I have used most, rather than all because generalizations are not laws which give no exceptions.  
Laws: Are statements of universal uniformities used as explanations of specific phenomena, which, because of their explanatory character can be viewed as predictive statements. Law talks of absolute properties with no exceptions. The unpredictable nature of human behaviour makes it difficult, if not impossible, to develop laws in the social sciences. It is difficult, for example, to say that “All human being love power,” because we would certainly find those, no matter how few, who would not love it. 
Theories: Are those explanations of uniformities that involve two or more generalizations but which, even though widely held, require empirical validation for confirmation. A theory is different from a law in that a theory offers at one and the same time less certainty and greater explanatory power; it explains in effect why laws work, but it is not as useful as a law in predicting particular events. 
Hypothesis: Tentative explanations, suppositions, or assertions that are formulated to be tested and, when extensively tested and confirmed by collected data, either themselves take on the character of laws or theories or else modify existing laws. There are two major hypotheses in scientific analysis, namely Null Hypothesis denotes by H0 and Alternative Hypothesis denotes by H1. 
Values: The importance individuals or groups attach to phenomena and ideals in terms of their views of the world. The scientific method aims at eliminating such values from analysis. 
What the Scientific Method Entails
The scientific method has two major aims, namely to explain and to predict on the basis of regularities which have been observed and found to be reliable. I shall elaborate briefly on these goals of science. 
Explanations: Let me illustrate this point with this example. If you were asked to explain why the All-Progressive Congress (APC) won the presidential election in Nigeria in 2015. You would probably say it won because of its attractive manifestos, the personality of its candidate, the quest for ‘change’ by Nigerian citizens and the charisma of its national leaders. This is an explanation. In scientific terms, we say that explanation entails specifying the conditions under which a particular event occurs. Survey Sampling Methods- Probabilistic & Non-Probabilistic
What is Sampling Method? 
Generally speaking, it is the process of selecting a group of people or products or items, or events to be used as a representative or random sample from a population. 
Sampling method refers to the way that observations are selected from a population to be in the sample for a sample survey.
The main reason for conducting a sample survey is to estimate the value of some attribute of a population

--- SLIDE ---

Population Parameter Vs Sample Statistics
A population parameter is the true value of a population attribute, while a Sample statistic is an estimate based on sample data, of a population parameter. Consider this example. 
A public opinion pollster wants to know the percentage of students in UI that are against legislation for same sex marriage. The actual percentage of all the students is a population parameter. The estimate of that percentage, based on sample data, is a sample statistic. 
The quality of a sample statistic (i.e., precision, meticulousness, representativeness) is strongly affected by the way that sample observations are chosen; that is, by the sampling method.

--- SLIDE ---

Importance of Drawing a Sample
1. It is economical because it is cheaper to work with a sample when the population is large. 
2. It saves time and energy.
3. Where a population is partly inaccessible, drawing a sample will be more appropriate.
4. Where members of the population can easily be destroyed while studying them, samples are more appropriate.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Sampling Techniques
The method of selecting a sample is called sampling procedure or sampling technique. 
As a group, sampling methods fall into one of two categories.
Probability samples. With probability sampling methods, each population element has a known (non-zero) chance of being chosen for the sample. In other words they have equal chance of being selected.
Non-probability samples. With non-probability sampling methods, we do not know the probability that each population element will be chosen, and/or we cannot be sure that each population element has a non-zero chance of being chosen. It favors the bias or interest of the researcher.

--- SLIDE ---

Non- probability
You should take note that Non-probability sampling methods offer two potential advantages - convenience and cost. 
The main disadvantage is that non-probability sampling methods do not allow you to estimate the extent to which sample statistics are likely to differ from population parameters. 
Only probability sampling methods permit that kind of analysis.

--- SLIDE ---

Probability Sampling Methods
The major types of probability sampling methods are 
simple random sampling, 
stratified sampling, 
cluster sampling, 
multistage sampling, and 
systematic random sampling. 
The main advantage of probability sampling methods is that they guarantee that the sample chosen is representative of the population. This ensures that the statistical conclusions will be valid.

--- SLIDE ---

Simple random sampling
This is the best sampling technique because it ensures that every member of the population has the same chance of being included in the sample. Simple random sampling refers to any sampling method that consists of - The population of N objects and the sample of n objects. If all possible samples of n objects are equally likely to occur, the sampling method is called simple random sampling.
There are many ways to obtain a simple random sample. One way would be the lottery or balloting method.
Random sampling helps produce representative samples by eliminating voluntary response bias and guarding against under-coverage bias. 
All probability sampling methods rely on random sampling.

--- SLIDE ---

Stratified sampling
With stratified sampling, the population is divided into groups, based on some characteristic.

SYSTEM AND STRUCTURAL FUNCTIONAL APPROACHES TO THE STUDY OF POLITICS
What is an approach?
An approach is a perspective or framework within which our phenomenon is analyzed. 
Within the context of political analysis, an approach can be defined as “a set of concepts, categories or terms that serves to focus attention on particular aspect of politics”.

--- SLIDE ---

The System Approach
The system approach is one of the most popular ways of organizing political study. 
It enables us to selectively identify and organize what is political when we look at the whole society. 
It also enables us to identify the interrelationships among political phenomena

--- SLIDE ---

What is a System
A system is an abstract construct to represent what goes on in the real world for purpose of analysis. It is a pattern of stable relationships among the parts which make it up. 
There are many kinds of systems, like the heating system in a house, the human physiological system and, of course, the political system. 
What makes any system a system is that it meets the five major characteristics of systems:

--- SLIDE ---

Characteristics of a System
A system is made up of parts. The human physiological system for example, is made up of the brain, liver, kidney, heart, lungs, etc. 
Each of these parts performs important functions which sustain the system and ensures its survival. 
The parts interact, i.e. that have patterned relationships. 
The parts are interdependent, meaning that what happens in one part directly or indirectly affects the other parts. 
A system has boundaries which can either be concrete or physical, as in the boundaries of a political system (which is not synonymous with the nation-state or country).

--- SLIDE ---

David Easton Input –Output Model of System Approach

--- SLIDE ---

According to this simple model, the major parts of the political system are the boundary, the total environment, the inputs, the structures of the political system concerned with the authoritative allocation of values, out-puts, and the feedback loop. 
All of these parts are inter-related and are in-interdependent, as the directions of the arrows in the figure above indicates.

--- SLIDE ---

Explanation on how it works
The total environment refers to the totality of the society in which we live and how its nature determines what we want, what we do, and so on.
From the total environment, come the inputs which consist of demands, supports and apathy. 
The inputs are transmitted to the decision-making centers where they are processed and converted into authoritative allocation of values as outputs. 
These outputs can be classified according to the functions of the three major organs of government, namely, rule-making by the legislature, rule-application by the executive, and rule-adjudication by the judiciary. 
The feedback loop represents the process by which the political system informs itself about the consequences of its outputs.

--- SLIDE ---

System approach
In summary, the approach has three major features.
 First, it is concerned with how order is maintained, because it suggests that the maintenance of the system depends on its ability to maintain order. 
Second, it recognizes that change is inevitable as it is interested in how political systems are able to meet the challenges posed by change. 
Third, it draws attention to the importance of goal-realization as a central aspect of the political system because it assumes that no political system can survive for long without articulating and pursuing identifiable goals.

--- SLIDE ---

Advantages or Merits
(i) It provides a framework for comparing political systems. 
(ii) It provides a standardized set of concepts such as inputs and outputs to describe activities which take place in all political systems. As such, they can be compared. 
(iii) The approach takes cognizance of the inevitability of change and addresses itself to how the system can adapt itself and survive when faced with changes.

The Debate Continues
The debate over whether a science of politics is possible or desirable is not likely to be completely resolved. 
The traditionalists, i.e. those political scientists who argue that it is not possible to be scientific and emphasize normative theories certainly have their points, as do the empiricists or behaviouralists who seek to be scientific. 
At the present stage, the agreement seems to be that political phenomena can be studied while those which cannot be subjected to scientific analysis be studied philosophically using normative theories.

--- SLIDE ---

A scientific analysis of political issues or scholarly work
A scientific analysis of political issues or scholarly work “should be reasoned, balanced, supported by evidence, and a bit theoretical.”
Reasoned analytical work requires you to spell out your reasoning, and it should make sense.
Another way by which you can minimize bias is by acknowledging that there are other ways of looking at your topic or issue at stake. This is what is called a balanced analysis. 
Also, your analysis must be supported with evidence. It is a major requirement for all scholarly or scientific analysis to be supported with quantifiable or qualitative evidence or both. 
Lastly, a thoughtful analysis is always connected, at least a little, to a theoretical point of view.

--- SLIDE ---

Political Analysis and the Relevance of Multi-Disciplinary Approach
The Social Science and the Multidisciplinary Approach
Political science, sociology, economics and human geography are called the Social Sciences, because they all are interested in the study of man as a social being; as a member of society. 
there are considerable overlaps in what we study because, certainly, man’s political and social relations would have implications for his economic behaviour. 
Studies are expected to be collaborative and complementary.
It is when such other relevant data are considered, that we talk of the interdisciplinary or multidisciplinary approach in the Social Sciences. As the name suggests, multidisciplinary analysis is analysis that uses data or method(s) from more than one discipline.

--- SLIDE ---

Political Science and other disciplines
At times, it is hard to tell where history, human geography, economics, sociology, anthropology, and psychology leave off and political science begins. Political science relates to other cognate disciplines particularly in the social sciences.
History: History is one of the chief sources of data for political scientists. But historians and political scientists look for different things and handle data differently. 
Human Geography: This aspect of Geography, though neglected by political scientists influences politics more than many realize.

--- SLIDE ---

Economics: Many political quarrels are economic: who get what? Sufficient economic development may be the basis for democracy: few poor countries are democratic. 
Sociology: Parts of sociology and political science merge. For instance, Seymour Martin Lipset demonstrates that there is close connection between democracy and level of wealth. 
Anthropology: The descriptive and interviewing techniques of anthropology have been heavily adopted by political scientists. The subfield of political culture could be viewed as a branch of anthropology. In Africa, voting and violence follow tribal lines.
Psychology: Psychology, particularly social psychology, contributes much to political science’s understanding of which personalities are attracted to politics, why and under what circumstances people obey authority figures, how people form national, group, and voting attachments.

--- SLIDE ---

The Basis of Multidisciplinary Political Analysis
For a long time, political scientists were concerned with the moral ends of the state as well as the formal structures (constitutions) of government.

The Nature of Political Analysis
Political analysis is the major task undertaken by Political Scientists. 
In simple terms, it involves study undertaken by an expert (Political Scientist) that requires studying a problem, decisions, issue or situation by organizing the information (data) that one has into categories or elements and then relating these to one another for the purpose of explaining. 
In short, political analysis is a detailed and critical examination of political phenomena with the aim of understanding them better. 
Thus, political analysis has three main goals.

--- SLIDE ---

Main Goals of Political Analysis
To know what is important in politics, i.e. those things that influence or determine the outcome of events. 
For instance, there are different factors that influence or determine voting behavior of an individual or group of individuals such as issues, class, ethnicity, party affiliation, ideology etc. 
If party affiliation seems to have a stronger influence on voting behavior, party affiliation is considered as important in your analysis.

--- SLIDE ---

Goals of Political Analysis
To know what is valuable, i.e. the difference every political outcome will make to our desires, both individually and collectively. 
The choice of party affiliation in the above example implies that special attention should be given to party affiliation when considering why voters behave they behaved. 
The preference for party affiliation shows your interest in using the factor to explain voting behavior and advance your argument.

--- SLIDE ---

Goals of Political Analysis
To know what is real or true by systematically subjecting our guesses, impressions, popular beliefs, even rumors, to verificatory tests. 
The hypothesis (an initial theory a researcher starts with, to be proved by evidence) that party affiliation determines voting behavior can be tested in another area or country for confirmation or rejection.

--- SLIDE ---

In Summary
Political analysis aims at political knowledge that is relevant to our values, that can be confirmed by empirical tests and experience, and that will enable us explain assess and predict outcomes. 
If therefore, you ask the question, why analyze politics, the answer is simple “Political analysis helps one to understand the world one lives in, to make more intelligent choices among the alternatives one faces, and to influence the changes inherent in all political systems.”

--- SLIDE ---

The Quest to be Scientific
As political analysts, we endeavour to be ‘objective in our analysis, so that our lives or dislikes, biases, values, or personalities’ do not distort our analysis. 
We also want to ensure that our studies provide explanations and generalizations which can be tested or verified by other analysts. 
By so doing, we seek to be “scientific”, i.e. to be systematic in our studies. 
This is the sense in which we are Political Scientists, i.e. we seek to use the scientific method.

--- SLIDE ---

You may have always thought that “science’ is exclusively used in relation to the natural sciences like Chemistry, Biology and Physics. 
This is not the case because science - from the Latin word ‘scire’- simply means ‘to know”, consequently, any study which advances knowledge is scientific. 
Today, most people think of science as precise and factual, supported by experiments and data. But this is not all. 
Science could be a matter of method, i.e. how to study, or of substance, i.e. what is studied, or both.

--- SLIDE ---

The natural sciences are scientific in both senses. Political Science like the other social sciences (Sociology, Economics, Psychology, Human Geography) is scientific only in the sense of its methods because it seeks to apply the systematic tools of study of man in society. 
Some political analysts have attempted to become like natural scientists; they quantify data and manipulate them statistically to validate hypotheses.

Neo-Realism/Structural Realism 
 
Introduction 
 
Realism is not a monolithic concept. As appropriately argued by Jeffrey W. Legro and 
Andrew Moravcsik, “realism is not a single theory but a family of theories—a paradigm”. 
Therefore, the belief that there is not one realism, but many, leads logically to a 
delineation of the different types of realism. Kenneth N. Waltz’s neo-realism also called 
as structural realism is considered to be the important category of realism. Neo-realism 
is an extension of classical realism in a redefined manner. It seeks to reformulate some 
of the basic postulates of classical realism. The neo-realist school began with the 
writings of Kenneth Waltz. In 1979, Waltz wrote one of the classics of international 
relations theory; ‘Theory of International Politics’. Waltz tried to provide a scientific 
basis to the realist thinking. In the cold war environment Waltz highlighted the value of 
understanding the systemic constraints upon the behaviour of the actors of 
international politics. Waltz explained that the bipolar system prevailing during the cold 
war meant stability in the system and hence relative peace. Today neo-realism is the 
most dominant theory of international politics. Most of the other new theoretical 
schools of international relations begin as a response to the argument of neo realist 
school. 
 
Neo-Realism/Structural Realism: The Emergence  
 
Hans J. Morgenthau (1904–1980) is credited with developing realism into a coherent 
theory of international politics in the post world war II period. But with the rise of 
Realism, there also came a barrage of criticisms from different directions. By the 
beginning of 1960s, the influence of scientific thinking in international relations was 
palpable. There were scholars who were engaged in making the study of international 
relations more scientific. These scholars severely criticized the classical realism as 
“wisdom literature”, without any scientific foundations. Under these conditions, the 
defense of realism came from Kenneth Waltz. Waltz reformulated the ideas of realism in 
the light of major criticisms. This led to the beginning of the new stream of realist 
thinking, known as neo-realism. 
 
Structural Realism: Kenneth Waltz  
 
Neo-realism has focused upon the absence of principal international authority which 
guides the behavior of states in an international setting. According to Waltz, it is anarchy 
which constraints states’ behaviour. This makes structure of the international system 

anarchical. The anarchical structure compels states to act in certain ways. That is why 
this theory is also known as structural realism. 
“Structural realism aims to set aside those features of international relations that 
depend on the character of the actors or the nature of their interactions in order to 
highlight the constraining impact of the structure of the international system”. So, the 
international power politics in rooted not in human nature but in the structure of the 
international system.  
Some of the important assumptions of structural realism are:  
(i) States are the rational actors in the international system. They always want to 
maximize benefits and minimize losses; 
(ii) The anarchic structure of the international system is the foremost important 
determinant of state’s behavior; 
(iii) In the anarchic international system, there is no central authority to impose the 
rules of the game.  
(iv) Under these circumstances, states are unaware about others intentions (security 
dilemma);  
(v) Survival is the most critical concern as a result of the anarchic structure of the 
international system.  
(vi) Power is not measured by the outcome; rather it is the combined capabilities of a 
state.  
(vii) The most important question for stability and peace in international system is 
balancing power in the system.

INTRODUCTION
Realism in the study of international politics and international relations places emphasis on the competitive and conflictual side of international relations or the interaction between state and non-state actors of the world, and since the World War II, It has been considered the most dominant school of thought, and it remains an ever-present in twenty-first century politics, and this theory posits five basic outlines:-
1. International politics are anarchic; 
2. Sovereign states are principal actors in international politics; 
3. States are rational unitary actors acting under their own national interests; 
4. The state’s primary goals are its own national security and survival; 
5. National power and capabilities are a key litmus test for relationships between states. 
This in summary means nation-states (or ‘states’) are the main characters in the unfolding tale of international relations. Other characters exist—individual people and businesses, in particular—but they have limited power. In times of war, states will speak and act as one with their own national interests in mind. 
The Realist theory, though drawing knowledge from the works of philosophers like Thucydides in his work titled “History of the Peloponnesian War, ” or the works of others like Niccolò Machiavelli, Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and Max Weber, it did not gain traction until the twentieth century with the effort of a  political scientist like Edward Hallet Cart who argued against the the deluded “idealism” of liberal internationalists and, in particular, their belief in the possibility of progress through the construction of international institutions such as the League of Nations.
CONCEPT OF OFFENSIVE REALISM
John Joseph Mearsheimer (born December 14, 1947, New York, USA), is a prominent American scholar of International Relations best known for his theory of "Offensive Realism".
Like most international relations scholars of his generation, Mearsheimer was deeply influenced by Kenneth Waltz, the founder of the school of international relations known as "Neorealism". In Waltz’s model, the absence of an authority above states (the condition of anarchy) forces them to make alliances in order to contain the threats posed by rival powers. The international order, in other words, is determined by the balance of power between states. According to Waltz, the need for security leads states to favour the status quo and to adopt a defensive position toward their competitors. Mearsheimer’s contrasting view which he called “offensive realism,” holds that the need for security, and ultimately for survival, makes states aggressive power maximizers. States do not cooperate except during temporary alliances, but constantly seek to diminish their competitors’ power and to enhance their own.
Indeed, in offensive realism, the international system provides great powers with strong incentives to resort to offensive action in order to increase their security and assure their survival. The international system characterised by anarchy (the absence of a central authority capable of enforcing rules and punishing aggressors) and uncertainty as to state intentions and available offensive military capabilities leads states to constantly fear each other and resort to self-help mechanisms to provide for their survival. In order to alleviate this fear of aggression each holds of the other, states always seek to maximise their own relative power, defined in terms of material capabilities. POS 205: Realist Theory of International Relations
Meaning and features of Realist Theory
Realism stands as one of the most influential and enduring theories in the study of international relations. It posits that the international system is essentially anarchic, lacking a central authority, and that states are the primary actors within it. Driven by a fundamental concern for their own survival and security, these states are seen as rational actors that prioritize their national interests and often engage in power politics to navigate this competitive landscape. Key concepts such as self-help, the balance of power, and the security dilemma are central to understanding the realist perspective, which views conflict as an inherent feature of international relations.
Realism is a theory of international relations that emphasizes the role of power and self-interest in shaping state behaviour. It suggests that states act primarily to advance their own interests, often in competition with one another, rather than for moral or ideological reasons. Realists believe that the international system is anarchic, meaning there is no overarching authority to enforce rules, leading states to prioritize their security and survival above all else. Key thinkers in realism include Thucydides, Niccolo Machiavelli, Thomas Hobbes, Hans Morgenthau, Edward Hallett Carr, John Mearsheimer, and Kenneth Waltz. 
Definition
Hans Morgenthau: “Political realism believes that politics, like society in general, is governed by objective laws that have their roots in human nature.”
Kenneth Waltz: “Realism is a theory of international politics that asserts that states, motivated by self-interest, compete with each other in an anarchic international system characterized by the absence of a central authority capable of enforcing binding rules.”
John Mearsheimer: “Realism is a view of international politics that stresses the competitive and conflictual side of international relations. It is pessimistic about the prospects for eliminating war and other forms of conflict among states.”
These definitions highlight the core tenets of realism, including the emphasis on state-centric behavior, self-interest, power dynamics, and the anarchic nature of the international system.
Key features of realism
1.Anarchy and State-Centric Focus : Realism emphasizes that the international system lacks a centralized authority (anarchy). States are the primary actors, and their actions drive global politics.
Realists believe the international system is anarchic not in the sense of chaos, but in the absence of a central authority to enforce rules, resolve disputes, or protect states. Here are some examples:
State Sovereignty: States possess supreme authority within their borders. There is no world government to tell them what to do. For example, a state's decision to go to war is ultimately its own, even if the UN Security Council advises against it.
Self-Help System: In the absence of a global enforcer, states must rely on their own capabilities to ensure their survival. If a state feels threatened, it must increase its military strength or form alliances because there is no world police to protect it.
Security Dilemma: When one state increases its power for defensive purposes, it can make other states feel less secure, leading them to increase their own power. This creates a spiral of insecurity. For example, the US and the Soviet Union during the Cold War both built up massive arsenals, each claiming it was for defense, but this buildup made the other side feel more threatened.
Lack of Enforceable Global Laws: International laws and treaties exist, but there is no guarantee that they will be enforced. For example, many states have signed treaties on human rights, but violations still occur because there is no world court with the power to force states to comply.

2. Theories of International Relations I: Realism and Liberalism
1. Overview of Theories in International Relations
In International Relations (IR), theories help us explain and predict the behaviour of states and other actors. The two most foundational theories – Realism and Liberalism – offer contrasting perspectives on human nature, power, and the potential for cooperation. We will examine these theories to understand how they interpret global politics and state interactions.
2. Realism: Key Concepts and Principles
Definition:
Realism is a school of thought that views international politics as a struggle for power in an anarchic system. It assumes that states act primarily in their own self-interest to ensure security and survival.
Historical Background:
Realism has roots in ancient texts, such as Thucydides’ History of the Peloponnesian War, and was further developed in modern times by theorists like Thomas Hobbes, Hans Morgenthau, and Kenneth Waltz.
Core Assumptions of Realism:
Human Nature is Self-Interested:
Realism assumes a pessimistic view of human nature, where individuals are inherently driven by self-interest, and this is mirrored in state behavior.
States are viewed as self-serving actors seeking power to secure their interests.
Anarchy in the International System:
The international system lacks a central authority (anarchy), meaning there is no global government to enforce laws or maintain order.
In this self-help system, states must rely on their resources and alliances to survive.
Primacy of Power and Security:
Power is the most important currency in international relations, often associated with military strength, economic capability, and political influence.
Realists argue that states pursue power both to ensure security and to counterbalance threats from other states.
State-Centric Approach:
States are the main actors in international politics, and non-state actors (like international organizations) have limited influence.
State sovereignty is central, with each state prioritizing its own national interest.
Balance of Power:
Realists believe that when power is balanced among states, the likelihood of conflict is reduced because no single state can dominate others.
Alliances and counterbalances are often seen as natural responses to prevent any one state from becoming too powerful.
Variants of Realism:
Classical Realism: Emphasizes the role of human nature as a driver of power politics. Hans Morgenthau, a key figure, argued that politics is governed by objective laws rooted in human nature.
Neorealism (Structural Realism): Developed by Kenneth Waltz, neorealism shifts the focus from human nature to the structure of the international system itself. Waltz argued that the anarchic system compels states to act in ways that maximize their security.
Key Concepts in Realism:
Security Dilemma: The notion that as one state seeks to increase its security (e.g., by building up its military), other states perceive it as a threat, leading to an arms race.
Relative Gains: Realists argue that states focus on gains relative to other states rather than absolute gains. States prefer outcomes where they are better off than their rivals.
•  Example of Relative Gains in Action:
If two rival states (e.g., the U.S. and China) enter a trade agreement, both might experience economic benefits. However, if one state gains more technological or economic leverage from the trade, the other might see this as a security threat.
In military alliances, states may worry about their partners gaining more military strength, as this could alter the alliance’s dynamics and shift the balance of power within it.
• Contrast with Absolute Gains:
Absolute gains refer to benefits that all parties derive, without regard to how gains are distributed. 
Critiques of Realism:
Realism’s emphasis on conflict and competition underestimates the potential for cooperation and peaceful coexistence.

Department of Political Science
POS 205: INTRODUCTION TO INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 
Lecturer: Prof. Olubukola S. ADESINA
Email: bukkystars@gmail.com
Course Outline & Reading list 2025/2026						 
This course provides an overview of International Relations, covering key theories and contemporary global issues. Students will explore the behaviour of states and non-state actors, and examine the complexities of global politics in today’s interconnected world.
Course Objectives
At the end of the course, students should be able to:
Explain the historical context of International Relations (IR).
Understand and critically evaluate major theories in IR.
Analyse key global issues through theoretical frameworks.
  1: Foundations of International Relations
Introduction to International Relations (IR) as a discipline.
Core concepts: state, sovereignty, power, anarchy, and security.
Historical context and evolution of the international system.
 2: Theories of International Relations I – Realism and Liberalism
Overview of realism (classical and neorealism) and liberalism (liberal institutionalism).
Key theorists and principles of each theory.
Application to historical and contemporary events.
 3: Theories of International Relations II – Constructivism and Critical Theories
Constructivism: social structures, norms, and identities in IR.
Introduction to Marxism, feminism, and post-colonial theories in IR.
Critical perspectives on traditional IR paradigms.
 4: The International System and Balance of Power
The concept of the balance of power in international politics.
Historical examples and the role of alliances.
Examination of unipolarity, bipolarity, and multipolarity in international relations.
 5: International Organizations and Global Governance
Role of international organizations, with a focus on the United Nations.
Mechanisms of global governance, including international law.
Challenges in addressing global issues through multilateral institutions.
 6: International Security and Conflict Studies
Traditional and non-traditional security concerns.
Causes of war and conflict resolution approaches.
Contemporary issues: terrorism, nuclear proliferation, and cyber warfare.
 7: International Political Economy (IPE)
Foundations of IPE: trade, development, and economic power.
The impact of globalization on state sovereignty.
Inequality and economic dependency in the global system.
 8: Human Rights and International Law
Development of human rights in the international context.
Sovereignty vs. humanitarian intervention.
Case studies on human rights, war crimes, and international tribunals.
 9: Environmental Politics and Transnational Issues
Climate change and the role of environmental policy in IR.
Resource conflicts and sustainable development.
The role of transnational actors, including NGOs, in environmental issues.
 10: Emerging Trends and Future Directions in International Relations
Analysis of contemporary and emerging trends: rise of China, nationalism, populism.
Technological change, cyber issues, and future global challenges.
Reflections on the future of the international order and evolving IR theories

Participation and Discussion

ABSTRACT 
 
This paper studies the realist theory of International Relations and attempts an 
explanation of how it illuminates our understanding of inter-state relations. We 
analyse the key assumptions of the realist theory and look at the main criticisms 
of the theory with the purpose of establishing how relevant it is to the study of 
International Relations and world problems today.  The thematic, chronological 
methods and secondary sources are employed in the gathering and presentation 
of data. The researchers conclude that, despite its criticisms, realism remains a 
key theory in explaining international relations issue.

the competitive and conflictual side of international relations.”2 Suffice it to say 
here, that available literatures show that, there is no single coherent definition 
of realism.

Theories of International Relations – Constructivism 
Constructivism in International Relations
Constructivism is a theory in International Relations (IR) that emphasizes the importance of ideas, beliefs, norms, and the shared understanding of reality in shaping international politics. Unlike theories like realism and liberalism, which focus primarily on material power and institutional structures, constructivism highlights how social interactions and shared meanings create the world we live in.
Key Features of Constructivism
Ideas Matter: Constructivism argues that the beliefs and ideas held by people, states, and organizations shape international relations.
Social Construction of Reality: International systems, such as alliances and rivalries, are created through shared meanings and social interactions, not just material factors like military power or economic resources.
Role of Norms and Identities: Norms (standards of appropriate behaviour) and identities (how actors see themselves and others) play a critical role in shaping state behaviour.
Agency and Structure: While structures like the international system influence actors (e.g., states), actors also shape these structures through their interactions.
Proponents of Constructivism
1. Alexander Wendt
Known as the “Father of Modern Constructivism”
Major Contributions
Core Idea: “Anarchy is What States Make of It”
Wendt’s 1992 article of the same name challenges the traditional realist and liberal understanding of anarchy in the international system.
According to Wendt, the meaning of anarchy is not fixed. Instead, it is shaped by the interactions, shared ideas, and norms of states.
For example:
Realists see anarchy as inherently conflictual.
Wendt argues that if states cooperate and trust one another, anarchy can lead to peaceful relationships.
Constructivist View of the State:
Wendt asserts that states are not just rational actors focused on material interests; they are also social entities shaped by their identities and norms.
The Role of Identity in International Relations:
Wendt explores how states develop identities (e.g., rival, ally, or neutral) through interactions with others. These identities shape their actions.
Example: The U.S. sees Canada as a friendly neighbor, while it views North Korea as a hostile state. These perceptions are socially constructed over time.
Key Works
“Anarchy is What States Make of It” (1992): A groundbreaking article that established constructivism as a significant IR theory.
“Social Theory of International Politics” (1999):
In this book, Wendt systematically develops the constructivist framework.
He introduces three cultures of anarchy:
Hobbesian Anarchy: States see each other as enemies.
Lockean Anarchy: States see each other as competitors but respect sovereignty.
Kantian Anarchy: States see each other as friends and cooperate extensively.
2. Nicholas Onuf
Coined the Term “Constructivism” in IR
Major Contributions
Introduction of Constructivism in IR:
Onuf is credited with formally introducing the term “constructivism” in his book “World of Our Making” (1989).
He argued that the international system is not naturally given but is constructed through language, actions, and shared understandings.
“Speech Acts” and Rule Formation:
Onuf emphasized how language (speech acts) creates rules and norms in international politics.
Example: When states sign treaties, they are not only expressing intentions but also creating new norms that shape future behaviour.
Focus on Human Agency:
Onuf highlighted the importance of human agency in shaping structures. Unlike realists who view structures as dominant, Onuf argued that individuals and states constantly recreate and reshape international structures.
Key Work
“World of Our Making” (1989): This foundational text explains how international relations are socially constructed and emphasizes the role of language in creating rules and norms.

1. Objectives
At the end of the teaching and learning hours, students should be able to:
(a) Define and understand basic terms and concepts in the subject area of Public Administration.
(b) Compare and contrast the differences and similarities in public organisations (public administration) and private organisations (private administration).
(c) Proffer explanations on the central role of public administration in Nigeria as well as any other modern political system.
2. Course Outline
(i) Introduction – Definition of Administration & its evolution.
(ii) Public Administration – Definition, evolution & growth, importance of public administration 
(iii) Differences & Similarities of public & private administrations.
(iv) Relevance & Ecology of Public Administration.
(v) Functions of an Administrator.
(vi) Debate on the Politics/Administration Dichotomy.
(vii) Elements & Theories of Organizations.
    – Bureaucratic Theory
(viii)Nature & Functions of civil service, civil service ethics etc. 
3. Teaching & Learning Techniques
The central purpose and objectives of this course of study are essentially student-focused. In the light of this, students will be encouraged to be involved as much as possible through interactions (question and answer sessions). Active students/participants in class interactive sessions will be commended while less active ones will be encouraged for greater participation. Class attendance is compulsory and will form part of continuous assessment.

Sixty (60) per cent will be for the final examination, while 30 and 10 per cent will be for pre-examination test and attendance respectively.

Introduction 
 
Welcome to POL 123: Introduction to Public Administration. 
 
This course is a three credit unit course for undergraduate students in 
Political science. The materials have been developed with the Nigerian 
context in view. This course guide gives you an overview of the course. 
It also provides you with information on the organization and 
requirements of the course. 
 
Course Aims 
 
The aims are to help you understand new ideas and concepts of Public 
Administration. Hence, there is a requirement for orienting your mind to 
the contemporary social situations. The course attempts: 
 
i. 
Introducing you to Public Administration and the basic principles 
and concepts. 
ii. 
Demonstrating how these principles can be applied 
iii. 
To expose you to current affairs and 
iv. 
To help you in widening your horizon of knowledge. 
 
Course Objectives 
 
To achieve the aims set out above, POL 123 has overall objectives. In 
addition, each unit also has specific objectives. The unit objectives are at 
the beginning of each unit. I advise that you read them before you start 
working through the unit. You may want to refer to them during your 
study of the unit to check your progress. 
 
Here are the wider objectives for the course as a whole. By meeting the 
objectives, you count yourself as having met the aims of the course. On 
successful completion of the course, you should be able to: 
 
•

Define the concept of administration in its various contextual usages.

1.1  Etymology and Meaning of Administration 
The English word 'administer' is derived from two Latin words — 'ad' and 'ministrare' — which 
together mean 'to serve', 'to care for', or 'to look after people'. In simple terms, 'administration' 
means the management of affairs or looking after the people. As an organised group activity, 
administration involves cooperation and coordination for the purpose of achieving desired goals or 
objectives. 
 
Administration as a concept appears in at least four distinct senses depending on the context in 
which it is used: 
 
THE FOUR CONTEXTUAL SENSES OF ADMINISTRATION 
As a Discipline: A branch of academic learning taught and studied in colleges and 
universities — the subject of formal intellectual inquiry. 
As a Vocation: A type of work, trade, or profession requiring specialised knowledge, 
training, and commitment — a career path. 
As a Process: The sum total of activities undertaken to implement public policy or to 
produce goods and services. It is administration as action. 
As a Synonym for Government/Executive: Used to refer to a specific ruling executive, 
e.g., the 'Tinubu Administration', the 'Biden Administration'.

Scholars across different traditions have offered definitions of administration that, while worded 
differently, all converge on two essential elements: cooperative effort and the pursuit of common 
objectives. The following are among the most cited definitions: 
 
 
Administration is a long and slightly pompous word, but it has a humble meaning, for it 
means to care for or look after people, to manage affairs... it is determined action taken 
in pursuit of conscious purpose. 
— E.N. Gladden

in a single organism, so adroitly that they shall operate as a unity. 
— Brooks Adams 
 
 
Administration is the organisation and use of men and materials to accomplish a 
purpose. 
— Felix A. Nigro 
 
 
The art of administration is the direction, co-ordination and control of many persons to

— L.D. White 
 
 
Administration has to do with getting things done, with the accomplishment of defined

— F.M. Marx

cooperating to accomplish common goals. 
— Herbert Simon, Smithburg and Thompson

2.1 Introduction: Meaning of 'Public' in Public Administration 
The term 'public administration' is a combination of two words — 'public' and 'administration'. The 
word 'public' stands for the people of a definite territory or state. Because the will of the people in a 
state is represented by the government, the word 'public' also carries a specialised governmental 
meaning. Public administration is therefore governmental administration — it refers to the 
application of a state's policies through its government machinery. 
 
The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines public administration as 'the application of a policy of a state 
through its government.' This highlights two key aspects: (1) it is the action part of government, and 
(2) it operates within a political and governmental setting. Public administration is distinct from 
private administration in that its purpose is service to the public, not the generation of profit.

broad categories: narrow definitions (restricting it to the executive branch) and broad definitions

application of law is an act of administration.

fulfilment or enforcement of public policy. This covers a multitude of operations including 
the delivery of a letter, the negotiation of a treaty, the quarantine of a sick child, and the 
management of public works. 
— L.D. White

3.1  Introduction 
The very term 'public administration' appears to suggest that there must be a non-public or private 
administration also. Administration is a universal process that occurs in all organised settings — 
governmental and non-governmental alike. Both types share the common features of management, 
coordination, and organisation to achieve objectives. However, the environment and goals of each 
type differ significantly, and these differences fundamentally shape their character, methods, and 
values. 
 
Public administration is governmental administration, concerned with achieving state purposes on 
behalf of the whole people of a territory. Private administration manages the affairs of business 
enterprises primarily to generate profit for owners. The distinction between them has been analysed 
by a number of scholars including Herbert Simon, Felix Nigro, Sir Josiah Stamp, Paul Appleby, and 
Peter Drucker.

4.1  Introduction: Why the Environment of Administration Matters 
No public administration system operates in a vacuum. The environment in which public 
administration operates is highly dynamic — technological, economic, physical, and cultural factors 
change with time, and societies differ significantly from country to country. Consequently, public 
administration's activities, structures, and methods also vary from nation to nation. The political and 
constitutional environments of a country are deeply inter-linked with its administrative systems. 
Understanding this inter-relationship is the central concern of the ecological approach to public 
administration. 
 
The ecological approach draws from biology, where 'ecology' refers to the study of the relationship 
between living organisms and their environment. Applied to public administration, ecology examines 
the mutual relationship between an administrative system and its surrounding social, cultural, 
economic, political, and historical environment. 
 
4.2  John M. Gaus: The Pioneer of Ecological Thinking 
John M. Gaus was among the first scholars to argue that public administration cannot be 
understood without reference to the environment in which it functions. In his 1947 work Reflections 
on Public Administration, Gaus argued that administrative systems are profoundly shaped by their 
environmental context, and that a theory of public administration must also be a theory of politics. 
 
 
A theory of public administration means in our time a theory of politics also. The factors 
which produce the environment of administration must be understood if administration 
itself is to be understood. 
— John M. Gaus 
 
Gaus identified the following seven environmental factors that shape administrative systems:

GAUS'S SEVEN ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS 
1. People: The population's size, composition, beliefs, values, literacy level, and 
expectations of government shape what administration must deliver and how it organises 
itself. 
2. Place: Geographical location — climate, topography, natural resources, and physical size 
of the territory — affects the nature and focus of administrative activities. 
3. Physical Technology: The level of scientific and technological development in

4. Social Technology: The state of knowledge about human behaviour — from psychology,

5. Wishes and Ideas: The dominant ideologies, values, political culture, and collective 
aspirations of the people determine what citizens demand of government and how they 
evaluate its performance.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES 
By the end of this topic, students should be able to: 
•

•

and order to complex welfare and development roles. 
•

effective public administrator. 
•

administrators in Nigeria. 
 
5.1  Who Is a Public Administrator? 
A public administrator is any official who works within the machinery of government to implement 
public policies, manage public resources, and deliver services to citizens. The range of individuals 
covered by this definition is extremely broad: it includes the Permanent Secretary at the Federal 
Secretariat in Abuja; the local government director of works; the NAFDAC inspector enforcing drug 
regulations in a Lagos market; and the primary school headmistress managing a government 
school in rural Oyo State. 
 
Corson and Harris (1963) provide a comprehensive description of what public administration 
involves: decision-making, planning the work to be done, formulating objectives and goals, working 
with the legislature to gain public support and funds, establishing and revising organisation, 
directing and supervising employees, providing leadership, communicating and receiving 
communications, determining work methods and procedures, appraising performance, and 
exercising controls. 
 
Administrators operate as the action part of the government — they are the means by which the 
purposes and goals of government are realised in the lives of citizens. 
 
5.2  Historical Evolution of the Functions of Public Administration 
The functions of public administration have expanded dramatically as civilisation has advanced. 
This evolution can be understood in three broad historical phases: 
 
HISTORICAL PHASES OF ADMINISTRATIVE FUNCTIONS 
Phase 1: Minimal State Functions (Pre-modern Period): At the beginning of civilisation, 
maintaining law and order was probably the only function performed by public administration. 
The state's role was to protect life and property, enforce basic rules of social conduct, and

Study Notes | 2025/2026 Session  |  For Student Use Only 
defend the territory from external enemies. The administrative machinery was 
correspondingly small. 
Phase 2: Regulatory and Infrastructure Functions (19th-early 20th Century): As 
industrialisation created new social problems — urban poverty, worker exploitation, 
environmental degradation — governments began regulating the economy and providing 
basic infrastructure (roads, railways, post offices). The functions of administration began to

IDEAS AND IDEOLOGIES IN POLITICS 
 
Richard Vernon 
Department of Political Science, University of Western Ontario, Canada 
Keywords: Ideologies, Liberal democracy, Modernity, Monarchy, Political ideas, Political 
philosophy, Political theory, Postmaterialism, Republicanism, Secularism. 
 
Contents 
 
1. Introduction 
2. From Monarchy to Modernity 
3. Three Challenges 
4. Contemporary Theory 
5. Current Ideologies 
Bibliography 
Biographical Sketch 
 
Summary 
 
Political ideas (known as “ideologies” when they are embedded in social or political 
movements) provide a framework for political action; they can be examined on their merits, 
as claims about what should or should not be done, and also in causal terms, as factors that 
influence political situations. Two powerful ideas, those of democracy and liberalism, 
together formed an idea of modern political organization that displaced traditional ideas of 
monarchical rule. Although important political theorists continue to defend the liberal-
democratic settlement, it faces long-standing challenges from socialists, nationalists and 
critics of secularism, as well as newer challenges—both philosophical and practical—from 
“post-materialist” points of view. To examine contemporary political ideas and ideologies 
is to confront basic questions about the legitimacy of states, and, indeed, the very idea of 
the state. 
1. Introduction 
 
When people act in politics, they have purposes in mind, and they use means, which they 
believe to be legitimate. They also have beliefs about the expectations and likely reactions 
of others; and they often wish to explain and justify themselves to others, or else persuade 
them to see things differently. These beliefs about what is desirable, possible and 
legitimate; these shared and reciprocal understandings about political behavior; these 
claims that are used to justify oneself to others, or to try to change others’ minds, all these 
are political ideas. And evidently we will not get far, in trying to understand political 
situations and political institutions—or in trying to change them—without learning 
something about the ideas which guide and constrain action, which make coordination 
possible and make conflict intelligible, and which provide the substance of public debate.

The author provides an overview about the field of international political economy
(IPE) along metatheoretical lines. The IPE communities in the United States and
Western Europe exhibit more differences than commonalities in their ontological,
epistemological and methodological assumptions. While the U.S. perspective is
solidly based on a materialist ontology, methodological individualism, and neo-
positivism as its epistemological foundation, the European IPE community is
considerably more heterogeneous in its theoretical, epistemological and
methodological approaches. The article ends with a view towards the future
introducing three possible scenarios for the IPE sub-discipline.

Balaam and Dillman thoroughly present the key theoretical debates in the ﬁeld, and issue areas

Summary 
International Political Economy (IPE) is an interdisciplinary social science field of 
study that emerged from the breakdown of the disciplinary barriers that divide 
International Economics from International Politics (or International Relations). IPE 
studies problems associated with international trade, international finance, North-South 
relations, multinational corporations, hegemony, and globalization. The domain of IPE 
is expanding beyond these issues, however, as IPE shifts from the traditional concerns 
of international politics to an even broader set of social, political, and economic issues.

COURSE DESCRIPTION
POL 223:  Foundations of Political Economy (3 Credit Units)
Political economy is an interesting field of study in the social sciences. It
dates back to the works of influential thinkers from the 17th and the 19th
centuries that were concerned with the workings of the capitalist system.
It is plausible to call those thinkers philosophers or political economists.
In the contemporary world system, political economy has become
multidisciplinary in nature that covers issues of wealth and power; hence
it is at the intersections of politics, economics and other disciplines such
as international relations, sociology among others This course, therefore,
examines the basic concepts in political economy, meaning, evolution
and scope of political economy; perspectives in political economy;
analysis of modes of production; primitive accumulation of capital;
globalisation; and the political economy of Nigeria.

What Is Political Economy?
Political economy is an interdisciplinary branch of the social
sciences. It focuses on the interrelationships among individuals,
governments, and public policy.
Political economists study how economic theories such as
capitalism, socialism, and communism work in the real world.
Any economic theory is a means of directing the distribution of a
finite amount of resources in a way that benefits the greatest
number of individuals. These ideas can be studied both
theoretically and as they are used in the real world. In the real
world, public policy is created and implemented around these
economic theories. Political economists study both the
underlying roots of these policies and their results.
In a wider sense, political economy was once the common term
used for the field we now call economics. Adam Smith, John
Stuart Mill, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau all used the term to
describe their theories.1 The shorter term "economy" was
substituted in the early 20th century with the development of
more rigorous statistical methods for analyzing economic
factors.23

• Socialism: This type of political economy promotes the idea
that the production and distribution of goods and wealth are
maintained and regulated by society, rather than a particular
group of people. The rationale behind this is that whatever is
produced by society is done so because of those who
participate, regardless of status, wealth, or position. Socialism
aims to bridge the gap between rich and poor, eliminating the
ability of individuals or groups to control the majority of power
and wealth.5
• Capitalism: This theory advocates profit as a motive for
advancement and the ability of free markets to regulate and
drive the economy on their own. The idea behind capitalism is
that private individuals and other actors are driven by their own
interests—they control production and distribution, set prices,
and create supply and demand.6
• Communism: Individuals often confuse communism with
socialism, but there is a distinct difference between these two
theories. Communism was a theory developed by Karl Marx,
who felt that capitalism was limited and created a big divide
between rich and poor. He believed in shared resources,
including property. Unlike socialism, however, under
communism production and distribution are overseen by the
government.7
