COURSE DESCRIPTION
POL 223:  Foundations of Political Economy (3 Credit Units)
Political economy is an interesting field of study in the social sciences. It
dates back to the works of influential thinkers from the 17th and the 19th
centuries that were concerned with the workings of the capitalist system.
It is plausible to call those thinkers philosophers or political economists.
In the contemporary world system, political economy has become
multidisciplinary in nature that covers issues of wealth and power; hence
it is at the intersections of politics, economics and other disciplines such
as international relations, sociology among others This course, therefore,
examines the basic concepts in political economy, meaning, evolution
and scope of political economy; perspectives in political economy;
analysis of modes of production; primitive accumulation of capital;
globalisation; and the political economy of Nigeria.

COURSE DESCRIPTION
POL 228 Introduction to Comparative Politics (3 Credit Unit)
This course, POL 228- Introduction to Comparative Politics, is a three
credit unit course for undergraduate students in Political Science and
other Social Science disciplines. The course compares political systems
across the world with a focus on different types of political systems. It
also introduces students to the foundation of comparative politics
particularly the works of its founding fathers and other scholars
particularly the perspectives they espoused. The materials have been
developed with special reference to Nigeria. It also provides you with
information on the organization and requirements for the course.
COURSE AIMS AND OBJECTIVES
The general aim of this course is to help you have the basic knowledge
and understanding of Comparative Politics, and to enable you appreciate
its usefulness in Political Science.
To achieve the general aim set out above, POL 228 has the following as
specific objectives:

educating you about the basic concepts and principles of
comparative politics

highlighting the value of comparison in political studies

acquainting you with the methods of comparative politics

educating you about how to analyse contemporary political issues
using comparative method.
In addition to the general objective of the course, each unit also has
specific objectives.  It is advisable that you read them before you start
working through the unit. Reference may be made to them in the course
of study of the units as self-assessments strategy.
Expected Outcomes
On successful completion of the course, you should be able to:

discuss the definitions, scope and origin of Comparative Politics

explain the approaches to the study of Comparative Politics

understand the importance and limitations of Comparative
Politics

comprehend the logic of comparative social inquiry

identify the focus and thrust of comparative politics

understand the role of concepts, models and theories in
Comparative Politics

explain the problem of conceptualisation in Comparative Politics

General Introduction and Course Overview 
The theory and practice of administration is a course in the field of public administration 
that discusses the meaning and purpose of government, bureaucracy, budgets, 
governance, and public affairs. It is a study that has developed more systematic patterns 
of inquiry about the substance of public organisational behaviour, public management, 
and public policy implementation. It has also contributed to an increasing reliability on 
the basic features and methods inherent in the study of public administration. The course 
therefore focuses on the explanation of public organisations methodological and 
theoretical form of analysis. 
     The course is divided into twelve lectures units. The first four lectures introduce the 
course with the explanation of administration as it applies to (1) Private and Public 
administration (2) debates on administration and politics (3) approaches to the study of 
public administration (4) schools of thought in public administration. Lectures five and 
six deal with the examination of bureaucracy and its models. Lectures seven and eight 
discuss policy and policy circles. Lecture nine is about planning and the problems 
attached to its attainment in an organisation. Lecture ten addresses different modes of 
distributing power in an organisation; while lectures eleven and twelve deal with the local 
government and issues related to its autonomy. Each lecture is accompanied with pre and 
post tests to guide the student’s study of the course materials. 
   
Aims of the Course 
     The overall aim of the course is to enable the students become aware of actions and 
processes involved in the analysis of structures in the study of public administration. This 
will give the students an insight into the interplay of political institutions on 
administrative patterns and behaviours, the study of bureaucracy, personnel 
administration and decision making. 
 
Objectives of the Course 
The students should be able to discuss the basic theories and practices involved in public 
administration. They should also be able to explain the various methods and processes of 
decision making for the attainment of organisational goals.   

 
3 
 
Specific Objectives 
At the end of this course, you should be able to: 
1. explain the term “administration”; 
2. define politics; 
3. discuss the general trend of politics and administration; 
4. explain different approaches to the study of public administration;  
5. describe different schools of thought in administration; 
6. discuss bureaucracy; 
7. describe the processes involved in the making of policy; 
8. describe the different forms of planning; 
9. discuss different levels of power distribution; and  
10. identify the basic features of local government administration. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
4

MEANING OF ADMINISTRATION

human resources are therefore put into use to achieve these goals. What is being done in 
such instances is called administration. 
In this, lecture therefore, I shall define the term “administration”, public and private 
administration, as well as their common features and differences.

1. _______ is a systematic attempt to provide answers to questions.  
Ans: Research

which they belong.  
Ans: Social Science 
3. Related group of disciplines specializing in the study of man in the social world is referred to as ______ 
Ans: Social Science 
4. _______ is the systematic investigation to human society and how it is organized.  
Ans: Social Research. 
5. Social Research can be divided into _____ and ______. 
Ans: Basic or Pure Research and Applied Research. 
6. Social Research should be ______, ______,_____,____ and ______. 
Ans: Empirical, systematic, logical, verifiable and transmittable and reductive.

4. Formulation of research design 
5. Identification and construction of instruments for observation and measurement.

Ans: Traditional period (up to 1950) and modern/behavioral period (from 1950s) 
9. What are the 4 approaches in the traditional period?  
Ans: The classical, the historical, the legalistic and the institutional. 

10. Major events that led to the criticism of the traditional approach are ______ and ______. 
Ans: The collapse of interwar German democracy and fascism. 
 
Chapter 3 
11. Methods of inquiry can be classified into _____ and _____. 
Ans: Scientific and Non-scientific 
12. ______ are methods of acquiring knowledge which are not based on scientific procedures and 
principles. 
Ans: Non-scientific methods.

Ans: Law of causation, empiricism and systematization

Ans: Empiricism.

Ans: Method

CLASSICAL REALISM: AN INTRODUCTION
One significant human trait is narratives, an attempt to explain phenomena within a coherent framework.
This human tendency towards seeking coherent narratives gives rise to theories, frameworks which try to explain our observations.
The political arena is a fertile field of theories, no less because political science is at its core, a study of the complex and multifaceted human nature. 
Hence, Aristotle crowned political science as the Master Science.
Competing theories have tried to explain interactions within the international political system.
Classical realism is one of such theories. What are its arguments and do these arguments hold up in the face of prevailing political realities?
Let’s examine the facts.
The classical realism is a realist state theory that argues that human nature influences the behavior of states. As such, all states seek to serve their national interests just like humans seek to maximize personal interest.
ORIGIN/ HISTORY OF CLASSICAL REALISM
The term " Classical Realism" was first used to describe the work that combines the fine drawing and design of the European academic tradition by Richard Lack (1928-2009) who was a pupil of Boston artist, R.H Ives Gammell ( 1893- 1931) during the early 1950s.  
As a political ideology, classical realism emerged in modern form during the interwar period between 1918- 1939 as the academic field of International Relations began to thrive during this era. It developed during the interwar period as a response to the prominence of idealist and utopian theories in International Relations during the time. 
After the Second World War, classical realism became more popular in academic and foreign policy setting. Central contributors to classical realism include George F.Kennan, Hans Morgenthau , Robert Gilpin ,E.H.Carr, Raymond Aron, etc.
Theoretical Origins and Proponents of Classical Realism
Classical realism has various approaches and theoretical traditions; however, classical realists have drawn from the ideas of earlier political thinkers such as Thomas Hobbes, Niccolo Machiavelli , Thucydides and so on to understand the development of the theory.

Thomas Hobbes was an English political philosopher who attempt to influence the classical realist theory by describing human nature, theories of the state and anarchy and his focus on politics as a contest for power. INTRODUCTION
Is Political Science a science or an art? Is the discipline a pure science? These questions have confounded practitioners and scholars of the discipline and better minds than we have failed to arrive at a consensus.
However, this paper is an attempt to tackle the age-long question. Note that we do not presume to proffer a conclusive answer to the question but to submit our own perspective on the matter.
What Is The Scientific Method?
To fully comprehend the scientific method, there is the need to understand where it originates from, which is 'science'?
What Is Science?
Science is from the Latin word 'scientia' meaning knowledge, awareness, understanding. Merriam Webster defined science as knowledge or a system of knowledge covering general truths or the operation of general laws especially as obtained and tested through scientific method. In the past, science was a synonym for knowledge or study such that a person who conducted scientific research was called a natural philosopher or man of science. Science may be old as human species and some of the earliest archaeological evidence for scientific reasoning is thousands of years old. The earliest written records in the history of science came from Ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia in around 3000 to 1200 BCE.
Modern science is divided into 4 branches;
Natural sciences: These are disciplines that study the physical world which include biology, chemistry and physics.
Social sciences: They study individuals, societies and how they influence one another, they include economics, sociology, psychology
Formal sciences: They study formal systems, governed by axioms and rules, they include logic, mathematics, theoretical computer science.
Applied sciences: These are disciplines that use scientific knowledge for practical purposes which include engineering and medicine.
THE SCIENTIFIC METHOD
It involves the empirical method for acquiring knowledge that has characterized the development of science since at least the 17th century. It involves careful observation, application of rigorous skepticism about what is observed, given that cognitive assumptions can distort how one interpret the observations. John Dewey defined it as an art of constructing true perceptions.
History Of The Scientific Method
Although the scientific method was not necessarily invented at a particular time because observations, hypotheses and experiments have been around as long as science has been around. However, Sir Francis Bacon (1561-1626) is generally considered the father of the scientific method, but was preceded by thinkers who inspired him. An example is Aristotle 384-322 BC) whom many people believed to be the first scientist due to his argument in favor of observation and empirical evidence. The English monk Roger Bacon (1219-1292) was among the first European scientific thinkers to promote experimental science, in one of his works "Opus Tertium" , he argued that other scientists should not only perform experiments but also record them so that others may repeat them, other early thinkers who influenced the philosophers and scientists who create and debate the scientific method include Galileo, Rene Descartes and Isaac Newton.
Elements Of The Scientific Method
For scientific research to be conducted, there are various elements that must be included and critically comprehended, they include;
1) Concept: This is the most important element of research used by researchers. It is abstractly used to describe a social or natural phenomenon. For instance, to illustrate voting among people, we have the concept of franchise, to illustrate population movement we have the concept of mobility and migration.
2) Variable: This is a concept with variety of values and it is a characteristic of the whole, for instance by looking at mobility we have age, sex, social class, height as variables.
3) Hypothesis: This is a tentative statement that establishes a relationship between two or more variables. The aim is to estab

COMPARATIVE POLITICS: NATURE AND MAJOR APPROACHES 
 
Comparative politics is the study and appraisal of domestic politics across countries. 
Comparative politics has a long and very eminent history dating back just before the 
origin of systematic political studies in ancient Greece and Rome. Even ancient people, 
compared their situations with those of other people's with whom they came in contact. 
The ancient Greeks performed the earliest systematic comparisons of a more modern 
and secular. 
Comparative politics is key area in political science, pigeonholed by an empirical 
approach based on the comparative method. To put it in another way, comparative 
politics is the study of the domestic politics, political institutions, and conflicts of 
countries. It often encompasses comparisons among countries and through time within 
single countries, emphasizing major patterns of similarity and difference. Many political 
theorists like Arend Lijphart argued that comparative politics does not have a functional 
focus in itself, instead a methodological one (Lijphart, Arend,1971). In simple form, 
comparative politics is not defined by the object of its study, but by the method it 
applies to study political phenomena. Peter Mair and Richard Rose gave modern 
definition of comparative politics and stated that comparative politics is elaborated by a 
combination of a substantive focus on the study of countries' political systems and a 
method of recognising and explaining similarities and differences between these 
countries using common models (Peter, 1996). 
In the field of Comparative politics, the term politics has three connotations such as 
political activities, political process and political power. Political activity consists of the 
efforts by which the conditions of conflicts are created and resolved in a way pertaining 
to the interest of people as far as possible who play in their part in struggle for power. 
Political process is an extension of political activity. Political power is the major topic 
in comparative politics. The term power has been defined by different writers. Friedrich 
described power as a certain kind of human relationship. Whereas Tawney explained 
power as a capacity of an individual or group of individuals to modify the conduct of 
other individuals in a manner which he desires (J. C. Johari, 1982). 
When applied to particular fields of study, comparative politics denotes by other names, 
such as comparative government (the comparative study of forms of government) or 
comparative foreign policy (comparing the foreign policies of different States in order to 
establish general empirical connections between the characteristics of the State and the 
characteristics of its foreign policy). 
Many theorists articulated that "Comparative political science" as a general term for an 
area of study, as opposed to a methodology of study, can be seen as redundant. The 
political only shows as political when either an overt or tacit comparison is being made. 

NATURE OF COMPARATIVE POLITICS: 
Nature and scope of comparative politics is fathomable only when one understands the 
main characteristics and significance of comparative government. Although the two 
terms 'Comparative Politics' and 'Comparative Governments' are used lightly and 
interchangeably, there is distinction between them. Conventionally, the comparative 
study of politics stands entitled as 'comparative government'. Comparative government 
includes the study of features and legal powers of political institutions existing in 
various states. It is the study of state and other political institutions in terms of their 
legal powers, functions, and positions on a comparative basis. 
Key characteristics of comparative government are mentioned below: 
 Stress upon the study of political institutions of various countries. 
 Focus on the study of major constitutions of the world. 
 Emphasis upon the study of powers and functions of various politic

Introduction to Comparative Politics 
 
Overview: This course presents an introduction to the study of comparative politics. 
Comparative political scientists study political systems and processes (contemporary and 
historical) in order to understand how they are similar, how they differ, and why. For example, 
why do some countries have democratic forms of government while others are ruled by 
authoritarian leaders? Do certain forms of government and economic systems have “better” 
outcomes? Why do revolutions occur? How does globalization affect the power of states? These 
are but a few of the interesting and important questions that we will analyze and discuss this 
semester.  
 
Objectives:  The class provides a conceptual framework for understanding political phenomena 
across the globe. Our objectives this semester are first, to understand the important concepts and 
theories in comparative politics; and second to acquire basic methods and tools to analyze important 
questions in comparative politics.  
 
Outcomes: After completing this class you will have a better understanding of what comparative 
political scientists do, and how to compare political phenomena in different countries. You will be 
able to identify the challenges facing countries across the globe and offer competing 
explanations for why these countries exhibit such divergent political and economic trajectories. If 
you are interested in political science as a concentration, this class will prepare you for more 
advanced subjects. If you just want to understand what is going on in the world, this class will 
provide you with useful theoretical frameworks.

INTRODUCTION
This course is a three-credit unit course for undergraduate students in
political science and other social sciences. The materials have been
developed with the Nigerian context in view. This course guide gives you
an overview of the course. It also provides you with information on the
organisation and requirements for the course.
COURSE AIMS
The main aim is to help you have the basic knowledge of statistics as it
relates to research in political science. However, the following broad aims
will also be achieved:
i)
Educating you about the basic concepts and principles of statistics
in decision-making process.
ii)
Highlighting the uses and limitations of statistics in the society.
iii)
Acquainting you with the methodology of data collection and
presentation in the political and other social sciences.
iv)
To educate you about how to analyse contemporary issues through
scientific logical deductions.
v)
To enable you understand some basic statistical theories and the
importance of measures of central tendencies.
COURSE OBJECTIVES
To achieve the aims set out above, POL212 has overall objectives. In
addition, each unit also has specific objectives. The objectives of each
unit are stated at the beginning of each unit. It is advisable that you read
them before working through the units. Reference may be made to them
in the course of studying the units as self-assessments strategy.
Listed below are the wider objectives for the course as a whole. By
meeting the objectives, you should be regarded as having met the aims of
the course. On successful completion of the course, you should be able to:
a)
Discuss the definitions, scope and origin of statistics
b)
Explain the approach to data collection
c)
Understand the importance and limitation of statistics
d)
Explain the tabulation and classification of data
e)
Appreciate the graphical and diagrammatical presentations of data
f)
Understand the frequency of distribution
g)
Understand measures of dispersion and measures of partition
define health care financing
h)
Explain the probability theory
i)
Discuss the Permutation and Combination theory

Democratic Practice and Governance 
in Nigeria 
This book examines the challenges confronting the practice of democracy 
and governance in Nigeria. 
The book examines the theoretical underpinnings and the procedural 
and institutional components of democratic practice in Nigeria, including 
the challenges associated with elections, the legislature, the media and 
gender issues. Approaching the pluralistic characteristics of the Nigerian 
state and how they impede democratisation through contributions by 
experts and scholars in the field, the book analyses the issues and nuances 
inherent to governance and democracy in Nigeria, as well as domestic 
policy process, global governance and human security. 
Democratic Practice and Governance in Nigeria will be of interest to students 
and scholars of African politics and democratisation. 
Ebenezer Oluwole Oni is a lecturer in the department of Political Science 
and International Studies at Crescent University Abeokuta, Nigeria. 
Omololu Michael Fagbadebo is a Research Fellow in the Department of 
Public Management and Economics, Durban University of Technology, 
Durban, South Africa. 
Dhikru Adewale Yagboyaju is an Associate Professor in the Department of 
Political Science, University of Ibadan, Nigeria.

Fragile states
Eghosa E. Osaghae
Since the 1990s, states that lack the capacity to discharge their normal functions and drive
forward development have been referred to as ‘fragile states’. This article focuses on Africa,
which not only has the largest concentration of prototypical fragile states, but has been the
focus of attention for scholars, international development agencies, and practitioners. The
author reviews competing analyses of the post-colonial African state and concludes that its
characteristics of weak institutions, poverty, social inequalities, corruption, civil strife,
armed conﬂicts, and civil war are not original conditions, but are rooted in speciﬁc historical
contexts. It is essential to understand both the external and internal factors of fragility if such
states are to get the assistance and empowerment that they need – not only for the beneﬁt of
their impoverished citizens, but also for the sake of global peace, prosperity, and security. Ulti-
mately, it is the citizens of the countries concerned who are responsible for determining when
states are no longer fragile – not ‘benevolent’ donors and the international community, whose
prime motivation for interventions supposedly to strengthen the state is to ensure that fragile
states ﬁnd their ‘rightful’ places in the hegemonic global order.

The discourse of ‘failed’, ‘weak’ or ‘fragile’ states has become widespread not only among
policymakers but also in academia and society more generally. Such terms, and the indices
used to delimit them, however, are often employed uncritically. Uses of the terms are often
blind to the contentiousness of the terms, have a tendency towards ahistoricity, seem
unaware of their own normative biases concerning ‘ideal’ governance or display a
limited understanding of the root-causes of violent conﬂict. In this accessible volume,
Brock et al. attempt to provide a more historically aware and nuanced account of state fra-
gility. The book provides an analysis of the historical origins of state fragility, the ‘core’
features that deﬁne a ‘fragile state’, and the relationship between state ‘fragility’ and
violent conﬂict. They argue that various historical and external forces have inﬂuenced
the trajectories of ‘fragile’ states, which is partly why they prefer to use the concept of
fragile rather than ‘failed’ or ‘weak’.
Despite arguments decrying the term’s normative and imperialist overtones, for the
authors ‘fragility’ is a valid concept because it describes an empirical reality. At core,
note the authors, ‘fragility’ is characterized ﬁrst by a state’s inability to maintain an exclu-

ideal, or as a system of citizens and institutions, which leads to a dependency on other

What is consciousness?

Introduction
-In its simplest, is sentience or awareness of internal and external 
existence
-Awareness of the external world & self including awareness of 
thoughts, perception and dreams
-Consciousness evolved in humans because it made it easier for us to 
communicate
3

How would YOU define consciousness?
• It is a state of awareness and responsiveness
• Your own mental processes and inner awareness
– Example: Your knowledge of your feelings, thoughts, 
and memories.
4

Consciousness occurs in a spectrum
It is a spectrum that ranges from low to high 
levels of awareness.
LOW
HIGH
Awake
Very Alert
Unconscious
5

Levels of Consciousness
Following states of consciousness are listed in 
decreasing order of arousal level, based on the 
extent of interaction between peripheral stimuli 
and the brain: 
i.
Maximum alertness
ii. Wakefulness
iii. Sleep (several different types)
iv. Coma
6

Let’s talk about sleep
7

Did you know?
Did you know that we spend about 1/3 of our lives 
asleep. If you live to be 75 years old you will have 
slept about 25 years!
An average 20 year old student has spent about 6 
years asleep!
8

Researchers have established what 
happens during sleep, but not why 
we sleep.
One theory is that we sleep because we are 
tired. 
In other words, sleep has a restorative function, 
like rebooting a computer.
9

Biological Clock
• Humans and other animals have an internal biological 
clock called the circadian rhythms
• These patterns vary over approximately a 24-hour cycle
and occur even in the absence of normal cues about 
whether it is day or night
• Responsible for body functions including:
– Hormone levels
– Sleep and wakefulness
– Blood pressure
– Body temperature
10

• Generated by the 
suprachiasmatic nucleus 
(SCN)
– Regulates the pineal 
gland’s secretion of the 
hormone – melatonin
– Increases in melatonin
produce drowsiness
Hypothalamus 
(SCN)
Pineal Gland
The Brain’s Control of Circadian Rhythms
11

Can your clock get out of whack?
• Yes, problems can occur if someone works 
through the night and sleeps during the day
• Also experienced with jet lag
– We are awake when our circadian rhythm cries 
“SLEEP!”
– To speed up resetting your biological clock after a 
long flight – spend time outdoors
• Bright lights help reset our biological clocks 
12

Morning People versus Evening People
• Morning people awaken early and full of 
energy – doing their best work before noon
– Most people over 65 are morning people
• Evening people take longer to warm up in the 
morning – doing their best work in the 
afternoon or evening
– Most young people are evening people
13

Isn’t sleep all the same?
• No, the use of the EEG shows variations in brain 
waves which determine different stages of 
sleep.
• There are 5 Stages of sleep
– (4) Non REM and (1) REM
• During an 8 hour period, people typically 
progress through all 5 full cycles,
– Each cycle lasts about 90 minutes
14

Non REM Sleep
• When awake, brain waves show a high 
frequency, low amplitude pattern
• NREM (non-rapid eye movement) sleep 
involves increasing bodily relaxation
– Slower EEG activity occurs
– The heart rate and respiration are slower during 
NREM
15

Non-REM Stages of Sleep
• NREM brain waves are of low amplitude and are 
fast, with mixed frequencies
– Brain activity changes with each stage
• People become more difficult to awaken as they 
progress through the four stages of NREM

Objectives
At the end of this lecture, students should be able to:   
1. Define perception and sensation

The meaning of sensation
• Sensations can be defined as the passive 
process of bringing information from the 
outside world into the body and to the brain.
• The process is passive in the sense that we do 
not have to be consciously engaging in a 
"sensing" process
3

Organs of Sensation
• Sense modalities such as taste (gustation), smell (olfaction), pain, 
and temperature provide sensory qualities 
• But not perceptual structures as do vision, audition, and touch, 
and thus are usually dealt with as sensory processes. 
4

Sensation Vs Perception?
• Although intimately related, sensation and perception play 
two complimentary but different roles in how we interpret 
our world.
• Sensation refers to the process of sensing our environment 
through touch, taste, sight, sound, and smell.
• This information is sent to our brains in raw form where 
perception comes into play.
5

Sensation Vs Perception?
• Perception is the way we interpret these sensations and 
therefore make sense of everything around us.
• chapter will describe various theories related to these two 
concepts and explain the important role they play in the field 
of psychology.
• Through this chapter, you will gain a better idea of how our 
senses work and how information is organized and 
interpreted.
6

7

The meaning of Perception
• “to become aware of something through the 
senses, or to comprehend or grasp a 
stimulus.” 
• A sense is any of the faculties by which one 
experiences the external world or the internal 
state organ. 
8

The meaning of Perception (2)
• Could also have different meanings. 
• Perception is the process, act, or faculty of perceiving. In another 
context, perception can be defined as the active process of 
selecting, organizing, and interpreting the information brought to 
the brain by the senses.  
• It involves the neurological processes by which such recognition 
and interpretation are effected. 
• In sum perception means insight, intuition, or knowledge gained 
by perceiving, as well as the capacity for such insight. 
9

Organs of Perception
• Since objects or events are not experienced only through vision, 
the term perception obviously applies to other sense modalities 
as well. 
• Certainly objects and their movement may be experienced 
through the sense of touch. 
• Such experiences derive from receptors in the skin (tactile 
perception), but more importantly, from the positioning of the 
fingers with respect to one another when an object is grasped, 
the latter information arising from receptors in the muscles and 
joints (haptic or tactile perception). 
10

Organs of Perception (2)
• The position of the parts of the body are also perceived with 
respect to one another whether they are stationary 
(proprioception) or in motion (kinesthesis), and the position of 
the body is experienced with respect to the environment through 
receptors sensitive to gravity such as those in the vestibular 
apparatus in the inner ear. 
• Auditory perception yields recognition of the location of sound 
sources and of structures such as melodies and speech. 
• Other sense modalities such as taste (gustation), smell (olfaction), 
pain, and temperature provide sensory qualities but not 
perceptual structures as do vision, audition, and touch, and thus 
are usually dealt with as sensory processes. 
11

physical stimulus in the environment.

and send them to the brain.

Background
• The peripheral nervous system (PNS) means all 
of the nervous tissue outside the brain and 
spinal cord. 
• It includes the cranial nerves apart from the

5

Introduction (1)
The peripheral nervous system (PNS) encompasses those neurons 
that connect the central nervous system (CNS) to the receptors, 
muscles, and organs at the periphery of the body. 
Most of the nerves of the PNS are made up of sensory nerve fibres
conveying afferent impulses from sensory end organs to the brain, 
and motor nerve fibres conveying efferent impulses from the brain 
through the spinal cord to effector organs. 
Each nerve has many nerve fibres compacted into a bundle.  
6

Introduction (2)
The PNS consists of:
•
31 pairs of spinal nerves
• 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 
• The autonomic part of the nervous system
7

1. The Spinal Nerves 
Are named according to the vertebrae with which they are 
associated. 
They arise from both sides of the spinal cord and emerge through 
the intervertebra foramina. 
Each nerve is formed by the union of a motor and sensory nerve 
root and is therefore a mixed nerve.
8

• 8 Cervical Nerves
• 12 Thoracic Nerves
• 5 Lumbar Nerves

A major goal of psychology is to predict behavior by understanding its causes. Making 
predictions is difficult in part because people vary and respond differently in different 
situations. Individual differences are the variations among people on physical or psychological 
dimensions. For instance, although many people experience at least some symptoms of 
depression at some times in their lives, the experience varies dramatically among people. Some 
people experience major negative events, such as severe physical injuries or the loss of 
significant others, without experiencing much depression, whereas other people experience 
severe depression for no apparent reason. Other important individual differences that we will 
discuss in the chapters to come include differences in extraversion, intelligence, self-esteem, 
anxiety, aggression, and conformity. 
Because of the many individual difference variables that influence behavior, we cannot always 
predict who will become aggressive or who will perform best in graduate school or on the job. 
The predictions made by psychologists (and most other scientists) are only probabilistic. We can 
say, for instance, that people who score higher on an intelligence test will, on average, do better 

Saylor URL: http://www.saylor.org/books 
 
Saylor.org 
 
 
15 
than people who score lower on the same test, but we cannot make very accurate predictions 
about exactly how any one person will perform. 
Another reason that it is difficult to predict behavior is that almost all behavior is multiply 
determined, or produced by many factors. And these factors occur at different levels of 
explanation. We have seen, for instance, that depression is caused by lower-level genetic factors, 
by medium-level personal factors, and by higher-level social and cultural factors. You should 
always be skeptical about people who attempt to explain important human behaviors, such as 
violence, child abuse, poverty, anxiety, or depression, in terms of a single cause. 
Furthermore, these multiple causes are not independent of one another; they are associated such 
that when one cause is present other causes tend to be present as well. This overlap makes it 
difficult to pinpoint which cause or causes are operating. For instance, some people may be 
depressed because of biological imbalances in neurotransmitters in their brain. The resulting 
depression may lead them to act more negatively toward other people around them, which then 
leads those other people to respond more negatively to them, which then increases their 
depression. As a result, the biological determinants of depression become intertwined with the 
social responses of other people, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of each cause. 
Another difficulty in studying psychology is that much human behavior is caused by factors that 
are outside our conscious awareness, making it impossible for us, as individuals, to really 
understand them. The role of unconscious processes was emphasized in the theorizing of the 
Austrian neurologist Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), who argued that many psychological 
disorders were caused by memories that we have repressed and thus remain outside our 
consciousness. Unconscious processes will be an important part of our study of psychology, and 
we will see that current research has supported many of Freud’s ideas about the importance of 
the unconscious in guiding behavior. 
KEY TAKEAWAYS 
• 
Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. 
• 
Though it is easy to think that everyday situations have commonsense answers, scientific studies have 
found that people are not always as good at predicting outcomes as they think they are.

HISTORIES AND SPECIAL EVENTS IN THE FIELD OF PSYCHOLOGY
The history of psychology is a dynamic narrative that spans centuries, evolving from philosophical inquiry to a rigorous scientific discipline. Below is an extended and updated outline, incorporating recent trends, events, and advancements.
1. Ancient Foundations of Psychology
Philosophical Roots:
Plato and Aristotle: Explored questions about memory, perception, and the nature of the soul.
Hippocrates: Linked mental processes to the brain, challenging earlier beliefs about the heart.
Mind-Body Dualism:
René Descartes argued for the separation of mind and body, influencing early psychological thought.
2. The Birth of Modern Psychology (19th Century)
Wilhelm Wundt:
Established the first experimental psychology lab in Leipzig, Germany (1879), marking psychology as a scientific discipline.
Edward B. Titchener: A student of Wundt
Focused on introspection and structuralism.
William James:
Published The Principles of Psychology (1890), introducing functionalism and concepts like "stream of consciousness."
G. Stanley Hall:
Founded the first U.S. psychology lab (1883) and the American Psychological Association (APA) in 1892.
3. Early Schools of Thought
Structuralism (Wundt and Titchener): Focused on analyzing the components of consciousness.
Functionalism (James): Emphasized the purpose of mental processes in adaptation.
Psychoanalysis (Freud): Introduced theories on unconscious processes, childhood development, and dream analysis.
Behaviorism (Watson, Skinner): Shifted focus to observable behavior, emphasizing conditioning and reinforcement.
4. Key Experiments and Milestones
1900: Freud published ”The Interpretation of Dreams”, formalizing psychoanalytic theory.
1920s–1930s: Ivan Pavlov’s work on classical conditioning influenced behaviorism.
1957: Leon Festinger introduced cognitive dissonance theory, revolutionizing social psychology.
1967: Ulric Neisser published Cognitive Psychology, establishing the cognitive revolution.
5. The Cognitive Revolution (1950s–1960s)
Shifted focus from behaviorism to internal mental processes like memory, perception, and problem-solving.
Influential Figures:
Jean Piaget: Studied cognitive development in children.
Noam Chomsky: Critiqued behaviorist views on language acquisition.
6. Integration with Neuroscience (1980s–2000s)
Advances in neuroimaging technologies like fMRI (Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) and EEG (Electroencephalography  allowed for detailed studies of brain-behavior relationships.
Emergence of biopsychology and Neuropsychology as a subfield integrating biology with psychology.
Modern Trends in Psychology (2000–2023)
a. Positive Psychology
Martin Seligman popularized positive psychology, focusing on human strengths, well-being, and resilience.
b. Technology in Psychology
Virtual Reality (VR) Therapy:
Used for treating PTSD and phobias by simulating controlled environments for exposure therapy.
Online Therapy Platforms:
The rise of apps like BetterHelp has increased access to mental health care globally.
c. Generative AI in Psychology
Tools like ChatGPT are being used for teaching, research, and therapy.
Emerging Subfield: "Machine Psychology" explores how AI systems process information.
d. Neuroscience Advancements
Research into brain correlates of disorders like schizophrenia has improved diagnostic tools and personalized treatments.
e. Multicultural Perspectives
Increased emphasis on diversity, equity, and inclusion in psychological research and practice.
f. Notable Achievements (2023)
Shelley E. Taylor received the National Medal of Science for her contributions to health psychology.
Thomas Joiner was honored for his research on suicide prevention.
8. Recent Special Events
a. Major Conferences in 2023
ICPS 2023: International Convention of Psychological Science held in Brussels.
APA Annual Convention 2023: Focused on workplace flourishing and global mental health challenges.
b. Influential Psychologists Today
Steve

HISTORY OF PSYCHOLOGY IN NIGERIA
The history of psychology in Nigeria reflects a journey from traditional practices to a formalized academic and professional discipline, marked by significant milestones and contributions to societal development.
Early Foundations and Traditional Practices
Before colonial influence, psychological practices in Nigeria were deeply rooted in traditional beliefs and methods. Mental health issues were addressed using herbal remedies, rituals, and spiritual interventions, reflecting indigenous understandings of human behavior and mental well-being. This period can be described as the "non-formal" era of psychology, where intuitive theories and cultural practices predominated.
Colonial Era and the Emergence of Modern Psychiatry
The introduction of modern mental health services began during the colonial period. In 1927, the first civil asylums were established in Lagos and Calabar to care for individuals with mental illnesses. A pivotal moment came in 1954 with the establishment of the Aro Psychiatric Hospital in Abeokuta under Professor Thomas Adeoye Lambo. Lambo integrated traditional African healing methods with Western psychiatric practices, laying the groundwork for culturally relevant psychological approaches in Nigeria.
Introduction of Psychology as an Academic Discipline
Psychology entered Nigerian academia formally in 1964 with the establishment of the first degree-awarding Department of Psychology at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. This department began with 11 students and was staffed by both Nigerian and American scholars. By the late 1960s and early 1970s, other universities, including the University of Lagos (1969) and University of Jos (1976), followed suit by creating psychology departments.
During this period, psychology was initially taught as part of other disciplines like philosophy, education, or medicine. However, its recognition as an independent field grew steadily. Early Nigerian psychologists like Professors Ugwuegbu, Omoluabi, Olowu, and Ebigbo made significant contributions by incorporating indigenous knowledge into psychological research.
Professionalization and Growth
The professionalization of psychology gained momentum with the establishment of organizations such as the Nigerian Psychological Association (NPA) in 1968 and the Nigerian Association of Clinical Psychologists (NACP) in 1978. These bodies advocated for the recognition of psychology as a vital profession in healthcare and education. By 2013, there were over 28 accredited departments of psychology across Nigerian universities.
The discipline diversified during the 1990s and early 2000s with specialized programs in clinical psychology, industrial-organizational psychology, and educational psychology. This period also saw an increase in local research output and publications.
Contemporary Developments
In recent decades, psychology in Nigeria has expanded its influence across various sectors. Efforts to integrate psychological services into primary healthcare systems have grown alongside initiatives to address mental health literacy and reduce stigma. The Psychology Bill (Senate Bill No. 624), awaiting presidential assent as of recent years, is expected to further regulate and institutionalize psychological practice in Nigeria.
Despite challenges such as limited resources, inadequate infrastructure, and a shortage of trained professionals, psychology continues to play a crucial role in addressing societal issues like education enhancement, mental health awareness, economic growth through consumer behavior insights, and social harmony through conflict resolution strategies.

COURSE PROFILE
Course Code and Title: PSY 101: Introduction to psychology
Credit Units: 2
Semester:	1st
Course Pre-requisite: NA
DESCRIPTION: This is a 2-Unit foundational course for Freshers in the discipline of psychology. It is carefully planned to introduce basic concepts and information preparatory to exposure of students to the knowledge of Psychology, what it is, its founding Fathers and various schools of thoughts among other interesting topics.
COURSE OBJECTIVE: 
1. Introduce students to the discipline of psychology 
2. Familiarize students with the schools of thoughts in the discipline
3. Highlight the various sub-disciplines within the core psychology discipline and how they can be applied in real life situations.
MODE OF DELIVERY: The course will be delivered through a series of lectures that introduce key concepts in the “psychology discipline” and the different schools of thoughts that emerged at different time points in the course of the growth of the discipline. Students will engage in assignments that reinforce their understanding of the course and encourage practical applications of the concepts learned in real-world contexts. Additionally, they will participate in discussions and group activities to enhance their critical thinking and collaborative skills related to psychological research.

INTRODUCTION TO PSYCHOLOGY
PSY 101INTRODUCTION TO PSYCHOLOGY

--- SLIDE ---

PSYCHOLOGY
The scientific study of human and animal behavior and their mental processes.

The field is scientific in that approaches (should be systematic in approach) to studies are done orderly and systematically in order to obtain objective evidence.

--- SLIDE ---

PSYCHOLOGY
Psychologists study overt and covert behavior.
 The overt behaviors are observable behavior, while covert behaviors include private mental processes that cannot be directly observed or measured and must be inferred from overt behavior.
Examples of overt behaviours are; laughing, walking, eating, gestures, facial expression etc and covert behaviour include the following; Perceiving, remembering, reasoning, thinking, creating, feelings etc

--- SLIDE ---

GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGY
Psychologists seek to do four things when studying behaviors:
Describe: What is the nature of the behavior? It gathers information on studied behavior and present what is known.
Explain: Why does it occur? Creating a hypothesis (educated guess) to understand why a behavior is practiced.
Predict:  By studying past behaviors, future behaviors can be predicted based upon theory 
Modify/Control behavior: What factors influence the behavior? Influence- using what is known to influence future behavior.

--- SLIDE ---

HISTORICAL APPROACH TO PSYCHOLOGY
Structuralism – Study of basic elements that make up human experiences.             
Wilhelm Wundt – In 1879, used people’s self observations about their thoughts (introspection) to map out structure of the thought process.
Functionalism – study of the function or how people & animals adapt to environment.  William James – known as the “father of psychology” taught first psych class in 1875 and wrote first textbook in 1890. He was concerned with ongoing conscious experience and the functions of mental processes.  His views gave rise to the branch of psychology called Functionalism.

--- SLIDE ---

HISTORICAL APPROACH (Cont’d)
Inheritable Traits – study of how heredity influences a person’s ability, character, and behavior. Is behavior determined by heredity or environment? 
Sir Francis Galton – Concluded that intelligence was hereditary / good marriages would supply the world with talented offspring. (1883).
Gestalt Psychology - Perception is more than the sum of its parts – it involves a whole pattern. German group that picked apart cognitive thought process.

--- SLIDE ---

HISTORICAL APPROACH (Cont’d)
Contemporary Approaches to Psychology (mid 1900’s to Present)
Psychoanalytic Psychology- study of unconscious motives & conflict determine behavior.  Sigmund Freud – used free association and dream analysis to study behavior (1940). 
Behaviorism – Study of how organisms learn or change behavior based upon responses to events in their environment. (Early-mid1900’s). it held the view that only overt behavior can be studied scientifically. They advocated the use of strict experimental procedure in psychology.

--- SLIDE ---

Contemporary Approaches to Psychology (mid 1900’s to Present)
Strict behaviorists believed that all behaviours are shaped by the environment.  “Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed,….. regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors”…….John Watson.
Ivan Pavlov – Classical conditioning experiment with dog’s salivation.
B.F. Skinner – Introduced concept reinforcement to show how behaviors repeat. 
John B. Watson –Behavior occurs due to stimuli in environment.

--- SLIDE ---

Contemporary Approaches
Humanistic Psychology – Belief that each person has freedom in directing his/her future an achieving personal growth. Humans are not controlled by environment, but by their own self concept. Humans are not being controlled by unconscious or environmental forces, we have free will, goals, aspirations and other positive motives which should be studied. It is influenced by Carl Rogers.
Abraham Maslow

Schools of Psychology

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
A group of psychologist having similar point of views and making similar approaches to study the human mind or behavior constitutes a school of thought in psychology.There are several schools of psychology and each has developed some systems of ideas which not only influenced the development of various trends and approaches for the study of behavior but also affected the process and product of education.

--- SLIDE ---

Major Schools of thought in Psychology
Early Schools of Thought. 
Structulism and Functionalism
Behaviorism
Psychoanalysis
Humanistic Psychology
Cognitive Psychology
Gestalt Psychology

--- SLIDE ---

Structuralism and Functionalism: Early Schools of Thought
Structuralism is widely regarded as the first school of thought in psychology. 
This outlook focused on breaking down mental processes into the most basic components. 
Major thinkers associated with structuralism include Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener. 
The focus of structuralism was on reducing mental processes down into their most basic elements. 
The structuralists used techniques such as  introspection to analyze the inner processes of the human mind.

--- SLIDE ---

CONTRIBUTIONS TO EDUCATION
1) Structuralism emphasized the systematic observation of the activities of the learner under controlled learning conditions.2) It is an experiment method for studying human behavior – experimental introspection.3) It initiated the spirit of science and experimentation in the field of education.

--- SLIDE ---

Functionalism
Functionalism formed as a reaction to the theories of the structuralist school of thought and was heavily influenced by the work of William James. 
It functioned on the mind's functions and adaptations. Unlike some of the other well-known schools of thought in psychology, functionalism is not associated with a single dominant theorist.
 Instead, there are some different functionalist thinkers associated with this outlook including John Dewey, James Rowland Angell, and Harvey Carr.

--- SLIDE ---

CONTRIBUTIONS TO EDUCATION
Functionalism revolutionized the curriculum by replacing theoretical overloaded curriculum with practical approaches.Study of various problems of the individual and their solutions is emphasized by Functionalism.
Functionalism gave utmost importance to learning by doing and developed activity oriented methods like project methods for teaching and learning.Functionalism gave birth to utilitarian theory of education. Only those subjects should be include in the curriculum which have practical utility and usefulness in the society.

--- SLIDE ---

The Behaviorist School of Thought in Psychology
Behaviorism became a dominant school of thought during the 1950s. It was based upon the work of thinkers such as:
John B. Watson
Ivan Pavlov
B. F. Skinner

--- SLIDE ---

Behaviorism suggests that all behavior can be explained by environmental causes rather than by internal forces. Behaviorism is focused on observable behavior. Theories of learning including classical conditioning and operant conditioning were the focus of a great deal of research.
The behavioral school of psychology had a significant influence on the course of psychology, and many of the ideas and techniques that emerged from this school of thought are still widely used today. 
Behavioral training, token economies, aversion therapy, and other techniques are frequently used in psychotherapy and behavior modification programs.

--- SLIDE ---

CONTRIBUTIONS TO EDUCATIONBehaviorism gave new ideas and innovations in the field of education. What is ethics?
• a set of values, principles and beliefs that guides the behaviour of a 
specified group – business people, engineers, health administrators, 
journalists, lawyers, manufacturers, physicians, surgeons, etc.  

Aim of ethics
Ethics aims to achieve two fundamental objectives:
(i)  to tell us how we ought to act in a given situation, and
(ii) to provide us with strong reasons for doing so

Meaning of Research 
• the systematic investigation into and study of materials and sources in order 
to establish facts and reach new conclusions
• an activity of systematic enquiry that seeks answers to a problem. 
• systematic investigation, including research development, testing and 
evaluation, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge.
• A Psychological research is conducted for the purpose of description, 
prediction, explanation, control of behaviour and application of knowledge 
generated in an objective manner
5

Meaning of Research Ethics
• Refers to the principles and guidelines that govern the conduct of 
research to ensure it is carried out responsibly, ethically, and with 
integrity.
• Focuses on protecting the rights, dignity, and well-being of participants, 
maintaining honesty and transparency, and promoting trustworthiness 
and accountability in the research process.
6

Research ethics
Objectives
• Protection of human participants
• Conduct of research in a way that serves interests of individuals, groups 
and/or society as a whole
• Examining specific research activities and projects for ethical 
soundness, protection of confidentiality and the informed consent 
process 

Importance of Research Ethics in Psychology
• Protection of Participants: Ethical guidelines ensure the rights, dignity, and well-being 
of participants are safeguarded, preventing harm and exploitation.
• Integrity in Research: Upholding ethical standards fosters honesty, transparency, and 
trustworthiness in the research process.
• Credibility and Trust: Ethical practices enhance the credibility of psychological studies, 
ensuring findings are respected and relied upon.
• Guidance for Professionals: Research ethics provide a framework for addressing 
complex moral dilemmas, promoting responsible conduct and informed decision-
making.
• Serves as the foundation for advancing psychological knowledge while respecting 
human values
8

Historical Context
• Early practices lacking formal ethical standards.
• Several records of harmful studies conducted are found in the 
literature
9

Unethical Historic Research in Psychology
• Little Albert Experiment (1920) by John Watson
• The Milgram Experiment (1961) 
• The Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) involved simulated prison roles, 
leading to abusive behavior and psychological harm. 
• David Reimer’s case (1965), an infant’s gender was reassigned after a medical 
error, resulting in lifelong psychological trauma. 
• The 1963-66 Willowbrook Study
10

Unethical Historic Research in Psychology
• Little Albert Experiment in 1920
• By John Watson and Rosalie Rayner
• A toddler was conditioned to fear furry objects through loud noises, 
disregarding the child's psychological well-being and informed consent.
• Milgram Experiment (1961)
• Obedience to authority. 
• Participants were instructed to administer electrical shocks to a learner, 
causing significant emotional distress despite the shocks being fake. 
• This raised ethical concerns about deception and participant protection.

text_snippet:
The interactions between biological, psychological, social, and environmental determinants of behavior are complex and reciprocal, influencing human behavior in a multifaceted way
Examples of Interactions
1. Stress and health: Chronic stress (environmental) can impact mental health (psychological), which can lead to physical health problems (biological).
2. Social media and self-esteem: Social media exposure (environmental) can influence self-esteem (psychological), which can impact relationships (social) and mental health (biological).
3. Education and socioeconomic status: Access to education (environmental) can influence socioeconomic status (social), which can impact health outcomes (biological) and cognitive development (psychological).
Environmental Influences
1. Urbanization: Exposure to urban environments (environmental) can influence mental health (psychological), social relationships (social), and physical activity (biological).
2. Climate change: Environmental stressors (environmental) can impact mental health (psychological), social relationships (social), and physical health (biological
1. Academic achievement: Genetic predisposition (biological) can be influenced by motivation (psychological), teacher support (social), and access to resources (environmental).
2. Learning disabilities: Neurobiological factors (biological) can be influenced by educational interventions (environmental), self-efficacy (psychological), and social support (social).
Health-Related Behaviors
1. Substance use: Genetic predisposition (biological) can be influenced by peer pressure (social), coping mechanisms (psychological), and access to substances (environmental).
2. Sleep habits: Circadian rhythms (biological) can be influenced by sleep hygiene practices (psychological), work schedules (social), and exposure to screens (environmental).
Mental Health
1. Trauma: Neurobiological response (biological) can be influenced by coping mechanisms (psychological), social support (social), and access to resources (environmental).
2. Resilience: Genetic predisposition (biological) can be influenced by self-efficacy (psychological), social support (social), and exposure to adversity (environmental).
Social Behaviors
1. Cooperation: Genetic predisposition (biological) can be influenced by empathy (psychological), social norms (social), and cultural values (environmental).
2. Conflict resolution: Emotional regulation (psychological) can be influenced by communication skills (social), cultural norms (environmental), and brain structure (biological).
Environmental Influences
1. Air pollution: Exposure to pollutants (environmental) can impact respiratory health (biological), cognitive development (psychological), and socioeconomic status (social).
2. Green spaces: Access to nature (environmental) can influence physical activity (biological), mental health (psychological), and social relationships (social).
Technology and Media
1. Screen time: Exposure to screens (environmental) can influence sleep habits (biological), cognitive development (psychological), and social relationships (social).
2. Social media: Social comparison (psychological) can be influenced by social media use (environmental), self-esteem (psychological), and cultural norms (social).

Quantitative Methods in Psychology
Dr. Opeyemi Fasanu

Department of Psychology,
University of Ibadan

Course Outline
2
Application of quantitative methods in psychological research: Basic concepts used in quantitative methods. 
Descriptive statistics
Nature of data: interval, ratio, ordinal, and nominal. 
Frequency distributions. 
Measures of central tendency: mean, median and mode.
Measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation, sample variance, standard deviation and many others. 
Practical exercises.
Application of inferential statistics to data analysis: 
Correlation and correlation coefficient, 
probability theory, 
T-test distribution, 
Chi-square, 
Z – test, 
Mann-Whitney 
U-test, 
Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, 
F-test
Introduction to ANOVA.
Practical.

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts in Quantitative Methods in Psychology
Week One
3

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts in QuantitativeMethods in Psychology
Psychology is the scientific study of behaviours and mental processes.
Behaviours are observable activities generated by an organism (man and animal) which can be measured.
Sometimes, behaviours are measured qualitatively. At other times, they are measured quantitatively.
4

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Quantitative Methods in Psychology
When behaviours are measured quantitatively, they generate scores that can be subjected to statistical computations.

These scores enable researchers to do data analyses whose results are used to make informed conclusions or decisions about the behaviours measured.
5

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts
6
Population and sample
Parameters
Measurements
Likert scale
Data (datum)
Data Validity
Data Reliability
Data Variability
Variables
Dependent variables
Independent variables

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts (cont’d)
Population: This refers to all individuals in geographical location. For example, students of the University of Ibadan, students in the Department of Psychology, residents in Ibadan North local government, etc.
Sample: This refers to a set of individuals selected from a population, who are intended to represent the population.
7

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts (cont’d)
Parameter: This refers to a value, usually a numerical value, that describes a population. 
A parameter is usually derived from measurements of the individuals in the population.
For example, the average score of intelligence of students in a class.
8

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts (cont’d)
Measurement: This refers to the process of systematically assigning numbers to characteristics and behaviours to enable statistical computations.
For example, gender is a characteristic that can be measured male and female. Male could assigned 0 while Female is assigned 1. Another example is age which could measured as 16 years.
9

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts (cont’d)
Likert scale: This refers to a set of numbers arranged from the smallest to the highest used to rate a behaviour. 
An example is rating this statement: “I am self-confident.”
4 = Strongly agree
3 = Agree
2 = Disagree
1 = Strongly disagree
10

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts: Data
Data: This refers to values generated from a measurement that represent a behaviours. Data is plural while datum is singular.
Dataset: This refers to a collection of measurements or observations.
For example, 18 years is a datum for age. Intelligence quotient (IQ) of 100 is a datum for intelligence. A collection of ages is called dataset.
11

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts: Data (cont’d)
Data validity: This refers to the extent to which the data represent what is intended. Valid data represent the intended construct or variable while invalid data does not.
For example, if a student gives a rating scale meant for patients with depression to her friends to respond, such data are not valid because the values generated do not represent depression from patients.
12

--- SLIDE ---

Basic Concepts: Data (cont’d)
Data reliability: This refers to the consistency of data for a construct or var

text_snippet:
Descriptive Statistics Concepts
Descriptive statistics summarize data features without inferences. Key terms include measures of central tendency and dispersion for psychology datasets like test scores. These help visualize trends in student behaviors or survey responses.
Population: Entire group of interest, such as all psychology freshmen at a university.
Sample: Subset of population selected for study.
Variable: Characteristic that varies, like anxiety levels.
Quantitative variable: Numeric data, e.g., reaction time in milliseconds.
Qualitative variable: Categorical data, e.g., gender or diagnosis type.
Univariate analysis: Examines one variable at a time.
Frequency: Number of occurrences of a value.
Frequency distribution: Table showing value frequencies.
Mean: Arithmetic average of scores.
Median: Middle value when data ordered.
Mode: Most frequent value.
Range: Difference between highest and lowest scores.
Variance: Average squared deviation from mean.
Standard deviation: Square root of variance, showing data spread.
Percentile: Value below which a percentage of scores fall.
Inferential Statistics Concepts
Inferential statistics use sample data to generalize to populations. Students apply these to test hypotheses on psychological effects, like therapy impacts. Concepts build on descriptives for decision-making.
Parameter: True population value, e.g., population mean.
Statistic: Sample-based estimate of parameter.
Hypothesis: Testable prediction, e.g., "treatment reduces anxiety".
Null hypothesis (H0): No effect or difference assumption.
Alternative hypothesis (H1): Effect or difference exists.
Significance level (alpha): Probability threshold, often 0.05.
P-value: Probability of results if null true.
Type I error: Rejecting true null hypothesis.
Type II error: Failing to reject false null.
Confidence interval: Range likely containing parameter.
Confidence level: Probability interval contains parameter, e.g., 95%.
Z-score: Standard deviations from mean.
T-test: Compares means of small samples.
Degrees of freedom (df): Independent information for estimation.
Normal distribution: Bell-shaped curve, symmetric.

text_snippet:
Neurones
being the title of a presentation by
Professor A. O. Adejumo 
MHSc(Canada) PhD(Ibadan) FWACN
Department of Psychology,
University of Ibadan
06 Apr, 2021
1

Outline
1. Definition of neurons
2. Structure of neurons
3. Parts of a neurone
4. Properties of neurons
5. Classification
6. Summary
2

Introduction
• Neurones are commonly referred to as nerve cells. 
• It is the basic structural unit of the Nervous System. 
• They are organized to form complex networks that perform the 
functions of the nervous system. 
• Each neurone consists of a cell body and its processes, one axon 
and many dendrites. 
• Bundles of axons bound together are called nerves. 
3

Introduction (2)
• Neurones can not divide. 
• For survival, they need a continuous supply of oxygen and 
glucose. 
• Unlike many other cells neurons can synthesize chemical 
energy adenosine tri phosphate (ATP) only from glucose.
4

Introduction (3)
• The nervous functions extremely rapidly
• Information and instructions travel speedily as electric impulses 
along nerves from one part of the body to another almost 
instantaneously. 
• The neurons are responsible for the electrical activities of the 
nervous system.     
• The nervous system relies on nerve impulses, or action 
potentials, which are similar to tiny electrical charges which it 
maintains throughout the length of the neurone.
5

Structure of a neurone
6

Parts of a Neurone
• Nerve cells or neurons, are specialized to carry "messages" 
through an electrochemical process.
• It consists of a nucleus, a membrane, one or more dendrites, a 
single soma, a single axon, one or more axon terminals,   
mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, vacuoles and 
other organelles / structures typical of animal cells. 
• Neurons are surrounded by a cell membrane
• The nucleus contains genes.
• Membrane- limits the flow of materials between the inside of the 
cell and the outside environment. 
• A few chemicals such as water, oxygen, and carbon dioxide, flow 
fairly freely across the membrane, while other substances flow 
fairly poorly, or not at all.
7

Parts of a neurone (2)
• The dendrite is one of the two types of synapses, the other being 
the axon terminal buttons. 
• Dendrites form protrusions in response to the axon terminal 
buttons. 
• These protrusions, or spines, are designed to capture the 
neurotransmitters released by the presynaptic neuron. 
• They have a high concentration of activated channels. 
• It is, therefore, here where synapses from two neurons 
communicate with one another. 
• These spines have a thin neck connecting a bulbous protrusion to 
the main dendrite. This ensures that changes occurring inside the 
spine are less likely to affect the neighbouring spines. The 
dendritic spine can, therefore, with rare exception, act as an 
independent unit.
8

Parts of a neurone (3)
• The dendrites then connect onto the soma. The soma houses the 
nucleus, which acts as the regulator for the neuron. 
• The fluid inside the cell membrane is known as the cytoplasm.  
• The mitochondrion is the site for the metabolic activities that 
provide energy the cell requires for its activities. 
• Ribosomes are for producing protein molecules. 
• Some ribosomes float freely, others are attached to the 
endoplasmic reticulum.
•
Vacuoles are fluid filled bubbles inside the cell.
9

Parts of a neurone (4)
• Unlike the spines, the surface of the soma is populated by voltage 
activated ion channels. 
• These channels help transmit the signals generated by the 
dendrites. 
• Emerging out from the soma is the axon hillock. 
• This region is characterized by having an incredibly high 
concentration of voltage activated sodium channels. 
• It is generally considered to be the spike initiation zone for action 
potentials.
• Multiple signals generated at the spines, and transmitted by the 
soma all converge here.
10

Parts of a neurone (5)
• Immediately after the axon hillock is the axon. 
• This is a thin tubular protrusion

An Overview of Experimentation 
Experimental psychology is the study of scientific methodology and the methods of experimentation. 
Experimental psychologists conduct research in almost all area of psychology – clinical, industrial, 
social, developmental, and so on. Experimental methods are the basis of experimental psychology. An 
understanding of the philosophy of science is important to an understanding of what science is, how 
the scientific method is used, and particularly of where experimentation fits into the more general 
framework of scientific methodology. With an understanding of the goals and functions of scientific 
methodology, the experimental psychologist is prepared to function efficiently, avoiding scientifically 
unsound procedures and fruitless problems. 
The Nature of science 
The questions that concern psychologists are singularly challenging – the complexity of the human 
mind. The study of psychological problems, therefore, requires the most effective research methods 
available. Experience over many centuries clearly indicates that scientific methods have yielded the 
soundest knowledge. 
Definitions of Science 
People define “science” in various ways, but generally they use either content or process definitions. 
A typical content definition is that “science is an accumulation of integrated knowledge,” whereas a 
process definition is that “science is an activity of discovering important variables in nature, of relating 
those variables, and of explaining those relationships (which are scientific laws).” A classical definition 
that incorporates content and process is “science is an interconnected series of concepts and 
conceptual schemes that have developed as a result of experimentation and observations” (Conant, 
1951, p. 25). A similar definition is that science is a systematically organized body of knowledge about 
the universe, obtained by the scientific method.” 
Scientific and Nonscientific Disciplines 
Sciences Use the Scientific Method. One common characteristic of the sciences is that they all use the 
same general approach in solving problems – a systematic serial process called the scientific method.  
Features of the Scientific Disciplines: 
(1) Solvable and Unsolvable Problems. The subject matter of the sciences are problems that can be 
solved. Briefly, a solvable problem is one that poses a question that can be answered with the 
use of normal capacities. An unsolvable problem raises a question that is unanswerable. 
Unsolvable problems often concern supernatural phenomena or questions about ultimate 
causes. For example, the question of what caused the universe is unsolvable and is typical of 
studies in religion and classical philosophy. 
(2) Science is Empirical. It is important to emphasize that “solvable” and “unsolvable” are technical 
terms so that certain vernacular meanings should not be read into them. The classification is not 
meant, for instance, to establish a hierarchy of values among the various disciplines by classifying 
them according to the type of problem studied. We are not necessarily saying, for example, that 
the problems of science are “better” or more important than the problem of religion. The 
distinction is that solvable problems may be empirically attacked. By empirical we mean relying 
on observations of natural events, such as behavior of other people. The person who attempts to 
solve problems through mysticism would not be using an empirical approach. Thus, solvable 
problems are susceptible to empirical solution by studying observable events. Unsolvable 
problems cannot be studied with the methods of empiricism. Consequently, science can be 

defined as the application of the scientific method to solvable problems. The study of solvable 
problems results in the accumulation of systematic knowledge.   
Psychology as a Science 
Psychology is Materialistic (Physicalistic), Objective, and Deterministic.

THE HYPOTHESIS 
Objective: To understand the scientific characteristics of hypotheses. 
What you are going to learn: 
1. That hypotheses are proposed relationships between variables and are tentative solutions to 
problems. 
2. That their basic format is that of a general implication wherein one variable implies another. 
3. That testable hypotheses always have a determinable degree of probability (they can never be 
absolutely true or false). 
At the end of the lecture:  
You should be able to state a hypothesis within the context of previous research, one that you can test in 
your own experiment. 
THE NATURE OF A HYPOTHESIS  
A scientific investigation must start with a solvable problem. A tentative solution is then offered in the 
form of a relevant hypothesis that is empirically testable - it must be possible to determine whether the 
hypothesis is probably true or probably false. If, after suitable experimentation, the relevant hypothesis 
is confirmed, it solves the problem. But if it is probably false, it obviously does not solve the problem.  
Explanatory Power of Hypotheses: Frequently, a confirmed hypothesis that solves a problem can be said to explain 
issues with which the problem is concerned. We use a hypothesis to state a possible relationship between one fact 
and another. If we find that the two facts are actually related in the manner stated by the hypothesis, then we have 
accomplished our immediate purpose – we have explained the first fact. 
What is a fact? Fact is a commonsense word, and as such its meaning is rather vague. We understand something 
by it, such as a fact is "an event of actual occurrence." It is something that we are sure has happened. Such 
commonsense words should be replaced, however, with more precise terms. For instance, instead of using the 
word fact, suppose we say a variable. Therefore, instead of saying that two facts are related, we may make the 
more productive statement that two variables are related. The advantages of this precision are sizable for we may 
now hypothesize a quantitative relationship – the greater the amount of time devoted to your study, the greater 
your score in a given course. With numbers we can say many more statements about the relationship between 
theses two variables. Later we will discuss quantitative statements of hypotheses. But for now, we may define a 
hypothesis as a testable statement of a potential relationship between variables that can explain "facts." 
The point to note is that an experiment is conducted to test an empirical relationship and, for convenience, we 
will usually refer to the statement of that relationship as a hypothesis. That a hypothesis is empirical means that it 
directly refers to data that we can obtain from our observation of nature. The variables contained in an empirical 
hypothesis are operationally definable and thus refer to events that can be directly measured. 
Hypothesis are synthetic statements. A synthetic statement may be either true or false; for example, the statement, 
“You are older than your sister” may be true or false. The important point for us is that a hypothesis must be a 
synthetic statement. Thus, any hypothesis must be capable of being established as (probably) true or false.  
MANNER OF STATING HYPOTHESES 
Granting, then, that a hypothesis is a statement of a potential empirical relationship between two or more variables, 
and also that it is possible to determine a degree of probability for it, we might ask what form that statement 
(proposition) should take; that is, precisely how should we state hypothesis in scientific work?

implication may be expressed as: "If..., then... "; that is, if certain conditions hold
