Psychology Research Ethics 
By Dr. Saul McLeod 
 
Ethics refers to the correct rules of conduct necessary when carrying out 
research. We have a moral responsibility to protect research participants from 
harm. 
However important the issue under investigation psychologists need to 
remember that they have a duty to respect the rights and dignity of research 
participants. This means that they must abide by certain moral principles and 
rules of conduct. 
In Britain, ethical guidelines for research are published by the British 
Psychological Society (BPS) and in America by the American Psychological 
Association (APA). The purpose of these codes of conduct is to protect 
research 
participants, 
the 
reputation 
of 
psychology, 
and 
psychologists themselves. 
  Ethical Issues in Psychology 
1. Informed Consent 
2. Debrief 
3. Protection of Participants 
4. Deception 
5. Confidentiality 
6. Withdrawal 
 
Moral issues rarely yield a simple, unambiguous, right or wrong answer. It is 
therefore often a matter of judgment whether the research is justified or not. 
For example, it might be that a study causes psychological or physical 
discomfort to participants, maybe they suffer pain or perhaps even come to 
serious harm. 
On the other hand, the investigation could lead to discoveries that benefit the 
participants themselves or even have the potential to increase the sum of human 
happiness. 
Rosenthal and Rosnow (1984) also talk about the potential costs of failing to 
carry out certain research. Who is to weigh up these costs and benefits? Who is 
to judge whether the ends justify the means? 
Finally, if you are ever in doubt as to whether research is ethical or not it is 
worthwhile remembering that if there is a conflict of interest between the 
participants and the researcher it is the interests of the subjects that should take 
priority. 

Studies must now undergo an extensive review by an institutional review board 
(US) or ethics committee (UK) before they are implemented. All UK research 
requires ethical approval by one or more of the following: 
(a) Department Ethics Committee (DEC): for most routine research. 
(b) Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC): for non routine research. 
(c) External Ethics Committee (EEC): for research that is externally 
regulated (e.g. NHS research). 
Committees review proposals assess if the potential benefits of the research are 
justifiable in the light of the possible risk of physical or psychological harm. 
These committees may request researchers make changes to the study's design 
or procedure, or in extreme cases deny approval of the study altogether. 
The British 
Psychological 
Society (BPS) 
and American 
Psychological 
Association (APA) have both issued a code of ethics in psychology that provides 
guidelines for the conduct of research.  Some of the more important ethical 
issues are as follows: 
 
Informed Consent 
Whenever possible investigators should obtain the consent of participants. In 
practice, this means it is not sufficient to simply get potential participants to say 
“Yes”. 
They also need to know what it is that they are agreeing to. In other words, the 
psychologist should, so far as is practicable explain what is involved in advance 
and obtain the informed consent of participants. 
Before the study begins the researcher must outline to the 
participants what the research is about, and then ask their 
consent (i.e. permission) to take part. An adult (18ys +) capable of 
giving permission to participate in a study can provide consent. Parents/legal 
guardians of minors can also provide consent to allow their children to 
participate in a study. 
However, it is not always possible to gain informed consent.  Where it is 
impossible for the researcher to ask the actual participants, a similar group of 
people can be asked how they would feel about taking part. 
If they think it would be OK then it can be assumed that the real participants 
will also find it acceptable

THE EXPERIMENTAL VARIABLES AND HOW TO CONTROL THEM 
Learning Objectives 
1. To analyze an experiment into its component variables and consider the potential relationships among them. 
2. To distinguish between stimulus and organismic variables. These two variables are subclassification of the 
independent variables (IV). 
3. Learn ways of measuring and evaluating dependent variables (DV). 
4. Know the empirical laws formulated as independent-dependent variable relationships. 
5. Learn methods of controlling extraneous variables. 
An experimental hypothesis is an assertion that systematic variation of (1) an independent variable produces 
lawful changes in (2) a dependent variable. If the findings of a suitably conducted experiment are in accord with 
the hypothesis, we increase our belief in that causal assertion. A critical characteristic of a sound experiment is 
that (3) the extraneous variables are controlled. The independent, dependent, and extraneous variables are, in 
an experiment, the three salient classes of variables that require special attention. Effective control of 
extraneous variables will allow us to reach a sound conclusion as to whether the IV does in fact causally affect 
the dependent variables. 
INDEPENDENT VARIABLES 
Stimulus Variables 
In experimentation the independent variable is a stimulus, where the word “stimulus” broadly refers to any 
aspect of the environment (physical, social, etc.) that excites the receptors. When we use the term "stimulus," 
though, we actually mean a certain stimulus class. A stimulus class is a number of similar instances of 
environmental events that are classified together.  
Examples of stimulus variables that might affect a particular kind of behaviour are the effects of different sizes 
or styles of type on reading speed, the effect of the intensity of light on the rate of eyelid conditioning, the effects 
of the number of people present at dinner on the amount of food eaten, and the effects of social atmosphere on 
problem-solving ability. 
Organismic Variables 
The possible relationships between organismic variables and behavior are studied using the method of 
systematic observation rather than experimentation. An organismic variable is any relatively stable physical 
characteristic of an organism such as gender, eye colour, height, weight, and body build, as well as such 
psychological characteristics as intelligence, educational level, neuroticism, and prejudice. The reason that we 
cannot study the effects of organismic variables in an experiment, at least with humans, is that we do not have 
the power to produce specific values of them, a point on which we shall shortly enlarge. 
DEPENDENT VARIABLES 
Response Measures 
Since in psychology we study behavior, and since the components of behaviour are responses, our dependent 
variables are response measures. “Response measures” is also an extremely broad class that includes such 
diverse phenomena as number of drops of saliva a dog secretes, number of errors a rat makes in a maze, time it 
takes a person to solve a problem, amplitude of electromyograms (electrical signals given off by muscles when 
they contract), number of words spoken in a given period of time, and judgements of people about certain traits. 
But whatever the response, it is best to measure it precisely as possible. In some experiments great precision can 
be achieved, and in others the characteristics of the events dictate cruder measures. Here are some standard 
ways of measuring responses. 

Page | 2

rifle at a target. Thus, a hit in the bull’s-eye might be scored a five, in the next outer circle a three, and in the next 
circle a one. Frequency of successes or errors is another response measure of accuracy (e.g., the number of errors 
one makes when taking a test).

Within-subjects design  
A within-subjects design refers to a study design where two or more measures are obtained from a 
sample of subjects. This type of design is also referred to as a repeated measures design.  
Three common circumstances lead to within-subjects designs.  
First, each subject is observed repeatedly in different conditions and the same measure is used as 
the outcome variable across the conditions. A main goal is to compare mean differences of the 
outcome variable across the conditions.  
Second, several related outcomes are measured collectively from each subject, such as an 
instrument with sub-scales, or related behavioural measures. 
In a within subject design, unlike a between subjects design, every single participant is 
subjected to every single treatment, including the control. 
This gives as many data sets as there are conditions for each participant; the fact that subjects act 
as their own control provides a way of reducing the amount of error arising from natural variance 
between individuals. 
 
These tests are common in many research disciplines. An education researcher might want to study 
the effect of a new program on children and test them before, and after, the new method has been 
applied. 
 
Psychologists often use them to test the relative effectiveness of a new treatment, often a difficult 
proposition. The sheer complexity of the human mind and the large number of 
potential confounding variables often renders between subjects designs unreliable, 
especially when necessarily small sample groups make a more random approach impossible. 
 
Examples of Within Subject Designs 
One of the simplest within subject designs is opinion - watch any formalized debate and you will see 
the process. The chairperson will take a vote before the debate, to establish a baseline opinion, and 
will ask the audience to vote again at the end. The team that gained the most votes obviously 
managed to sway opinion in the same subjects much better, so can be announced as the winner. 
Another common example of a within-subjects design is medical testing, where researchers try to 
establish whether a drug is effective or whether a placebo effect is in order. The researchers, in 
the crudest form of the test, will give all of the participants the placebo, for a time, and monitor the 
results. They would then administer the drug for a period and test the results. 
 
Of course, the researchers could just as easily administer the drug first and then the placebo. This 
ensures that every subject acts as their own control, so there are few problems with matching age, 
gender and lifestyle, reducing the chance of confounding factors. 
 
The Advantages of Within Subject Designs 
The main advantage that the within subject design has over the between subject design is that it requires fewer 
participants, making the process much more streamlined and less resource heavy. 
 
For example, if you want to test four conditions, using four groups of 30 participants is unwieldy and expensive. 
Using one group, which is tested for all four, is a much easier way. Ease is not the only advantage, because a 

well planned within subject design allows researchers to monitor the effect upon individuals much more easily and 
lower the possibility of individual differences skewing the results. 
Within-subjects is typically used for longitudinal studies or observational studies conducted over an 
extended period of time. It may be appropriate to use a within-subjects design if factors in the subjects' past 
may influence the results of the experiment. It is best to use a within-subjects design if there is a likelihood 
that the participants' previous experiences will have an effect on the experiment.

HOW TO READ AND WRITE RESEARCH REPORTS 
HOW TO DO A LITERATURE SEARCH



 Introduction

WRITING A RESEARCH REPORT 
 
Format 
 
Trying to read a psychology journal article for the first time can be a challenging experience. Researchers write 
articles for other researchers, so they use jargon and a terse writing style. These features aid communication 
among scholars in a particular field, who can read short reports and understand them. But such writing can be 
difficult to comprehend for students beginning their study of a field. This chapter is designed to prepare you 
for your first encounter with the literature of experimental psychology.  
Because psychology is a science, progress is measured by the accumulation of knowledge in the various fields. 
Researchers spend a great deal of their time reading and writing journal articles in an effort to contribute to 
this body of knowledge. Even if your career in psychology extends no further than this course, you will discover 
that critical thinking and writing skills are invaluable for living in a world that revolves around information. To 
help you become fluent in the art of reading and writing research reports, we describe the format and style 
most often used in journal articles.  
Hints are provided to help you become a critical reader, skilled at objectively evaluating an article. With some 
practice, you will acquire skills on how to understand every psychology article you read. This note ends with 
some recommendations for writing a research report. 
 
 ▼ HOW TO DO A LITERATURE SEARCH 
Once you have come up with a research idea, the next step is usually to conduct a literature search. The 
purpose of a literature search is to find out what other researchers have previously discovered about a 
particular topic. This is done by tracking down published articles in which researchers have reported their 
scientific findings. 

2 | P a g e 
 
The easiest way to conduct a literature search is by computer. Many libraries allow you to access electronic 
databases that contain abstracts of articles from journals that publish psychological research. More will be 
said about abstracts later, but typically they are short summaries (sometimes 180 words or less) of the 
experiments in the article. One of the most important electronic databases is PsycINFO, which currently 
contains more than 2 million records. With an electronic database, you provide a topic and the computer scans 
for abstracts related to that topic. Some databases also allow you to scan for government documents and 
technical reports that often do not have abstracts.  
Another popular way to conduct a computerized literature search is to use the Internet search engine Google 
Scholar (http://scholar.google.com/), which scans scholarly literature in many disciplines, including 
psychology. An excellent electronic resource for learning about the latest research findings is the Social Science 
Citation Index. By entering information about a key article that you have  already found,  you  can  obtain  a 
list of more  recent  articles  that have  cited  your article  and view  their abstracts. Because these articles 
contain a discussion of your key article, it is very likely that they are directly related to your topic of interest. 
This is an extremely efficient way to bring yourself up to date in some specific content area. 
After you  have  found  an abstract  of interest  to you,  you  can  then  find the entire article  in your  library  
or send  a note to the author  requesting a reprint  of the article  or additional information. Many libraries now 
provide access to electronic versions of research journals, so you may be able to download the article directly 
from a computer.

COURSE OUTLINE

2

EMPLOYEE TRAINING AND DEVELOPMENT
3

Employee Training and Development
After applying for jobs, screened, interviewed, and “courted” to 
some extent by your employer, you will be anxious to get to work—
to show them what you can do and to make your mark on the 
company. 
However, before you are able to get started, the company sends 
you to a training center where you will learn the basics of the job, 
learn company policies and procedures, and learn about the 
culture of your new organization.
Employee training is a planned effort by an organization to facilitate 
employees’ learning, retention, and transfer of job-related 
behavior. 
In most organizations, training is not limited to new employees, as 
various types of training and development programs are offered at 
all stages of an employee’s career.
4

Employee Training and Development (Cont.)
1) We will begin by examining areas of employee training. 
2) We will also examine the fundamentals of the learning 
process and how learning applies to employee training and 
development. 
3) We will then look at factors that affect the success of training 
programs. 
4) Next, we will look at how employee training needs are 
assessed and study general training methods. 
5) Finally, we will examine how training programs are 
evaluated.
5

(1.) Areas of Employee Training 
Training, like learning, is a lifelong process. Organizations need to 
provide for the wide variety of training needs of workers to stay 
competitive.
a.)  New employee orientation and training
Orientation programs are typically designed to introduce 
employees to the organization and its goals, philosophy, policies, 
and procedures. 
They can also acquaint workers with both the physical structure 
and the personnel structure of the organization, such as the chain 
of supervisory command and the various relevant departments and 
divisions. 
During orientation new employees also learn about compensation, 
benefits, and safety rules and procedures.
6

(1.) Areas of Employee Training (Cont.)
Initial training should provide enough information so that new employees can 
quickly become productive members of the organization’s workforce. 
In fact, there is some evidence that when it comes to employee orientation 
and early training, more is better (Saks, 1996). 
An additional function of an orientation program is to help newcomers deal 
with the stresses of adjusting to a new work environment (Wanous, 1993; 
Waung, 1995).
Although new employee orientation and training are a large part of most 
organizations’ training programs, many do not give sufficient attention or 
resources to this area, despite its very important role in creating a productive 
and dedicated workforce. 
In fact, research shows that new workers are often eager and willing to learn 
(Morrison, 1993). Moreover, evidence suggests that employees receiving

HUMAN RESOURCE PLANNING
Human resource planning (HRP), sometimes referred

right number of qualified people into the right job at 
the right time.” 
HRP is the system of matching the supply of people 
– internally (existing employees) – and externally
(those to be hired or searched for) – with the 
openings the organization expects to have over a 
given time frame.

Human Resource Planning (Cont.)
The first challenge of HRP is to translate the 
organization’s plans and objectives into a timed 
schedule of employee requirements. 
Once the employee requirements have been 
determined, HRP must devise plans for securing the 
necessary employees. 
Basically, all organizations engage in human 
resource planning either formally or informally. Some 
organizations do a good job and others a poor job.

In essence, the human resource demands and 
needs are derived from the strategic and operating 
planning of the organization and then compared 
with human resource availability. 
Then a variety of programs such as recruiting,

gaps.

derived from the organization’s short-term 
performance objectives.

been called the cascade approach to 
objective setting.

JOB ANALYSIS
One of the most basic personnel functions is job analysis, or 
the systematic study of the tasks, duties, and responsibilities 
of a job and the knowledge, skills, and abilities  needed to 
perform it. 
Job analysis is the starting  point  for nearly all personnel 
functions, and  job analysis is critically important for 
developing the means for assessing personnel (Wheaton & 
Whetzel,  1997).  
Before  a worker can be hired  or trained and  before  a 
worker’s performance can be evaluated, it is critical to 
understand exactly what the  worker’s job entails.

Such job analyses should
also be conducted on a
periodic basis to ensure that the information on jobs is up
to date. In other words, it needs to reflect the work
actually being performed.
For example, as time goes by, an administrative assistant in
a small organization might assume additional tasks and
responsibilities that did not exist earlier. If the company has
to replace this person, but does not have an up-to-date job
analysis for the position, it is doubtful that the company
would be able to hire an individual with all the knowledge,
skills, abilities, and other characteristics needed to perform
the job as it currently exists.

Job Analysis (Cont.)
Because  most  jobs consist  of a variety of tasks and  duties,  gaining  a full 
understanding of a job is not always easy. Therefore, job analysis methods 
need to be comprehensive and precise.  
Indeed, large  organizations have specialists whose primary responsibilities are to 
analyze the various jobs in the company and develop extensive and current 
descriptions for each.
Most jobs are quite complex and require workers to possess certain  types 
of knowledge and skills to perform a variety of different tasks. 
Workers may need to operate complex machinery to perform their jobs or they might  
need to possess a great deal of information about  a particular product or service. 
Jobs might also require workers to interact effectively with different
types of people, or a single job might require a worker to possess all these
important skills and knowledge.
As jobs become more  and  more  complex, the need for effective and  
comprehensive job analyses becomes  increasingly  important.

To perform a good job analysis, the job analyst must be
well trained in the basic research methods.
Job
analysis
typically

the
objective

performed by actual

Therefore, a job analyst must be an expert
in objective

In fact, a review of research on job analysis suggests that
experience and training in job analysis methods are critical
for effective job analysis (Landy,
1993; Voskuijl & van
Sliedregt, 2002).

A job analysis leads directly to the development of
several other important personnel “products”:
a job description,

J O B    D E S I G N

Job design is the process of structuring work and 
designating the specific work activities of an individual 
or group of individuals to achieve certain organizational 
objectives.
Designing a job involves making decisions as to 
who, 
what, 
where, 
when, 
why, and 
how the job will be performed.
JOB DESIGN

1.
The specification of individual tasks: What different 
tasks must be performed?
2.
The specification of the method of performing each 
task: Specifically, how will each task be performed?
3.
The combination of individual tasks into specific jobs 
to be assigned to individuals: How will the different 
tasks be grouped to form jobs?
The job design process can generally be divided 
into three phases:

Phase 1 and 3 determines the content of the job, while 
phase 2 indicates precisely how the job is to be 
performed. 
The overall goal of job design is 
to develop work assignments that meet the 
requirements of the organization and the technology; 
and 
satisfy the personal and individual requirements of the 
jobholder. 
Process of job design (contd.)

The key to successful job design is to balance the 
requirements of the organization and the jobholder. 
For many years, the prevailing practice in designing jobs 
was to focus almost entirely on simplifying the tasks to be 
undertaken. This usually resulted in making jobs as 
specialized as possible. 
While job specialization has many advantages it can 
result in boredom and even degradation of the 
jobholder. 
A classic example of specialization is the automobile 
assembly line. The idea is to specialize but not to overdo it.
Process of job design (contd.)

1.
Fewer skills required per person, which makes it 
easier to recruit and train employees.
2.
Increased proficiency through repetition and 
practice of the same tasks.
3.
More efficient use of skills by primarily utilizing each 
employee’s best skills.
4.
Low wages due to the ease with which labour can 
be substituted.
5.
More conformity in the final product or service.
6.
Different tasks performed concurrently.
Advantages of Job Specialization

Job scope and job depth are two important 
dimensions of job design.
Job scope refers to the number and variety of 
different tasks performed by the jobholder.
In a job with narrow scope, the jobholder 
performs a few different tasks and repeats those 
tasks frequently. 
The negative effects of jobs limited in scope vary 
with the jobholder, but can result in more errors 
and lower quality. 
JOB SCOPE AND JOB DEPTH

Job depth refers to the freedom of jobholders to 
plan and organize their own work, work at their 
own pace, and move around and 
communicate as desired.
A lack of job depth can result in job 
dissatisfaction, which in turn can lead to 
tardiness, absenteeism, and even sabotage.
Job Scope and Job Depth (contd.)

A job can be high in job scope and low in the job 
depth, or vice versa.
For example, newspaper delivery involves the same 
few tasks each time, but there is considerable 
freedom in organizing and pacing the work. 
Therefore, the job is low in scope but high in depth.
Of course, many jobs are low in (or high) in both job 
scope and job depth.

DEFINITION AND NATURE OF DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY 
 
Developmental Psychology is one of the sub-fields of Psychology. It is an ontogenetic study of 
human organism from conception to death. Developmental Psychology seeks understanding and 
controls the basic processes and dynamics underlying human behavior at the various stages of 
life. Its investigations encompass the growth and maturation of the individual organism, its 
cognitive and emotional powers, as well as its personality structure. 
Developmental Psychology, as a science of growth, deals with all the processes contributing to 
becoming an infant, a child, an adolescent, and a mature adult. 
According to Hurlock, "Developmental Psychology is the branch of psychology that studies 
intraindividual changes and interindividual changes within these intraindividual changes. Its task 
is not only description but also explication of age-related changes in behavior in terms of 
antecedent consequent relationship." 
Some developmental psychologists study developmental changes covering the life span from 
conception to death. Others cover only a segment of the life span, childhood or old age. 
Developmental Psychology is a scientific discipline that attempts: (i) to devise methods for 
studying organisms as they evolve over time (ii) to collect facts about individuals of different 
ages, backgrounds and personalities and (iii) to construct a theoretical frame work that can 
account for the observed behaviors as well as for the changes occurring throughout the life 
cycle. 
 
Aspects of Development 
There are four aspects of development which are closely intertwined. Each aspect of 
development affects the other. 
• 
Physical development 
• 
Intellectual development 
• 
Personality development 
• 
Social development 
 
We will now discuss each of these in brief. 
1. Physical development. Physical development consists of changes in the body, brain, sensory 
capacities and motor skills. They exert major influences on both intellect and personality. For 
example, much of an infant's knowledge comes from the senses and from motor activity. A child 
who has a hearing loss is at risk of delayed language development. In late adulthood, physical 
changes in the brain as in Alzheimer's disease which has been estimated to affect about 10 
percent of people over the age of 65 (Evans et aL 1989) can result in intellectual and personality 
deterioration. 
2. Intellectual development. Changes in mental abilities such as learning, memory, reasoning, 
thinking and language are aspects of intellectual development. These changes are closely related 
to both motor and emotional development. A baby's growing memory, for example, is related to 
separation anxiety, the fear that the mot

Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
simplypsychology.org/kohlberg.html
Saul McLeod, updated 2013
Lawrence Kohlberg (1958) agreed with Piaget's (1932) theory of moral development in
principle but wanted to develop his ideas further. 
He used Piaget’s storytelling technique to tell people stories involving moral dilemmas.  In
each case, he presented a choice to be considered, for example, between the rights of
some authority and the needs of some deserving individual who is being unfairly treated.
One of the best known of Kohlberg’s (1958) stories concerns a man called Heinz who lived
somewhere in Europe.
Heinz’s wife was dying from a particular type of cancer. Doctors said a new drug might save
her. The drug had been discovered by a local chemist, and the Heinz tried desperately to buy
some, but the chemist was charging ten times the money it cost to make the drug, and this was
much more than the Heinz could afford.
Heinz could only raise half the money, even after help from family and friends. He explained
to the chemist that his wife was dying and asked if he could have the drug cheaper or pay the
rest of the money later.
The chemist refused, saying that he had discovered the drug and was going to make money
from it. The husband was desperate to save his wife, so later that night he broke into the
chemist’s and stole the drug.
Kohlberg asked a series of questions such as:
1. Should Heinz have stolen the drug?
2. Would it change anything if Heinz did not love his wife?
3. What if the person dying was a stranger, would it make any difference?
4. Should the police arrest the chemist for murder if the woman died?
By studying the answers from children of different ages to these questions, Kohlberg hoped
to discover how moral reasoning changed as people grew older. The sample comprised 72
Chicago boys aged 10–16 years, 58 of whom were followed up at three-yearly intervals for
20 years (Kohlberg, 1984).
1/6

Each boy was given a 2-hour interview based on the ten dilemmas. What Kohlberg was
mainly interested in was not whether the boys judged the action right or wrong, but the
reasons given for the decision. He found that these reasons tended to change as the
children got older.
He identified three distinct levels of moral reasoning each with two sub-stages. People can
only pass through these levels in the order listed. Each new stage replaces the reasoning
typical of the earlier stage. Not everyone achieves all the stages.
Level 1 - Pre-conventional morality
At the pre-conventional level (most nine-year-olds and younger, some over nine), we don’t
have a personal code of morality. Instead, our moral code is shaped by the standards of
adults and the consequences of following or breaking their rules.
Authority is outside the individual and reasoning is based on the physical consequences of
actions.
• Stage 1. Obedience and Punishment Orientation. The child/individual is good in order
to avoid being punished. If a person is punished, they must have done wrong.
• Stage 2. Individualism and Exchange. At this stage, children recognize that there is not
just one right view that is handed down by the authorities. Different individuals have
different viewpoints.
Level 2 - Conventional morality
At the conventional level (most adolescents and adults), we begin to internalize the moral
standards of valued adult role models.
Authority is internalized but not questioned, and reasoning is based on the norms of the
group to which the person belongs.
• Stage 3. Good Interpersonal Relationships. The child/individual is good in order to be
seen as being a good person by others. Therefore, answers relate to the approval of
others.
• Stage 4. Maintaining the Social Order. The child/individual becomes aware of the wider
rules of society, so judgments concern obeying the rules in order to uphold the law and to
avoid guilt.

NOBA
Social and Personality Development in
Childhood
Ross Thompson
Childhood social and personality development emerges through the interaction of social
influences, biological maturation, and the child’s representations of the social world and the
self. This interaction is illustrated in a discussion of the influence of significant relationships,
the development of social understanding, the growth of personality, and the development of
social and emotional competence in childhood.
Learning Objectives
• Provide specific examples of how the interaction of social experience, biological maturation,
and the child’s representations of experience and the self provide the basis for growth in
social and personality development.
• Describe the significant contributions of parent–child and peer relationships to the
development of social skills and personality in childhood.
• Explain how achievements in social understanding occur in childhood. Moreover, do
scientists believe that infants and young children are egocentric?
• Describe the association of temperament with personality development.
• Explain what is “social and emotional competence“ and provide some examples of how it
develops in childhood.

Introduction
“How have I become the kind of person I am today?” Every adult ponders this question from
time to time. The answers that readily come to mind include the influences of parents, peers,
temperament, a moral compass, a strong sense of self, and sometimes critical life experiences
such as parental divorce. Social and personality development encompasses these and many
other influences on the growth of the person. In addition, it addresses questions that are at
the heart of understanding how we develop as unique people. How much are we products of
nature or nurture? How enduring are the influences of early experiences? The study of social
and personality development offers perspective on these and other issues, often by showing
how complex and multifaceted are the influences on developing children, and thus the
intricate processes that have made you the person you are today (Thompson, 2006a).
Understanding social and personality
development requires looking at children
from three perspectives that interact to
shape development. The first is the social
context in which each child lives,
especially the relationships that provide
security, guidance, and knowledge. The
second is biological maturation that
supports developing social and emotional
competencies and underlies temperamental
individuality. The third is children’s
developing representations of themselves
and 
the 
social 
world. 
Social 
and
personality development is best understood
as the continuous interaction between
these social, biological, and representational
aspects of psychological development.
Relationships

infants and their parents in the first year. Virtually all infants living in normal circumstances
develop strong emotional attachments to those who care for them. Psychologists believe that
the development of these attachments is as biologically natural as learning to walk and not
simply a byproduct of the parents’ provision of food or warmth. Rather, attachments have

Endocrine System
being the title of a presentation by
Professor Adebayo O. Adejumo
MHSc(Canada) PhD(Ibadan) FWACN
Department of Psychology,
University of Ibadan
17 May, 2021
1

Outline
i.
Introduction
ii. Anterior Pituitary Hormones
iii. Posterior Pituitary Hormones
iv. Disorders (Oversecretion / Undersecretion)
v. Summary
2

Introduction 1
• The endocrine system consists of glands widely separated from 
each other with no direct anatomical links. 
• Endocrine glands consist of groups of secretory cells surrounded 
by an extensive network of capillaries which facilitates diffusion 
of hormones from the secretory cells in the blood stream. 
• They are commonly referred to as the ductless glands because 
the hormones are secreted and diffuse directly into the blood 
stream.    
3

Introduction 2
• Human and animal behaviour is a collective role of the genetic 
make-up, nervous system, endocrine system as well as the 
environment of an organism. 
• The nervous and endocrine systems play a major role in 
establishing and regulating behaviours on the basis of a stimulus-
response relationship. 
• The endocrine system works correspondingly with the nervous 
system to control consistent patterns of responding to internal 
and external cues in an organism’s effort to maintain physiological 
and psychological balance. 
4

Introduction 3
• To achieve this, the nervous system harmonizes rapid and 
very accurate responses to stimuli, using action potentials, 
while the endocrine system 
• The nervous system coordinates rapid and precise responses 
to stimuli using action potentials while the endocrine system 
maintains homeostasis and long-term control using chemical 
signals. 
5

Introduction 4
• The nervous and endocrine systems are involved in a feedback 
mechanism which regulates body functions and maintains 
homeostasis. 
• The endocrine and nervous systems are so closely linked that they 
are often are considered a single system – The Neuro-Endocrine 
System. 
• Both nerve impulses and hormones elicit a response however, 
nerve impulses prompt a nearly instantaneous response to a 
change in the environment while hormones on the other hand are 
released more slowly than nerve impulses, but their effects 
usually last longer.
• Effects of some hormones can last 10 to 20 minutes while others 
can last for several hours. 
6

Introduction 5
• A hormone is any of a large number of chemical substances 
secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood stream by an 
endocrine gland. 
• This secretion is transported to another part of the body where 
it binds to a specific type of receptor. 
• At the receptor site, the hormone exerts a particular effect. 
• The effect enables the endocrine system to function as a 
communication system between cells and alongside and 
independently of the nervous system. 
• Most hormones are produced from amino acids (proteins) and 
fats.  
7

Major Endocrine Glands
• The endocrine system consists of a number of distinct glands and 
some other tissues in other organs.  
• Although the hypothalamus is classified as a part of the brain and 
not as an endocrine gland it controls the pituitary gland and has 
an indirect effect on many others. 
• The endocrine glands are:
•
1 pituitary gland
•
1 thyroid gland
•
4 parathyroid glands
•
2 adrenal (suprarenal) glands
•
1 Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)
•
1 pineal gland or body
•
1 thymus gland
•
2 ovaries in the female
•
2 testes in the male  
8

Diagram showing locations of the endocrine 
glands in the body
9

Release of Hormones (1)
• The level of a hormone in the blood is variable and self regulating 
within its normal range. 
• A hormone is released in response to a specific stimulus and 
usually its action reverses or negates the stimulus through a 
negative feedback mechanism.

Psycho-biological Study of Behaviour
By Dr. Adejumo
Department of Psychology
University of Ibadan
1

Abstract
Biological psychology provides the link between biology and psychological events such as how
the nervous and endocrine systems influence conscious and unconscious overt and covert
behaviours in humans and non-humans. It rests on the belief that transient and repetitive
behaviours are related to neural, hormonal, and other bio-psychosocial events in an organism,
and that the organism’s behavior is a product of known or unknown brain activities. 
       The course is laid out in three units. Unit One provides a general introduction the nervous
system, a little deeper than the level of information obtained in our earlier PSY 101 and PSY
207. Unit Two explores the human brain and its role in human behavior, while Unit Three
discusses the link between neuro-endocrinology and behavior. These topics were laid, mindful of
the information obtained in earlier pre-requisite courses, with deeper attention to diagrammatic
illustrations in relating theoretical information to practical skills required in biological
psychology. 
      Instructions follow a logical sequence, such that knowledge flows from simple to complex.
Although, it is recommended that practical the instructions should be practically demonstrated,
students are advised to make use of the diagrammatic illustrations included in this course
material. Learners require deliberate effort not only to learn the topics, but to make conscious
efforts to appropriately apply the concepts to real life situations as often as possible.
2

General Course introduction and objectives 
        This course is designed to explain human and animal behavior from psycho-biological
perspective. Psychobiology is a biological discipline that focuses on the mind and mental
process. Biological psychology is a branch or type of psychology that brings together biology
and psychology to understand behavior and thought. Biological psychology looks at the link
between biology and psychological events such as how information travels throughout our
bodies (neural impulses, axons, dendrites, etc.), how different neurotransmitters affect sleep,
dreams, and other behaviors, among others. 
        There is close association between the domains of behavioral neuroscience, biological
psychology, biopsychology, and psychobiology. One thing is common to them all; they consider
the application of the biological principles (especially neurobiology), to the study of
physiological, genetic, and developmental mechanisms of behavior in human and non-human
animals. It investigates at the level of nerves, neurotransmitters, brain and endocrine mechanisms
and the basic biological processes that underlie normal and abnormal human and animal
behavior. 
           Psycho-biology relies heavily on research, examinations, and investigations. Knowledge
about most human and animal behavior is gained from deliberate, planned, scientific, and many
times experimental studies. Specialised equipment items and techniques are often used in
identifying the role of biological, developmental, socio-psychosocial, and environmental factors
in psychological functioning across ages. Biological psychology is an interdisciplinary research
field aimed at understanding and explaining psychological and overall functioning. 
        With these, the pupil psychologist is expected to have basic, yet sufficiently in-depth
biological understanding of why people do what they. This helps to concretize cause and effect
relationship, as a foundation for providing scientific explanation for human and animal
behaviours.
3

DEFINITION AND NATURE OF DEVELOPMENTAL PSYCHOLOGY 
 
Developmental Psychology is one of the sub-fields of Psychology. It is an ontogenetic study of 
human organism from conception to death. Developmental Psychology seeks understanding and 
controls the basic processes and dynamics underlying human behavior at the various stages of 
life. Its investigations encompass the growth and maturation of the individual organism, its 
cognitive and emotional powers, as well as its personality structure. 
Developmental Psychology, as a science of growth, deals with all the processes contributing to 
becoming an infant, a child, an adolescent, and a mature adult. 
According to Hurlock, "Developmental Psychology is the branch of psychology that studies 
intraindividual changes and interindividual changes within these intraindividual changes. Its task 
is not only description but also explication of age-related changes in behavior in terms of 
antecedent consequent relationship." 
Some developmental psychologists study developmental changes covering the life span from 
conception to death. Others cover only a segment of the life span, childhood or old age. 
Developmental Psychology is a scientific discipline that attempts: (i) to devise methods for 
studying organisms as they evolve over time (ii) to collect facts about individuals of different 
ages, backgrounds and personalities and (iii) to construct a theoretical frame work that can 
account for the observed behaviors as well as for the changes occurring throughout the life 
cycle. 
 
Aspects of Development 
There are four aspects of development which are closely intertwined. Each aspect of 
development affects the other. 
• 
Physical development 
• 
Intellectual development 
• 
Personality development 
• 
Social development 
 
We will now discuss each of these in brief. 
1. Physical development. Physical development consists of changes in the body, brain, sensory 
capacities and motor skills. They exert major influences on both intellect and personality. For 
example, much of an infant's knowledge comes from the senses and from motor activity. A child 
who has a hearing loss is at risk of delayed language development. In late adulthood, physical 
changes in the brain as in Alzheimer's disease which has been estimated to affect about 10 
percent of people over the age of 65 (Evans et aL 1989) can result in intellectual and personality 
deterioration. 
2. Intellectual development. Changes in mental abilities such as learning, memory, reasoning, 
thinking and language are aspects of intellectual development. These changes are closely related 
to both motor and emotional development. A baby's growing memory, for example, is related to

Kohlberg's Stages of Moral Development
simplypsychology.org/kohlberg.html
Saul McLeod, updated 2013
Lawrence Kohlberg (1958) agreed with Piaget's (1932) theory of moral development in
principle but wanted to develop his ideas further. 
He used Piaget’s storytelling technique to tell people stories involving moral dilemmas.  In
each case, he presented a choice to be considered, for example, between the rights of
some authority and the needs of some deserving individual who is being unfairly treated.
One of the best known of Kohlberg’s (1958) stories concerns a man called Heinz who lived
somewhere in Europe.
Heinz’s wife was dying from a particular type of cancer. Doctors said a new drug might save
her. The drug had been discovered by a local chemist, and the Heinz tried desperately to buy
some, but the chemist was charging ten times the money it cost to make the drug, and this was
much more than the Heinz could afford.
Heinz could only raise half the money, even after help from family and friends. He explained
to the chemist that his wife was dying and asked if he could have the drug cheaper or pay the
rest of the money later.
The chemist refused, saying that he had discovered the drug and was going to make money
from it. The husband was desperate to save his wife, so later that night he broke into the
chemist’s and stole the drug.
Kohlberg asked a series of questions such as:
1. Should Heinz have stolen the drug?
2. Would it change anything if Heinz did not love his wife?
3. What if the person dying was a stranger, would it make any difference?
4. Should the police arrest the chemist for murder if the woman died?
By studying the answers from children of different ages to these questions, Kohlberg hoped
to discover how moral reasoning changed as people grew older. The sample comprised 72
Chicago boys aged 10–16 years, 58 of whom were followed up at three-yearly intervals for
20 years (Kohlberg, 1984).
1/6

Each boy was given a 2-hour interview based on the ten dilemmas. What Kohlberg was
mainly interested in was not whether the boys judged the action right or wrong, but the
reasons given for the decision. He found that these reasons tended to change as the
children got older.
He identified three distinct levels of moral reasoning each with two sub-stages. People can
only pass through these levels in the order listed. Each new stage replaces the reasoning
typical of the earlier stage. Not everyone achieves all the stages.
Level 1 - Pre-conventional morality
At the pre-conventional level (most nine-year-olds and younger, some over nine), we don’t
have a personal code of morality. Instead, our moral code is shaped by the standards of
adults and the consequences of following or breaking their rules.
Authority is outside the individual and reasoning is based on the physical consequences of
actions.
• Stage 1. Obedience and Punishment Orientation. The child/individual is good in order
to avoid being punished. If a person is punished, they must have done wrong.
• Stage 2. Individualism and Exchange. At this stage, children recognize that there is not
just one right view that is handed down by the authorities. Different individuals have
different viewpoints.
Level 2 - Conventional morality
At the conventional level (most adolescents and adults), we begin to internalize the moral
standards of valued adult role models.
Authority is internalized but not questioned, and reasoning is based on the norms of the
group to which the person belongs.
• Stage 3. Good Interpersonal Relationships. The child/individual is good in order to be
seen as being a good person by others. Therefore, answers relate to the approval of
others.
• Stage 4. Maintaining the Social Order. The child/individual becomes aware of the wider
rules of society, so judgments concern obeying the rules in order to uphold the law and to
avoid guilt.

Individual judgment is based on self-chosen principles, and moral reasoning is based on

Social and Personality Development in
Childhood
Ross Thompson
Childhood social and personality development emerges through the interaction of social
influences, biological maturation, and the child’s representations of the social world and the
self. This interaction is illustrated in a discussion of the influence of significant relationships,
the development of social understanding, the growth of personality, and the development of
social and emotional competence in childhood.
Learning Objectives
• Provide specific examples of how the interaction of social experience, biological maturation,
and the child’s representations of experience and the self provide the basis for growth in
social and personality development.
• Describe the significant contributions of parent–child and peer relationships to the
development of social skills and personality in childhood.
• Explain how achievements in social understanding occur in childhood. Moreover, do
scientists believe that infants and young children are egocentric?
• Describe the association of temperament with personality development.
• Explain what is “social and emotional competence“ and provide some examples of how it
develops in childhood.

Introduction
“How have I become the kind of person I am today?” Every adult ponders this question from
time to time. The answers that readily come to mind include the influences of parents, peers,
temperament, a moral compass, a strong sense of self, and sometimes critical life experiences
such as parental divorce. Social and personality development encompasses these and many
other influences on the growth of the person. In addition, it addresses questions that are at
the heart of understanding how we develop as unique people. How much are we products of
nature or nurture? How enduring are the influences of early experiences? The study of social
and personality development offers perspective on these and other issues, often by showing
how complex and multifaceted are the influences on developing children, and thus the
intricate processes that have made you the person you are today (Thompson, 2006a).
Understanding social and personality
development requires looking at children
from three perspectives that interact to
shape development. The first is the social
context in which each child lives,
especially the relationships that provide
security, guidance, and knowledge. The
second is biological maturation that
supports developing social and emotional
competencies and underlies temperamental
individuality. The third is children’s
developing representations of themselves
and 
the 
social 
world. 
Social 
and
personality development is best understood
as the continuous interaction between
these social, biological, and representational
aspects of psychological development.
Relationships
This interaction can be observed in the development of the earliest relationships between
infants and their parents in the first year. Virtually all infants living in normal circumstances
develop strong emotional attachments to those who care for them. Psychologists believe that
the development of these attachments is as biologically natural as learning to walk and not
simply a byproduct of the parents’ provision of food or warmth. Rather, attachments have

text_snippet:
Humanistic theories
These  are a group of psychological theories that emphasize the uniqueness and potential of the individual. They focus on the subjective experience of the person, rather than on external factors such as behavior, personality traits, or unconscious conflicts.
There are several humanistic theories, but two of the most influential ones are:
• Maslow's hierarchy of needs: proposed by Abraham Maslow, this theory suggests that human needs are arranged in a hierarchy, with basic physiological and safety needs at the bottom, followed by social, esteem, and self-actualization needs at the top. According to Maslow, people are motivated to satisfy their needs in order to achieve self-actualization, which is the realization of their full potential.
• Rogers' person-centered theory: developed by Carl Rogers, this theory emphasizes the importance of empathy, unconditional positive regard, and authenticity in the therapeutic relationship. According to Rogers, people have an innate tendency towards growth and self-actualization, but this can be blocked by negative experiences and conditions of worth imposed by others. The role of the therapist is to create a supportive environment that allows the client to explore their feelings and develop their own solutions to their problems.
Purpose of personality assessment 
Personality assessment is an important aspect of psychology, and it is used for a variety of reasons. Some of the main reasons for personality assessment include:
• Understanding the individual: Personality assessment helps to understand an individual's traits, behaviors, and characteristics. It can provide insight into how they think, feel, and interact with others.
• Diagnosis: Personality assessment can be used to diagnose personality disorders, such as borderline personality disorder or narcissistic personality disorder. It can also be used to assess the severity of symptoms and determine the most appropriate treatment.
• Career counseling: Personality assessment can be used in career counseling to help individuals identify their strengths, weaknesses, and interests. It can also provide insight into the types of jobs or careers that are likely to be a good fit for them.
• Research: Personality assessment is used in research to study the relationships between personality traits and various outcomes, such as health, job performance, and relationships.
• Personal growth and development: Personality assessment can be used to identify areas for personal growth and development. It can also help individuals to understand how they can improve their relationships, increase their well-being, and achieve their goals.
Personality assessment is a valuable tool in psychology that can be used for a variety of
reasons, including understanding the individual, diagnosing personality disorders, career counseling, research, and personal growth and development
Methods of personality assessment 
There are various methods of personality assessment that psychologists use to understand an individual's traits, behaviors, and characteristics. Some of the most commonly used methods are:
Self-report questionnaires: These are standardized questionnaires that ask individuals to rate their own personality traits and characteristics. Examples include the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI), the Big Five Inventory (BFI), and the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI).
Projective tests: These are tests that ask individuals to interpret ambiguous stimuli, such as inkblots or pictures, in order to reveal unconscious aspects of their personality. Examples include the Rorschach Inkblot Test and the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT).

What is Sensation?
A stimulus is any form of energy that can be detected by a specialized sense organ.

Examples are lights, sound, taste, temperature, touch, etc.

It is important to note that sense organs are specialized. In order words, they have specific stimuli they can detect and not others. For example, eyes can see objects but cannot hear sounds.
17/04/2024
3

--- SLIDE ---

Senses and their Stimulus
17/04/2024
4

--- SLIDE ---

The Stimulus
As earlier mention, stimulus is any form of energy that can be detected with a specialized sense organ. 
The stimulus could be existing both “out there,” in the environment, and within the person’s body.
Internal stimulus comes from within. Examples include the feeling of stomach pain, headaches, etc.
17/04/2024
5

--- SLIDE ---

The Stimulus
External stimulus also called environmental stimulus come from outside of the person. They are all the things we can potentially sense around us.
Usually, there are numerous stimuli in the environment and each of them is picked by our senses. However, we do not respond to all of them at once.
17/04/2024
6

--- SLIDE ---

The Stimulus
Usually, we attend to stimuli selectively. This is called selective attention and the stimulus we attend to at a point in time is called the attended stimulus.
An attended stimulus becomes the stimulus on the receptor because it has been “picked up” by the sense organ.
17/04/2024
7

--- SLIDE ---

The Stimulus
Sense organs have specialized cells called receptors that enable them to sense stimulus both within and outside the body. 
For example, when the eye sees a tree, the tree is transferred to the retina where the image is formed. Consequently, the tree becomes attended stimulus.
17/04/2024
8

--- SLIDE ---

The Stimulus
Most of the stimuli around us are picked up but not processed and are not stored in memory. If we have to process all the information coming to our senses, life will be weird and confusing.
The ability to make selective attention, therefore, helps our memory formation and organization.
17/04/2024
9

Environmental Stimulus
Attended Stimulus

10

--- SLIDE ---

Electrical Process in Perception
One of the central principles of perception is that everything we perceive is based on electrical signals in our nervous system.
These electrical signals are created in the receptors, which transform energy from the environment (such as the light on Ellen’s retina) into electrical signals in the nervous system—a process called transduction.
17/04/2024
11

--- SLIDE ---

Transduction
Transduction is the transformation or conversion of the stimulus in its natural energy form into electrical energy that can be transferred to the brain.
For example, light energy coming into the eyes become converted into electrical energy in the retina of the eyes that can be transferred to the brain for further processing.
17/04/2024
12

--- SLIDE ---

Transmission
Once electrical signals are formed in the receptors of the sense organ, they are transported to the brain. This transportation process is called transmission. The transmitted signal is picked up by specialized neural cells which further trigger another series of other neural cells until the electrical energy is interpreted. This process is called neural processing.
17/04/2024
13

--- SLIDE ---

Transmission
Neural processing eventually produces a meaningful interpretation of the electrical signal received from the sense organs. It is at this point that perception has taken place.

PERSONAL GUIDE 
 
💥 THE FOUNDING FATHERS OF SOCIOLOGY — FULL EXPLANATION 
 
 
1️⃣ Auguste Comte (1798-1857) 
 
Who he was: The person who gave sociology its name. Called the Father of Sociology. 
 
What he believed: Society grows in stages—first people explain things through 
religion (Theological stage), then through abstract ideas (Metaphysical stage), and 
finally through science and reason (Positive stage). 
 
Example (UI): Think of UI as a society that started small, maybe based on traditions or 
missionary foundations (theological), grew with philosophical and cultural ideas 
(metaphysical), and today runs mostly on research, logic, and science (positive 
stage). 
 
 
 
--- 
 
2️⃣ Herbert Spencer (1820-1903) 
 
Who he was: The thinker who borrowed from Charles Darwin’s ideas. 
 
What he believed: Societies are like living things that grow naturally. The strong 
survive, and we shouldn’t interfere too much—just let society develop on its own. 
 
Example (UI): Imagine if no one tried to change how UI is run. If some faculties, 
student groups, or departments struggle while others thrive, that’s just natural 
growth—no need for intervention. 
 
 
 
--- 
 
3️⃣ Emile Durkheim (1858-1917) 
 
Who he was: A scientist in the true sense who wanted sociology to focus on facts. 
 
What he believed: What keeps a society together are shared values, beliefs, and 
institutions like schools, churches, and families. He focused on social facts—things 
in society that guide how we behave. 
 
Example (UI): The way students follow UI’s dress code, respect lecturers, and attend 
convocation ceremonies—these are social facts that maintain order in the school 
community. 

 
 
 
--- 
 
4️⃣ Karl Marx (1818-1883) 
 
Who he was: More than just a sociologist—his ideas shaped economics, politics, 
history, and more. 
 
What he believed: Society is divided between those who own things (the rich) and 
those who work for them (the poor). Change happens through their struggles (class 
conflict). 
 
Example (UI): Think of workers at UI demanding better pay or students protesting 
high fees. Marx would say these struggles between those in power and those without 
power drive change. 
 
 
 
--- 
 
5️⃣ Max Weber (1864-1920) 
 
Who he was: A critic of Marx, focused on understanding people’s actions and 
meanings. 
 
What he believed: Before explaining people’s behaviour, you must understand their 
viewpoint (empathy). His focus was on individual actions and how they influence 
society. 
 
Example (UI): Instead of just looking at students protesting, Weber would say: try to 
understand why—maybe they feel oppressed or unheard. 
 
 
 
--- 
 
6️⃣ Talcott Parsons (1902-1979) 
 
Who he was: An American who built on Durkheim and Weber’s ideas. 
 
What he believed: Society is like a machine where everyone has a role, and these 
roles keep things working smoothly. Shared values and norms guide action. 
 
Example (UI): In UI, lecturers teach, students learn, admin staff manage 
records—everyone’s role helps the university work as a whole system. 
 

 
 
--- 
 
7️⃣ Ibn Khaldun (1332-1402) 
 
Who he was: An early Arab thinker who talked about society before modern sociology 
existed. 
 
What he believed: Societies rise and fall like living things—they grow, mature, and 
decline. 
 
Example (UI): If you see how UI grew from a small college to a large, famous 
university, and consider that without care it could decline, you’re seeing Khaldun’s 
idea of a society’s cycle.

He lived during the time of the Industrial Revolution when Europe was changing fast;

He saw that people needed to understand these changes and bring order to society.

SOC 101 
INTRODUCTION TO 
SOCIOLOGY 1
TOPIC 1: GENERAL INTRODUCTION 
/ SUBJECT MATTER
Dr. Olufunke Adegoke

LEARNING OUTCOMES
• How did Sociology emerge as a discipline in the study 
of human society? 
• What is the relevance of Sociology in Societal 
Arrangement and Stability.
• What are the Basic Sociological Theories to Societal 
understanding

GENERAL INTRODUCTION
• This course introduces students to the Tenets of Sociology. 
• It attempts to bring out, with illustrations, the importance of Sociology to the 
understanding of human behaviour; how Sociologists undertake this task; their 
methods and theories; as well as the concepts they employ in achieving their 
purposes. 
• Critical analyses are attempted to demonstrate that the practice of sociology is 
not absolute. 
• Students are to ‘practice’ Sociology themselves as they become integrated into 
this new discipline

General Introduction Contd. 2
A key insight of Sociology is the simple fact of being in a group 
changes your behaviour. The group is a phenomenon that is more 
than the sum of its parts. 
Why do we feel and act differently in various types of social 
situations? Why might people of a single group exhibit different 
behaviours in the same situation?
Why might people acting similarly not feel connected to others 
exhibiting the same behaviour? 
These are some of the many questions Sociologists ask as they 
study people and societies.

General Introduction Contd. 3
Sociology critically analyses the ‘society’/individual nexus: 
How does the society ‘create’ the individual and how does 
the individual influence the stability, or otherwise, of the 
society?
Sociologists are interested in understanding the ‘macro’ and 
‘micro’ level analyses of human behavior.
To undertake the above, Sociologists use both theories and 
research to arrive at a ‘tentative’ explanation of societal 
arrangement.

General Introduction Contd. 4
Tentative explanations are given because social 
change is inevitable.
Thus, Sociologists also examine social change: the 
why, how, what, when and where of social change?
Who are the ‘stakeholders’ in social change?
What are the possible consequences of social 
change: on the individual stakeholders and the society?

General Introduction Contd. 5
Sociology, simply put, is the scientific study of human society. It focuses on 
studying human social behaviour and interaction, the pattern of relationships, 
cultural way of life, social change, causes and consequences of human 
behaviour. 
In other words, Sociologists want to know, understand, and explain why 
people behave as they do. To achieve this, Sociologists do not start with 
individuals - this is the preoccupation of psychologists - but with the group, 
society or community. That is, how do people interact within these contexts.

Definitions of Sociology
The word “sociology” is derived from the Latin word socius (companion) and the 
Greek word logos (speech or reason), which together mean “reasoned speech about 
companionship”.
• Sociology is the science of social phenomena subject to natural and invariable 
laws
• Sociology is a science which attempts the interpretive understanding of social 
action in order thereby to arrive at a causal explanation of its course and effects 
(Max Weber).
• Sociology is the Science of Social Institutions (Emile Durkheim)
• Sociology is a general science of society (Kingsley Davis) 
• Sociology is the science that deals with social groups (Harry M. Johnson)
• Sociology is the discipline that attempts to understand the forces outside us that 
shape our lives, interests, and personalities (Eitzen and Zinn)

SUBJECT MATTER OF SOCIOLOGY
• Sociology is said to have its roots in the works of philosophers such as Plato, 
Aristotle and Confuscius.
The Age of Enlightenment (1685 – 1815) was that of the 17th century when 
philosophers and scientists had scientific discoveries. It started with the works 
of Galileo’s a Greek philosopher who had proof that the earth w

SOC 101 
INTRODUCTION TO 
SOCIOLOGY 1

Sociology
• Highlighting their contributions to the Discipline 
of Sociology

INTRODUCTION
Before the emergence of Sociology as an established discipline, there had been earliest 
thoughts by people like Ibn Khaldun, an Arabic scholar, who advocated for the need of a 
new science that would help in understanding human society. He employed the term, Al-
Umram, translated to mean, Sociology, to describe the new science that would help to 
provide understanding of human society. However, Ibn Khaldun is not recognized as the 
founding father of Sociology, Auguste Comte is.   

FOUNDING FATHERS  
AUGUSTE COMTE (1798-1857) referred to as the Founder of Sociology. He coined the 
word Sociology. Comte was a European (French) and he lived during the years of industrial 
revolution which affected the social structure or fabric of the European society which 
destabilized and altered the pre-existing social order. He described the epistemological 
perspective of the new science (Positivism). He posited that society moves gradually from 
the lowest to the highest levels in the order of: Theology, Metaphysical and Positive stage. Implicit 
in this analysis is that his society is in the positive stage - age of rationality and 
reasoning. He believed that human beings always desire order which to him was to be 
found in the European society. Such desires, he posited, are made possible by the social 
institutions which control the individual. It is also the society that to him can bring out 
change and not the individual.

Founding Fathers Contd.
Herbert Spencer (1820- 1903): he (Spencer) identified with the virtues expatiated by Charles 
Darwin. The basic principle behind Darwin’s contribution to knowledge was based on his 
explanation of evolution of the human species. He employed such terminologies as "struggle 
for existence" and "survival of the fittest" being the method of development of human 
species. He attributed the development of society to nature. For him, whatever hardship a 
society is going through is natural and that ultimately, development shall result. In other words, 
there is no need to interfere in societal processes. Spencerian analysis postulated a natural 
order which societies would pass. It does not explain what will bring about the societal changes.
Emile Durkheim ((1858-1917): He believed in the gathering of data and observation with 
which to test theories and make predictions about behaviour. He was interested in 
understanding how society is held together and how common values and beliefs and patterns 
of behaviour came to be. Study of the society is to study the large institutions functioning to 
maintain the whole structure. He was preoccupied with gathering 'social facts' about 
institutions and how these 'facts' maintain order. 

Founding Fathers Contd. 3
Karl Marx (1818-1883): It is not right to refer to Marx as only a Sociologist because his 
writings have influenced Economists, Philosophers, Political scientists, Historians, among 
others. He was concerned with explaining the processes of change in society as well as taking 
part in the changes. He was against the existing 'order' and believes that it should change to a 
further stage. Social change can never be explained by the inevitability of people's struggle for 
survival. Human beings enter relationships either as owner of means of production or non-owner of 
the means (Capitalist or Bourgeiosies against Proletariat) .When the latter is the case, he (Proletariat) is 
oppressed and in conflict with the interests of his oppressor. It is this conflict position that 
explains change and order in societies.
Max Weber (1864- 1920): Weber has been posited as arguing against the 'ghost' of Karl Marx. 
He championed a value-free sociology and the need to understand (empathy) before one can

INTRODUCTION
Sociologists have terms which help them to explain complex ideas. These are referred to
as concepts. These are abstract ideas that corresponds to themes and realities in society.
Basic concepts in Sociology is a book written by Maximilian Weber, a German Economist
and Sociologist. The original edition was published in German but various translations to
English exist. The first known of these was written in 1952. Let us look at some of the
Sociological concepts:

BASIC CONCEPTS IN SOCIOLOGY
• Society: it is derived from the Latin word socius which means companionship or
friendship. It is a group of people who share a common culture, occupy a particular
territorial area and feel themselves to constitute a unified and distinct entity. It is the mutual
interactions and interrelations of individuals and groups.
• Social Institutions: refer to associations, customs, or relationships consciously approved
by a society, organized and maintained through prescribed rules and agencies. Thus, a SI
consists of all the structural components (mores, folkways, and patterns of behaviour) of a
society through which the main concerns and activities are organized, and social needs (such
as those for order, belief, and reproduction) are met. Examples are Family, Religious,
Educational, Economy, Political (Government or State), and Health, which are the major
Institutions.

Basic Concepts in Sociology contd. 1
Group Organisation: these shapes people's behaviour. As human beings we hold 
opinions, possess beliefs and ascribe values, thus this will have effect on the organization. 
However, it is the organisation that helps to concretise these values, beliefs and opinions. 
Organisation is set up for certain explicit purpose of achieving certain goals and possess 
both rules and formal status structure with clearly marked lines of communication and 
authority”. Nonetheless, in certain cases, the purposes of organisation may not be explicit 
and the goals of this organisation may change over time. 
Culture: this concept was rigorously defined by E.B Taylor in 1862 “the complex whole which 
includes knowledge, belief, art , law, morals , customs and any other capabilities acquired by man as a 
member of society”. Simply defined as the total way of life of people in society. Material 
aspect of culture includes those things that can be visibly seen such as houses, hoes, 
clothes, and so on. Non-material aspect of culture consists of those things that one 
cannot physically see or touch in a given society. These include belief systems, norms, 
values, and so on; these can be felt and cannot be seen. 

Basic Concepts in Sociology contd. 2
Authority: It is the same as “the right to direct and command others” Max Weber identifIied three 
ways by which one can gain authority. These include: Tradition(authority obtained through ascribed), 
Charisma (authority obtained through personal attributes) and Legality (authority obtained through office of the 
individual and not the person). From the authority one possesses derive the power which legitimates the 
authority. Power may be employed through persuasion and influence, offer of material, social or 
political benefits; and through negative incentives such as withholding benefits and the use of 
threats, coercion or force.
Sub-culture: is when culturally distinct people within a larger culture fails to assimilate fully or has

SOC 101 PRINCIPLES OF SOCIOLOGY
TOPIC 8: SOCIALIZATION

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
Sociology is the scientific study of human behavior and their interaction in groups. 
Trying to understand and make sense on their social actions – different from psychology
This is done in a scientific and systematic way – Research (Science of Knowing)
Concepts are developed to explain these social phenomenon

--- SLIDE ---

Socialization  
It is an unconscious process where by a newborn child learns the values, beliefs, rules and regulations of society or internalizes the culture by conforming. The most important aspect of the socialization process takes place during infancy, usually within the family. Socialization is a lifelong process and not confined to childhood.

--- SLIDE ---

AGENTS OF SOCIALIZATION
There are various socializing agents which helps to inculcate in an individual the society’s norms, values and roles. 
Such agents are the family, education, politics, health, economy, mass media etc.

--- SLIDE ---

LEVELS OF SOCIALIZATION
Primary Socialization: refers to the way a new born child is moulded into a social being who can interact with others according to the expectations of society. It usually occurs within the family and other intimate groups in the child’s social environment.

--- SLIDE ---

Secondary Socialization: it occurs in later childhood and adolescence, when the child enters school and comes under the influence of adults and peers outside the household and immediate family.

Adult Socialization: this is when the individual learns the norms associated with new statuses such as wife, husband, journalist, grandparent etc.

--- SLIDE ---

CONTROVERSIES ON SOCIALIZATION
The concept of socialization has to do with “Nature” and “Nurture”.  Social scientists have studied the socialization process trying to develop theory to address the issue of “Nature” which is innate or inborn and “Nurture” which is learned. This is explained using theories.

--- SLIDE ---

Theory is an idea to explain something or set of guiding principles.
It is also an explanation to observable facts which have being proven 
A rational type of abstract thinking about a phenomenon or the results of such thinking.

--- SLIDE ---

SOME THEORIES ON SOCIALIZATION ARE:
1. Freudian Approach
Sigmund Freud was the first social scientist to develop a theory addressing the socialization process of human existence. For Freud, the social self develops primarily in the family wherein the child is gradually forced to control the  biological functions and needs: sucking, eating, defecation, genital stimulation, warmth, sleep and so on.

--- SLIDE ---

According to him, infant are taught on how to delay physical gratification and to channel their biological urges into socially accepted forms of behaviour. For instance Toilet Training.
He divided personality into three functional areas  which permits the self to function well in the society namely: 
ID - the part from which the infant’s unsocialized drives arise. Such as immediate gratification.

--- SLIDE ---

Superego - the moral codes of adults especially parents become incorporated into the part of the personality. This part of the personality consist of all the internalized norms, values and feelings that are taught in the socialization process 
Ego- is the conception of ourself in relation to others. It is in contrast with Id which represents self centeredness

--- SLIDE ---

To Freud, infant wants to receive sexual stimulation from the opposite sex parent, thus competing with the same sex parent. The same sex parent happens to be the most powerful socializing influence on the child. 
The ideology of same sex attraction and imitation of the same sex parent behaviour are used by other theorists to explain differences between men and women. Parents serve as models of behaviour whom children will emulate throughout their lives. Oedipus and Electra Complexes.

ACADEMIC SESSION 2025/2026 FIRST SEMESTER
This course introduces students to the subject matter of Sociology. How it emerged
