Social Sciences and Public Policy 
 
 
 
Political Science and Public Policy 
As a discipline in the social sciences, political science deals with the work- 
ings of government and governance especially in relation with local, state 
and national (or as defined relative to the structure of each nation) gover- 
nance. Political science also studies international relations, power politics, 
power relations and acquisition, public administration and finance as well 
as resource allocation. Political science uses both theory and empirical 
methods to understand governance in domestic and international envi- 
ronments and proffers policy options for good governance and peoples’ 
advancement (Dunleavy 2014; Corbett 2011). A recognised geographical 
space internationally accepted as a nation constitutes a state. Structures of 
state differ from one nation to another. However, the more popular ones 
since the nineteenth century include liberal democracies (for instance, the 
USA, France and Great Britain), the Socialist States (e.g., defunct USSR, 
China, Cuba and North Korea), monarchical systems (Saudi Arabia, 
Swaziland and Oman, for instance) (e.g., see Schumpeter 2013; Singer 
and Weir 2006; Laibman 1992; Torres 1989). Irrespective of the structure 
of government practised, there is a connection between state and policy- 
making and constituted governments thus play vital and principal roles in 
policymaking. Also, the structure and process of governance influence 
policymaking in every nation (Dunleavy 2014). For example, liberal 
democracies usually apply laissez fare policies with private capital as a pri- 
mary essence of production. Socialist systems prioritise state ownership of 
means of production, and monarchical systems attribute all social benefits 
and production as the benefaction of a hereditary sovereign to the citizens 
(Singer and Weir 2006). 
Irrespective of the system of government practised, governance is vital 
in state administration and public policy. According to Edwards, Halligan, 
Horrigan and Nicoll (2012: 9), “Governance is concerned with how40 
A. O. OMOBOWALE ET AL. 
societies, governments and organisations are managed and led. Importantly, 
this includes how they structure and otherwise order their affairs, make 
decisions and exercise powers, and manage their relationships and account- 
abilities.” The principles of governance, which a nation adopts, have direct 
implication for public policy.7 For example, liberal principles favour the 
primacy of private capital in policy formulation while conservative, social- 
ist and welfarist structures would advance some form of populist orienta- 
tion in public policy. Irrespective of the structure of governance, the ethos 

of good governance, transparency and accountability for efficient and 
effective implementation are most important to achieve successful public 
policy (Singh, Ansari and Singh 2009). In most Third World countries, 
and African nations, in particular, good governance is not a readily given 
phenomenon. It is influenced by the politics of resource allocation and 
power relations (Palaniswamy and Krishnan 2012, Wong 1994). In Africa, 
ethnicity, patronage, nepotism and corruption among other socio-political 
vile influence power relations and determine resource allocation and pub- 
lic policy (Galiani and Schargrodsky 2011; Omobowale and Olutayo 
2007, 2010; Olarinmoye 2008). Such political vile frustrate good gover- 
nance and render public policy ineffective for social and political 
development. 
By extension, the political economy of governance structures public 
policy in contextual terms. Within a political economy, local (local politi- 
cians and businesses) and global actors (the globalisation process, multina- 
tional corporations, international organisations and developed economies) 
play strategic roles in politics and the economy influence and structure the 
context of public policy (Rausser and Swinnen 2011; Galston 2006).

TOPIC ONE: WHAT IS SOCIOLOGY? 
Sociology, simply put, is the study of human behaviour. In other words, sociologists want to 
understand in order to know, and therefore to explain why people behave as they do. In order to 
achieve this, sociologists do not start with individuals - this is the preoccupation of psychologists 
- but with the group, society or community. 
This implies that sociologists agree that there are factors in the society which affect individual 
behaviour. For these societal factors to possibly affect individuals, it means that individuals live 
in groups. These groups are organised such that different roles are allocated to different people 
e.g. working in an office or being in the class. 
Sociologists do not take organisations as they are but try 'to study in a scientific and systematic 
way as much as possible, how societies operate' (Thompson, 1982, p.1). We want to explain the 
how and why of these placements/ phenomena which other members of the society may likely 
take for granted (Nabb, 1983). For example, sociologists will want to ask why people within the 
same environment behave differently or similarly, in order to generalize about characteristics of 
human behaviour and social organisation. Furthermore, sociologists have developed concepts to 
explain in a shorthand form, complex ideas.  
SOCIOLOGY AND OTHER SOCIAL SCIENCES 
Sociology is related to other disciplines such as economics, anthropology and political science 
because they all study some aspects of human behaviour. In actual fact, some institutions do not 

2 
 
separate them from each other (Wallerstein, 1980). They are referred to as the social sciences 
(see Otite and Ogionwo, 1979 for further classification).  
Nonetheless, there are certain differences of emphasis. For example, political scientists interest 
themselves with the government and power distribution in societies; geographers look at how the 
society and physical environment influence each other; economists concern themselves with 
trading arrangements in the societies and anthropologists study human behaviour historically.All 
of these may, however be limited in what is called Political-Economy. 
SOCIOLOGY AS A SCIENCE 
Around the mid-19th century, 'science' as a discipline became what all other disciplines aspired 
to be. The idea of objectivity i.e presenting a value-neutral position became the most desired- 
probably because of the contributions of physical sentence to human development. 
Sociology won no exception more so when the discipline itself became recognised in Western 
Europe, at about this period. Attempts began to be made to study human behaviour with the use 
of theories. These theories were formed through systematic collection of data with specialist 
skills. There are, however, a great deal of disagreements over these theories and skills. 
Due to the fact that sociologists concentrate on social 'problems' which therefore directly concern 
human beings, the idea of objectivity has become a problem -itself- even among sociologists. 
While some sociologists believe that their interests should only be to 'describe', explain, and 
understand, others posit that practitioners should go further to present what ought to be. 
The former position has earned the criticism of the impossibility of neutrality, since 'sociologists 
are also human with human values, prejudices and traditions', it is argued, they cannot but be 
affected by human conditions. For example an academic sociologist is not likely to agree with 
the note that 'teachers rewards are in heaven' neither will a poor sexually starved sociologists see 
anything wrong with a rapist. In the same vein, a sociologist who is a mother will not agree that

Subject Matter of Sociology

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
The discipline of sociology emerged after the European Industrial Revolution of the 18th century 
The revolution caused disorder in the European economy
The subject matter of sociology, therefore, was to understand the problem of order in the European society: why disorder?

--- SLIDE ---

Order and disorder in society
The positions of most of the founding fathers of sociology was that there was disorder in the European society
Their positions were, therefore, how to reinstate order
However, they did not have the same position on the form of order to be established

--- SLIDE ---

Order!
The type of order they all envisaged was that in which there should be a ‘structured’ and ‘predictable’ relationship in the society
As such, institutions were assigned certain ‘roles’ and the functions they perform towards the stability of the structure/society were identified
Where such institutions cannot be clearly seen to be performing their assigned functions, they are seen as ‘dysfunctional’

--- SLIDE ---

Order and social change
The founding fathers of sociology expected that societies are never static but dynamic (always changing)
However, such changes are expected to be ‘orderly’
The changes in one institution affect the other institutions and a new institution is formed

--- SLIDE ---

Order and social change
For instance, a change in the family institution is expected to affect, and be affected by, the educational institution which, in turn, may affect, and be affected by the economic institution, and so on
Think of the roles of the extended family institution and its change to nuclear family type. What effects has this had on the economic institution?

--- SLIDE ---

Order and social change
Can you identify any form of order and/or disorder in the Nigerian society?

--- SLIDE ---

Order and change at the micro-level
Sociologists are not only interested in disorder at the macro-level. They are also interested in how order is maintained at the micro-level
How is order maintained in your home?
Have you ever noticed any form of disorder in the relationship at home?
How about the nature of relationship between you and your friend?

--- SLIDE ---

Order and disorder
Is order inevitable in relationships?

BY 
DR. U. A. Ojedokun

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
When anthropologists and sociologists study religion, they are not trying to confirm whether God exist or not, or whether certain religious beliefs are valid, or whether one religion is better than the other. 

Nevertheless anthropologists agree that all religions are characterized by the belief in supernatural beings and in their powers to assist or harm man. 

Belief systems deal with everything that human beings perceive and wish, everything they can imagine. It is through belief systems that human beings give meanings to their experiences.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of belief systems
Hunter and Whittens (1976) identified two kinds of belief systems:

Instrumental belief systems: concerned primarily with practical life: day-to-day subsistence activities, travel, nourishment, health and so forth. concerned primarily with practical life: day-to-day subsistence activities, travel, nourishment, health and so forth.

Transcendental belief systems: take us beyond daily concerns. They provide structure through which human beings give meaning and purpose to existence. In other words, they address the central question of human existence

--- SLIDE ---

The Universality of Religion
Religious practices have been traced to Neanderthal man at least 100, 000 years ago.

Man’s view of the world has always included the natural and supernatural. 

The natural order is that of the visible, the seen, the ordinary or commonplace. The supernatural is invisible, the unseen realm beyond the natural world, unobserved, hidden from common sight, mysterious and unobservable (Stewart, 1973).

--- SLIDE ---

Theories on the Universality of Religion
Psychological theories: They suggested that religion is a response to anxieties and uncertainties which affect all of us personally and as a consequence, threaten to disrupt the social group. Carl Jung, a notable psychoanalyst argued that religion can be used for therapeutic purposes when emotional problems erupt.

Sociological theories: suggest that religion is a reflection of society and societal needs. Emile Durkheim, in his book, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, argued that religion’s primary function is to provide human groups with the symbolic forms through which they can ritually strengthen the group’s integration and thus, become more socially integrated and stable. These theorists believe that religion is a creation of the society to maintain group solidarity.

--- SLIDE ---

Other theories: these are essentially a combination of psychological and sociological approaches. In this context, religion is seen as a means of cultural revitalization. In other words, religion acts to recharge the batteries of a flagging culture, particularly when the stability of a society is threatened by internal or external forces. This means that the threat of societal breakdown forces people to think of a new way to survive.

--- SLIDE ---

Religious Practitioners
In all societies, there are certain individuals who are solely responsible for performing certain activities by means of which supernatural beings are propiated or influences. 

It is a fact that prayers of individuals or similar activities form the bulk of religious acts.

Nonetheless, these are often supplemented or guided by religious practitioners who may be full-time or part-time specialists, depending on the complexity of the society.

--- SLIDE ---

The Two Major Practitioners
The two major practitioners recognized throughout the world are: the shaman and the priest.

The Shaman: otherwise known as healer or curer is a kind of intermediary between man and the supernatural. In many societies, he is usually a part-time religious practitioner. A major goal of psychology is to predict behavior by understanding its causes. Making 
predictions is difficult in part because people vary and respond differently in different 
situations. Individual differences are the variations among people on physical or psychological 
dimensions. For instance, although many people experience at least some symptoms of 
depression at some times in their lives, the experience varies dramatically among people. Some 
people experience major negative events, such as severe physical injuries or the loss of 
significant others, without experiencing much depression, whereas other people experience 
severe depression for no apparent reason. Other important individual differences that we will 
discuss in the chapters to come include differences in extraversion, intelligence, self-esteem, 
anxiety, aggression, and conformity. 
Because of the many individual difference variables that influence behavior, we cannot always 
predict who will become aggressive or who will perform best in graduate school or on the job. 
The predictions made by psychologists (and most other scientists) are only probabilistic. We can 
say, for instance, that people who score higher on an intelligence test will, on average, do better 

Saylor URL: http://www.saylor.org/books 
 
Saylor.org 
 
 
15 
than people who score lower on the same test, but we cannot make very accurate predictions 
about exactly how any one person will perform. 
Another reason that it is difficult to predict behavior is that almost all behavior is multiply 
determined, or produced by many factors. And these factors occur at different levels of 
explanation. We have seen, for instance, that depression is caused by lower-level genetic factors, 
by medium-level personal factors, and by higher-level social and cultural factors. You should 
always be skeptical about people who attempt to explain important human behaviors, such as 
violence, child abuse, poverty, anxiety, or depression, in terms of a single cause. 
Furthermore, these multiple causes are not independent of one another; they are associated such 
that when one cause is present other causes tend to be present as well. This overlap makes it 
difficult to pinpoint which cause or causes are operating. For instance, some people may be 
depressed because of biological imbalances in neurotransmitters in their brain. The resulting 
depression may lead them to act more negatively toward other people around them, which then 
leads those other people to respond more negatively to them, which then increases their 
depression. As a result, the biological determinants of depression become intertwined with the 
social responses of other people, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of each cause. 
Another difficulty in studying psychology is that much human behavior is caused by factors that 
are outside our conscious awareness, making it impossible for us, as individuals, to really 
understand them. The role of unconscious processes was emphasized in the theorizing of the 
Austrian neurologist Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), who argued that many psychological 
disorders were caused by memories that we have repressed and thus remain outside our 
consciousness. Unconscious processes will be an important part of our study of psychology, and 
we will see that current research has supported many of Freud’s ideas about the importance of 
the unconscious in guiding behavior. 
KEY TAKEAWAYS 
• 
Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. 
• 
Though it is easy to think that everyday situations have commonsense answers, scientific studies have 
found that people are not always as good at predicting outcomes as they think they are.

HISTORIES AND SPECIAL EVENTS IN THE FIELD OF PSYCHOLOGY
The history of psychology is a dynamic narrative that spans centuries, evolving from philosophical inquiry to a rigorous scientific discipline. Below is an extended and updated outline, incorporating recent trends, events, and advancements.
1. Ancient Foundations of Psychology
Philosophical Roots:
Plato and Aristotle: Explored questions about memory, perception, and the nature of the soul.
Hippocrates: Linked mental processes to the brain, challenging earlier beliefs about the heart.
Mind-Body Dualism:
René Descartes argued for the separation of mind and body, influencing early psychological thought.
2. The Birth of Modern Psychology (19th Century)
Wilhelm Wundt:
Established the first experimental psychology lab in Leipzig, Germany (1879), marking psychology as a scientific discipline.
Edward B. Titchener: A student of Wundt
Focused on introspection and structuralism.
William James:
Published The Principles of Psychology (1890), introducing functionalism and concepts like "stream of consciousness."
G. Stanley Hall:
Founded the first U.S. psychology lab (1883) and the American Psychological Association (APA) in 1892.
3. Early Schools of Thought
Structuralism (Wundt and Titchener): Focused on analyzing the components of consciousness.
Functionalism (James): Emphasized the purpose of mental processes in adaptation.
Psychoanalysis (Freud): Introduced theories on unconscious processes, childhood development, and dream analysis.
Behaviorism (Watson, Skinner): Shifted focus to observable behavior, emphasizing conditioning and reinforcement.
4. Key Experiments and Milestones
1900: Freud published ”The Interpretation of Dreams”, formalizing psychoanalytic theory.
1920s–1930s: Ivan Pavlov’s work on classical conditioning influenced behaviorism.
1957: Leon Festinger introduced cognitive dissonance theory, revolutionizing social psychology.
1967: Ulric Neisser published Cognitive Psychology, establishing the cognitive revolution.
5. The Cognitive Revolution (1950s–1960s)
Shifted focus from behaviorism to internal mental processes like memory, perception, and problem-solving.
Influential Figures:
Jean Piaget: Studied cognitive development in children.
Noam Chomsky: Critiqued behaviorist views on language acquisition.
6. Integration with Neuroscience (1980s–2000s)
Advances in neuroimaging technologies like fMRI (Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) and EEG (Electroencephalography  allowed for detailed studies of brain-behavior relationships.
Emergence of biopsychology and Neuropsychology as a subfield integrating biology with psychology.
Modern Trends in Psychology (2000–2023)
a. Positive Psychology
Martin Seligman popularized positive psychology, focusing on human strengths, well-being, and resilience.
b. Technology in Psychology
Virtual Reality (VR) Therapy:
Used for treating PTSD and phobias by simulating controlled environments for exposure therapy.
Online Therapy Platforms:
The rise of apps like BetterHelp has increased access to mental health care globally.
c. Generative AI in Psychology
Tools like ChatGPT are being used for teaching, research, and therapy.
Emerging Subfield: "Machine Psychology" explores how AI systems process information.
d. Neuroscience Advancements
Research into brain correlates of disorders like schizophrenia has improved diagnostic tools and personalized treatments.
e. Multicultural Perspectives
Increased emphasis on diversity, equity, and inclusion in psychological research and practice.
f. Notable Achievements (2023)
Shelley E. Taylor received the National Medal of Science for her contributions to health psychology.
Thomas Joiner was honored for his research on suicide prevention.
8. Recent Special Events
a. Major Conferences in 2023
ICPS 2023: International Convention of Psychological Science held in Brussels.
APA Annual Convention 2023: Focused on workplace flourishing and global mental health challenges.
b. Influential Psychologists Today

HISTORY OF PSYCHOLOGY IN NIGERIA
The history of psychology in Nigeria reflects a journey from traditional practices to a formalized academic and professional discipline, marked by significant milestones and contributions to societal development.
Early Foundations and Traditional Practices
Before colonial influence, psychological practices in Nigeria were deeply rooted in traditional beliefs and methods. Mental health issues were addressed using herbal remedies, rituals, and spiritual interventions, reflecting indigenous understandings of human behavior and mental well-being. This period can be described as the "non-formal" era of psychology, where intuitive theories and cultural practices predominated.
Colonial Era and the Emergence of Modern Psychiatry
The introduction of modern mental health services began during the colonial period. In 1927, the first civil asylums were established in Lagos and Calabar to care for individuals with mental illnesses. A pivotal moment came in 1954 with the establishment of the Aro Psychiatric Hospital in Abeokuta under Professor Thomas Adeoye Lambo. Lambo integrated traditional African healing methods with Western psychiatric practices, laying the groundwork for culturally relevant psychological approaches in Nigeria.
Introduction of Psychology as an Academic Discipline
Psychology entered Nigerian academia formally in 1964 with the establishment of the first degree-awarding Department of Psychology at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. This department began with 11 students and was staffed by both Nigerian and American scholars. By the late 1960s and early 1970s, other universities, including the University of Lagos (1969) and University of Jos (1976), followed suit by creating psychology departments.
During this period, psychology was initially taught as part of other disciplines like philosophy, education, or medicine. However, its recognition as an independent field grew steadily. Early Nigerian psychologists like Professors Ugwuegbu, Omoluabi, Olowu, and Ebigbo made significant contributions by incorporating indigenous knowledge into psychological research.
Professionalization and Growth
The professionalization of psychology gained momentum with the establishment of organizations such as the Nigerian Psychological Association (NPA) in 1968 and the Nigerian Association of Clinical Psychologists (NACP) in 1978. These bodies advocated for the recognition of psychology as a vital profession in healthcare and education. By 2013, there were over 28 accredited departments of psychology across Nigerian universities.
The discipline diversified during the 1990s and early 2000s with specialized programs in clinical psychology, industrial-organizational psychology, and educational psychology. This period also saw an increase in local research output and publications.
Contemporary Developments
In recent decades, psychology in Nigeria has expanded its influence across various sectors. Efforts to integrate psychological services into primary healthcare systems have grown alongside initiatives to address mental health literacy and reduce stigma. The Psychology Bill (Senate Bill No. 624), awaiting presidential assent as of recent years, is expected to further regulate and institutionalize psychological practice in Nigeria.
Despite challenges such as limited resources, inadequate infrastructure, and a shortage of trained professionals, psychology continues to play a crucial role in addressing societal issues like education enhancement, mental health awareness, economic growth through consumer behavior insights, and social harmony through conflict resolution strategies.

1964: Creation of Nigeria’s first Department of Psychology at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka.
1968: Formation of the Nigerian Psychological Association.

INTRODUCTION TO PSYCHOLOGY
PSY 101INTRODUCTION TO PSYCHOLOGY

--- SLIDE ---

PSYCHOLOGY
The scientific study of human and animal behavior and their mental processes.

The field is scientific in that approaches (should be systematic in approach) to studies are done orderly and systematically in order to obtain objective evidence.

--- SLIDE ---

PSYCHOLOGY
Psychologists study overt and covert behavior.
 The overt behaviors are observable behavior, while covert behaviors include private mental processes that cannot be directly observed or measured and must be inferred from overt behavior.
Examples of overt behaviours are; laughing, walking, eating, gestures, facial expression etc and covert behaviour include the following; Perceiving, remembering, reasoning, thinking, creating, feelings etc

--- SLIDE ---

GOALS OF PSYCHOLOGY
Psychologists seek to do four things when studying behaviors:
Describe: What is the nature of the behavior? It gathers information on studied behavior and present what is known.
Explain: Why does it occur? Creating a hypothesis (educated guess) to understand why a behavior is practiced.
Predict:  By studying past behaviors, future behaviors can be predicted based upon theory 
Modify/Control behavior: What factors influence the behavior? Influence- using what is known to influence future behavior.

--- SLIDE ---

HISTORICAL APPROACH TO PSYCHOLOGY
Structuralism – Study of basic elements that make up human experiences.             
Wilhelm Wundt – In 1879, used people’s self observations about their thoughts (introspection) to map out structure of the thought process.
Functionalism – study of the function or how people & animals adapt to environment.  William James – known as the “father of psychology” taught first psych class in 1875 and wrote first textbook in 1890. He was concerned with ongoing conscious experience and the functions of mental processes.  His views gave rise to the branch of psychology called Functionalism.

--- SLIDE ---

HISTORICAL APPROACH (Cont’d)
Inheritable Traits – study of how heredity influences a person’s ability, character, and behavior. Is behavior determined by heredity or environment? 
Sir Francis Galton – Concluded that intelligence was hereditary / good marriages would supply the world with talented offspring. (1883).
Gestalt Psychology - Perception is more than the sum of its parts – it involves a whole pattern. German group that picked apart cognitive thought process.

--- SLIDE ---

HISTORICAL APPROACH (Cont’d)
Contemporary Approaches to Psychology (mid 1900’s to Present)
Psychoanalytic Psychology- study of unconscious motives & conflict determine behavior.  Sigmund Freud – used free association and dream analysis to study behavior (1940). 
Behaviorism – Study of how organisms learn or change behavior based upon responses to events in their environment. (Early-mid1900’s). it held the view that only overt behavior can be studied scientifically. They advocated the use of strict experimental procedure in psychology.

--- SLIDE ---

Contemporary Approaches to Psychology (mid 1900’s to Present)
Strict behaviorists believed that all behaviours are shaped by the environment.  “Give me a dozen healthy infants, well-formed,….. regardless of his talents, penchants, tendencies, abilities, vocations, and race of his ancestors”…….John Watson.
Ivan Pavlov – Classical conditioning experiment with dog’s salivation.
B.F. Skinner – Introduced concept reinforcement to show how behaviors repeat. 
John B. Watson –Behavior occurs due to stimuli in environment.

--- SLIDE ---

Contemporary Approaches
Humanistic Psychology – Belief that each person has freedom in directing his/her future an achieving personal growth. Humans are not controlled by environment, but by their own self concept. Humans are not being controlled by unconscious or environmental forces, we have free will, goals, aspirations and other positive motives which should be studied. It is influenced by Carl Rogers.
Abraham Maslow

Schools of Psychology

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
A group of psychologist having similar point of views and making similar approaches to study the human mind or behavior constitutes a school of thought in psychology.There are several schools of psychology and each has developed some systems of ideas which not only influenced the development of various trends and approaches for the study of behavior but also affected the process and product of education.

--- SLIDE ---

Major Schools of thought in Psychology
Early Schools of Thought. 
Structulism and Functionalism
Behaviorism
Psychoanalysis
Humanistic Psychology
Cognitive Psychology
Gestalt Psychology

--- SLIDE ---

Structuralism and Functionalism: Early Schools of Thought
Structuralism is widely regarded as the first school of thought in psychology. 
This outlook focused on breaking down mental processes into the most basic components. 
Major thinkers associated with structuralism include Wilhelm Wundt and Edward Titchener. 
The focus of structuralism was on reducing mental processes down into their most basic elements. 
The structuralists used techniques such as  introspection to analyze the inner processes of the human mind.

--- SLIDE ---

CONTRIBUTIONS TO EDUCATION
1) Structuralism emphasized the systematic observation of the activities of the learner under controlled learning conditions.2) It is an experiment method for studying human behavior – experimental introspection.3) It initiated the spirit of science and experimentation in the field of education.

--- SLIDE ---

Functionalism
Functionalism formed as a reaction to the theories of the structuralist school of thought and was heavily influenced by the work of William James. 
It functioned on the mind's functions and adaptations. Unlike some of the other well-known schools of thought in psychology, functionalism is not associated with a single dominant theorist.
 Instead, there are some different functionalist thinkers associated with this outlook including John Dewey, James Rowland Angell, and Harvey Carr.

--- SLIDE ---

CONTRIBUTIONS TO EDUCATION
Functionalism revolutionized the curriculum by replacing theoretical overloaded curriculum with practical approaches.Study of various problems of the individual and their solutions is emphasized by Functionalism.
Functionalism gave utmost importance to learning by doing and developed activity oriented methods like project methods for teaching and learning.Functionalism gave birth to utilitarian theory of education. Only those subjects should be include in the curriculum which have practical utility and usefulness in the society.

--- SLIDE ---

The Behaviorist School of Thought in Psychology
Behaviorism became a dominant school of thought during the 1950s. It was based upon the work of thinkers such as:
John B. Watson
Ivan Pavlov
B. F. Skinner

--- SLIDE ---

Behaviorism suggests that all behavior can be explained by environmental causes rather than by internal forces. Behaviorism is focused on observable behavior. Theories of learning including classical conditioning and operant conditioning were the focus of a great deal of research.
The behavioral school of psychology had a significant influence on the course of psychology, and many of the ideas and techniques that emerged from this school of thought are still widely used today. 
Behavioral training, token economies, aversion therapy, and other techniques are frequently used in psychotherapy and behavior modification programs.

--- SLIDE ---

Akinsola Akiwowo: Indigenous Sociologist and Father of Glocal Sociology 
 
Akinsola Akiwowo was a pioneering Nigerian sociologist who introduced a powerful and 
original approach to sociological thinking by drawing from African, especially Yoruba, 
traditions. His main contribution lies in the development of indigenous sociology—a school of 
thought that believes that African societies should be studied using African ideas, languages, 
and worldviews, not just Western theories. 
 
Instead of relying only on thinkers like Marx, Durkheim, or Weber, Akiwowo looked inward to 
his own culture to find valid sociological tools and concepts. Through his work, he 
challenged the Western dominance in sociology and showed that African societies have their 
own methods of understanding the world, building community, and maintaining social order. 
 
 
Ajọbi and Ajogbe: Understanding Social Relations 
 
Akiwowo introduced the Yoruba concepts of Ajọbi and Ajogbe to explain how social bonds 
form in African settings. 
 
Ajọbi refers to kinship by blood. It includes family ties based on descent—your parents, 
siblings, cousins, etc. These blood relations define one's rights, responsibilities, and sense of 
belonging in traditional society. 
 
Ajogbe, on the other hand, means kinship by co-residence or association. It refers to the 
bond created by living together in the same community, worshipping together, or sharing 
common values and goals—even if you’re not related by blood. 
 
 
Together, these two concepts show that social identity in Yoruba society is both inherited 
(Ajọbi) and built (Ajogbe). Akiwowo used them to show that African communities operate 
with a dual sense of belonging—based on both lineage and shared living—which differs from 
individualistic Western models. 
 
 
 
 Ifá: A Sociological Knowledge System 
 
Akinwowo did something bold—he used Ifá, the Yoruba divination system, as a legitimate 
source of sociological theory. While outsiders may see Ifá as spiritual or mystical, Akiwowo 
saw it as a coded library of Yoruba philosophy and ethics. 
 
Ifá verses (Odu) contain stories and moral lessons about justice, cooperation, punishment, 
leadership, and personal conduct. In this way, Ifá plays the role of what Westerners might 
call a sociological textbook—guiding how society should be organized and how people 
should behave. 
 
 

Omolúàbí and Ọmọ Bùrúkú: Social Control in Yoruba Society 
 
To explain morality, deviance, and social control, Akiwowo referenced two key Yoruba moral 
categories: 
 
Omolúàbí: This is the ideal citizen—a person of good character, respect, truthfulness, 
discipline, and social responsibility. Every child is raised to become an Omolúàbí because it 
reflects the community’s moral expectations. 
 
Ọmọ Bùrúkú: This refers to the bad child—someone who disrespects elders, disobeys 
norms, and brings shame to the family or community. It represents deviance, and it attracts 
social disapproval or punishment. 
 
 
Through these, Akiwowo showed how Yoruba society defines acceptable and unacceptable 
behaviour, without needing foreign theories of deviance. These concepts help maintain order 
and peace in the community. 
 
From Indigenous to Glocal Sociology 
 
Akiwowo’s ideas connect to a broader movement known as Southern Theory, which argues 
that people in the Global South should not only be subjects of sociological research but also 
creators of sociological theory. 
 
By drawing from Yoruba culture, language, and philosophy, Akiwowo didn’t just localize 
sociology—he redefined it from the South, making it stronger and more global in scope. 
 
 
Final Takeaway:  
 
Akiwowo’s theory was focused on Glocal Sociology – 
“It is relevant globally, locally useful.” 
         This means that the concepts he developed from Yoruba traditions - Ajọbi, Ajogbe, 
Ifá, Omolúàbí, and Ọmọ Bùrúkú are not only useful for understanding African societies but

Isidore Auguste Marie François Xavier Comte (/kɒnt/; French: [oɡyst kɔ̃t]
ⓘ; 19 January 1798 – 5

doctrine of positivism. He is often regarded as the first philosopher of science in the modern sense
of the term.[2] Comte's ideas were also fundamental to the development of sociology, with him
inventing the very term and treating the discipline as the crowning achievement of the sciences.[3][4]
Influenced by Henri de Saint-Simon,[1] Comte's work attempted to remedy the social disorder caused
by the French Revolution, which he believed indicated an imminent transition to a new form of
society. He sought to establish a new social doctrine based on science, which he labeled positivism.
He had a major impact on 19th-century thought, influencing the work of social thinkers such as
John Stuart Mill and George Eliot.[5] His concept of Sociology and social evolutionism set the tone
for early social theorists and anthropologists such as Harriet Martineau and Herbert Spencer,
evolving into modern academic sociology presented by Émile Durkheim as practical and objective
social research.
Comte's social theories culminated in his "Religion of Humanity",[1] which presaged the development
of non-theistic religious humanist and secular humanist organizations in the 19th century.[6] He may
also have coined the word altruism (altruism).[7]
Auguste Comte was born in Montpellier,[1] Hérault on 19 January 1798, at the time under the rule of
the newly founded French First Republic. After attending the Lycée Joffre[8] and then the University
of Montpellier, Comte was admitted to École Polytechnique in Paris. The École Polytechnique was
notable for its adherence to the French ideals of republicanism and progress. The École closed in
1816 for reorganization, and Comte continued his studies at the medical school at Montpellier.
When the École Polytechnique reopened, he did not request readmission.
Following his return to Montpellier, Comte soon came to see unbridgeable differences with his
Catholic and monarchist family and set off again for Paris, earning money by small jobs. Comte had
abandoned Catholicism under the influence of his first teacher and Protestant pastor Daniel
Encontre.[9][10]

Founding Fathers of Sociology
1. Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406)
Background:
Ibn Khaldun was a North African Arab Muslim scholar and is widely regarded as the forerunner of
modern sociology, historiography, and economics. Born in Tunis, he lived during a time of political
turmoil and intellectual flourishing in the Islamic world.
Major Work:
Muqaddimah (Introduction): A preface to his universal history, this monumental work is considered a
foundational text in the philosophy of history and social science.
Key Contributions:
- Social Cohesion (Asabiyyah): Ibn Khaldun introduced the concept of Asabiyyah, meaning social
solidarity or group feeling, which he argued was crucial for the rise and fall of civilizations.
- Cyclical Theory of History: He proposed that societies and empires rise, flourish, and fall in a
cyclical pattern, often due to internal decay and loss of social cohesion.
- Scientific Approach to Society: He insisted that historical and social phenomena should be studied
using empirical observation and logic rather than superstition or legend.
Relevance:
Although often overlooked in Western sociology, Khaldun's work predated and anticipated many
ideas later developed by European sociologists. His emphasis on the scientific study of society and
change aligns with core sociological principles today.

2. Auguste Comte (1798-1857)
Background:
A French philosopher and mathematician, Comte is traditionally known as the "father of sociology."
He sought to apply the scientific method used in natural sciences to the study of society.
Major Work:
- Course of Positive Philosophy
- A General View of Positivism
Key Contributions:
- Positivism: Comte argued that knowledge should be derived from scientific observation and
empirical data. He proposed three stages of societal development: theological, metaphysical, and
positive.
- Social Statics and Dynamics: He distinguished between the study of social structures (statics) and
social change (dynamics).
- Hierarchy of Sciences: Comte placed sociology at the top of a hierarchy of sciences, believing it
would unify all scientific knowledge.
Relevance:
Comte laid the groundwork for sociology as a systematic, scientific discipline. His ideas about
positivism greatly influenced early sociologists like Durkheim.

Georg Simmel
Georg Simmel (/ˈzɪməl/; German: [ˈzɪml̩]; 1 March 1858 – 26 September 1918) was a German
sociologist, philosopher, and critic. Simmel was influential in the field of sociology. Simmel was one
of the first generation of German sociologists: his neo-Kantian approach laid the foundations for
sociological antipositivism, asking "what is society?"—directly alluding to Kant's "what is nature?"—
presenting pioneering analyses of social individuality and fragmentation.
Simmel discussed social and cultural phenomena in terms of "forms" and "contents" with a
transient relationship, wherein form becomes content, and vice versa dependent on context. In this
sense, Simmel was a forerunner to structuralist styles of reasoning in the social sciences.
Through "The Metropolis and Mental Life" Simmel was a precursor of urban sociology, symbolic
interactionism, and social network analysis. An acquaintance of Max Weber, Simmel wrote on the
topic of personal character in a manner reminiscent of the sociological ideal type. He broadly
rejected academic standards, however, philosophically covering topics such as emotion and
romantic love. Both Simmel and Weber's nonpositivist theory informed the eclectic critical theory of
the Frankfurt School.
Early life and education
Georg Simmel was born in Berlin, Germany, as the youngest of seven children to an assimilated
Jewish family. His father, Eduard Simmel (1810–1874), a prosperous businessman and convert to
Roman Catholicism, had founded a confectionery store called "Felix & Sarotti" that would later be
taken over by a chocolate manufacturer. His mother Flora Bodstein (1818–1897) came from a
Jewish family who had converted to Lutheranism. Georg, himself, was baptized as a Protestant
when he was a child.[1] His father died in 1874, when Georg was 16, leaving a sizable inheritance.[2]
Georg was then adopted by Julius Friedländer, the founder of an international music publishing
house known as Peters Verlag, who endowed him with the large fortune that enabled him to
become a scholar.[3]
Beginning in 1876, Simmel studied philosophy and history at the Humboldt University of Berlin,[4]
going on to receive his doctorate in 1881 for his thesis on Kantian philosophy of matter, titled "Das
Biography

Wesen der Materie nach Kants Physischer
Monadologie" ("The Nature of Matter According
to Kant's Physical Monadology").[4]
In 1885, Simmel became a privatdozent at the
University of Berlin, officially lecturing in
philosophy but also in ethics, logic, pessimism,
art, psychology and sociology.[5] His lectures were
not only popular inside the university, but
attracted the intellectual elite of Berlin as well.
Although his applications for vacant chairs at
German universities were supported by Max
Weber, Simmel remained an academic outsider.
However, with the support of an inheritance from
his guardian, he was able to pursue his scholarly
interests for many years without needing a
salaried position.[6]
Simmel had a hard time gaining acceptance in
the academic community despite the support of
well known associates, such as Max Weber,
Rainer Maria Rilke, Stefan George and Edmund
Husserl. This was partly because he was seen as
a Jew during an era of anti-Semitism, but also
simply because his articles were written for a
general audience rather than academic
sociologists. This led to dismissive judgements
from other professionals. Simmel nevertheless
continued his intellectual and academic work, as
well as taking part in artistic circles.

structures that shape them. It seeks to understand how social institutions, relationships and 
cultural norms influence individual and group behavior within a societal concept. According to 
Auguste Comte, the founding father of Sociology, Sociology is a distinct field of study, distinct 
study of the society and a distinct intellectual realm through which we can understand the society. 
Similarly, Emile Durkheim in his book “The Rules of Sociological Method (1895) defined 
Sociology as the science of social institutions. He emphasized the need to study social facts as 
things external to and coercive over individuals. Max Weber also defined Sociology as the

for the action. 
Sociology is a discipline that is very organic and evolving. It is a discipline that attempts to 
understand the society and every aspect of human behavior. Whenever we have social relations, 
Sociology is very important. Whenever there is social problems, Sociology is needed there to

Talcott Parsons: Historical Thoughts or 
Contemporary Relevance? 
Talcott Parsons was one of the greatest sociologists in the 20th century. He was born in the 
United States of America in Colorado in the year 1902 and died in Munich Germany in 1979. He 
contributed greatly to sociology. He was more of a theorist than an empirical analyst, meaning 
that he had more abstract ideas and thoughts about how society should work, rather than 
observing and gathering of data and facts. He published a book called "The Structure of Social 
Actions" in 1937, and he also developed theories like structural functionalism and the AGIL

think his ideas are outdated and not useful today. Others believe they still help us understand 
how modern societies should work.  
Talcott Parsons was a very broad-minded sociologist, he was not just restricted to one thought 
but had many thoughts. Thoughts ranging from social stability, to gender, to religion, medical 
sociology, and so on.  
The Theories/Thoughts of Talcott Parsons.  
Structural Functionalism 
Talcott Parsons’ structural functionalism sees society as a system like a machine where different 
parts work together to keep things running smoothly. These parts are things like the family, 
school, religion, and the economy. If one part stops working, the system feels it. According to 
Talcott Parsons, as long as each part does its job, society will stay stable and balanced 
He believed that institutions like family, education, religion, and government each have specific 
functions that contribute to the overall functioning of society. For example, the family is 
responsible for the proper upbringing of children, who will later grow up to be valuable 

individuals to society, while schools prepare individuals for their roles in careers and the social 
workforce. 
This basically suggests that when all parts of society work properly, social order is maintained. 
But however, if one part fails, it can disturb the entire system. Talcott Parsons’ approach points 
out the importance of social institutions in sustaining social stability.

must perform to survive, It is a way of breaking down what every society needs in order to 
survive and grow.

HISTORICAL OVERVIEW ON GEORG SIMMEL 
Georg Simmel was born in the heart of Berlin on March 1, 1858. He studied a wide range of subjects at 
the University of Berlin. However, his first effort to produce a dissertation was rejected, and one of his 
professors remarked, “We would do him a great service if we do not encourage him further in this 
direction” (Frisby, 1984:23). Despite this, Simmel persevered and received his doctorate in philosophy in 
1881. He remained at the university in a teaching capacity until 1914, although he occupied a relatively 
unimportant position as Privatdozent from 1885 to 1900. In the latter position, Simmel served as an 
unpaid lecturer whose livelihood was dependent on student fees. Despite his marginality, Simmel did 
rather well in this position, largely because he was an excellent lecturer and attracted large numbers of 
(paying) students (Frisby, 1981:17; Salomon, [1963] 1997). His style was so popular that even cultured 
members of Berlin society were drawn to his lectures, which became public events (Leck, 2000). 
  

Simmel wrote innumerable articles (“The Metropolis and Mental Life”) and books (The Philosophy of 
Money). He was well known and influential in German academic circles. His Berlin home was a center of 
cultural life where he and his wife, Gertrud, hosted important figures including poets Rainer Rilke and 
Stefan George, philosophers Edmund Husserl and Heinrich Rickert, and sociologists Max and Marianne 
Weber (Helle, 2013). Hans Georg Gadamer noted that Simmel’s essays on metaphysics influenced 
philosopher Martin Heidegger’s (1953|2010) monumental book, Being and Time. Simmel even had an 
international following, especially in the United States, where his work was of great significance in the 
birth of sociology. Finally, in 1900, Simmel received official recognition, a purely honorary title at the 
University of Berlin, which did not give him full academic status. Simmel tried to obtain many academic 
positions, but he failed in spite of the support of scholars such as Max Weber.

academic status)

For Simmel, society does not exist independently of the individuals who make it up. 
Society is constantly being constructed and reconstructed through dyadic (2-person) and triadic (3-person)

Simmel said: “Society exists where a number of individuals enter into interaction.”

Form is how interaction is structured (e.g., cooperation, competition, subordination)

Introduction
The enduring debate about the relevance of Karl Marx's ideas in the 21st century is a rich
and complex one. Marx, known for his critique of capitalism and his foundational role in
socialism and communism, wrote extensively about class struggle, exploitation, and the
capitalist mode of production. While many argue that his work is outdated, rooted in the
19th-century industrial era, others assert that the core of his analysis remains sharply
relevant in today’s globalized and technologically advanced world. This essay will explore
the relevance of Marxist thought in contemporary society using real-world examples and
theoretical analysis.
1. Karl Marx’s Key Ideas
Marx’s philosophy revolves around the critique of capitalism and the understanding of
historical and material conditions. Some of his most important contributions include:
     
     - **Historical Materialism**: The idea that material conditions and economic practices
shape society and history.
     - **Class Struggle**: The belief that history is a series of conflicts between oppressors
(bourgeoisie) and the oppressed (proletariat).
     - **Alienation**: The concept that under capitalism, workers are disconnected from their
labor, the product, and themselves.
     - **Surplus Value**: Capitalists gain profit by paying workers less than the value of what
they produce.
     - **Base and Superstructure**: The economic base shapes the societal superstructure
(politics, ideology, culture).
2. Case Studies in the Contemporary World
a. **The Gig Economy**:
     Gig workers, such as those on Uber, Bolt, and freelance platforms like Fiverr and Upwork,
often work long hours without employment benefits, job security, or a minimum wage.
These platforms maximize profits by minimizing labor costs, mirroring Marx’s concern with
exploitation.
     
     b. **Sweatshop Labor and Global Supply Chains**:
     Multinational companies often outsource production to countries with lax labor laws.
Workers in countries like Bangladesh, Vietnam, and parts of Africa endure low wages and
hazardous conditions, aligning with Marx’s theory of surplus value extraction.
     
     c. **Inequality in Developed Nations**:
     Even in countries like the U.S. or the U.K., wealth disparity is vast. CEOs earn hundreds of

times more than average workers, and many employees live paycheck to paycheck.
Capitalism fosters this inequality, proving Marx's predictions true in new contexts.
     
     d. **Welfare Capitalism in Scandinavia**:
     While nations like Norway and Sweden have extensive welfare systems, they still operate
on capitalist principles. Exploitation is less overt, but the class structure and capital
accumulation persist.
3. Everyday Life and Capitalist Dynamics
Capitalism pervades everyday experiences: paying tuition, renting homes, working jobs with
rigid hours and low pay. A student hiring a cleaner to fetch water up multiple flights of stairs
for a small fee is one example. Another is a university lecturer depending on an underpaid
driver to work late into the night. These examples may appear benign but reveal layers of
inequality and labor exploitation consistent with Marx’s analysis.
4. The Illusion of Choice and Alienation
Marx argued that capitalism creates an illusion of freedom. Today, people believe they have
freedom of choice—between jobs, products, and lifestyles—but in reality, their options are
limited by economic necessity. Most people cannot afford to stop working or pursue
passions without worrying about survival. Additionally, many workers feel disconnected
from the purpose of their work, experiencing what Marx described as alienation.

Introduction 
Sociology is an essential discipline that studies human society, social behavior, relationships, and 
institutions. It emerged during the French and Industrial Revolutions. Its primary goal is to 
understand the complex ways in which individuals, groups, and institutions interact with one 
another in society. Sociology plays a crucial role in helping us understand the social dynamics 
that shape our world and the ways in which they impact individuals, communities, and society as 
a whole. It involves understanding the social interactions of human behavior or the interpretive 
understanding of human actions. 
 
At its core, sociology looks at the connections between individuals and society. No one exists in 
isolation; our identities, beliefs, and actions are influenced by the communities we belong to, the 
traditions we inherit, and the systems that govern us. Sociology emerged in the 19th century, 
pioneered by thinkers like Auguste Comte, Karl Marx, and Emile Durkheim, who sought to 
explain social order, change, and conflict—and earlier in the 14th century by Ibn Khaldun, who 
some refer to as the original father of sociology, although he is often forgotten. Since then, it has 
expanded to explore the most pressing issues of our time. 
 
In the family of the social sciences, sociology is comparatively a new entrant. But because of its 
dealing with social problems, social relationships and social interactions, the importance of the 
study of this subject has considerably increased in methodology, scope and approach. Attempts 
are now being made to study every social problem objectively, scientifically or empirically, 
eliminating subjectivity to a large extent. As a field of study, sociology has a very broad scope. It 
deals with families, groups, gangs, business firms, computer networks, political parties, schools 
and religions. It is also concerned with conformity, order, equilibrium, discrimination, love, 
poverty, alienation and community. 
 
In the 21st century, Nigeria, a nation with a population exceeding 220 million and marked by 
rapid urbanization, technological disruption, rising inequality, youth unemployment, insecurity, 
and cultural diversity, stands at a critical crossroads. These social transformations have 
intensified the demand for a deeper, empirically grounded understanding of human behavior, 

group dynamics, and institutional structures. In this context, sociology offers a uniquely 
powerful lens to explore and interpret the changing landscape of Nigerian society. Far from 
being an abstract academic discipline, sociology equips policymakers, development practitioners, 
educators, and civil society actors with the tools to critically engage with pressing societal 
challenges.

that have significantly slowed its national development. From industrial decline and widespread

gender-based violence, child labour, youth restiveness, religious intolerance, corruption, a 
decaying education system, and a shortage of basic social infrastructure. These problems are not 
isolated; they are deeply interconnected and rooted in the social structures and relationships that 
shape Nigerian life.

INTRODUCTION: 
Ibn Khaldun was a 14th century renowed Tunsian historian and sociologists. Khaldun was a proto-
sociological thinker. He is the mostly considered as a social scientist. He lived during a time of great 
political conflict and change. His most famous book is the al –Muqqaddmiah(the-introduction). It is known 
for its deep reflections on how societies rise and fall. In the book, he talks about ideas like group 
unity(asabiyyah), the role of economy, and the patterns of history. Because of this, some people today say 
that was “the father of sociology”, although that is not widely accepted as that term is generally attributed 
to August Conte for coining the word “sociology”.  
The Muqaddimah has attracted attention from scholars across discilplines and eras for its remarkable 
attempts to understand the forces shaping civilisations. Also, his concept of Asabiyyah, or social cohesion, 
has been the subject of much academic interest, which has earned him recognition from time to time as a 
precursor to modern sociology. Muqaddimah is considered a foundational work in sociology, history, 
philosophy. 
One of his central concepts is the distinction between ʿumran badawi (rural or nomadic civilization) and 
ʿumran hadari’ (urban or sedentary civilization). Ibn Khaldun argued that nomadic societies are 
characterized by strong ʿasabiyyah’, simplicity, and collective strength. These qualities, he believed, make 
them capable of conquering and establishing rule over more luxurious and sedentary urban societies. 
However, as these nomadic groups settle, adopt city life, and grow accustomed to luxury, their solidarity 
weakens, leading to social decay and eventual decline. This rise-and-fall dynamic formed the basis of his 
cyclical view of history. 
Despite all these accolades, the relevance of Ibn Khaldun’s thoughts to contemporary sociology deserves 
critical examination. While it is true that some of his thoughts appear proto-sociological in nature , his 
thoughts were deeply embedded in a specific historical and cultural context namely, the Islamic world of 
the 14th century. Unlike modern sociology, which is grounded in empirical methodologies and built upon 
range of competing theoretical paradigms, Ibn Khaldun’s analysis leans heavily on philosophical reflection, 
anecdotal observation, and cyclical views of history. 
Take for his example, his famous theory of Asabiyyah, which he used to explain how tribes rise to power 
and eventually form states, only to be replaced by other groups with stronger internal solidarity. Ibn 
KHaldun formed this theory based on his observations of Berber tribes and dynastic changes in North Africa 
and Andalusia. While insightful for understanding the political dynamics of tribal socieites , asabbiyah does 
not easily map out modern forms of collective action, social cohesion, or institutional stability. Today,

Ibn Khaldun and His Contribution to Sociology
Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) was a North African scholar, historian, and philosopher who is often regarded as one of the founding figures of modern sociology, historiography, and economics. Long before Western sociologists like Auguste Comte or Karl Marx, Ibn Khaldun developed ideas about social organization, political systems, and the rise and fall of civilizations. His most famous work, the Muqaddimah (Introduction), is considered one of the earliest texts on sociology and historical analysis.
Who Was Ibn Khaldun?
Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis (present-day Tunisia) in 1332. He came from an educated family and received training in Islamic law, philosophy, mathematics, and history. He worked as a government official, diplomat, and historian across North Africa and the Middle East, which gave him firsthand experience of political instability, tribal conflicts, and the rise and fall of dynasties.
His greatest intellectual achievement was the Muqaddimah, written in 1377, where he analyzed how societies develop and decline over time. His work laid the foundation for later sociological theories, making him one of the earliest social thinkers.
Key Contributions of Ibn Khaldun to Sociology
1. Theory of Social Change and the Rise & Fall of Civilizations
One of Ibn Khaldun’s most important contributions is his theory of social change, which explains how societies grow, strengthen, and eventually decline.
Stages of Civilization: He argued that societies go through a cycle of growth, peak, and decline, just like human life (childhood, adulthood, old age).
Tribal Societies vs. Urban Societies: 
Tribal societies (Bedouins or Nomads) are strong because of their unity, discipline, and simple lifestyles.
Urban societies (Cities and Empires) grow wealthy and powerful but become corrupt and weak over time.
Luxury and Decay: Ibn Khaldun observed that when societies become wealthy and comfortable, people become lazy and lose their original strength, making them vulnerable to conquest.
Example (Nigerian Context):
Think of pre-colonial Nigerian empires like the Oyo Empire or Sokoto Caliphate. They started as strong warrior societies, expanded their territories, but later became weakened by corruption, internal conflicts, and colonial conquest.
2. Asabiyyah (Social Solidarity or Group Cohesion)
Ibn Khaldun introduced the concept of Asabiyyah, which means group solidarity or social cohesion.
He argued that strong societies are built on unity, trust, and collective purpose.
Asabiyyah is strongest in tribal or rural societies, where people rely on each other for survival.
In urban societies, asabiyyah weakens due to luxury, individualism, and political corruption, leading to the downfall of civilizations.
Example (Nigerian Context):
In rural villages, people cooperate and support each other through communal work (e.g., farming together, helping during ceremonies).
In urban cities like Lagos, people become more individualistic, and crime or corruption can increase as traditional bonds weaken.
3. Economic and Political Sociology
Ibn Khaldun also contributed to the study of economics and politics in society.
Taxation and Economic Growth: He argued that excessive taxation weakens the economy and leads to a decline in state power. 
If a government overtaxes its people, businesses collapse, and economic activities slow down.
A wise government should balance taxation to encourage trade and productivity.
Example (Nigerian Context):
If the Nigerian government overtaxes businesses, many entrepreneurs may shut down, leading to unemployment and economic decline.
But if taxation is moderate, businesses thrive, and the country’s economy grows.
Leadership and Corruption: He warned that leaders often become corrupt when they gain too much power, leading to oppression and economic decline.
Good leadership maintains social order, while corrupt leaders weaken society and invite rebellion or foreign conquest.

Max Weber
Maximilian Carl Emil Weber (/ˈveɪbər/; German: [ˈveːbɐ];[1] 21 April 1864 – 14 June 1920) was a
German sociologist, historian, jurist, and political economist who was one of the central figures in
the development of sociology and the social sciences more generally. His ideas continue to
influence social theory and research.
Born in Erfurt in 1864, Weber studied law and history in Berlin, Göttingen, and Heidelberg. After
earning his doctorate in law in 1889 and habilitation in 1891, he taught in Berlin, Freiburg, and
Heidelberg. He married his cousin Marianne Schnitger two years later. In 1897, he had a breakdown
after his father died following an argument. Weber ceased teaching and travelled until the early
1900s. He recovered and wrote The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. During the First
World War, he initially supported Germany's war effort but became critical of it and supported
democratisation. He also gave the lectures "Science as a Vocation" and "Politics as a Vocation".
After the war, Weber co-founded the German Democratic Party, unsuccessfully ran for office, and
advised the drafting of the Weimar Constitution. Becoming frustrated with politics, he resumed
teaching in Vienna and Munich. He died of pneumonia in 1920 at the age of 56, possibly as a result
of the post-war Spanish flu pandemic. A book, Economy and Society, was left unfinished.
One of Weber's main intellectual concerns was in understanding the processes of rationalisation,
secularisation, and disenchantment. He formulated a thesis arguing that such processes were
associated with the rise of capitalism and modernity. Weber also argued that the Protestant work
ethic influenced the creation of capitalism in The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. It was
followed by The Economic Ethics of the World Religions, where he examined the religions of China,
India, and ancient Judaism. In terms of government, Weber argued that states were defined by their
monopoly on violence and categorised social authority into three distinct forms: charismatic,
traditional, and rational-legal. He was also a key proponent of methodological antipositivism,
arguing for the study of social action through interpretive rather than purely empiricist methods.
Weber made a variety of other contributions to economic sociology, political sociology, and the
sociology of religion.
After his death, the rise of Weberian scholarship was slowed by the Weimar Republic's political
instability and the rise of Nazi Germany. In the post-war era, organised scholarship began to appear,
led by Talcott Parsons. Other American and British scholars were also involved in its development.
Over the course of the twentieth century, Weber's reputation grew as translations of his works
became widely available and scholars increasingly engaged with his life and ideas. As a result of
these works, he began to be regarded as a founding father of sociology, alongside Karl Marx and

Émile Durkheim, and one of the central figures in
the development of the social sciences more
generally.

ASSIGNMENT QUESTION 
THE THOUGHTS OF IBN KHALDUN ARE NOTHING BUT HISTORY WITHOUT ANY RELEVANCE IN CONTEMPORARY SOCIOLOGY, DISCUSS WITH RELEVANT EXAMPLES. 
INTRODUCTION:
Ibn Khaldun was a 14th century renowed Tunsian historian and sociologists. Khaldun was a proto-sociological thinker. He is the mostly considered as a social scientist. He lived during a time of great political conflict and change. His most famous book is the al –Muqqaddmiah(the-introduction). It is known for its deep reflections on how societies rise and fall. In the book, he talks about ideas like group unity(asabiyyah), the role of economy, and the patterns of history. Because of this, some people today say that was “the father of sociology”, although that is not widely accepted as that term is generally attributed to August Conte for coining the word “sociology”. 
The Muqaddimah has attracted attention from scholars across discilplines and eras for its remarkable attempts to understand the forces shaping civilisations. Also, his concept of Asabiyyah, or social cohesion, has been the subject of much academic interest, which has earned him recognition from time to time as a precursor to modern sociology. Muqaddimah is considered a foundational work in sociology, history, philosophy.
One of his central concepts is the distinction between ʿumran badawi (rural or nomadic civilization) and ʿumran hadari’ (urban or sedentary civilization). Ibn Khaldun argued that nomadic societies are characterized by strong ʿasabiyyah’, simplicity, and collective strength. These qualities, he believed, make them capable of conquering and establishing rule over more luxurious and sedentary urban societies. However, as these nomadic groups settle, adopt city life, and grow accustomed to luxury, their solidarity weakens, leading to social decay and eventual decline. This rise-and-fall dynamic formed the basis of his cyclical view of history.
Despite all these accolades, the relevance of Ibn Khaldun’s thoughts to contemporary sociology deserves critical examination. While it is true that some of his thoughts appear proto-sociological in nature , his thoughts were deeply embedded in a specific historical and cultural context namely, the Islamic world of the 14th century. Unlike modern sociology, which is grounded in empirical methodologies and built upon range of competing theoretical paradigms, Ibn Khaldun’s analysis leans heavily on philosophical reflection, anecdotal observation, and cyclical views of history.
Take for his example, his famous theory of Asabiyyah, which he used to explain how tribes rise to power and eventually form states, only to be replaced by other groups with stronger internal solidarity. Ibn KHaldun formed this theory based on his observations of Berber tribes and dynastic changes in North Africa and Andalusia. While insightful for understanding the political dynamics of tribal socieites , asabbiyah does not easily map out modern forms of collective action, social cohesion, or institutional stability. Today, societies operate within nation-states with formal bureaucracies, legal institutions, and mass-communication systems-mechanisms that did not exist in ibn Khaldun’s time and which demand different sociological explanations.
This write-up argues that Ibn Khaldun’s thought, though remarkable for their time, are primarily historical in nature and offer limited applicability to modern sociology theory and practice. His concepts were shaped by the unique socio-political conditions of the medieval Islamic world, they lack the empirical foundations that strengthen modern sociology, and contribute little to the theoretical framework that dominate contemporary sociological discourse. His contributions are best understood as part of the intellectual history of historiography

BIOGRAPHY 
Ibn Khaldun was born in 1332 in Tunis, which is in present-day Tunisia, North Africa. He came 
from a respected Arab family with a long tradition of public service and scholarship. From a 
young age, he was trained in Islamic studies, the Qur’an, mathematics, logic, Arabic grammar, 
and philosophy.He lived during a time of political instability and often worked as a judge, 
diplomat, and scholar. His exposure to politics and administration gave him real-life experience 
in government, which influenced his writings. 
INTRODUCTION 
Ibn Khaldun was a 14th-century North African scholar known for his book Al-Muqaddimah, 
where he wrote about how societies grow and collapse. Even though he lived many centuries 
ago, his ideas are still very relevant today, especially when we look at who controls knowledge 
in our world. In this essay, I will explain some of Ibn Khaldun’s major ideas—especially 
asabiyyah, which means group unity or social solidarity—and show how his ideas help us 
question today’s dominance of Western (European) ways of thinking in academics, a situation 
we call intellectual hegemony. I will also give examples and connect some of these ideas to what 
we learn in sociology. 
WHO WAS IBN KHALDUN AND WHAT DID HE BELIEVE? 
He is often called one of the first sociologists because he tried to explain how society works, 
even before famous European thinkers like Auguste Comte or Karl Marx. In his book Al-
Muqaddimah, he argued that: 
• 
Societies rise when people have strong unity (asabiyyah). 
• 
This unity is strongest in small groups like tribes. 
• 
When such groups come to power, they start civilizations and build states. 
• 
Over time, they become too comfortable and selfish, and they lose their unity. 
• 
Then, another stronger group takes over, and the cycle continues. 
This idea of rise and fall of states based on group unity can be compared with modern political 
theories about the strength of state institutions and national identity. 
 
WHY IS IBN KHALDUN NOT  ALWAYS TAKEN SERIOUSLY IN THE 
WEST? 
Even though Ibn Khaldun’s work came before many European scholars, he is not always taught 
in political science or sociology classes, especially in the Western world. This is because of 
intellectual hegemony—a term we can understand as when one group (usually the West) controls 
what is seen as “true” or “serious” knowledge. 

     Scholars like Edward Said, who wrote Orientalism, have said that Western countries often 
ignore or downplay non-Western knowledge. This means scholars like Ibn Khaldun are 
sometimes called “precursors” or “pre-modern,” instead of being recognized as full thinkers in 
their own right.As a result, African, Asian, and Arab thinkers are pushed to the side, while 
European thinkers are seen as the main sources of political and social theory. This is unfair and 
shows how power can affect what we learn and what we see as knowledge 
     However, despite his intellectual brilliance, Ibn Khaldun is often overlooked in Western 
academic history. This raises an important question: Why are non-Western scholars like Ibn 
Khaldun not given the same recognition as their Western counterparts? The answer lies in the 
idea of intellectual hegemony. In this essay, I will explain what intellectual hegemony means, 
how Ibn Khaldun has been affected by it, and why his work should be taken seriously in global 
knowledge systems today. 
UNDERSTANDING INTELLECTUAL  HEGEMONY 
      Intellectual hegemony is a term that refers to the dominance of certain ideas, knowledge, or 
theories over others—especially when one group controls what is considered “valid” or 
“superior” knowledge. This concept comes from the Italian thinker Antonio Gramsci, who said 
that powerful groups in society (like colonial powers or ruling elites) use not only military or 
political force but also cultural and intellectual control to maintain power.

Assignment: Write a well-illustrated essay on the meaning and relevance of Sociology in Contemporary Global Society
Sociology comes from two words: socius (Latin for society) and logos (Greek for study). This means that
sociology is the study of society. But what exactly does this mean?  
Imagine walking down a busy street in Lagos. You see traders calling out to customers, bus conductors
shouting destinations, and young people scrolling through their phones. At the same time, news headlines talk
about protests, government policies, and rising unemployment. These daily activities and events are part of
society. Sociology helps us understand why they happen and how society functions.  
One of the earliest thinkers in sociology, Auguste Comte, believed that society operates under certain laws,
just like the natural sciences. He proposed that sociology should study society in a systematic way to
understand human behavior and social change. Similarly, the 14th-century Islamic scholar Ibn Khaldun
studied how societies rise and fall. He argued that civilizations decline when they lose their cultural values.
Their ideas remain relevant today in understanding globalization, social change, and governance.  
Sociology is essential in modern society because it helps us understand social institutions, globalization, social
problems, technological advancements, and health-related issues.  
1. Understanding Social Institutions and Their Impact  
Every society has institutions that structure human interactions. These include family, education, religion,
government, and the economy. Sociology helps us understand how these institutions function and change over
time.  
For example, Nigeria's education system faces many challenges like underfunded universities and ASUU
strikes. A sociologist does not just focus on the strikes alone but asks deeper questions: Why are universities
underfunded? How does this affect students and society? This kind of analysis helps in finding long-term
solutions. The same applies to governance-corruption, poor policy implementation, and political instability all
affect the quality of education.  
Similarly, family structures in Nigeria have changed over time. In the past, extended families were common,

but now, nuclear families (just parents and children) are more popular in urban areas. Sociologists study these
changes and their effects on social behavior.  
Sociologists like Émile Durkheim studied how institutions create stability in society. He believed that when
institutions fail to function properly, society experiences disorder. His ideas can be applied to understanding
the breakdown of governance in Nigeria and the increasing level of crime.  
2. Sociology and Globalization  
Globalization connects countries through trade, technology, and culture. While it has many benefits, it also
comes with challenges. Sociology helps us understand both.  
For instance, Nollywood has gained global recognition, which benefits Nigeria's economy. But at the same
time, many Nigerian youths are adopting Western lifestyles, sometimes at the cost of traditional values. A
sociologist would ask: How does globalization shape cultural identity? Can modernization and tradition exist
together?  
The brain drain phenomenon is another effect of globalization. Many Nigerian doctors, engineers, and IT
professionals leave for countries like Canada, the UK, and the US in search of better opportunities. This
weakens Nigeria's economy. Sociologists study how this migration affects local communities and national
development.  
Ibn Khaldun's theory of Asabiyyah (social cohesion) explains how societies decline when they lose their sense
of unity. If Nigerian professionals continue leaving, it could lead to weakened institutions, affecting economic
growth.  
3. Addressing Social Problems  
Sociology also helps in understanding and solving social problems like poverty, crime, and gender inequality.
