Theories of Social Change 
 
The Meaning of Social Change: 
 
The word “change” denotes a difference in anything observed over some period of 
time. Social change, therefore, would mean observable differences in any social 
phenomena over any period of time. 
 M. D. Jenson. “Social change may be defined as modification in ways of 
doing and thinking of people.” 
 
 Anderson and Parker. “Social change involves alteration in the 
structure or functioning of social forms or processes themselves.” 
 
 
 Lundberg and others. “Social change refers to any modification in 
established patterns of inter human relationships and standards of 
conduct.” 
 
 Koenig, S. “Social change refers to the modifications which occur in the 
life patterns of a people.” 
 
 
 Jones. “Social change is a term used to describe variations in, or 
modifications of, any aspect of social processes, social patterns, social 
interaction or social organisation.” 
 

 Mazumdar, H. T. “Social change may be defined as a new fashion or 
mode, either modifying or replacing the old, in the life of a people, or in 
the operation of a society.” 
 
social change refers to the modifications which take place in the life 
patterns of people. It does not refer to all the changes going on in the 
society. The changes in art, language, technology; philosophy etc., may 
not be included in the term ‘Social change’ which should be interpreted in 
a narrow sense to mean alterations in the field of social relationships. 
 
The main characteristics of the nature of social change are as follows: 
 
 Social change is a universal phenomenon:  
Social change occurs in all societies. No society remains completely static. This 
is true of all societies, primitive as well as civilized. Society exists in a universe 
of dynamic influences. 
The population changes, technologies expand, material equipment changes, 
ideologies and values take on new components and institutional structures 
and functions undergo reshaping. The speed and extent of change may differ 
from society to society. Some change rapidly, others change slowly. 
Social change is community change:  
Social change does not refer to the change in the life of an individual or the life 
patterns of several individuals. It is a change which occurs in the life of the 
entire community. Social change is social and not individual. 

 Speed of social change is not uniform:  
While social change occurs in all societies, its speed is not uniform in every 
society. In most societies it occurs so slowly that it is often not noticed by 
those who live in them. Even in modern societies there seems to be little or no 
change in many areas. Social change in urban areas is faster than in rural 
areas. 
Social change occurs as an essential law: 
Change is the law of nature. Social change also is natural. It may occur either in 
the natural course or as a result of planned efforts. By nature we desire 
change. Our needs keep on changing. To satisfy our desire for change and our 
changing needs social change becomes a necessity. The truth is that we are 
anxiously waiting for a change. 
 Definite prediction of social change is not possible: 
It is difficult to make any prediction about the exact forms of social change. 
There is no inherent law of social change according to which it would assume 
definite forms. We may say that on account of the social reform movement 
untouchability will be abolished from the Indian society; that the basis and 
ideals of marriage will change due to the marriage laws passed by the 
government; that industrialization will increase the speed of urbanisation but 
we cannot predict the exact forms which social relationships will assume in 
future. Likewise it cannot be predicted as to what shall be our attitudes, ideas, 
norms and values in future.

The speed of social change is not uniform in each age or period in the same

ABSTRACT 
Nigeria is no doubt blessed with diverse natural resources. However, this essay seeks to 
examine the distribution of these resources along the geo-political divisions in the country 
and how each geo-political zone differs in terms of the natural resources available in each of 
them. We will first try to understand what natural resources are, the classifications and why 
they are important for a nation’s growth. 
Afterwards, we will go on to examine the diversity of the various natural resources available 
in Nigeria; from the very source of energy (the Sun), the climate harnessed by the 
atmosphere, water resources and its bye products and their accruing benefits, arable land 
distribution and its consequent effects on vegetation and then of course solid mineral 
deposits. All the above will be discussed in relation to how they are spread across the geo-
political zones. 
Maps and graphs will be an integral part this essay as illustrations to drive home certain 
points made in the essay. The discussions of the essay will be under major headings which 
will be the various types of natural resources and under these headings the diversity of each 
will be discussed as well as the factors that cause or have caused the availability or hitherto 
unavailability of the said resources. 
NATURAL RESOURCES 
Definition 
The term NATURAL means anything or material that occurs in the environment without the 
input of man. That is, Natural is anything that is not man made. Resources on the other hand 
are materials or objects that of benefit to man. These benefits could be economic or aesthetic 
in nature. We can therefore define Natural resources as materials or objects that are of benefit 
to man which exist without any input from human kind. Or we can simply put; Natural 
resources are resources that exist without any action from human kind (Oxford Dictionary, 
2014). Also, yourdictoonary.com defines natural resources as an actual or potential form of 
wealth supplied by nature. In essence, natural resources are resources provided by nature. 
Having defined natural resources we will now examine the classifications of these natural 
resources. Natural resources can be classified according to their ability to replenish and under 
this classification we have two types namely: 
1. Renewable Resources 
2. Non Renewable Resources 
Renewable resources are those resources that are capable of being replaced naturally. That is, 
renewable resources are naturally replenished. Some examples of Renewable resources are 
water, air, sunlight and wind. Their availability does not usually vary over short periods but 
they may experience depletion from over use. 
Non Renewable resources on the other hand usually experience depletion at a rate faster than 
its replenishing ability from use. The most prominent example of non Renewable resources is 
solid minerals. They are not usually available naturally or take a very long time to form. 
Nigeria has the above types of resources in abundance. Although they intensity of natural 
resources such as water and wind vary across geo-political zones because the climates differ. 

For instance. Water is less available up north because of drier climate and high rate of 
evaporation. 
Having discussed renewable and non renewable natural resources we will now discuss natural 
resource diversity.  
Natural resource diversity refers to the variation of natural resources over a given area. The 
Oxford Dictionary defines diversity as a state of being diverse or having variety. Hence 
natural resource diversity across the borders of the geo-political zones in Nigeria refers to the 
variety of natural resources in each geo political zone.  
Nigeria has six geo-political zones namely: 
1. North East 
2. North West 
3. North Central 
4. South East 
5. South West 
6. South-South 
We will now progress in this essay by discussing the variety of these natural resources in 
each of the geo-political zones.

APPROACHES TO SYSTEMATIC ANALYSIS – CONFLICT PERSPECTIVE
Dr A.O. Omobowale

--- SLIDE ---

Marx_Captalist Society (Contd)
Bourgeoisie are the owners of the means of production: Land, Offices, Machinery 

The proletariat are non-owners of the means of production, but they possess labour

The proletariat yield their labour to the bourgeoisie in order to produce and earn wages in return

--- SLIDE ---

Karl Marx
Karl Marx claims that the history of mankind have been denominated dialectic relations between two major groups:

Slavery Society: Master Vrs Slaves

Estates: Noble Vrs Serfs

Class Society: Bourgeoisie Vrs Proletariat

--- SLIDE ---

Conflict Perspective: Introduction
Conflict Perspective opines that the society is divided into two unequal parts, where the dominant exploit the dominated.

Unlike the consensus perspective, it opines that stratification is not functional, but exploitative

--- SLIDE ---

Slavery Society
Slavery: Master – Servant Relationship

The slave is a purchased property of the Master

The slave works for the master without compensation

A slave has no right

--- SLIDE ---

Estates
Estates: Nobles and Serfs

Nobles (Aristocracy and Clergy): Land owners

Serfs (farmers and masons): Land/farm workers

Serfs yielded all they produced to nobles in exchange for protection

--- SLIDE ---

Marx on Capitalist Society
Karl Marx opines that the capitalist society was divided into two dialectic groups

The Bourgeois

Proletariat

--- SLIDE ---

Marx_Captalist Society (Contd)
The bourgeoisie appropriates the product and wealth produced by the proletariat



In short, the wealth the bourgeosie claims, is appropriated from the product produced by the proletariat, while the proletariat earns low wages

--- SLIDE ---

Marx_Captalist Society (Contd)
The bourgeoisie alienates the Proletariat in Four ways

Alienation from the production process
Alienation from co-workers
Alienation from the product
Alienation from self

--- SLIDE ---

Marx_Captalist Society (Contd)
The proletariat does not take note of the exploitative and alienation processes because he is in a state-in-itself, hence has false consciousness

The proletariat will eventually gain consciousness, transit from a state-in-itself to a state-for-itself and engage the bourgeoisie in class revolution, that it would win.

Hence, the society will become classless and the means of production will belong to the state.

Soc 215: Social Processes

--- SLIDE ---

Social process defined
Social processes are the ways in which individuals and groups interact, adjust and readjust and establish relationships and pattern of behaviour which are again modified through social interactions.

Social interactions are reciprocal relationships which not only influence the interacting individuals but also the quality of relationships. 

According to Gillin and Gillin, social interaction refers to social relations of all sorts in functions – dynamic social relations of all kinds – whether such relations exist between individual and individual, between group and group and group and individual, as the case may be”.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of social process
Socialisation:  Process of internalizing norms and ideologies

Cooperation: Working together to achieve a common goal 

Conflict: Deliberate attempt to oppose

Competition: Social struggle 

Accommodation: Process of social adjustment 

Acculturation: Acquisition or adjustment to a new culture 


Assimilation: Process by which different cultures are united

--- SLIDE ---

Classification of social process
Loomis classified social processes into two categories; 

 The elemental process: are those by which the separate elements of the social system are articulated.

The comprehensive or master processes:  are those by which several or all of the elements are articulated or involved. These elements are beliefs (knowledge), sentiment, end or goal, norm, status-role (position), rank, power, sanction, and facility.

--- SLIDE ---

Social Processes
Man has an inherent nature to interact.

Interaction is pivotally essential for man’s existence and survival

 As man interacts, he builds his structures, cultures, institutions, norms and values that support human existence and survival

--- SLIDE ---

Critical factors in social process
Social evolution

Borrowing and diffusion

Discovery and invention: New technology

Assimilation: weaker cultural group subsumed into stronger cultural group

Acculturation: 2 cultural knowledge converge (melting pot)

Cultural loss: cultural extinction

Planned and guided change: deliberate initiation of policies by the government, cultural groups, etc.

--- SLIDE ---

Basic essentials of social processes
a. Culture—Total ways of life of a people…

b. Language—a veritable medium of communication, socialization and cultural diffusion

--- SLIDE ---

Social Processes
c. Social Institutions and Structures– social institutions and social structures comprise of interacting individuals within a particular society/culture with distinctive norms, values, roles and practices. Social institutions impact peoples norms, values, and in fact the totality of their ways of life. 

A society is made up of diverse structures as defined by the society. Sociologists have however identified five basic social institutions with which every society is comprised. 

These are the family, economic, political, religious and educational institutions.

--- SLIDE ---

Social Processes
All these institutions contribute to the processes of the social construction of human beings. 

But for these institutions, structures and inherent cultures, human beings would just be biological/physiological frames.

Poser: describe the “personality” of an individual who has been isolated from birth

--- SLIDE ---

Social Processes
d. Norms and values: norms are rules that guide behaviour while values are standards of expected behaviour

e. Socialization process: the process through which norms, values and cultures are transferred from one generation to another.

f. Internalization: this happens when cultural patterns, norms and values become parts and parcel of an individual.

--- SLIDE ---

Social Processes
g. Agents of socialization: 

Family

Education 

Religion 

Political institution

Economic institution and

Mass media (e.g. newspapers and periodicals, TVs radio and quite recently but very phenomenal, cable TV.)

SOCIAL INSTITUTIONS DEFINED



“According to Ekpenyong (2003), “social institutions refers to the
organisations, patterned, accepted and standardized procedures and
conduct designed toward the attainment of society’s basic needs.”
 
Adeola (1987) sees it “as complex, or clusters of roles, which are knit
together for the accomplishment of certain needs”.
 
Giddens (1982) observes that social institutions are basic modes of
social activities which are followed by majority of members of a given
society with a quest for achieving basic needs. This may include
folkways, mores, laws, customs, traditions, values, etc.
 Department of Sociology Seminar Series

CHARACTERISTICS OF SOCIAL INSTITUTIONS






Institutions are purposive in the sense that each has its objectives or goals to
satisfy social needs.
 
They are relatively permanent in their structure.
 
They tend to become traditional and enduring.
 
Each institution is a uniﬁed structure and functions as a unit.
 
The institution is necessarily value laden and tends to become a code of conduct.
 
Each institution is afﬁliated and derive rights from some or other society.
 
Department of Sociology Seminar Series

TYPES OF SOCIAL INSTITUTIONS





Family institution
 
Religious institution/system
 
Economic institution/system
 
Educational institution/system
 
Political institution/system
Department of Sociology Seminar Series

FAMILY INSTITUTION/SYSTEM (A)




Family - the most basic institution
 
George Peter Murdock (1949) deﬁnes the family as a universal institution.
According to him, the family is a ‘social group characterised by common
residence, economic corporation and reproduction. It includes adults of
both sexes at least two of whom maintain a socially approved sexual
relationship and one or more children owned or adopted of the sexually
cohabiting adults’.
 
The United States Census Bureau (2007) deﬁnes the family as a relatively
permanent group of two or more people who are related by blood, marriage
or adoption and who live under the same roof.
 
Dubermn and Hartjen (1979) deﬁnes family as a universal institution whose
most important functions are to socialize and nurture the younger
generation.
Department of Sociology Seminar Series

FORMS AND TYPES OF FAMILY










a) Family based on structure and compositions
Nuclear family – Father, mother and the children
Single parent family – Only biological parent takes care of the children
Extended family – consists two or more nuclear families
 
b) Family based on residence
Neolocal family residence: New couple establishes a new residence
Patrilocal family residence: Couple lives with the husband’s family
Matrilocal/uxorilocal residence: Couple lives with the wife’s family
Bilocal/ambilocal residence: Residence in either the wife or husband’s immediate
family
Avunculocal residence: Marital residence where the couple settle with his mother’s
relatives
Amitilocal residence: Couple lives with the wife’s father’s sister
Uxiri-virilocal residence: Couple lives with the wife’s family and later to the
husband’s family.
Department of Sociology Seminar Series

FORMS AND TYPES OF FAMILY (CONTD.)






c) Family based on authority and power
Patriarchal family: Authority resides in paternal side.
Matriarchal family: Authority resides in the maternal or the oldest
female.
Egalitarian family: Authority is neither dominated by the husband nor
the wife.
 
d) Family based on descent
Patrilineal family: Tracing ancestry to the father’s lineage
Matrilineal family: Tracing ancestry to the mother’s lineage
Bilateral family: Tracing ancestry to both sides of the family

SOC 215: STRUCTURE OF NIGERIAN SOCIETY
TOPIC: SOCIAL PROBLEM
JANUARY 2020

--- SLIDE ---

Social Problem Defined
Social problem can be defined as: 

The problems that emerge from social interactions, caused by strains in social systems and which threaten the realisation of societal norms or values (Adenugba, 2009).


The problems which a large segment of the society perceive as creating undesirable difference between socially prescribed norms or ideals and social realities.

Any condition or behavior that has negative consequences for large numbers of people and that is generally recognized as a condition or behavior that needs to be addressed. This definition has both an objective component and a subjective component.

--- SLIDE ---

Social Problem: Objective Component vs Subjective Component
a) The objective component: 

For any condition or behavior to be considered a social problem, it must have negative consequences for large numbers of people.


b) The subjective component: 

There must be a perception that a condition or behavior needs to be addressed for it to be considered a social problem. This component lies at the heart of the social constructionist view of social problems (Rubington, & Weinberg, 2010).

--- SLIDE ---

Conditions for Social Problem
The problem must be perceived to be a social problem by the public.

The problem must create an undesirable gap between social ideals and reality.

It must be solvable through collective action.

The problem should have some effect on a large percentage of the population.

--- SLIDE ---

Causes of Social Problem(s)
There are usually multiple causes of social problems in the society. According to Adenugba (2009) these causes include, but not limited, to the following:

Chaos: The occurrence of disorderliness in the society.

Deviance and misbehaviour e.g. armed robbery, theft, exam malpractice, etc.

Socio-cultural, political and demographic changes: sudden change in the societal values or policies e.g. a ban on okada riding, exposure of youths to material culture (gang culture), internet/ICT, etc.

Social conflicts e.g. social inequality, injustice, ethnicity, etc.

--- SLIDE ---

Stages in Life Cycle of Social Problem
There are five (5) evolutionary process or stages in the life cycle of social problems (Blumer, 1997 cf. Adenugba, 2009):

Discovery stage. The problem gets discovered at this point, the point when the people notice the existence of the problem for the first time.

Confirmation stage. The reality and the extent of the problem would be ascertained. The society confirms that the problem is actually a social problem.

Prevention stage. The society usually embarks on advocacy to bring the problem to the awareness of other members of the public in a bid to prevent its spread.

Eradication stage. The society draws up plans to eradicate the problem. 

Implementation stage. The strategies that had been mapped out in the earlier phase will be set in motion at this point. The goal is mainly to solve the problem through collective action.

--- SLIDE ---

Some social problems in contemporary Nigeria
There are a number of contemporary social problems in Nigeria. Each of them also comes with its consequences. These include:
 
Unemployment & underemployment: Absence of jobs/not using trained skills

Youth unemployment e.g. unemployed graduates and youths with vocation that lack job to do (the major cause of youth unemployment is misconception about office jobs). 

Militancy & insurgency e.g. boko haram insurgency in the north-east Nigeria, militancy in the Niger Delta region, hostage taking, etc.

Kidnapping e.g. kidnapping for ransom and rituals are common in Nigeria today

Ethnicity: Suspicion of one another based on membership of ethnic group (Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo), the issue of prebendalism (most times employment/political appointment is based on ethnic identity.

Individuality and Social Networks
Introduction
From the last topic, the urban social structure, it would be observed that the characteristics identified with the urban space have nothing to do with the physical infrastructures. This implies that, for Sociologists, what we are interested in are the things that have implications for the human beings living in the urban space. Yes, ‘the good things of life’, good roads, electricity, pipe-borne water, and so on, are, most often, largely located in the urban space, they do not, in the last instance, define the survival of the urban people. Yes, they may assist in ‘making life easier’, yet, they may constitute untold burdens for the people in terms of their availability, sustainability and affordability, among others. For us, as Sociologists, how people navigate the complex social relations characterizing the urban space is of utmost importance. The complex social relations are compounded by the rolling back of the fundamental roles of family, the foundation of almost every society, in the urban space. These roles are, in the main, reallocated to other social institutions. For instance, the educational institutions, especially the formal type, which someone once referred to as the source of the ‘meal ticket’, have become a very important socializing agency through which access to other institutions, including the economic and politics, are determined. Indeed, formal educational institution is also becoming the defining factor even in the family and religion!
Some examples of changing roles and relevance of formal social institutions
The above, of course, is totally different from the social networks created through the earlier known social institutions in sociological studies such as the family, education, religious, political, economic and the mass media. Ideally, the experiences in these social institutions are expected to be the bedrock of their social networks, which some people refer to as the net worth. More often than not, the socialization processes experienced from these institutions are physical. And, it is often assumed, it is the extent to which one is socialized by these institutions that determines the person’s life chances. But, to what extent does family socialization, no matter how deep, implicate its relevance to the individual? Religion that used to be in the family is now independent of it. Even religion, it seems, is more in the realm of the ‘profane’ rather than the ‘sacred’. Individuals, mainly, define their religions by themselves: it is what suits me that is ‘my’ religion! It is no longer, it seems, determined by a ‘community’ of believers. Indeed, the ‘community’ is no longer physical but digital! But, don’t some people still go to the physical mosque/church for networking? Is this still the practice or, isn’t it that the personality factors now determine the extent to which we are socialized into the religious practices. Who is this individual? How is s/he defined?
In the formal educational institution, individuality seems to be the fulcrum! The individual’s certificate is meant only for her/him and almost all the processes of certification are individualized. Her/his certificate cannot be inherited by any other person as s/he sits for all the examinations alone. Such individuality percolates into other social institutions through the achieved, or is it acquired, certificate(s). Yet, the extent to which the individual succeeds in the examination, even in gaining access to the educational institution, is, to a large extent, defined by factors external, one way or the other, to her/him. For instance, family status may inform access to and performance in the formal educational institution. Yet, only the individual is expected to enjoy the fall-outs of the successes, if any. 
The ‘individual’ in the new social network
Seemingly more interesting in the ways by which the individual is being socialized is the fact that the individual is now dissociated from her/h

PHENOMENOLOGY AND ETHNOMETHODOLOGY 
 
 
 
Phenomenology is a methodology of philosophical research initiated in 1900 by 
mathematician Edmund Husserl (1859-1938). The core of phenomenological method 
consists in the disciplined use of the reflective techniques of ‘bracketing’ and ‘reduction’ 
to disclose the essential features of intentional objects (objects perceivable or imaginable 
by conscious human beings). Applied to the dispositions, anticipations, and intuitions of 
the intending subject, the same techniques disclose the ‘transcendental’ conditions and 
processes of subjectivity as such (i.e., of the rational subject of the European 
Enlightenment). Husserl developed first eidetic, then transcendental phenomenology in 
an endeavor to clarify the foundations of the sciences, a project that was well underway 
in mathematics when he began his investigations. His realization in 1931 that 
‘transcendental intersubjectivity… constitutes the world as an objective world, as a world 
that is identical for everyone’ (quoted in Moran 2000: 179) may be considered, at least 
honorifically, as the founding moment of phenomenological sociology. His most 
important contribution to the social sciences is the concept the lifeworld (Lebenswelt), 
the pregiven, unproblematicized, pretheoretical ground of shared language, familiar 
objects, and tacit meanings that the intending subject inhabits ‘prepredicatively.’  
Ethnomethodology is a partial offshoot of phenomenological sociology with deep 
roots in classical social theory and sociolinguistics (Hilbert 1992). It is the descriptive 
study of the reporting and accounting practices (‘methods’) through which socially 
embedded actors come to attribute meaning and rationality to their own and others’ 
behavior. Ethnomethodologists study interactive, ad hoc sense making at the sites where 
social structures are produced and reproduced through talk and coordinated action. The 
central claim of ethnomethodology is that ‘[p]henomena of order are identical with the 
procedures for their local endogenous production and accountability’ (Garfinkel 2002: 
72).   
While phenomenology and ethnomethodology differ in their disciplinary 
orientations, research questions, and levels of analysis, they share a common problematic 
in the constitution of objectivities. The term ‘constitution’ refers to the precipitation of a 
unified meaning from a cascading series of overlapping and synchronous perceptual, 

 
2
apperceptual, and categorical processes, whose redundancy confirms the objectivity of 
the identity thus produced. What serial constitution ultimately produces is not the 
furniture of the universe, but the known structures and processes upon which human 
beings premise and account for their actions. When dealing with affirmed bodies of 
knowledge—whether in science, the professionals, or everyday life—phenomenology 
and ethnomethodology seek to show how such knowledge is possible:  They strive to 
retrace the steps through which articulated descriptions, definitions, axioms, concepts, or

RESEARCH DESIGN, PURPOSE AND TYPES  
 
Research design is regarded as the total plan of a given study (Agbaje & Alarape, 2006). It is the 
process for deciding what aspects we shall observe, of whom, and for what purpose.  It involves a 
set of decisions regarding what topic is to be studied, among what population, with what research 
methods, for what purpose.  It is the process of focusing your perspective for the purposes of a 
particular study. Social research can serve many purposes. These purposes can affect the way in 
which we design our research  
Three purposes of research: 
(1) Exploratory purpose: Much of social research is conducted to explore a topic, that is, to 
start to familiarize a researcher with that topic. This approach occurs when a researcher 
examines a new interest or when the subject of study is relatively new.  For example, you 
might want to find out about the emergence of Save Nigeria Group- SNG in Nigeria; you 
might want to learn more about the group: how widespread is it; what level and degrees of 
support are there within the community? How is the movement organized? Explorative 
studies are also appropriate for more persistent phenomena.  
Explorative studies are most typically done for three purposes: (i) to satisfy researchers’ 
curiosity and desire for better understanding, (ii) to test the feasibility of undertaking a 
more extensive study and (iii) to develop the methods to be employed in any subsequent 
study. 
Explorative studies are quite valuable in social scientific research. They are essential 
whenever a researcher is breaking new ground, and they almost yield new insights into 
topic for research. However, the chief shortcoming of explorative study is that they seldom 
provide satisfactory answers to research questions, this is because the people studied might 
not be representative enough to make conclusion about general population.  
(2) Descriptive purpose: A major purpose of social scientific studies is to describe situations 
and events. The researcher observes and then describes what was observed.  Many 
qualitative studies aim primarily at description, an ethnographer may try to detail the 
particular culture of some society. Most of the time, studies are not limited to description, 
researcher usual go on to examine why the observed pattern exists and what they imply. 
(3) Explanatory purpose: The purpose of research is to explain things. For instance, a 
descriptive research may report the poll result or voting intentions of the people in 
Anambra, reporting why some people plan to vote for Soludo is explanatory. This is where 
the causal explanation for a pattern is given. 
 
Time Dimension to Research Design 
Observations can be made more or less at one time or over a long period. Time plays many roles 
in the design and execution of research aside from the time it takes to do research.  For instance, 
do the description and explanation resulting from a particular study accurately represent the 
situation of ten years ago or ten years from the conduct of the study. 
(i) 
Cross-sectional study involves observations of a sample, or cross section, of a 
population or phenomenon that are made at one point in time. Exploratory and 
descriptive studies are often cross-sectional. A researcher conducting a large 
national survey on demographic and health survey is likely to be cross-sectional, 
taking a snapshot at a particular point in history. Shortcoming of such study is the 

need of social research which often involves revisiting phenomena and building on 
the result of earlier research. 
(ii) 
A longitudinal study is designed to permit observations of the same phenomenon

cult group from inception to demise. Longitudinal studies can be more difficult for

Abstract 
Taking an interactional perspective on creativity, the authors examined the influence of social networks 
and conformity value on employees' creativity. They theorized and found a curvilinear relationship 
between number of weak ties and creativity such that employees exhibited greater creativity when their 
number of weak ties was at intermediate levels rather than at lower or higher levels. In addition, 
employees' conformity value moderated the curvilinear relationship between number of weak ties and 
creativity such that employees exhibited greater creativity at intermediate levels of number of weak ties 
when conformity was low than when it was high. A proper match between personal values and network 
ties is critical for understanding creativity. 
 
Keywords: Cross-cultural differences, Modesty, Negativity, Self-evaluations

QUESTION: Using symbolic interactionist perspective account for the various ways that Nigerian's make sense out of the current Hardship in the country.
Introduction
Nigerians interpret their current hardships through personal and collective meanings shaped by social interactions. Symbolic interactionism approach emphasizes how individuals construct their realities based on symbols and language, allowing them to navigate challenges like economic instability and political strife. By sharing experiences and narratives within communities, they create a shared understanding of resilience and adaptation. They even go about with a slogan “E go better, God go help us” This perspective highlights the active role of Nigerians in redefining their identities and coping strategies amidst adversity, illustrating that hardship is not merely a structural issue but also a deeply personal experience influenced by social contexts.
The symbolic interactionist perspective, rooted in the ideas of George Herbert Mead and Herbert Blumer, emphasizes how individuals interpret and give meaning to their experiences. George Herbert Mead (1934) posits that human interactions are shaped by symbols, particularly language, which facilitates social communication.  Blumer (1969) defines symbolic interactionism as a framework that allows individuals to make sense of complex social phenomena through shared meanings and interactions For instance, many might share anecdotes about resilience, framing their experiences as part of a broader narrative of survival. Additionally, social media serves as a platform for Nigerians to express frustrations and solidarity, reinforcing community bonds. Symbolic interactionism provides a valuable framework for understanding the subjective of Nigerians facing hardship. This perspective emphasizes the micro-level interactions and meanings individuals attach to their circumstances, allowing for a nuanced exploration of how people navigate their challenges. It  reveals how personal interactions and shared symbols shape their understanding of adversity, transforming hardship into a collective identity of resilience and hope.
Context of which Nigeria faces several socio-economic challenges
Approximately 38.9% of the population lives below the poverty line, with about 87 million Nigerians affected. In the context of unemployment,  there is high youth unemployment rates, exacerbated by economic mismanagement and the COVID-19 pandemic, lead to job losses and reduced salaries. There is also the issue of  insecurity causing the widespread violence from banditry, kidnappings, and terrorist activities disrupt daily life and economic stability. The issue of persistent corruption undermines governance and the effective distribution of resources, hindering development efforts.
Individual Interpretations
Individuals interpret these hardships through various lenses. For example, through coping mechanisms Nigerians use support systems, by relying on family and local networks for assistance during tough times e.g. We can see on Twitter now know as X where people donated some amount of money to a woman called Deborah for a efforts in cooking very early for her husband before he goes to work due to high cost of mama put. People often express their struggles through symbolic communication e.g. cultural narratives using of stickers and memes on WhatsApp, Facebook, etc., art, and, fostering a sense of shared experience. They share a resilience narratives by viewing hardships as challenges to be overcome, promoting a culture of resilience that emphasizes hope and perseverance amidst adversity. We can see in our society how guys greet themselves shaking one another when they meet.

Topic 2:  Descriptive Statistics 
Descriptive statistics is often used to: 
o To describe the characteristics of the sample  
o To check the variables for any violation of the assumptions underlying the 
statistical techniques that will be used to address the research questions 
o To address specific research questions

SOC 311: STATISTICAL METHODS IN SOCIOLOGY
Course Manual
General Introduction
This course introduces Sociology majors to statistics in social research. You will be introduced to the concepts underlying probability sampling, what a sampling distribution is, and the role of a sampling distribution in statistical inference. When you complete this course you should be capable of deciding the appropriate statistical (analytical) design for your research needs: knowing, for example, when and how to use correlation and regression to describe the relationship between a pair of variables and to test hypotheses about means, proportions etc. Interpretation of computed Regression analysis will also be discussed. Most of the practical examples and exercises for this manual were extracted from Elementary Statistics: A Step by Step Approach and Complete Business Statistics listed in the reference section.
LECTURER: Dr Olufunke Fayehun

The Normal Distribution

Statistics is the science of conducting studies to collect, organizes, summarize, analyze and draw conclusion from data.  
A statistic is any numerical information describing a characteristic of a sample e.g age of a student. 
Population consists of all subjects (human or otherwise) that are being studied. It is the sent representing all measurement of interest to the research. 
A sample is a group of subject selected from a population. Most of the time, it is not possible to use the entire population for statistical study due to size, expense, medical reasons and time.

LECTURE ONE
Meaning of Human Resource Management (HRM)

3
Introduction
In this lecture, we shall discuss the meaning of Human Resource Management. To start with, we
shall consider many definitions, then distinguish between HRM and Personnel Management and
discuss its centrality to organizations.
Objectives
At the end of this lecture, students should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of HRM
2. Relate it to the overall activities of organizations
Pre-Test
1. What is Human Resource management?
2. How central is it to organizations?
CONTENT
The terms "Human Resource Management" and "Human Resources" (HR) have largely replaced
the term "personnel management" as a description of the processes involved in managing people
in organizations. The term HRM is increasingly being used in business as an alternative to
personnel management because more and more people feel that it is in tune with the realities of
organizational life.
What then is Human Resources Management? The term has been widely defined by scholars and
practitioners. Some definitions are offered below:
HRM is a process of bringing and keeping people and organizations together so that the goals of
each are met;
HRM encompasses those activities designed to provide for and coordinate the human resources
of an organization.
HR functions refer to those tasks and duties performed in organizations to provide for and
coordinate human resources.
HRM is the function performed in organizations that facilitates the most effective use of the
employees to achieve organizational and individual goals.

4
Human Resource Management (HRM) is defined as the policies, practices and systems that
influence employees’behaviour, attitude and performance while Ogunbameru, (2008) sees it as
the strategic and coherent approach to the management of an organization’s most valued assets -
the people working there who individually and collectively contribute to the achievement of the
objectives of the business.

Study Session 1: Conceptualizing Research  
Introduction 
In this session, we describe the dynamics of research in terms of fundamental and 
critical functions in the social sciences. The section is designed to give students an 
understanding of the concept of research. The section will also introduced to the 
students, the meaning of research and explain its role in decision-making processes. 
This section will also discuss the nature and scope of research and explain is roles in 
social science research. Finally, the section will discuss the relationship between 
social research and natural science highlighting the basic similarities between two.  
Learning Outcomes for the study session 1 
After completing this chapter, the students should be able to: 
(a) Define research as both an operational function and a process  
(b) Define research and be able to explain the purpose (s) for doing research 
(c) Identify and define all the major elements of research 
(d) Explain the components of the research process    
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
3
1.1 What is research?  
What is research? Depending on whom you ask, you will likely get very different 
answers to this seemingly innocent question. Some people will say that they routinely 
research different online platforms to find the best place to buy goods or services they 
want. Television news channels supposedly conduct research in the form of viewer or 
opinion polls on topics of public interest such as forthcoming elections or government 
policies. University undergraduate often search the Internet to seek information to 
complete assignments or compliment lectures. Graduate students working on research 
projects may see research as collecting or analyzing data related to their thesis or 
dissertations. Businesses and consultants search potential solutions to correct 
organizational challenges such as a supply chain bottleneck or to identify customer 
purchase patterns. However, none of the above can be considered “scientific research” 
unless: (1) it contributes to a body of knowledge, and (2) it follows the scientific 
process.  Following from the above, research can therefore be defined as a systematic, 
formal, rigorous and precise process employed to gain solutions to problems or to 
discover and interpret new facts and relationships. (Waltz and Bausell, 1981). Payton, 
(1979) defined research as the process of looking for a specific answer to a specific 
question in an organized, objective, reliable way. For Kerlinger (1973), Research is 
systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation of hypothetical 
propositions about the presumed relations among natural phenomena. And Kothari 
(2006) views Research as the pursuit of truth with the help of study, observation, 
comparison and experiment; the search for knowledge through objective and 

 
4
systematic method of finding solutions to a problem. A research therefore is a 
systematic investigation of a social phenomenon in an attempt to explain, describe or 
explore a situation, social setting or relationships. Research is defined as 
“methodological investigation into a subject in order to develop a plan of action based 
on the facts discovered”. In a nutshell, research is organized study for a specific 
purpose. It is formal work undertaken systematically to increase the stock of 
knowledge, including knowledge of humanity, culture and society, and the use of this 
stock of knowledge to devise new applications (OECD (2002). Research is used to 
establish or confirm facts, reaffirm the results of previous work, solve new or existing 
problems, support theorems, or develop new theories.

INTRODUCTION 
This manual is going to discuss on Social Research in the Social Sciences also known as the 
Behavioural Sciences as it deals with the scientific processes in human thought and behavior. 
Specificity will be on Sociology as a discipline engaged in the channel and art of Social 
Research. Generally, the lives of humans are affected by their environment as a result of their 
social interaction. The various scenes where there are human social interactions such as market 
place, religious gatherings, political rallies, schools etc. are all subject to human inquiry with the 
aim of enhancing situations and changing social conditions. For instance one might learn that 
women often go to religious gatherings than men. The process of learning and reflecting on one‘s 
knowledge is a remarkable endeavor which subjects an individual on ―how do you know that?‖. 
The scenes earlier mentioned are environments subjected to as a laboratory experiment using the 
art of social sciences. How do one identify a social problem and or social condition and subject it 
to inquiry to have an understanding of that social problem and or social condition. What are the 
methods most suitable to engage in by the researcher to have an insight into the social 
phenomenon under study to get good research findings? What medium should be implored to 
disseminate the research findings and the challenges and errors in the conduct of social research? 
Of importance are the principles guiding the ethics of a social research. It is expected that at the 
end of this manual, you will be able to understand and undertake social research, since you 
would have learnt and developed the practical skills required in the art of social research with its 
applicability in academic and professional sceneries.

STUDY SESSION 1:  
WHAT IS SOCIAL RESEARCH? 
Introduction   
In this study session, you will learn about the art of social research in the social or behavioural 
sciences. However, specificity will be on Sociology as a discipline engaged as a channel in social 
research. The conceptualization on identifying a social problem and the processes involved in 
inquiry of a social phenomenon will be discussed. 
Learning Outcomes for Study Session 1 
At the end of the session, students should be able to: 
a. Give an account on the emergence of Sociology as a social science discipline, and the 
concepts used in the conduct of research.  
      b. The relevance of theory and its applicability in the conduct of a social research. 
1.1 Sociology as a Social Science Discipline 
Sociology is said to have its roots in the works of philosophers such as Plato, Aristotle and 
Confuscius. As a discipline it was precipitated by the Age of Enlightenment in the 17th and 18th 
Century and subsequently the Age of Revolution (French Revolution). The Age of 
Enlightenment also known as the Age of Reason was an era when philosophers and scientists 
had scientific discoveries. The writings of the Philosophers and Scientists such as Galileo, 
Francis Bacon, Rene Descartes and Isaac Newton emphasized the idea of progress guided by 
human reason and opposed to the dominant notion that the human condition was ordained by 
God and could not be improved by human actions. It was a period preceded by and closely 
associated with the Scientific Revolution. The Scientific Revolution was a period marked by 
Modern Science which gave birth to developments in Mathematics, Astronomy, Physics, 
Biology, Chemistry etc. which transformed societal views about nature. Then came the Age of 
Revolution (Industrial Revolution).

FUNCTINALISST THEORY OF SOCIAL STRAATIFICATION – TALCOT 
PARSONS 
 
DR. AUSTIN 
 
 
 

1 
 
ABSTRACT 
Social stratification, the hierarchical division of individuals and groups within a society, has 
captivated the attention of scholars across various disciplines. It is “the differential ranking of 
the human individuals who compose a given social system and their treatment as superior and 
inferior relative to one another in certain socially important respects” (Parsons, 1940). This 
paper examines Talcott Parsons' functionalist theory of social stratification, focusing on its core 
elements and their application to understanding the social stratification in the Nigerian society. 
Drawing upon Parsons' work in “An analytical approach to the theory of social stratification” 
(1940), this paper discusses Talcott Parsons analysis on social stratification. 
At the heart of the functionalist approach lies the analogy of society as an organism, with each 
part contributing to the whole. Different social institutions, like the family, education system, 
and economy, fulfil distinct yet interconnected functions (Merton, 1949). Functionalists argue 
that inequality is inherent and unavoidable in this system, as not all roles contribute equally to 
its smooth operation. Some roles, like doctors and engineers, are deemed functionally more 
important due to the demanding skills, extensive training, and crucial contributions they offer 
to societal well-being. 
Furthermore, he mentions the importance of socialization in maintaining this stratified order. 
Through various institutions, particularly the family and education system, individuals are 
socialized into accepting their designated roles within the social hierarchy (Parsons, 1951). 
This internalization of societal norms, they argue, promotes stability and social cohesion by 
fostering a sense of duty and commitment to fulfilling one's assigned role. Applying Parsons' 
theory to Nigeria sheds light on functional roles in Nigerian society, showcasing how diverse 
groups like farmers, entrepreneurs, and educators contribute to societal needs (Fabo, 2021). 
Furthermore, it advocates for meritocracy, underlining the significance of merit and skills in 
rewarding individuals' contributions (Okeke, 2019).  
However, the functionalist perspective has also drawn significant criticism. Critics highlight 
its overly simplistic portrayal of social stratification, neglecting the historical and power 
dynamics that often contribute to its formation and perpetuation. Moreover, the emphasis on 
meritocratic ideals can obscure the systemic inequalities that may restrict upward mobility for 
certain groups based on factors like race, gender, and socioeconomic background (Collins, 
1971). It’s limitations in relation to the Nigeria society includes its oversimplification of social 
mobility, disregarding the impact of ethnicity, gender, and family background on social 

2 
 
position beyond merit (Okonjo, 2013). Additionally, it overlooks power dynamics inherent in 
social stratification, neglecting how privileged groups maintain their status through societal 
structures (Ake, 1981). Thus, while the functionalist theory offers valuable insights into the 
potential stability-enhancing functions of social stratification, it is crucial to acknowledge its 
limitations. By engaging in critical reflection on both its strengths and weaknesses, we can gain 
a more nuanced understanding of the complex and dynamic nature of social stratification within 
societies.

SOC 405: Sociology of Development  
 
Course outline 
 
This course, Sociology of Development seeks to examine the factors that instigate economic, social 
and political changes in the society. As much as development is germane to human survival, it 
remains a phenomenon that is quite contentious and seemingly difficult to achieve amongst The 
Third World Countries”. This contentious nature of development is further aggravated and 
amplified by opposing inclinations which struggled for adherents, most especially during the 20th 
century. From the Capitalist orientations of the West to the Socialist orientations of the East, the 
need to develop reverberating in spite of the divergent channels recommended. Of course, 
capitalism seems to have dominated the space after the collapse of the socialist empire in 1990. 
Sociology of Development as a course will not supply or offer solutions for problems linked to the 
development, it will rather activate constructive discourse that will enable learners to explore and 
understand the various dimensions of developmental issues. Since the concept of Development is 
beyond systemic (or non) poverty alleviation etc.. The course will bring to forte the meaning of 
development to include social change, the changes in values and norms and the overview of 
political, social and economic structures that supports or hinders development. Thus, the main 
concern of the course will be to interrogate what capitalism portents for the s0-called “Third World 
Countries”.

PREFACE TO THE FIRST EDITION 
   
In 1893 we published a ‘Preliminary Communication’¹ on a new method of examining and treating hysterical 
phenomena. To this we added as concisely as possible the theoretical conclusions at which we had arrived. 
We are here reprinting this ‘Preliminary Communication’ to serve as the thesis which it is our purpose to 
illustrate and prove. 
   We have appended to it a series of case histories, the selection of which could not unfortunately be 
determined on purely scientific grounds. Our experience is derived from private practice in an educated and 
literate social class, and the subject matter with which we deal often touches upon our patients’ most 
intimate lives and histories. It would be a grave breach of confidence to publish material of this kind, with 
the risk of the patients being recognized and their acquaintances becoming informed of facts which were 
confided only to the physician. It has therefore been impossible for us to make use of some of the most 
instructive and convincing of our observations. This of course applies especially to all those cases in which 
sexual and marital relations play an important aetiological part. Thus it comes about that we are only able to 
produce very incomplete evidence in favour of our view that sexuality seems to play a principal part in the 
pathogenesis of hysteria as a source of psychical traumas and as a motive for ‘defence’ - that is, for 
repressing ideas from consciousness. It is precisely observations of a markedly sexual nature that we have 
been obliged to leave unpublished. 
   The case histories are followed by a number of theoretical reflections, and in a final chapter on 
therapeutics the technique of the ‘cathartic method’ is propounded, just as it has grown up under the hands 
of the neurologist. 
   If at some points divergent and indeed contradictory opinions are expressed, this is not to be regarded as 
evidence of any fluctuation in our views. It arises from the natural and justifiable differences between the 
opinions of two observers who are agreed upon the facts and their basic reading of them, but who are not 
invariably at one in their interpretations and conjectures. 
J. BREUER, S. FREUD

The Interpretation of Dreams
Sigmund Freud (1900)
 
PREFACE TO THE THIRD EDITION
Wheras there was a space of nine years between the first and second editions of this book, the need of a third edition was apparent when little 
more than a year had elapsed. I ought to be gratified by this change; but if I was unwilling previously to attribute the neglect of my work to its 
small value, I cannot take the interest which is now making its appearance as proof of its quality. 
 The advance of scientific knowledge has not left The Interpretation of Dreams untouched. When I wrote this book in 1899 there was as yet no 
"sexual theory," and the analysis of the more complicated forms of the psychoneuroses was still in its infancy. The interpretation of dreams was 
intended as an expedient to facilitate the psychological analysis of the neuroses; but since then a profounder understanding of the neuroses has 
contributed towards the comprehension of the dream. The doctrine of dream-interpretation itself has evolved in a direction which was 
insufficiently emphasized in the first edition of this book. From my own experience, and the works of Stekel and other writers, [1] I have since 
learned to appreciate more accurately the significance of symbolism in dreams (or rather, in unconscious thought). In the course of years, a mass 
of data has accumulated which demands consideration. I have endeavored to deal with these innovations by interpolations in the text and 

footnotes. If these additions do not always quite adjust themselves to the framework of the treatise, or if the earlier text does not everywhere come 
up to the standard of our present knowledge, I must beg indulgence for this deficiency, since it is only the result and indication of the increasingly 
rapid advance of our science. I will even venture to predict the directions in which further editions of this book - should there be a demand for 
them - may diverge from previous editions. Dream-interpretation must seek a closer union with the rich material of poetry, myth, and popular 
idiom, and it must deal more faithfully than has hitherto been possible with the relations of dreams to the neuroses and to mental derangement. 
 Herr Otto Rank has afforded me valuable assistance in the selection of supplementary examples, and has revised the proofs of this edition. I have 
to thank him and many other colleagues for their contributions and corrections. 
 Vienna, 1911 - 
 [1] Omitted in subsequent editions.  
PREFACE TO THE SECOND EDITION
That there should have been a demand for a second edition of this book - a book which cannot be described as easy to read - before the 
completion of its first decade is not to be explained by the interest of the professional circles to which I was addressing myself. My psychiatric 
colleagues have not, apparently, attempted to look beyond the astonishment which may at first have been aroused by my novel conception of the 
dream; and the professional philosophers, who are anyhow accustomed to disposing of the dream in a few sentences - mostly the same - as a 
supplement to the states of consciousness, have evidently failed to realize that precisely in this connection it was possible to make all manner of 
deductions, such as must lead to a fundamental modification of our psychological doctrines. The attitude of the scientific reviewers was such to 
lead me to expect that the fate of the book would be to fall into oblivion; and the little flock of faithful adherents, who follow my lead in the 
therapeutic application of psycho-analysis, and interpret dreams by my method, could not have exhausted the first edition of this book. I feel, 
therefore, that my thanks are due to the wider circle of cultured and inquiring readers whose sympathy has induced me, after the lapse of nine 
years, once more to take up this difficult work, which has so many fundamental bearings.

INTRODUCTION AND
ANALYSIS
The Republic of Plato is the longest of his works with the exception of the Laws,
and is certainly the greatest of them. There are nearer approaches to modern
metaphysics in the Philebus and in the Sophist; the Politicus or Statesman is
more ideal; the form and institutions of the State are more clearly drawn out
in the Laws; as works of art, the Symposium and the Protagoras are of higher
excellence. But no other Dialogue of Plato has the same largeness of view and
the same perfection of style; no other shows an equal knowledge of the world,
or contains more of those thoughts which are new as well as old, and not of
one age only but of all. Nowhere in Plato is there a deeper irony or a greater
wealth of humour or imagery, or more dramatic power. Nor in any other of his
writings is the attempt made to interweave life and speculation, or to connect
politics with philosophy. The Republic is the centre around which the other Di-
alogues may be grouped; here philosophy reaches the highest point (cp, especi-
ally in Books V, VI, VII) to which ancient thinkers ever attained. Plato among the
Greeks, like Bacon among the moderns, was the ﬁrst who conceived a method
of knowledge, although neither of them always distinguished the bare outline
or form from the substance of truth; and both of them had to be content with
an abstraction of science which was not yet realized. He was the greatest me-
taphysical genius whom the world has seen; and in him, more than in any other
ancient thinker, the germs of future knowledge are contained. The sciences of
logic and psychology, which have supplied so many instruments of thought to
after-ages, are based upon the analyses of Socrates and Plato. The principles
of deﬁnition, the law of contradiction, the fallacy of arguing in a circle, the dis-
tinction between the essence and accidents of a thing or notion, between means
and ends, between causes and conditions; also the division of the mind into
the rational, concupiscent, and irascible elements, or of pleasures and desires
into necessary and unnecessary–these and other great forms of thought are all
of them to be found in the Republic, and were probably ﬁrst invented by Plato.
The greatest of all logical truths, and the one of which writers on philosophy are

strenuously insisted on by him (cp. Rep.; Polit.; Cratyl), although he has not
always avoided the confusion of them in his own writings (e.g. Rep.). But he
does not bind up truth in logical formulae,– logic is still veiled in metaphysics;
and the science which he imagines to ’contemplate all truth and all existence’ is
very unlike the doctrine of the syllogism which Aristotle claims to have disco-
vered (Soph. Elenchi).

THE SOCIAL SYSTEM 
In the history of sociological theory, Talcott Parsons holds a very special place. His The 
Structure of Social Action (1937), was a pioneer work that has influenced many social 
scientists. The present work, The Social System, presents a major scientific and 
intellectual advance towards the theory of action first outlined in his earlier work. 
‘Social science is concerned with human beings interacting with one another in terms 
of mutually accepted standards of conduct. Their interaction takes place in an 
environment of what one might call “brute fact”, which comprises, among other things, 
climate, material resources, the population structure and the physical possibilities of 
communication. To study this vast complex of material some scheme of concepts is 
required, by means of which we can pick out what is significant, and so pave the way for 
discovering “what goes with what”. It is such a scheme that Professor Talcott Parsons has 
worked out, in his latest book. It is an important book.’

Prof. Victoria O. Adetunji
Department of Veterinary Public Health and Preventive Medicine,
University of Ibadan

--- SLIDE ---

ONE HEALTH
One Health is a collaborative, multisectoral, and transdisciplinary approach — working at the local, regional, national, and global levels — with the goal of achieving optimal health outcomes recognizing the interconnection between people, animals, plants, and their shared environment.

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
Veterinarians play an important role in One Health by striving to keep animals healthy, which helps ensure the food supply's safety and reduces disease spread from animals to humans.

--- SLIDE ---

Specific areas in which veterinarians contribute to One Health include:
Disease surveillance — Veterinarians are on the front lines of zoonotic disease surveillance, reporting outbreaks and unusual cases in animals that could impact human health.
Antibiotic stewardship — Veterinarians understand how antibiotic resistance develops in people, pets, and food animals, and take steps to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.
Education — Veterinarians educate their clients, colleagues, and communities about One Health, encouraging interdisciplinary collaboration.

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
Research — Veterinarians involved with research can directly contribute to One Health by studying disease transmission, emerging pathogens, and treatments. Veterinarians can set an example by actively collaborating and sharing knowledge with other medical professionals.
Policy — Veterinary organizations with lobbying power can advocate for One Health-friendly policies, focusing on infrastructure, veterinary care access, and environmental regulations at local and large-scale levels.

One Health is not a new concept, but it has become more important in recent years because many factors have changed the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment. These changes have caused the emergence and reemergence of many diseases.

--- SLIDE ---

One Health concept
The One Health concept recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal and ecosystem health. 
A One Health approach involves applying a coordinated, collaborative, multidisciplinary and cross-sectoral approach to address potential or existing risks that originate at the animal-human-ecosystems interface. 
The overarching aim of One Health is to achieve optimal health for humans, animals and the ecosystem.

--- SLIDE ---

Zoonotic Diseases
Diseases that can be passed between animals and humans



At least 61% of all human pathogens are zoonotic.

~75% of all emerging pathogens in the past decade have been zoonotic.

Why is this true?
We interact with animals in our daily lives.
We raise animals for food or enjoyment.
We keep them in our homes as pets.
We come into close contact with animals at fairs and zoos.
We encounter wildlife when we are outdoors or bugs that transmit disease.

text_snippet:
FVM 101Introduction to Veterinary Medicine2025/2026Topic: Pharmacology and the Veterinarian
Dr  Bisi  O. Adeoye
Department of Veterinary Pharmacology and Toxicology
17/07/2026
1

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
Veterinary Pharmacology: The study of drug actions and uses in animals.



To ensure effective treatment and preventing harm to animals and humans.
2

--- SLIDE ---

Branches of Veterinary Pharmacology
• Pharmacokinetics: ADME.
• Pharmacodynamics: how drugs interact with body to produce their effects. 
• Toxicology: Studies the harmful effects of chemicals, drugs, and toxins on living organisms and the methods for prevention or treatment of these effects.
Clinical Pharmacology: Focuses on the diagnosis,
treatment, and prevention of diseases in animals using drugs.
3

--- SLIDE ---

Branches of Veterinary Pharmacology…
Regulatory Pharmacology: Concerns the approval, regulation, and monitoring of veterinary drugs.

Ethnopharmacology: Investigates the use of traditional and herbal medicines in veterinary practice. Focuses on natural remedies and their pharmacological properties.
4

--- SLIDE ---

Branches of Veterinary Pharmacology…
Comparative Pharmacology: Studies the differences in drug effects and metabolism across animal species. Essential for understanding species-specific responses.

Pharmaceutical Science: Involves the development and formulation of drugs for veterinary use.
5

--- SLIDE ---

Commonly Used Drugs in Veterinary Medicine
• Antibiotics: Amoxicillin, Enrofloxacin.
• Analgesics: NSAIDs like Meloxicam.
• Vaccines: For diseases like rabies, distemper.
• Antiparasitics: Ivermectin, Fenbendazole.
• Multivitamins.
6

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary Toxicology
Deals with the adverse effects of chemicals, drugs, and toxins on animals.
Also on the relationship between toxicants and animal health and well-being. 
• Sources of toxins:
   - Natural: Plants, mycotoxins, venom.
   - Synthetic: Pesticides, industrial chemicals.
• Routes of exposure: Oral, dermal, inhalation.
.
7

--- SLIDE ---

Common Toxins in Veterinary Practice
• Household Toxins: Chocolate, xylitol, cleaning agents.

• Environmental Toxins: Lead, pesticides, antifreeze (ethylene glycol).

• Pharmacological Toxins: Overdose of NSAIDs or other drugs.

• Case examples of toxic effects on animals.
8

--- SLIDE ---

Branches of Veterinary Toxicology
Clinical Toxicology: Focuses on the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of poisoning in animals.

Environmental Toxicology: Studies the impact of environmental pollutants on animal health.

Forensic Toxicology: Concerned with the legal aspects of toxicology, such as investigating animal deaths caused by poisoning.
9

--- SLIDE ---

Branches of Veterinary Toxicology…
Nutritional Toxicology: Examines the effects of contaminants or imbalances in animal feed.

Toxicopathology: Studies the pathological effects of toxins on animal tissues and organs.

Food Safety Toxicology: Focuses on ensuring that veterinary drugs and chemicals in animal products (e.g., meat, milk, eggs) do not pose a risk to human consumers.
10

--- SLIDE ---

Diagnosis and Treatment of Toxicities
• Steps in diagnosis:
   - Clinical signs, history, and toxicology tests.

• Treatment protocols:
   - Decontamination: Induced vomiting, activated charcoal.
   - Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen therapy.
   - Antidotes: Pralidoxime(2-PAM) for organophosphates, Vitamin K for anticoagulants.
11

--- SLIDE ---

Regulatory Aspects
• Drug Approval and Safety: Role of organizations like FDA-CVM, EMA.

• Toxicology Regulations: Testing and setting permissible levels of toxins.
12

--- SLIDE ---

Challenges and Advancements
• Emerging challenges:
   - Antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
   - Environmental contamination by Veterinary drugs.

• Technological advancements:
   - Precision medicine.
   - Nanotechnology in drug delivery.
13

--- SLIDE ---

Conclusion
we are to protecting animal health, welfare, and public safety.
14

--- SLIDE ---

Thank you
15

Importance of Veterinary 
Anatomy in the making of a

FVM 101

Introduction
•Anatomy is a cornerstone of 
medicine, 
•Veterinary anatomy provides the 
foundation for understanding the 
structural organization of different 
animal species. 

Understanding Animal Structure:
•This knowledge is essential for 
veterinarians to accurately diagnose and 
treat animals.

Veterinary anatomy is the study of the structure and 
organization of animal bodies. It encompasses:
•Gross anatomy: Study of visible structures (organs, 
tissues, systems)
•Microscopic anatomy: Study of cellular and tissue 
structure
•Comparative anatomy: Study of similarities and 
differences between species
•Functional/Clinical  anatomy: Study of how structures 
function and interact and how to apply this knowledge in 
CLINICS

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
•Diagnostic Accuracy: Knowledge of anatomy enables 
veterinarians to:
•Identify normal and abnormal structures
•Localize lesions or diseases
•Interpret diagnostic images (e.g., X-rays, MRI)
•Perform surgical procedures with precision
•Minimize complications and risks
•Develop innovative surgical techniques

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
In therapeutic Interventions,anatomy informs:
•Medication administration (e.g., injection sites)
•Anesthesia and pain management
•Rehabilitation and physical therapy

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
In Preventive Medicine, knowledge of anatomy helps 
veterinarians to: 
•Identify risk factors for diseases
•Develop preventive strategies (e.g., vaccination, parasite 
control)
•Counsel clients on animal care and husbandry

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
Anatomy provides a common language for 
veterinarians to:
•Communicate with colleagues and clients
•Document medical records accurately
•Educate students and professionals

Applications of Veterinary Anatomy 1
Clinical Practice: 
Anatomy informs daily decision-making in:
•Companion animal practice
•Livestock production
•Equine medicine
•Zoological medicine

Applications of Veterinary Anatomy 2
Research and Development: 
Anatomy drives advancements in :
•Veterinary pharmaceuticals
•Surgical innovations
•Diagnostic technologies

Applications of Veterinary Anatomy 3
Education and Training: 
: Anatomy is essential for:
•Veterinary curriculum development
•Training of paravet/animal science/zoology,biological
science undergraduate and postgraduate research
•Continuing education programs
•Professional certification

Recommendations for Students:
•Engage actively with anatomy coursework
•Supplement studies with ONLINE resources, 
Artificial Intelligence/ imaging, and interactive 
resources
•Seek mentorship from experienced veterinarians
•Participate in clinical rotations and externships
•By embracing veterinary anatomy, you'll become 
proficient, confident, veterinarians, equipped to 
provide exceptional expertise

Conclusion
Veterinary anatomy is the bedrock of veterinary 
medicine. It provides the essential foundation for 
accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and 
compassionate care. 
As future veterinarians, it's crucial to:
Develop a thorough understanding of veterinary anatomy
Apply anatomical knowledge in clinical practice
Stay updated with advancements in veterinary anatomy

Additional Resources:
"Veterinary Anatomy" by K.M. Dyce, W.O. Sack, and 
C.J.G. Wensing; “
Anatomy of Domestic Animals" by R. Nickel
Online resources: Kenhub, Veterinary Anatomy 
online courses, 3D anatomy software
Professional organizations: International Association 
of Veterinary Anatomists (IAVA)

text_snippet:
EMERGENT PROPERTIES
When the Whole Is Greater Than the Sum

--- SLIDE ---

A) Something that appears suddenly
B) Something new that arises from interactions
C) Something hidden inside parts
D) Something unimportant
Question: Before we start, what do you think "emergent" means?

--- SLIDE ---

WHAT ARE EMERGENT PROPERTIES?
A characteristic of a system that arises from the INTERACTIONS between its components, but is NOT present in the individual components themselves.
The whole has properties the parts don't have

--- SLIDE ---

EXAMPLE: WATER (H₂O)
Hydrogen (H)
• Flammable gas
• Explosive
• Colorless
Oxygen (O)
• Supports combustion
• Makes fires burn
• Colorless gas
Water (H₂O)
• EXTINGUISHES fire
• Liquid at room temp
• Essential for life
Property of 'extinguishing fire' is EMERGENT - doesn't exist in H or O alone!

--- SLIDE ---

KEY PRINCIPLE
You CANNOT predict emergent properties
just by studying the parts in isolation.

You must study:
• How parts interact
• How they're organized
• How they relate

--- SLIDE ---

Hydrogen and oxygen are both gases
This property doesn't exist in H or O alone
 Water is more important than its parts
 It's a chemical reaction
Question: Water's ability to extinguish fire is emergent because:?

--- SLIDE ---

THE BIOLOGICAL HIERARCHY
Life is organized in levels - new properties emerge at EACH level
BIOSPHERE
ECOSYSTEMS
COMMUNITIES
POPULATIONS
ORGANISMS
ORGANS
TISSUES
CELLS

--- SLIDE ---

LEVEL 1: ATOMS → MOLECULES
EMERGENT PROPERTY:

Information storage (DNA)

--- SLIDE ---

LEVEL 2: MOLECULES → ORGANELLES
EMERGENT PROPERTY:

Energy production (ATP)

--- SLIDE ---

LEVEL 3: ORGANELLES → CELLS
EMERGENT PROPERTY:

LIFE ITSELF

--- SLIDE ---

LEVEL 4: CELLS → TISSUES
EMERGENT PROPERTY:

Coordinated movement

--- SLIDE ---

LEVEL 5: TISSUES → ORGANS → ORGANISMS
EMERGENT PROPERTY:

Consciousness, behavior

--- SLIDE ---

LEVEL 6: ORGANISMS → ECOSYSTEMS
EMERGENT PROPERTY:

Climate regulation, biodiversity

--- SLIDE ---

A) Atoms
B) Molecules
C) Organelles
D) Cells
Question: Life emerges at which level??

--- SLIDE ---

A) Individual neurons
B) Brain tissue alone
C) The network of neurons working together
D) DNA
Question: Consciousness is an emergent property of ?

--- SLIDE ---

WHY EMERGENCE MATTERS
Forces us to think differently about complex systems

--- SLIDE ---

TWO WAYS TO UNDERSTAND COMPLEXITY
REDUCTIONISM

Break it down
Study the parts

Works for simple systems
Limited for emergence
SYSTEMS THINKING

Look at the whole
Study interactions

Essential for emergent
properties

--- SLIDE ---

WE NEED BOTH APPROACHES
Reductionism: tells us what the parts are and what they do

Systems Thinking: tells us what emerges from their interactions
Examples:
• Medicine: Study proteins + understand disease systems
• Engineering: Design components + predict system behavior
• Ecology: Study species + understand ecosystem dynamics

--- SLIDE ---

THE CHALLENGE: UNPREDICTABILITY
Emergent properties can be UNPREDICTABLE
Even knowing all the parts doesn't guarantee predicting what emerges
This is why:
• Drug side effects happen
• Ecosystems collapse unexpectedly
• AI systems behave unexpectedly
• Protein folding is hard to predict

--- SLIDE ---

A) ) Wrong and should never be used
B) The only way to understand complex systems
C) Useful for understanding parts, but limited for emergent properties
D) The same as systems thinking
Question: Reductionism is…… ?

--- SLIDE ---

EXAMPLES ACROSS FIELDS

--- SLIDE ---

🏥 MEDICINE: Immune System Memory
Individual white blood cells: patrol, do their jobs
No single cell remembers past infections

But the immune SYSTEM:
• Has MEMORY of pathogens
• Remembers vaccines
• Responds faster to repeat infections

Memory is EMERGENT

🐜 ECOLOGY: Ant Colony Intelligence
Single ant: follows simple rules
No individual ant is intelligent

Ant colony:
• Division of labor
• Efficient food collection
• Temperature regulat

laboratory environment.

risk of injury as a result of chemical spill, broken glassware,
fire/explosion, infectious agents etc.
Laboratory hazards can cause acute injuries (e.g. burns, cuts,
fractures), chronic diseases (e.g. cancer, respiratory diseases),
nausea, vomiting etc.
Three common laboratory hazards include:
Chemical hazards
Biological hazards
Physical hazards.

CHEMICAL HAZARDS
Chemical hazard is caused by chemical agents that can pose health risks
such as toxicity, corrosivity flammability and reactivity. Some of the
chemicals in the laboratory that cause hazards include ethanol, sulphuric
acids, mercury, hydrogen peroxide, sodium hydroxide etc.
Chemical hazard exposure may occur by
Skin absorption or contact
Injection
Spill or splash
Aerosol distribution with exposure on skin
Contact with eyes
Inhalation
Ingestion
Explosion (such as a flammable chemical fire ignition).

BIOLOGICAL HAZARDS
Biological hazards are infectious agents or hazardous biological materials that 
present a risk or potential risk to the health of humans.
Biological hazardous materials include: 
• Recombinant DNA.
• Organisms and viruses infectious to humans, animals or plants (e.g. parasites, 
viruses, bacteria, fungi, prions,  rickettsia). 
• Biologically active agents (i.e. toxins, allergens, venoms) that may  cause 
disease.

PHYSICAL HAZARDS
Physical hazards are environmental factors or conditions that can cause
immediate harm, injury or illness in a laboratory.

• Slips, Trips and Falls
