text_snippet:
INTRODUCTION TO BIOLOGICAL DRAWINGS
For students of biology, it is important to note that biological presentation of specimens is quite different from an artist’s impression of the same specimens/objects on paper. The under-listed serve as guide towards making biological drawings:
Draw on only one side of the paper.
The diagram must represent the specimen given.
The diagram should be centrally located and should occupy ½ - ¾ of any particular page used.
There must be no broken or wobbly lines and no shading. If lines are broken or wobbly it gives an impression of an anatomical defect in the specimen provided. Faint diagrams make features look like they are disappearing (atrophy).
An appropriate title (written under drawing) should be given to each specimen. For example: Diagrammatic representation of whole specimen of stuffed Rattus norvegicus (white rat). This indicates whether the specimen is a part, whole or slide presentation to the examiner. Title of drawing and magnification (the relative proportion of the actual specimen to the drawing on paper: mag: x) should be indicated below the drawing.
It is important to classify specimens. Thus, for white rat:
Phylum:	Chordata
Class:		Mammalia
Order:		Rodentia
Genus:		Rattus
Species:	norvegicus
Classification should be written on top left corner of your paper. Notes of Zoological Interest (for examples: External features like dermal milk gland for white rat) should be at the bottom left corner of your diagram.
 Guidelines for labels must be ruled with appropriate tools like rulers. They must not overlap as this automatically cancels it out. Labels must be horizontal, neat and at least ¾ should be to one side. Labels must also be well outside the diagram.
Scientific names must be underlined. When using upper and lower case letters, the first letter for the generic name must be a capital letter while for the species name, it must be a lower-case letter, e.g. Rattus norvegicus. If capital letters are used throughout then all letters can be in capital e.g. RATTUS NORVEGICUS.
It may be necessary to draw different views of specimens provided, that is; anterior view, posterior view, dorsal view, ventral view and lateral view. Terms like front view, back view, side view are no longer acceptable at this level. For most biological drawings, however, the lateral view will suffice. All these guidelines (if strictly adhered to) will enhance a student’s interpretation of biological drawings.
EXERCISE 1:
External Features of selected animals
Specimens:  Any biological specimen of your choice ( Rat, frog, lizard, Cockroache, Centipede, Millipede, bird, insect etc)
Exercise: Draw the dorsal and lateral view of the any 2 specimens. Write short notes of Zoological interest on the observable features of each specimen.

PRACTICAL I
LABORATORY SAFETY PRINCIPLES AND PROCEDURES
PREVENTION OF FIRE AND EXPLOSION
Some vapours are flammable and sometimes explosive; in order to prevent fire and explosions in the laboratories, the following precaution should be taken.
1.	Only small quantities of explosive reagents should be kept on the working bench in the laboratory.
2.	Large quantities of explosive reagents should be kept separately in a special storage, cool room which is well ventilated, fire proof, and provided with fire extinguisher.
3.	Gas burners should not be kept within six feet of any flame.
4.	Flammable solvents should not be used in confined spaces where vapours may accumulate.
5.	Solutions containing flammable solvents should never be heated over a burner; boiling water bath or electrical hot plates should be used.
6.	Do not use force when assembling glass apparatus or when inserting glass tubes in stoppers.
HANDLING OF FIRE
1.	For small fires involving a beaker or any small container, cover with a larger vessel, smother with a wet cloth or use a carbon IV oxide foam type of fire extinguisher.
2.	For fire involving spilled flammable reagents which covers a large portion of the bench or floor, warn people around and use foam type of extinguisher. If the fire cannot be brought under control immediately, evacuate the room and call the fire department.
3.	In the absence or failure of fire extinguisher, sand bags or sand buckets are useful in putting out fire.
HANDLING OF POISONOUS, CORROSIVE AND CAUSTIC REAGENTS
Strong acids and bases: These are dangerous substances; it is essential that proper attention be paid to their handling. Burns should be washed with large quantities of water immediately the accident occurs in order to remove the acid. Any remaining acid may be removed by neutralization with sodium bicarbonate.
Acids:
1.	Acids should never be pipetted by mouth
2.	When pouring, or making dilutions of strong acids, splashing must be prevented by slow pouring and by the use of bottles with pouring lips.
3.	Automatic or semi-automatic pipetting devices should be used for acids.
4.	When diluting acids, it is best to add acid to water always, and do it slowly.
Strong bases:
1.	Burns caused by bases should be flushed immediately with large quantities of water. Saturated solution of boric acid should then be used to neutralize any remaining alkali.
	Dissolving solid sodium and potassium hydroxides in water generates a great deal of heat that may crack a thick-walled glass vessel, and should be done with the same precautions as used for strong acids.
Poisonous compounds:
These include methanol, cyanides, arsenical compounds, mercury compounds, oxalates, nitroprussides, zinc compounds, lead compounds, barium compounds, elemental iodine, acrylamide, aromatic amines, hydrocarbons, etc. 
These poisonous substances may be carelessly ingested by:
Transfer to the hand during handling, which may then be transferred to mouth or food, etc.
Careless pipetting of solution.
Contamination of cigarettes pipes or pipettes.
BURNS AND SCALDS
1.	Burns are caused by hot dry objects like glass or metal apparatus.
2.	Scalds are caused by hot fluids or vapours.
3.	Excessive exposures to infrared or ultraviolet radiations cause burns.
4.	Glass wares should not be handled with bare hands until it is cold.
5.	Heating the lower portion of a fluid in a test tube rapidly should be avoided.
6.	Heating liquid in a thick-walled container and pouring the hot liquid into a cold container should be avoided.
7.	Thin-walled flask should not come directly in contact with heat, or a burner; an asbestos centered wire should be used. 
Quartz chips (also called smooth boiling granules) may be added to a container before heating of liquid is started, to prevent or control violent boiling with splashing.

Clothing

The ﬁrst person to describe cells was

cubicles in monasteries where monks

He gave that name to the liƩle

living plants and idenƟﬁed cells there

centuries conƟnued the microscopic examinaƟon and study of

MaƩhias Schleiden and 
Theodor Schwann, and

recognizes the cell as the basic unit of life. 

The Cell Theory further states that: 
all organisms are composed of cells and all cells arise 
from preexisƟng cells. 
This theory is one of the major principles in biology.

magnify extremely small details of the cell using an

An Introduction to Computer Science 
(CSC 101)

--- SLIDE ---

CSC 101 Objective
This course is to prepare the students on the Fundamentals of Computer science and Computing.
 It teaches the basics concepts, Data representation, Computer Organization & Architecture, Problem Solving with Algorithm, Computer Networks and the Internet and programming in Visual Basics. 
The course will feature activities like teaching, demonstration, laboratory activities, chatting, assignment and group discussion. 
Course evaluation will be based on class attendance, online activities, quizzes, lab work and examination. 
Go to moodle learning system to see the course outline
		 lms.ui.edu.ng

--- SLIDE ---

How to get maximum benefits  from the Lecture
Attend class regularly
Read the related chapters in the textbook
Visit Moodle regularly
Visit lecturer whenever you have questions
Use your IT gadget to foster understanding of the course by checking up new concepts online. Go to U-tube and download lecture videos on topics you don’t understand
Attend Discussion Groups after studying
Think more!

--- SLIDE ---

Lesson Objectives
To Introduce Computer science through an understanding of what computer scientists do
To examine COMPUTER SCIENCE AS A DISCIPLINE
To present an understanding of the nature of computational tools and theories.
To explain the Founding Traditions of Computer Sc
QUALITIES OF A GOOD COMPUTER SCIENTIST
To introduce six major criteria that computation tools must be built to satisfy.
i.E  correctness, efficiency, security, fault-tolerance, user-friendliness and intelligence

--- SLIDE ---

Understanding Computer science
Computer Scientists have been in increasing demand since the advent of the modern computer.
The pervasiveness of the modern computer has accentuated the need to train more people in the discipline.
These people must be able to meet the need of the society in helping to achieve the effective use of computers.

--- SLIDE ---

What Computer Scientists do
In order to understand the discipline, it is important to answer the question: what do computer scientists do?
They create and manage tools that support and enhance  the use of the modern computer(computation tools for short).
In order to create effective computation tools it is important to create models of these tools before they are built.

--- SLIDE ---

What Computer Scientists do
Most of the models created are mathematical in nature.
Models need to be built around discrete mathematical structures(e.g. sets, lists, orderings etc.)
Computer scientists use these existing structures to create mathematical theories
A theory is a body of knowledge that facilitates the creation of models. 
Tools are built based on these theories

--- SLIDE ---

Definitions of Computer Science
The systematic study of algorithmic processes that describe and transform information: their theory, analysis, design, efficiency, implementation and application. (automation)
Computer Science is about building computers and writing computer programs, how we use computational tools, and what we find out when we do
Computer Science is also about problem solving. Solving problem computationally involves the followings:

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in Computational Problem Solving
ABSTRACTION
AUTOMATION
IMPLEMENTATION

 ABSTRACTION: Building clean abstract models (abstractions) of real-world. Computer Science is a means of solving real-world problems, and it all starts with abstractions. 
A representation of the actual problem
A mental model that removes complex details at the moment of abstraction
This is a key concept on CSC.  Abstraction will reappear throughout the course – be sure you understand it!

--- SLIDE ---

E.G of Abstraction
Abstraction of the car functionalities
You don’t bother about the internal details that make a car work while driving
Internal details of the engine and how it works are hidden when driving, it is an abstract view of a car

Introduction
It took thousands of years for the computer to develop in to the present state.

5,000 additions per second

All modern computer systems are called Von Neumann machines

Von Neumann - Biography
Born 28 December 1903, Budapest, Hungary; Died 8 February 1957, Washington DC; Brilliant mathematician, synthesizer, and promoter of the stored program concept, whose logical design of the IAS became the prototype of most of its successors - the von Neumann Architecture.
Von Neumann was a child prodigy, born into a banking family is Budapest, Hungary. When only six years old he could divide eight-digit numbers in his head. He received his early education in Budapest, under the tutelage of M. Fekete, with whom he published his first paper at the age of 18. Entering the University of Budapest in 1921, he studied Chemistry, moving his base of studies to both Berlin and Zurich before receiving his diploma in 1925 in Chemical Engineering. He returned to his first love of mathematics in completing his doctoral degree in 1928. he quickly gained a reputation in set theory, algebra, and quantum mechanics. At a time of political unrest in central Europe, he was invited to visit Princeton University in 1930, and when the Institute for Advanced Studies was founded there in 1933, he was appointed to be one of the original six Professors of Mathematics, a position which he retained for the remainder of his life. At the instigation and sponsorship of Oskar Morganstern, von Neumann and Kurt Gödel became US citizens in time for their clearance for wartime work. There is an anecdote which tells of Morganstern driving them to their immigration interview, after having learned about the US Constitution and the history of the country. UNIT 4 
Introduction to Writing 
 
4.1 Getting Started 
For the purpose of this course, writing is conceived as a process because it 
involves a series of actions or steps. Some of these actions take place at 
different times while some happen simultaneously, but they all ultimately lead 
to the production of what is to be read. However, the idea of what is to be read 
at this level and in this course goes beyond just anything scribbled down. Here, 
we are talking about a sustained and comprehensive piece of writing on a given 
idea. It is a writing that consists of interrelated paragraphs on a given subject. 
One very important thing often taken for granted about writing is the fact that 
it involves or requires skill. No evidence better supports this than the fact that 
putting down codes or signifiers of a language (alphabetic forms/letters) is a 
skill usually taught at the elementary level of literacy development. Although 
some people may have greater potentials than others when it comes to writing, 
writing skills can be acquired and developed by anyone who cares enough to 
cultivate them. The skills can be further honed or sharpened to a point of 
distinction. Interestingly, as academic success today still depends to a great 
extent on writing, cultivating its skills and putting them into practice can, 
therefore, not be over-emphasised. This is why this chapter introduces you to 
certain fundamentals about writing and forms of writing. 
4.2 Learning Outcomes 
At the end of this unit, students should be able to: 
a. recognise features of different forms of writing; 
b. apply features of different forms of writing; 
c. recognise steps and skills involved in writing; 
d. apply relevant skills in different forms of writing; and 
e. generally, improve their writing competence. 
4.3 Contents 
4.3.1 Forms of Writing 
Having made our conception of writing clear in the introduction above, we can 
now briefly examine the different forms of writing. 
 
 
 

a. Correspondence 
Correspondence refers to written communication from one individual or group 
to another. Basically, there are two types of correspondence, namely, official 
and unofficial correspondences.  
i. 
Unofficial Correspondence is a written exchange between individuals 
on private affairs. It usually comes in a letter form, also referred to as 
informal letter. Besides its informal language, it has the following as 
its basic features: writer’s address, date, salutation (for example Hi 
Fa’iz, Dear Sola, My Honey, Dear Dad, and so on), the body 
(introduction, main body and conclusion) and complimentary close 
(such as Yours sincerely, Your sweetheart, Your loving daughter, 
Yours affectionately, and the like). 
ii. 
Official Correspondence is one that deals with official or business 
concerns between two or more parties. The basic forms of official 
correspondence are formal letter and memorandum. A fundamental 
difference between formal letter and memorandum is that the 
circulation of memorandum is limited to within an organisation 
whereas letters can circulate within and as well go beyond an 
organisation. Their formats or styles of presentation also differ. The 
following are what characterises each of them:

CHAPTER FOUR
Nigeria History, Culture and Art Up To 1800: Non-Centralised and Minority States
Olawale Isaac YEMISI
Introduction
From the earliest origins of humanity, through the development of human civilisations and societies, the organisation, governance, and process of state formation have been crucial indices. As part of early man's survival process, state formation emerged through the governance of socio-economic structures. The pre-colonial history of Nigeria also underwent this process, resulting in the emergence of several centralised and non-centralised states in Nigeria. In several territories in pre-colonial Nigeria, there was evidence of original small polities. Isiche (1983) argued that there were approximately 2,780 of these among the Igbo East of the Niger, 100 in Akoko, northeast of Yorubaland, 140 among the Edo speakers, and about 90 among the Idoma and related peoples. However, unlike the centralised states discussed in the first chapter, non-centralised or small-scale states are also civilised and have rich histories, cultures, and arts. These non-centralised and small-scale states also have several alternative myths of political origins and possess organised socio-economic and political structures. The non-centralised states in pre-colonial Nigeria include the Igbo, Isoko, Urhobo, Ibibio, and Ijo city-states.
Non-centralised states are states in which power and authority are not concentrated in the hands of a single ruler.  These categories of states are small-scale in size, generally organised around a village or a small town or into chiefdoms. The exercise of power was distributed among the elders and associations of young people (age grades). The governance process was decentralised, and there was no need to build strong armies to expand. Communal interests among non-centralised states are built around trade and trading associations, with an orderly society regulated by sanctions through the power of religion and control exercised by the head of clans. However, two important notions must be clarified. That non-centralised states are small-scale in terms of organisation does not appear to be the case. These states also have enormous populations, which are central to their socio-cultural and economic features. Additionally, the fact that non-centralised states are described as stateless societies does not imply that they were foragers or belonged to wanderer-hunter-gatherer societies. They are described as stateless due to the absence of a central authority structure, as in the case of centralised states. Non-centralised states were agriculturally based and sedentary societies, rather than pastoralist or nomadic.
In the pre-colonial history of Nigeria, non-centralised states also had a rich socio-cultural identity. Nok (Nok culture) can be regarded as a foremost example of a decentralised state. The Nok society was a composition of people with standard socio-cultural practices, norms, and interactions, and it lacked strict hierarchical governance processes. In present-day northern Nigeria, the Nok culture was characterised by sedentary settlements with rich cultural artefacts, including clay figurines, iron tools, stone axes, and ornaments. These archaeological excavations testify to a relatively sophisticated socio-cultural space and a diversified society with economic specialisation, allowing for a functional society. Additionally, in other non-centralised states, archaeological excavations have uncovered material culture, underscoring the rich history of these non-centralised states. For instance, Isiah Anozie accidentally discovered the Igbo-Ukwu artefacts in 1939 while digging a well in his compound. Thurstan Shaw's archaeological works, conducted in 1959 and 1964, uncovered the rich history of Igbo Ukwu material culture. text_snippet:
DEVELOPMENT POLICIES AND 
IMPLEMENTATION IN NIGERIA, 1970-1999
Mutiat T. Oladejo

Introduction
•
As nations and international organisations looked for methodical ways to direct economic
growth
and
social
transformation,
particularly
during
decolonisation,
the
concept
of
development policy changed around the world in the years following World War II (Chete,
Adeoti, Ajakaiye, & Olorunfemi, 2016). As nations and international organisations looked for
methodical ways to direct economic growth and social transformation, particularly during
decolonisation, the concept of development policy changed around the world in the years
following World War II (Chete, Adeoti, Ajakaiye, & Olorunfemi, 2016).
•
Following independence, African countries adopted these frameworks to demonstrate
economic independence and promote unified nationhood; Nigeria, recovering from the
devastation of the 1967-1970 Civil War, immediately gave organised planning top priority
with its Second National Development Plan (1970-1974), signalling a significant change
towards economic revitalisation, national integration, and reconstruction (Onitiri, 1971;
Ikeanyibe, 2009).
•
The Third (1975-1980) and Fourth (1981-1985) national plans that followed each other
reflected changing goals and difficulties. Despite improvements in industry and construction,
the Third Plan's efforts to diversify and provide universal primary education only allocated a
small portion of its budget to agriculture, which led to a decline in output (Ibietan et al.,
2013). The Fourth, supported by high oil earnings, prioritised infrastructure expenditures and
export promotion, but it eventually failed because of unstable oil prices and financial
limitations (Ibietan et al
2013; Falola et al

Gender and Nigerian Cultures
Exploring gender practices in contemporary Nigerian society, from pre-colonial traditions to modern challenges. Understanding how culture shapes expectations for men and women across Nigeria's 250+ ethnic nationalities.

--- SLIDE ---

Understanding Gender vs. Sex
Sex
Biological identity as male, female, or ambiguous. Fixed physiological aspects like menstruation, lactation, spermatogenesis.
Gender
Social construct defining femininity and masculinity. Culturally determined roles, expectations, and opportunities based on sex identity.
Gender Roles
Behaviours society expects from men and women.
Men: hunting, fishing, repairing, rituals.
Women: cooking, childcare, house care.
These roles are learned through culture and socialization.
They can limit opportunities and slow down development when people are restricted.
Gender roles differ across societies and can change over time.
Sex Roles
Biological functions determined by anatomy and physiology, and they are exclusive to each sex (not interchangeable).
Female sex roles: childbearing, pregnancy, breastfeeding.
Male sex roles: sperm production, fertilization, determining child’s sex.

--- SLIDE ---

Key Gender Concepts
Gender Equality
Equal rights, freedoms, and opportunities for all genders to realize full potential and contribute to development.
Gender Equity
Fairness in representation and benefits according to respective needs, ensuring equal access to opportunities.
Gender-Based Violence
Violence directed at individuals based on gender identity, rooted in power imbalances and discrimination.

--- SLIDE ---

Gender Stereotypes and Socialization
Male Stereotypes
Expected to be sexually assertive, independent, competitive, unemotional, objective, active, adventurous, rational, and courageous.
Female Stereotypes
Assumed to be dependent, passive, emotional, nurturing, submissive, talkative, sensitive, and lacking self-confidence, generalized to be poor.
These stereotypes are formed through socialization by family, schools, peer groups, religious institutions, and media - reinforcing traditional gender roles across generations.

--- SLIDE ---

Types of Feminism
Liberal Feminism
Focuses on equal rights within existing society. Promotes legal reforms, equal pay, workplace equality.
Radical Feminism
Challenges patriarchal culture entirely. Declares "personal is political," questions reproductive roles and traditional institutions.
Marxist Feminism
Links gender inequality to capitalism. Views economic empowerment as key to ending women's subjugation.
Socialist Feminism
Combines Marxist and radical insights. Sees gender relations as embedded in all social systems throughout history.

--- SLIDE ---

Pre-Colonial Women's Power
Religious Leadership
Women served as priestesses in Osun, Ogun, and Sango cults. Titles like Iya Sango and Iya Osun recognized their authority.
Economic Power
Yoruba women dominated distribution and services, forming trade associations (egbe). Economic power led to political authority.
Political Participation
Dual-sex political systems existed. Igbo omu (Female Chief) and obi (Male Chief) shared community leadership responsibilities.

--- SLIDE ---

Colonial Impact on Women
1
Pre-Colonial Era
Women held significant power in religious, economic, and political spheres. Complementary roles with men in society.
2
Colonial Period
Victorian ideology imposed "woman-as-housewife" concept. Alternative structures favored men while marginalizing women's traditional power bases.
3
Educational Response
Elite women like Oyinkan Abayomi agitated for girls' education. Queens' College established in 1927, 10 years after Kings' College.
4
Women's Organizations
Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti formed Abeokuta Women's Union (1945). Margaret Ekpo founded Aba Market Women's Association.

--- SLIDE ---

Contemporary Gender Challenges
Economic Disparity
Women's wages represent only 55% of men's wages. Labour income largely controlled by men across Sub-Saharan Africa.

        INDIGENOUS EDUCATION IN NIGERIA
Introduction
This chapter examined indigenous education in Nigeria and the 
relationship between  culture and environment. It also examined how the environment has influenced the culture in Nigeria and finally the two

Indigenous Education in Nigeria
Every society in the world, no matter how small or large, has its own way of transmitting its cultural heritage from one generation to another. The objectives and methods of transmitting the societal culture vary from one society to another. In the context of traditional education generally, an educated man in Nigeria is “a warrior, a hunter, a nobleman, and a man of character”. Anyone who combined the latter feature with a specific skill was considered to be a well-educated and well-integrated citizen of Nigeria (Fafunwa 1974). According to Fafunwa, functionalism was the main guiding principle of Nigerian education, and that education is a means to an end and not an end in itself. It has been observed that traditional education is holistic in nature, and it helps in the realization of the Nigerian culture, among other things. Perhaps, it may be regarded as a branch of Nigerian culture. Traditional education may be regarded as the Nigerian way of imparting their culture into the younger ones in such a way that their culture will not go into an extinction. Traditional education generally begins at home, where the parents become the child's first teachers. The first child's lesson is teaching about his environment as well as the culture of his society, including numbers and numeracy. Specifically, Nigerian education is geared towards social responsibility, job orientation, and political participation, as well as spiritual and moral values. There is a proverb in Nigeria that "a child is not intelligent, and his parents do not want him to die; what will eventually kill a child who is not intelligent?" This means that traditional education goes beyond  acquisition of reading and writing skills. In the pre-literate period of Nigerian society, people who were knowledgeable in their vocations,  societal ethics and were indeed repositories of the culture of their societies were considered educated. In other words, Nigerian traditional education prepares the younger ones for adulthood life in addition to preparing them to become useful members of their society.
A critical examination will reveal that the content and methods of traditional education are interwoven, as they are not divided into separate compartments as we have in formal education. It is true that Nigerian  education was not formalized, including its curriculum, but according to Babarinde (2016), it can still be compared with the western form of education. For instance, it involves parents as first teachers, and this perhaps is comparable with the primary level of formal system of education. According to him, the neighborhood education is the secondary level; the community education may be compared with the higher level, while the last stage of Nigerian traditional education is the one that is received from the secret societies, which is designed for initiation, and this is another form of higher education. It should, however, be noted that most of the features of Nigerian traditional education in the past are still in existence today despite the importation of the foreign culture into Nigeria specifically.

What is Nation Building?
There is hardly any acceptable definition of nation building, as it means different things to different people.

Nation building is largely about whether the citizens of a state see themselves as one, with common identities and aspirations or otherwise.

Nation building, no doubt, is a global challenge, Nigeria inclusive. 
From independence from British colonial rule on October 1, 1960, Nigeria has faced numerous challenges in its nation-building efforts. Nigerian Indigenous Trade and Market Systems
Before colonial economic structures were imposed, Nigerian societies organized production, exchange, and distribution within locally defined norms and values. These indigenous trade and market systems were essential to human development, embedded within societal institutions of kinship, religion, and governance.

--- SLIDE ---

The Foundation of Indigenous Markets
Reciprocity & Exchange
Markets operated on principles of reciprocal commerce, where economy was inextricably linked to kinship and social bonds.
Cultural Logic
Non-Western market economies needed understanding within their cultural context, not purely neoclassical economic models.
Trust Networks
Complex relationships of trust, credit agreements, and social laws supported economic independence without formal institutions.
From the trans-Saharan trade linking West Africa to the Mediterranean, to the Indian Ocean commerce connecting East African societies, these systems demonstrated remarkable diversity and tenacity across the continent.

--- SLIDE ---

Pre-Colonial Market Organization (Up to 1897)
Yoruba Markets (Oja)
Urban centers like Ibadan grew around thriving market economies. Market days were cyclical, connected to four to eight-day customary weeks, serving as commercial hubs and venues for political negotiations.
Iyaloja and Iyalode leadership
Female authority over regulation
Dispute settlement mechanisms
Hausa Trading Networks
The kola trade exemplified how single commodities organized vast caravan circuits, connecting forest producers in the south to urban consumers and Islamic learning centers.
Sarkin Kasuwa market officials
Long-distance trade networks
Integration with farming calendars
Igbo Periodic Markets
Four-day market cycles (Eke, Orie, Afo, Nkwo) organized dispersed producers into predictable meeting points, avoiding local market clashes while coordinating seasonal production.
River port specialization
Onitsha as major hub
Ritual and commerce integration

--- SLIDE ---

Skills and Apprenticeship Systems
Skill acquisition took place through apprenticeship in crafts and trades rather than formal schools. This created a self-sustaining economic base where knowledge transfer was embedded in market systems.
Blacksmithing
Master craftsmen taught metalworking techniques, tool making, and innovation. Apprentices learned both technical skills and business ethics essential for market trust.
Weaving & Textiles
Traditional weaving techniques passed through generations, creating distinctive regional patterns and maintaining quality standards through guild-like associations.
Pottery & Crafts
Ceramic arts, leatherwork, and other artisanal vocations maintained local production capacity and cultural identity through hands-on mentorship.

--- SLIDE ---

Colonial Disruption (1897-1960)
Colonial rule reoriented indigenous markets by subordinating local economic logics to metropolitan fiscal and commercial imperatives. The introduction of cash crops, monetized taxes, and infrastructure realignments fundamentally altered native market systems.
Taxation & Monetization
Colonial tax regimes forced rural producers to monetize goods and enter cash crop markets, creating new vulnerabilities to global price fluctuations.
Transportation Revolution
Rail and steamboat networks transformed traditional market towns, concentrating wholesale functions in colonial entrepôts while bypassing others.
Market Regulation
Municipal reforms introduced licensing, official relocations, and registration systems that conflicted with established governance structures.

--- SLIDE ---

Women's Economic Leadership
"Market women and traders' unions honed their political roles by organizing petitions, strikes, and collective bargaining to protect trading territories, secure infrastructure, and oppose harmful municipal relocations."
Iyaloja System
Female market heads wielded significant authority over stall allocation, dues collection, and dispute resolution acr

Quantities, Units and Dimensions
There are two groups of physical or measurable 
quantities. 
These are fundamental and derived quantities.
A Fundamental quantity: Does not depend on prior 
knowledge of any other quantity.
A derived quantity: It is derived from the knowledge 
of some other quantities. 
The seven fundamental quantities are 
Mass, Time, Length,  Temperature, Electric current, Amount 
of substance and Luminous intensity.
1

All other quantities such as volume, density, force, energy, 
resistance, specific heat, current etc. are derived from these  
fundamental quantities.
Unit of a Quantities
The unit of a quantity tells us the scale in which its
measurement is made.
A value without its unit of measurement has incomplete 
meaning. In Systeme Internationale d’Unites (SI) units, the 
fundamental units are: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, 
seconds (s) for time, Kelvin (K) for temperature, mole (mol) for amount of

PHY 103: Basic Principle of Physics II
2023/2024 Session
Introductory Heat and Thermodynamics
LECTURE 1

Recommended Note andTexts
PHY 103 Lecture notes (Slides)
Modern Engineering Physics by A. S. Vasudeva;
Physics for scientists and engineers 5th edition 
by Serway and Beich;
Essential Principle of Physics by Whelan and 
Hodgson;
Physics part 1 and 2 by Hallidey and Reslick;
Advanced level physics by Nelckon and Parker. 

Course Contents
Temperature scales. 
1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamics.
Application of the laws thermodynamics (e.g. to 
calorimetry, gas properties and expansion of liquids).
Application of 1st and 2nd laws to heat engines,heat
pumps and refrigeration.
Third law and absolute zero of temperature. 

Course ContentS contd.
Thermal conductivity.
Types of radiation and energy 

The following terms are  keys to studying Heat and 
Thermodynamics:
Temperature
Heat
Thermal Contact
Thermal Equilibrium
Zeroth Law
Temperature scales
Thermometers

Temperature and “Zeroth Law” (cont’d)
HEAT is the transfer of energy from one object 
to another object as a result of a difference in 
temperature between them.
NOTE: (i)The two bodies must be in thermal 
contact.
(ii)Heat always flow from a higher temperature 
body to a lower temperature body
Two objects are said to be in thermal contact 
with each other if energy can be exchanged 
between them.

Temperature and “Zeroth Law”    
(contd)
Zeroth Law of thermodynamics
This law states that if two objects A and B, which are not in 
thermal contact, are separately in thermal equilibrium with a 
third object C, then objects A and B are in thermal equilibrium 
with each other.
This law allows the development of thermometers. Object C is 
our thermometer in this case.
For example, the length of a mercury column (object C in the 
zeroth law as defined above) may be used as a measure to 
compare the temperature of the two other objects.

Temperature and “Zeroth Law” contd.
Thermal equlibrium
This is a situation in which two objects would not exchange 
energy by heat or electromagnetic radiation if they were in 
thermal contact.
In other words, This occurs when two objects in thermal 
contact with each other cease to exchange energy by the 
process of heat or by electromagnetic radiation.

Thermometer and temperature scales
• let’s take for instance, if two objects of different thermal 
conductivities (e.g a metal tray and a plastic bottle) are removed from 
the freezer, the two objects are at the same temperature but will feel 
different when touched.
• The object with the higher conductivity (the metal tray) will feel 
colder than the one with lower conductivities if we touch them. This 
will give a false idea that it is at a lower temperature.
Inference: our senses is a qualitative indicator of temperature but it 
is unreliable and could be misleading. 
Thermometers: These are devices used to measure the temperature of 
a system.

Thermometer and temperature scales
Temperature of an object depends on measuring devices for its 
measurements and on the temperature scale adopted. 
The Most common temperature scales are:
Thermodynamic (Kelvin)
Celsius
Fahrenheit
Though few scales have been used, there are many types of 
devices for measuring temperature. 

Thermometer and temperature 
scales
All thermometers are based on the principle that some physical 
properties change as temperature changes. This properties are 
known as the thermometric properties.
Some of the physical properties that change with temperature 
(thermometric properties) are:
The volume/length of a liquid 
The length of a solid
The pressure of a gas at constant volume (as in constant-
volume gas thermometer)
The volume of a gas at constant pressure (as in constant-
pressure gas thermometer)

Thermometer and temperature scales 
contd.
The electric resistance of a conductor (as in 
resistance thermometer)
The colour of an object 
The emf of a thermo couple

TEMPARATURE SCALES

Thermal expansion of solids and liquids
If the temperature of a liquid increases, its volume will consequently 
increase.
Exception to this is water, 
❖From temperature of less than 00C to 00C, water expands like the other 
liquids;
❖From 00C to 40C, water contracts (contrary to any other material,
❖Then from 40C upwards, water expands normally like any other 
material. 
For solids, as temperature increases, its dimensions increase. 
This phenomenon is known as thermal expansion. It has many 
applications.
For example, thermal joints are included in buildings, railroad tracks, concrete 
highways and bridges to compensate for dimensional changes that occur as 
temperature changes.

Expansion is a consequence of the change in the average 
separation between the constituents atoms in an object.

INTRODUCTION
• In this lecture, we shall discuss the nature and scope of statistics and relate the course to 
our day-to-day activities. 
• Essentially, what we study in statistics are data. So, in this course we shall understand 
the distinct types of data available and their sources. The issue of data quality is a major 
concern not only to data producers but also to users as well. 
• The course will also itemize the basic measures of data quality. In concluding this 
course, we shall discuss measurement scales. This is because, as you will discover later 
in the course that it helps you to know the appropriate method to use to analyze your 
data.

the quantity, quality, fact, statistics, other basic units of meaning, or simply sequences of

• A datum is an individual value in a collection of data. 
• Data is usually organized into structures such as tables that provide additional context 
and meaning, and which may themselves be used as data in larger structures. Data may be 
used as variables in a computational process. 
• Data may represent abstract ideas or concrete measurements. 

Data is commonly used in scientific research, economics, and in virtually every other form

STA 114 - DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS
Module Two - Presentation of Data
DR. VICTORIA E. LAOYE
Department of Statistics, 
University of Ibadan
5th February, 2026

An Overview of Lecture
⇒ Tabular presentation
⇒ Classification
⇒ Guidelines for the construction of tables
⇒ Definition of some terms under classification and tabulation
⇒ Steps for constructing a frequency distribution table from raw data
⇒ Diagram presentations (Bar Chart, Histogram, Frequency
Polygon, Stem & Leaf)

Tabular Presentation
qThis is an orderly and precise arrangement of numerical information in columns and 
rows.
qTabulation of data forms the basis for reducing and simplifying the details given in a 
mass of data into such a form that the main features may be brought out to make the 
assembled data easily understood.
Classification
This is a process of arranging observations into logical, meaningful, useful categories in 
accordance with the nature of property under-study.
The idea is to group like things together to facilitate comparison of likes with like and also 
to reduce a large number of data to a form suitable for statistical analysis and processing.

Classification Cont’d
Ideally, a group or class must be homogenous, that is, it should include all items and only 
those items with definite characteristic of data.
Each item must have a class to which it belongs (Exhaustive). Each item must belong to 
only one class (Exclusive)

Example of Classisfication

Guidelines For Consturuction of a Table
• We have seen from the Tables above most of the desirable features of a good 
table.
• The construction of statistical tables does not require expert thoughts or a great 
skill.
• All that is necessary is to pay attention to the more obvious and simple points.
• The following guidelines for the drawing of tables should be noted:
• The table should have a title which should be short and self explanatory.
• It should present the data clearly, highlighting important details.

Guidelines For Consturuction of a Table Cont’d
• Table should be simple and unambiguous. It must be easily interpreted.
• It should save space but attractively designed
• Self - sufficiency of the table in the sense of not requiring supporting tables or evidence. 
This is because, quite often, a text table could be used by some other person as a 
reference material.
• Abbreviations and symbols should be avoided as much as possible. Approximation and 
omission should be explained in footnote.
• Always indicate the source(s) of the data at the bottom of the table so as to know the 
origin of the table.

Frequency Distribution Table
• Frequency distribution is a tabular arrangement of data by classes together with the 
corresponding class frequencies.
• A frequency table is also called a frequency distribution because such a table shows 
how the values of the variable are distributed.
• However we need not use exact values as the classes. We could use intervals as we 
shall see very soon.
• The frequency distribution tables are of fundamental importance in statistics.
• Apart from being a useful summary method of presenting data, they form a basis 
for the discussion of probability ideas

BIO 102 
 
     Prof SG Jonathan 
 
      Viruses 
A virus Viruses may be defined as acellular organisms whose genomes consist of nucleic 
acid, and which obligatory replicate inside host cells using host metabolic machinery and 
ribosomes to form a pool of components which assemble into particles called VIRIONS, 
which serve to protect the genome and to transfer it to other cells. When infected by a 
virus, a host cell is forced to produce many thousands of identical copies of the original 
virus. Unlike most living things, viruses do not have cells that divide; new viruses are 
assembled in the infected host cell. But unlike still simpler infectious agents, viruses 
contain genes, which gives them the ability to mutate and evolve. Over 5,000 species of 
viruses have been discovered yet 
 
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites characterized by a simple structure of 
genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), and sometimes a 
lipid envelope. They lack metabolic machinery, requiring a host cell's resources for 
replication and assembly, and exhibit both living traits like genetic variation and 
reproduction within a host, and non-living traits like inactivity outside a host and lack 
of cellular structure. Viruses are extremely small, can infect all types of life, and have 
various shapes and sizes. 
A virus is a submicroscopic infectious agent (small parasite) that cannot reproduce by 
itself. All viruses are obligatory replicates only inside the living cells of an organism. 
Also viruses can infect all types of life forms, from animals and plants to 
microorganisms, including bacteria and archaea. When infected by a virus, a host cell 
is forced to produce many thousands of identical copies of the original virus.. 
 
Most viruses have either RNA or DNA as their genetic material. The nucleic acid 
may be single- or double-stranded of genetic material. The entire infectious 
virus particle, called a virion, consists of the nucleic acid and an outer shell of 
protein. The simplest viruses contain only enough RNA or DNA to encode four 
proteins. The most complex can encode 100 – 200 proteins. 
 
Viral infections can cause disease in humans, animals and even plants. Antibiotics 
have no effect on viruses, but antiviral drugs have been developed to treat life-
threatening infections. Vaccines that produce lifelong immunity can prevent some 
viral infections. 
Viruses reproduce rapidly because they have only a few genes compared to humans who 
have 20,000–25,000. For example, influenza virus has only eight genes and rotavirus has 
eleven. These genes encode structural proteins that form the virus particle, or non-
structural proteins, that are only found in cells infected by the virus. 

 
Size of Viruses 
A small virus has a diameter of about 20 nm. Parvovirus. A large virus has a diameter of 
up to 400 nm. Poxviruses. Viruses are among the smallest infectious agents, and most of 
them can only 
 
Shape of Viruses: - 
Viruses vary in shape from the simple helical and icosahedral to more complex 
structures. A virus consists of two or three parts: genome and capsid or genome, 
capsid and envelope 
 
Characteristics of viruses: 
1.  Acellular: 
Viruses are not made of cells and lack cellular structures such as a cell membrane, 
cytoplasm, and organelles like ribosomes.  
2.  Genetic Material: 
They possess a genome, which is genetic material composed of either DNA or RNA, but 
not both simultaneously.  
3.  Protein Coat (Capsid): 
A protein coat, called a capsid, encases the viral genome and provides protection.  
4. Optional Envelope: 
Some viruses are "enveloped" and have an outer lipid layer, while "naked" viruses lack 
this envelope.  
5.  Obligate Intracellular Parasites: 
Viruses are obligate parasites, meaning they can only reproduce and carry out metabolic 
activities inside a living host cell.  
6. 6. Metabolic Inertness: 
Outside of a host cell, viruses are metabolically inactive and inert

text_snippet:
NATURE OF LIVING ORGANISM
What are living organisms?
These are organisms characterized by performance of certain life processes such as Movement, Respiration, Nutrition, Irritability, Growth, Excretion, Reproduction Intractability and Aging.  Non living things may
be able to perform one or more to these process, for instance, a machine can move, it is only living
organism that can perform all of the activities.
Plant nutrition, Elements and their function
Plant nutrition is the study of the chemical elements that are necessary for plant growth. There are
several principles that apply to plant nutrition. Some elements are directly involved in plant metabolism. Metabolism is the life sustaining chemical activity, i.e. The series of processes by which food is converted into the energy and products needed to sustain life.
A nutrient that is able to limit plant growth according to Liebig's law of the minimum, is
considered an essential plant nutrient and if the plant can not complete its full life cycle without
it. Macronutrients are Elements that when are  present at low levels may cause deficiency symptoms, and toxicity is possible at levels thatare too high. Further, deficiency of one element may present as symptoms of toxicity from anotherelement, and vice-versa.
Micronutrients (trace levels) These are elements that are vital to plant growth but are only
required in minute amounts, very much like vitamins in human diets
Plants uptake essential elements from the soil through their roots and from the air (mainly
consisting of nitrogen and oxygen) through their leaves. Nutrient uptake in the soil is
achieved by cation exchange, wherein root hairs pump hydrogen ions (H+) into the soil
through proton pumps. These hydrogen ions displace cations attached to negatively charged
soil particles so that the cations are available for uptake by the root. In the leaves, stomata
open to take in carbon dioxide and expel oxygen. The carbon dioxide molecules are used as
the carbon source in photosynthesis
Functions of nutrients

Phosphorus can also be used to modify the activity of various enzymes by phosphorylation, and can be used for cell signalling. Since ATP can be used for the biosynthesis of many plant biomolecules, phosphorus is important for plant growth and flower/seed formation.

Potassium regulates the opening and closing of the stoma by a potassium ion pump. Since stomataare important in water regulation, potassium reduces water loss from the leaves and increases drought tolerance. Potassium deficiency may cause necrosis or interveinal chlorosis.

RESPIRATION IN PLANTS
The breakdown of complex molecules to yield energy takes place in the cytoplasm and in the mitochondria (also only in eukaryotes). The breaking of the C-C bonds of complex compounds through oxidation within the cells, leading to release of considerable amount of energy is called respiration. The compounds that are oxidised during this process are known as respiratory substrates. Usually carbohydrates are oxidised to release energy, but proteins, fats and even organic acids can be used as respiratory substances in some plants, under certain conditions. During oxidation within a cell, all the energy contained in respiratory substrates is not released free into the cell, or in a single step. It is released in a series of slow step-wise reactions controlled by enzymes, and it is trapped as chemical energy in the form of ATP. Hence, it is important to understand that the energy released by oxidation in respiration is not (or rather cannot be) used directly but is used to synthesize ATP, which is broken down whenever (and wherever) energy needs to be utilized. Hence, ATP acts as the energy currency of the cell. This energy trapped in ATP is utilized in various energy-requiring processes of the organisms, and the carbon skeleton produced during respiration is used as precursors for biosynthesis of other molecules in the cell. Plants, unlike animals, have no specialized organs for gaseous exchange but they have stomata and lenticels for this purpose. 
C6H12O6 + 6O2                   6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy
If this energy is to be useful to the cell, it should be able to utilize it to synthesize other molecules that the cell requires. The strategy that the plant cell uses is to catabolize the glucose molecule in such a way that not all the liberated energy goes out as heat. The key is to oxidize glucose not in one step but in several small steps enabling some steps to be just large enough such that the energy released can be coupled to ATP synthesis. During the process of respiration, oxygen is utilized, and carbon dioxide, water and energy are released as products. The combustion reaction requires oxygen. But some cells live where oxygen may or may not be available. Even among present-day living organisms, we know of several that are adapted to anaerobic conditions. Some of these organisms are
facultative anaerobes, while in others the requirement for anaerobic condition is obligate. In any case, all living organisms retain the enzymatic machinery to partially oxidize glucose without the help of oxygen. This breakdown of glucose to pyruvic acid is called glycolysis. 
GLYCOLYSIS
The term glycolysis has originated from the Greek words, glycos for sugar, and lysis for splitting. The scheme of glycolysis was given by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof, and J. Parnas, and is often referred to as the EMP pathway. In anaerobic organisms, it is the only process in respiration. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm of the cell and is present in all living organisms. In this process, glucose undergoes partial oxidation to form two molecules of pyruvic acid . In plants, this glucose is derived from sucrose, which is the end product of photosynthesis, or from storage carbohydrates. Sucrose is converted into glucose and fructose by the enzyme, invertase, and these two monosaccharides readily enter the glycolytic pathway. Glucose and fructose are phosphorylated to give rise to glucose-6- phosphate by the activity of the enzyme hexokinase. This phosphorylated form of glucose then isomerises to produce fructose-6- phosphate. Subsequent steps of metabolism of glucose and fructose are same. In glycolysis, a chain of ten reactions, under the control of different enzymes, takes place to produce pyruvate from glucose. ATP is utilized at two steps: first in the conversion of glucose into glucose 6-phosphate and second in the conversion of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1, 6-bisphosphate. DR. ADEOLA A. ONI

--- SLIDE ---

OUTLINE
Briefs on physiology to include:
Nutrition;
Respiration;
Circulatory systems; 
Excretion;
Reproduction; 
Growth and Development in Animals

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
Living cells require a consistent flow of nutrients to sustain their metabolic needs.

As a result, most animals spend considerable time and energy in acquiring and digesting food.

The ingested food is used primarily by the animal’s body cells to produce Adenosine Tri-Phosphate (ATP), the main energy currency which the cells use to carry out all their metabolic activities. 

In addition, it also provides raw materials such as amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins, minerals necessary for growth, maintenance and repair of the body tissues, as well as for reproduction and regulation of body processes. 

Nutrition in animals encompasses all the processes involved in assimilation and utilization of food for energy, growth, maintenance and reproduction.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
The structurally complex food substances of animals are broken down into simple absorbable units by enzymes in a process known as digestion. 

Digestion in animals evolved from intracellular to extracellular digestion. In intracellular digestion, it is only food items small enough to be internalized by the cells that can be digested. 

As a result, intracellular digestion is limited to only few lower animal groups. These include:

Protozoans – Unicellular organisms that ingest tiny food particles and digest them inside food vacuoles.

Sponges (Phylum: Porifera) multicellular animals that use specialized cells to engulf food particles from the water and digest them inside the cells.
In extracellular digestion, larger quantities of food can be broken down and stored.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
Extracellular digestion
An animal’s digestive tract is mainly a hollow sac or tube with an entrance (mouth) and an exit (anus).

Even though this tube, i.e. the digestive tract lies within an animal’s body, the openings at both ends (mouth and anus) are in contact with the outside world and so the digestive tube or gut can therefore be thought of as being continuous with the external environment.

Until the nutrients in food conducted down this tube are broken down into simpler units and absorbed across the walls of the tube into the body cells, they are not considered as “inside” the body, hence the term “extracellular” digestion because food breakdown occurs outside the body cells within the gut.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
Evolution of the digestive tract in animals
The first digestive systems probably evolved as an in-folding of the epidermis into an interior sac (such as those found in Cnidarians), allowing the animal to capture much larger quantities of food.

The sac later fused with the opposite end of the body to form a complex tube known as the gut with an entrance (the mouth) and an exit (the anus).

Cells lining this digestive tube could evolve specialized functions: 
some could be specialized and compartmentalized for acidic digestion (e.g. the parietal or oxyntic cells in mammals, birds and lower vertebrates); 
others for alkaline digestion (e.g. intestinal epithelial cells), some for receiving and storing food (e.g. the crop) and others for processing wastes.

--- SLIDE ---

Overview on Nutrition
The gut in most animals can be divided into the foregut, mid-gut and the hind gut. 

Some animals like hydra, jellyfish, sea anemones and flatworms carry out both intracellular and extracellular digestion. 

Most invertebrates like annelids and arthropods, and all vertebrates practice extracellular digestion.

24  ANIMAL EVOLUTION—THE INVERTEBRATES

   389
CORE CONCEPTS
  24.1 Medicines from the Sea
Animal life began in the sea, and the oceans remain 
the greatest reservoir of animal diversity. In the oceans, 
as on land, the majority of animals are invertebrates, 
which means they do not have a backbone. Only about 
5 percent of animals have a backbone and thus are 
considered vertebrates. Invertebrates evolved long 
before vertebrates, and they remain the most diverse 
and numerous animals. The longevity and diversity 
of invertebrate lineages attests to how well they have 
adapted to their environment. 
Many marine invertebrates produce secondary 
metabolites (Section 22.9) that help them survive. These 
compounds may protect an animal from predators, 
help it fend off pathogens, or assist in the capture of 
prey. Some such compounds also have effects in the 
human body, and so can be useful as medicines. 
Consider the venom that some fish-eating cone 
snails inject into their prey to subdue it (FIGURE 24.1). 
The snail’s venom anesthetizes and paralyzes a fish, 
thus preventing it from struggling with and possibly 
harming the snail as it is captured and consumed. 
Human nerves and fish nerves use the same chemi-
cal communication signals, so compounds used by a 
cone snail to drug fish can also affect the function of 
the human nervous system. A person stung by a fish-
eating cone snail may become numb at the site of injec-
tion, suffer from temporary paralysis, or even die. 
A synthetic version of one peptide in cone snail 
venom is now used as a pain reliever. The drug, 
ziconotide (Prialt), is injected to suppress severe 
pain that cannot be controlled by other means. Other 
peptides isolated from cone snail venom are being 
tested as treatments for epilepsy, diabetes, or cancer.

Links to Earlier Concepts
This chapter discusses how a protist ancestor 
(Section 21.8) could have given rise to 
animals. Understanding the geologic time 
line (16.5) will help you put the events we 
discuss in perspective. We draw on earlier 
discussions of homeotic genes (10.3), 
comparative genomics (15.5), and patterns of 
development (18.5). 
Evolution
Evolution underlies the unity and diversity 
of life.
Shared core processes and features provide 
evidence that all living things are descended  
from a common ancestor. All animals have 
unwalled cells connected by cell junctions and a 
collagen-containing extracellular matrix. Animals 
evolved from a colonial protist ancestor by about 
600 million years ago.
Pathways of Transformation
Organisms exchange matter and energy 
with the environment in order to grow, 
maintain themselves, and reproduce.
Animals are heterotrophs that ingest and digest 
their food. In the simplest animals, the gut is saclike 
and nutrients diffuse through tissues. Animals with 
more complex body plans have a tubular gut, 
and some have a circulatory system. All animals 
undergo development and move from place to 
place during part or all of the life cycle.
Information Flow
Living systems store, retrieve, transmit, and 
respond to information essential for life. 
Homeostatic mechanisms that involve feedback 
control allow living things to maintain themselves 
by responding dynamically to internal and external 
conditions. Many animals have organ systems that 
allow them to control the solute level of their body 
fluids. Most have sensory organs that alert them to 
changes in their environment.

N 1883 THE ZOOLOGIST FRANZ SCHULZE 
noticed something unusual in his Austrian labora-
tory: transparent, flattened organisms were crawl-
ing on the sides of his saltwater aquarium. These 
organisms, which Schulze had collected acciden-
tally along with the sponges that were his primary 
interest, appeared to be animals, but they were 
unlike any animals previously described—espe-
cially since they continually changed shape as they 
moved.
Further examination revealed that the new 
organisms were indeed animals. Structurally, how-
ever, they were among the simplest animals that 
Schulze—or anyone else—had ever observed, 
being made up of only four types of cells. He 
named the new species Trichoplax adhaerens, which means 
“sticky hairy plate,” and argued that the new species had 
no close relationships with other major animal groups. For 
decades, however, most biologists dismissed Schulze’s find-
ings, insisting that the transparent organisms must be larval 
forms of other, well-known, animals.
In the 1960s more detailed studies confirmed the distinc-
tive nature of Trichoplax. Even then, this odd animal contin-
ued to be known almost exclusively from aquariums. Only in 
the past decade have biologists located natural populations 
of T. adhaerens growing on hard surfaces in tropical and 
subtropical coastal regions. A few additional closely related 
species have been discovered (although most have not 
yet been formally named). Collectively, these species are 
known as placozoans (Greek, “flat animals”).
The more biologists have studied Trichoplax, the 
odder this animal appears. It has the smallest genome of 
any animal studied to date. The mature stages lack body 
symmetry and have no mouth, gut, or nervous system. Is 
Trichoplax a relict representative of a group of animals that 
appeared early in animal evolution?
Which groups of organisms are at the root of the 
animal tree is currently a subject of considerable inves-
tigation and debate. Several possible hypotheses of 
relationships are being explored with genomic analyses. 
The structural simplicity of Trichoplax is now considered 
by most biologists to be an evolutionary reversal from a 
more complex body form. Most genomic studies point to 
other groups of animals as forming the earliest split with 
the remaining species.
This chapter explores the 
earliest branches on the animal 
tree and shows how a few funda-
mental “body plans” have been 
modified to yield the remark-
able variety of animal forms 
described in this and the follow-
ing two chapters.

placozoans are morphologically simple and have the smallest genome

with more complex body plans.

 Despite their stunning diversity,  animals form a monophy-
letic group, sharing key traits: 
• All animals are multicellular eukaryotes whose cells lack cell 
walls but have an extensive  extracellular matrix (ECM); 
( Ch.  11 ,  Section  11. 1 ) . The ECM includes proteins specialized 
for cell–cell adhesion and communication. 
• All animals are heterotrophs , meaning that they obtain carbon 
compounds from other organisms (rather than via photosyn-
thesis as autotrophs do). Most ingest (“eat”) their food, rather 
than absorbing it across their exterior body surfaces. 
• All animals move under their own power at some point in their 
life cycle. 
• All animals other than sponges have  (1)  neurons (nerve cells) 
that transmit electrical signals to other cells; and  (2)  muscle 
cells that can change the shape of the body by contracting. 
 Multicellular fungi and animals are similar in that they are 
both multicellular heterotrophs that digest (break down) and 
absorb nutrients. However, animals are the only multicellular 
heterotrophs on the tree of life that usually ingest their food first, 
before they digest it. As a result, digestion in animals typically 
occurs within the space, or lumen, of the digestive tract rather 
than in the open exterior, as occurs with fungi. 
 In most animals, neurons connect to each other, forming a 
nervous system, and some neurons connect to muscle cells—
which may contract in response to electrical signals from neu-
rons. Muscles and neurons are adaptations that allow a large, 
multicellular body to move efficiently. What does the combina-
tion of multicellularity, heterotrophy, and efficient movement 
produce? Eating machines—animals are the largest detritivores, 
herbivores, and carnivores on Earth. 
 The radiation of animals began around  550 million years 
ago during an event called the  Cambrian explosion  ( Ch.  25 ,

appear in the fossil record with not only muscles and nerves

mented bodies. The Cambrian explosion was arguably the most

Agnathans, Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes
Dr. Adeola A. Oni (Agnathans)

--- SLIDE ---

Agnathans (jawless fishes)
Specimens provided: Genus – Petromyzon (dissected adult)
                                Ammocoete larva, i.e. the larval stage of a lamprey - Petromyzon
Classification:
Kingdom: Animalia
Phylum: Chordata (have a notochord – a characteristic feature of chordates)
Subphylum: Vertebrata (have a backbone or vertebral column, even though the vertebrae are rudimentary
Infra-phylum: Agnatha (jawless vertebrates)
Superclass: Cyclostomata (possess a circular opening, the mouth)
Class: Petromyzontida or Petromyzonti
Order: Petromyzontiformes
Family: Petromyzontidae
Subfamily: Petromyzontinae
Genus: Petromyzon (Originates from two Greek words – “Petro” meaning “stone” + “myzon” meaning “sucker”. This is because they tend to grasp stones or attach to rocks to hold their position in water amidst the current or during nest building and mating
Common name: Sea Lamprey

--- SLIDE ---

General features of Agnathans
The body is slender and eel-like
They lack jaws 
Their skeleton is fibrous and made up of cartilage rather than bone (a similarity they share with the cartilaginous fishes – Chondrichthyes, the difference with this group is that cartilaginous fishes have jaws)
They lack scales 
They have dorsal fins but no paired fins or appendages
They have pore-like gill openings
They have sucker like oral disc and a tongue with well developed keratinized (i.e. contains keratin, a strong natural protein) teeth
Sexes are separate and there is a long larval stage known as Ammocoete larva.

The Sea Lamprey is a parasitic fish.

They attach themselves by their sucker-like mouth to other fishes such as Rainbow trout, Herrings and with their sharp keratinized teeth  rasp through the flesh and suck out their body fluids, leaving a gaping wound that can prove fatal.

Quantum Numbers, Atomic Orbitals, 
and Electron Configurations 
Each electron in an atom is described by
four different quantum numbers. The first
three (n, l, ml) specify the particular

orbital of interest, and the fourth (ms)
specifies
how
many
electrons
can
occupy that orbital.

1. Principal Quantum Number (n): n = 1,
2,…,8.
This
number
describes
the
average distance of an electron from the
nucleus,
like
the
innermost
electron
shell,

which has a principal quantum of 1.This
specifies the energy of an electron and
the size of the orbital.

All orbitals that have the same value of n
are said to be in the same shell (level).
For a hydrogen atom with n=1, the
electron is in its ground state;

if the electron is in the n=2 orbital, it is in
an excited state. The total number of
orbitals for a given n value is n2.
Orbitals for which n=2 are larger those
for which n=1, for example.

Because they have opposite electrical charges,
electrons are attracted to the nucleus of the atom.
Energy must therefore be absorbed to excite an
electron from an orbital in which the electron is
close to the nucleus (n=1) into an orbital in which
it is further from the nucleus (n=2).

The principal quantum number therefore
indirectly describes the energy of an orbital.
As n increases, the energies of the orbitals
also increase. The principal quantum number
n may have any positive integral value
between n=1 and n= ∞.

The n corresponds to the orbital energy
level or ‘‘shell”. The shell with n=1 is
called the 1st shell, the shell with n=2 is
called the second shell and so forth.

For a particular energy level, there may
be subshell, the number of which is
defined by the quantum number l.

2. Angular or orbital Quantum Number (l): l =
0, ..., n-1. Specifies the shape of an orbital
with a particular principal quantum number.
The angular quantum number divides the
shells into smaller groups of orbitals called
subshells (sublevels).

Usually, a letter code is used to identify l
to avoid confusion with n:
l
0 1
2 3 4 5 . . .
Letter s
p d
f g h . . .
The subshell with n=2 and l=1 is the 2p
subshell; if n=3 and l=0, it is the 3s
subshell, and so on.

The value of l also has a slight effect on 
the energy of the subshell; the energy of 
the subshell increases with l (s < p < d < 
f)

3. Magnetic Quantum Number (ml):
ml = -l, ..., 0, ..., +l.
Specifies the orientation in space of an
orbital of a given energy (n) and shape
(l).

This
number
divides
the
subshell
into
individual orbitals which hold the electrons;
there are 2l+1 orbitals in each subshell. Thus
the s subshell has only one orbital, the p
subshell has three orbitals, and so on

4. Spin Quantum Number (ms): ms = +½
or -½. Specifies the orientation of the
spin axis of an electron. An electron can
spin in only one of two directions
(sometimes called up and down).

The Pauli exclusion principle (Wolfgang
Pauli, Nobel Prize 1945) states that no two
electrons
in
the
same
atom
can
have
identical values for all four of their quantum
numbers. What this means is that no more
than two electrons can

occupy the same orbital, and that two
electrons in the same orbital must have
opposite spins. Because an electron spins,
it creates a magnetic field, which can be
oriented in one of two directions.

For two electrons in the same orbital, the
spins must be opposite to each other; the
spins are said to be paired. These substances
are not attracted to magnets and are said to
be diamagnetic.

Atoms with more electrons that spin in
one
direction
than
another
contain
unpaired electrons. These substances are
weakly attracted to magnets and are said
to be paramagnetic

CHE 176 – ORGANIC CHEMISTRY I 

PROF. O O. SONIBARE 
OFFICE: F104, CHEMISTRY DEPT. 

LECTURE OUTLINE  
Basic concept of organic chemistry – definition and 
importance of organic chemistry,  atom and molecular 
orbitals including bonding, unique nature of carbon and 
hybridization  
 
Determination of molecular composition and structure of 
organic compounds 
 
Functional group classes of organic compounds and 
nomenclature 
 
Reaction mechanism and Kinetics  
 
Organic reactions- types and factors affecting them. 
 
  

DEFINITION OF ORGANIC CHEMISTRY  
What is Chemistry? 
Chemistry is the branch of physical science that deals with 
the study of composition, properties and reactions of 
substances. 
 
What is Organic Chemistry? 
Branch of chemistry that deals with carbon compounds. 
This branch of chemistry is very important because of the 
large numbers of organic compounds and their 
occurrences and applications.  

IMPORTANCE OF ORGANIC CHEMISTRY 
Most of the substances we use in our daily life are organic 
in nature:  
   (a) The food types that sustain human body are  made up of  
        organic compounds, e.g. carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils,  
        vitamins etc. 
    (b) the clothes we wear (wool and cotton- cellulose) 
    (c) the commodities we use (wood- cellulose, plastic- polymer  
          of hydrocarbons) 
    (d) the source of primary energy (petroleum, natural gas, coal) 
     (e) The medicine we take  
    (f) In agriculture (fertilizers and agrochemicals) 
 

UNIQUE NATURE OF CARBON  
What makes carbon special? Why is a whole field of 
organic chemistry dedicated to carbon? 
Carbon is very unique due to many reasons: 
 
1. Tetravalent nature: Due to its tetravalent nature, 
carbon always form covalent bonds by sharing 
electrons with one, two, three or four carbon atoms or 
atoms of other elements or group of atoms. Carbon 
can form single, double or triple bonds with other 
atoms because of its bonding ability.  

 
  

2. Catenation: The tetra-covalency of carbon atom 
allows it to combine easily with other carbon to 
form stable chain like structure.  
 
Catenation: Catenation is the ability of an element 
to form chains and rings in which its atoms are 
bonded to one another i.e. ability to exhibit self–
linkage. 
 

3. Formation of strong C-C covalent bonds: The 
single bond formed between the carbon atoms is strong. 
This results in the formation of stable compounds. 
Carbon atoms also form stable bonds with other atoms 
e.g. H, Cl, Br, O etc. 
 
 3. Formation of C-C multiple bonds: Due to its small 
size, the C-atom can also form multiple bonds. This 
gives rise to a variety in the carbon compounds.  
 
4. Hybridisation:  Formation of hybrid orbitals allows 
carbon to form double and triple bonds. 
 

ATOMS, ATOMIC AND MOLECULAR ORBITALS – 
Refer to your CHE 156 Note 

HYBRIDISATION OF ORBITALS IN CARBON 
Hybridization simply means mixing 
 
Hybridization of orbitals involves mixing of atomic 
orbitals to form new identical orbitals known as 
hybrid orbitals.  
 
These hybrid orbitals are subsequently used in 
bonding to give more stable compounds. 
 

 
3 types of Hybridization exist in carbon:  
 
sp3, sp2 and sp  
 
All the three types involve mixing of s and p 
orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals. 

sp3 HYBRIDIZATION IN CARBON  
Atomic Number of Carbon = 6   
Electronic configuration of Carbon in ground state =  
   1s2 2s2 2p2 [2p1
x 2p1y 2pz], thus implying that valency of    
   carbon should be 2.  
However, carbon exhibits a valency of 4 i.e. its tetravalent.        
WHY IS THIS SO? 
One electron is promoted from the 2s orbital to the vacant 2pz 
orbital giving rise to four (4) unpaired electrons viz - the new 
electronic configuration of carbon = 1s2 2s1 2p1
x 2p1
y 2p1
z 
1s electrons are considered to be core electrons and are not 
available for bonding. 

Furthermore, there is mixing between the 2s orbital and 
the three 2p orbitals to form four (4) new sp3 hybrid 
orbita

HYBRIDIZATION AND SHAPES OF 
SIMPLE MOLECULES

•Hybridization, in Chemistry, is defined as the
concept of mixing two atomic orbitals to give
rise to a new type of hybridized orbitals. This
intermixing usually results in the formation of
hybrid orbitals having entirely different energy,
shapes e.t.c.

The process of merging two atomic orbitals to
produce a new variety of hybridized orbitals is
described as hybridization. Usually, this mixing
creates
hybrid
orbitals
with
entirely
distinct
energies, forms, and other characteristics. Atomic
orbitals with the same energy level are principally

responsible for hybridization. However, if the
energies of the orbitals are equivalent, the
process can involve both fully filled and
partially filled orbitals.

The concept of hybridization is an extension
of
valence
bond
theory
that
helps
us
understand bond formation, bond energies,
and bond lengths. When two atomic orbitals
combine to form a hybrid orbital in a

molecule, the energy of the orbitals of
individual atoms is redistributed to give
orbitals of equivalent energy. When two
atomic orbitals combine to form a hybrid
orbital in a molecule,

the energy of the orbitals of individual atoms 
is redistributed to give orbitals of equivalent 
energy. This is known as hybridization.

Hybridization helps us to explain what is
actually
going
on
during
such
bonding
processes. In molecular bond formation, only
the valence electrons are utilized, that is, the
electrons in the outermost shell of the atom
(K, L, M, N, O etc.)

The process of hybridization gives us some insight
into the shapes or structures of simple molecules.
Consider the molecule CCl4 (carbon tetrachloride).
The carbon atom must bond to four chlorine atoms for
2-electron/2-centre
bonding
to
be
in
operation.
However, there are only two unpaired electrons
available for bonding here (scheme 1).

Since all the bonding electrons must be

from the 2s-orbital into 2p-orbital (Scheme 2)

The process is called Hybridization

the expenditure of energy.

is

to

the promotion
of the electron in the
2s-orbital into the 2p-orbital.

Therefore, there are four unpaired electrons
from four hybrid orbitals which can now
overlap with the p-orbitals
of the chlorine
atom
to
form
chemical
bonds.
The
combination of these four hybrid orbitals to
form

four tetrahedrally arranged orbitals of the
same energy content can be represented as
shown in figure 1.

Figure 1: combination of s and p orbitals of 
C in CCl4

These
tetrahedrally
arranged
hybrid
orbitals
of the carbon atom now overlap
with
the appropriate p-orbitals of the

bonds
(figure

containing

from s-

and

from
p-

the process is called sp3 hybridization. Thus,
sp3
hybridization
gives
rise
to
a
tetrahedral geometry or structure.

An Atom
Matter is anything that takes up

All matter is made of atoms.
Atoms are the building blocks of

*1. Each element is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms

*2. Atoms of an element cannot be converted to atoms of another

substances (change the way they are bound to each other).
*3. The atoms of a given element are identical, and different from 
those of any other element.
*4. Atoms of one element can combine with atoms of other elements 
to form compounds. A given compound always has the same relative 
numbers and types of atoms.

The proton & neutron are found in the

nucleus.
The electrons orbit the nucleus. 
Elements are made of atoms. While the
