EXTRACTION OF METALS
The process of extracting metal ores buried deep underground is called mining. The metal ores are found in the earth’s crust in varying abundance. The extraction of metals from ores is what allows us to use the minerals in the ground. The ores are very different from the finished metals that we see in buildings and bridges. Ores consist of the desired metal compound and the impurities and earthly substances called gangue. The extraction of metals and their isolation occurs over a few major steps:
1

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION OF METALS
Extraction of metals and the reactivity series:
The most reactive metals are at the top of the series
The tendency to become oxidised is thus linked to how reactive a metal is and therefore its position on the reactivity series
Metals higher up are therefore less resistant to oxidation than the metals placed lower down which are more resistant to oxidation
The position of the metal on the reactivity series determines the method of extraction
2

--- SLIDE ---

REACTIVITY SERIES OF METALS
3

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION OF METALS
Concentration of Ore –  the ore is separated from earthy impurities.
Isolation of metal from concentrated Ore – Here the ore is converted to its oxide form and then reduced. The steps involved are either calcination or roasting and then heating with a reducing agent.
Purification of the metal – Here the metal is purified for practical purposes.
4

--- SLIDE ---

Metals extraction method table
5

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION FLOW CHAT
6

--- SLIDE ---

7

--- SLIDE ---

The extraction method depends on the position of a metal in the reactivity series
Higher placed metals (above carbon) have to be extracted using electrolysis as they are too reactive and cannot be reduced by carbon
Lower placed metals can be extracted by heating with carbon which reduces them
8

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in the extraction of metals from their ores.
Concentration of Ores
The very first step, which is the concentration of ore, involves the removal of gangue particles that can be achieved using gravity separation, froth floatation, magnetic separation, and leaching processes.
9

--- SLIDE ---

EXTRACTION OF METALS
The gravity separation method is used when gangue particles are lighter than the ore. This method is generally used for the concentration of oxides and carbonate ores. The method involves the passing of crushed ore particles through a stream of water during which the lighter gangue particles are washed away.
10

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in the extraction of metals from their ores.
The froth floatation method is used to remove gangue particles from sulfide ores. In this method, the crushed ore and water are added to a tank in which a frother, such as pine oil, is added and then air is blown under pressure to create the froth. The gangue particles will be wetted by water and the metal comes up with the froth.
11

--- SLIDE ---

Steps in the extraction of metals from their ores.
The magnetic separation method is used when either metal or gangue particles have magnetic properties. In this method, the crushed ore is passed over conveyor belts with magnetic rollers.
The leaching method is used to concentrate ores of aluminium, silver, and gold, etc. In this method, the crushed ore is treated with a solvent that dissolves the ore leaving behind the impurities.
12

--- SLIDE ---

Metal Extraction Processes
Roasting and Calcination
Roasting is the heating of concentrated metal ore in presence of air. It is mainly done for metal sulfide ores to convert them into their respective oxides. For example, cinnabar is a sulfide ore of mercury with the chemical formula of HgS. When the ore is heated in presence of air, it is first converted into mercuric oxide and then upon further heating, liquid mercury is formed:

Allotropy
Allotropy is the phenomenon in which an element
exists in multiple forms with different structures and
properties. The different forms arise from the different
ways in which the atoms are bonded together and as
such they may vary in chemical and physical properties.
Allotropes are also called polymorphs.

History of Carbon
Carbon is denoted by the letter ‘C’ and it is the number 6 element in
the periodic table. It is the 4th most common element, found
everywhere and unarguably one of the most abundant and most
important in life.
In the study of climate change, carbon is often generally referred to as
carbon dioxide which is the primary greenhouse gas being emitted by
humans.

Allotropes of Carbon
• Carbon is a unique element that exhibits allotropy with three well-
known allotropes: graphite, diamond, and graphene. In recent years, 
a fourth allotrope of carbon has been discovered, known as Fullerene.

contributes to the molecule's stability. These pi electrons are
responsible for many of the unique properties of fullerenes, including
their ability to act as electron acceptors in organic solar cells.

--- SLIDE ---

At the end of this lecture you should be able to
Define HIV and AIDS
Understand the difference between HIV and AIDS
Know the HIV types and subtypes 
Understand how HIV causes AIDS
Understand the global epidemiology of HIV infection
Define opportunistic infections 
Understand the steps involved in diagnosing HIV infection
Understand the need to know your HIV status
Understand and explain the HIV situation in Nigeria
Learning Objectives

--- SLIDE ---

VIRUS
 A virus is the smallest known infective agent.
 They are also known as ‘filterable agent’ 
 Depend absolutely on the mechanisms of host cells for survival. 
Outside the host, a virus is inert i.e they are non-living. 
Unlike other organism that possess both RNA and DNA, the genetic material of viruses are either DNA or RNA. 
Not every virus will infect every cell; they have affinity for specific host cell. 
For example HIV has affinity for CD4 bearing cells 
Hepatitis B virus has affinity for hepatocytes of the liver.
Definitions

--- SLIDE ---

Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome.
Acquired 
means that the disease is not hereditary but from contact with a disease-causing agent (in this case, HIV).
Immunodeficiency 
means that the disease is characterized by a weakening of the immune system. 
Syndrome 
refers to a group of symptoms that indicate or characterize a disease.
AIDS

--- SLIDE ---

Acronym for the Human Immunodeficiency virus, the 
virus that causes  acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). 
It is a retrovirus that has an RNA genome and a reverse transcriptase enzyme. 
The usual direction of flow of genetic material is DNA →RNA  
but retroviruses can go from RNA→DNA with the aid of the reverse transcriptase (RT) enzyme
The viral DNA integrates itself into the DNA of the host and then take over the activity of the cell.
HIV

--- SLIDE ---

AIDS is the late stage of HIV infection – the presence of clinical disease
HIV infected – the virus is present in the body
Not everyone that is infected with HIV that has AIDS
Most HIV infected individuals will develop AIDS if not on anti-retroviral drugs
Difference B/W HIV and AIDS

--- SLIDE ---

Diagram of Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1
Function of HIV proteins
Gp 120: part of envelope- for attachment of virus to cell
 Gp 41: part of envelope- used to internalize virus into cell 
 Lipid Membrane:  envelope provides external covering to the virus
 Integrase: enzyme used to integrate virus genome to host genome
Reverse transcriptase: enzyme used to convert viral  RNA to viral cDNA that gets integrated into the host genome
Viral RNA: Genome of the virus

Capsid: protein that surrounds the genome/nucleic acid

--- SLIDE ---

HIV is a highly variable virus which mutates very readily/easily

This means there are many different strains of HIV, even within the body of a single infected person. 

Based on genetic similarities and differences, HIV has been classified into two types, HIV-1 and HIV-2. 

Both types are transmitted through the same mode and appear to cause clinically indistinguishable AIDS.

Worldwide, the predominant virus is HIV-1

HIV-2 type is concentrated in West Africa and among those who has lived or interacted with those from West Africa

GLOBAL DISTRIBUTION OF HIV INFECTION

SIMLARITIES AND DIFFERENCES BETWEEN HIV-1 AND HIV-2

--- SLIDE ---

HIV types are classified into groups which are further classified into subtypes. 

HIV-1 can be classified into four groups: the "major" group M, the "outlier" group O and two new groups, N and P. 

More than 90 percent of HIV-1 infections belong to HIV-1 group M. 

Within group M, at least nine genetically distinct subtypes (or clades) of HIV-1 have been identified. 
These include subtypes A(A1-A4), B, C, D, F (F1 & F2), G, H, J and K.

It refers to a state of well-being that is complete, whole or full  
It has several components including physical, mental and social  
It is dynamic i.e. it is active and ever changing  
All persons regardless of age, sex, race, have a right to it  
It is more than absence of discomfort, pain, disease or infirmity  
Determinants of Health  
Structural factors  
Environment, income, education, policies

Lifestyle or behavior simply refers to

It is also called habits of individuals  
Lifestyles are important because of their contributions to between health, disease and quality 
of life  
Lifestyle can ADD or DECREASE a person’s years of potential life (Green & Kreuter, 1991) 
Importance of lifestyle 
Every disease whose cause is known has a behavioral component 
For example, the cause of AIDS is HIV 
HIV is transmitted through four behaviors 
Sexual intercourse 
Breastfeeding  
Sharing of skin-piercing instrument 
Transfusion of infected blood

GES 107 CRAMMABLE HANDBOOK
Compiled by FOLUBI
Sometimes the smallest seeds planted in the mind blossom into revolutions unseen. Knowledge is the first quiet step on
the journey to influence. May this guide serve not just for this exam, but for the many decisions that shape legacies.
SECTION 1: FOUNDATIONAL DEFINITIONS & CONCEPTS
Health: A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being.
Nutrition: The science of food intake and utilization.
Balanced Diet: Includes carbs, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water.
Malnutrition: Result of insufficient or excessive nutrients.
Kwashiorkor: Protein deficiency.
Marasmus: Calorie and protein deficiency.
Macro vs Micro Nutrients: Macro = Carbs, proteins, fats. Micro = Vitamins, minerals.
SECTION 2: DISEASES & INFECTIONS
Communicable Diseases: Spread between people.
Non-Communicable Diseases: Chronic, non-infectious.
HIV/AIDS: Viral immune system attack, managed by ART.
HIV Transmission: Sex, blood, sharps, mother-to-child.
STIs: Gonorrhea, Syphilis, Chlamydia, Herpes, HPV.
Prevention: Abstinence, condoms, sterilization.
Chain of Infection: Agent -> Reservoir -> Exit -> Transmission -> Entry -> Host.
SECTION 3: REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH & ADOLESCENCE
Adolescence: Ages 10-19.
Menstrual Cycle: Monthly hormone-regulated cycle.
Reproductive Organs: Male: testes, penis. Female: ovary, uterus.
Early Sexual Risks: Pregnancy, STIs, emotional impact.
Mother-To-Child Transmission (MTCT): HIV transfer during pregnancy, birth, breastfeeding.
SECTION 4: NUTRITION & METABOLISM
Carbs: Energy. Proteins: Growth. Fats: Storage.
Water-Soluble: Vitamins B, C. Fat-Soluble: A, D, E, K.
Fibre aids digestion but isn't digested.
Diabetes: Insulin deficiency. Hyponatremia: Excess water intake danger.

SECTION 5: MENTAL & SOCIAL HEALTH
Substance Abuse: Impairs judgment.
Determinants: Genetics, environment, income, education.
Promotion: Hygiene, exercise, safe sex.
Nosocomial Infections: Hospital-acquired.
SECTION 6: MEMORY TRIGGERS & MNEMONICS
HIV: ABC = Abstinence, Be faithful, Condom.
STIs: GSHC = Gonorrhea, Syphilis, Herpes, Chlamydia.
Chain of Infection: Agent -> Reservoir -> Exit -> Transmission -> Entry -> Host.
Macronutrients: CPF = Carbs, Proteins, Fats.

HIV COUNSELLING AND TESTING(HCT),  TREATMENT, CARE AND SUPPORT
A.O. Adefolarin  
Department of  Psychiatry, College of Medicine , UI
Dr Akande
Department of  Medicine, College of Medicine, UI

--- SLIDE ---

LESSON OBJECTIVES
Understand  the integration of HIV  Counselling and Testing                   into HIV prevention programmes
Discuss Health providers’ role in maintaining confidentiality
Provide information about HIV testing
Explain the meaning of positive and negative HIV test results
identify needs of the newly diagnosed HIV-positive patients
After completing this LESSON, the participants will  be able to:

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
HIV/AIDS is one of the world most devastating epidemics with physical, social, psychological and economic effects on individuals, families and society. 
The young people are particularly at risk for HIV infection for a number of reasons:
 incorrect and incomplete knowledge about the virus, the risk associated with its transmission, its prevention/control measures and available treatment and support services in our society

--- SLIDE ---

Definitions
HIV counselling is an interaction between a counsellor and a counsellee on HIV and AIDS issues with the purpose of empowering the counsellee to make informed decisions and face the challenges associated with his/her HIV status.

It is a  Confidential discussion(s) between an individual and the care provider to examine HIV transmission risk and explore HIV testing

Counselling can be:
Pre-HIV test Counselling
Post-HIV test Counselling
On-going HIV counselling

--- SLIDE ---

Information on HIV status kept private
Information shared only with providers directly involved in care—and only on a “need to know” basis 
Medical records kept in safe place
Guiding Principles for  Counselling and Testing

--- SLIDE ---

Importance of HIV Counselling and Testing (CT)
Is  vital for identifying HIV-positive persons to provide services
Provides an entry point to comprehensive HIV/AIDS treatment, care and support
Helps identify and reduce behaviors that increase HIV transmission risks
Becomes available to all Young people and women of childbearing age and their male partners

--- SLIDE ---

Counseling  and Testing as an Entry Point to MCH/HIV Prevention

--- SLIDE ---

Components of HIV Counseling and Testing
Informed Consent
Pre-test Counselling /HIV Education
HIV testing 
Post-test counselling
Referral to HIV prevention and care services

--- SLIDE ---

Informed Consent
Counselling and testing must be truly voluntary and individuals should be able to opt out or refuse counselling or testing if they do not think that it is in their best interest.

--- SLIDE ---

Information on HIV status kept private
Information shared only with providers directly involved in care—and only on a “need to know” basis 
Medical records kept in safe place
Guiding Principles for  Counselling and Testing

--- SLIDE ---

Pre-HIV test Counselling
This is a counselling session taken before HIV test is performed

This session provides the opportuinity to discuss issues related to:
Level of counsellee’s knowledge of HIV and AIDS
Updating the counsellee’s knowledge of HIV and AIDS
HIV risk assessment
HIV test results and interpretation
Assurance of confidentiality
Management/coping strategies
Linkage with service points and other support systems
Consent to undergo the test

--- SLIDE ---

Types of pre-HIV test counselling technique
‘Opt-in’ technique
The counsellee requests for the service

‘opt-out’ technique 
The counsellor offer the service

--- SLIDE ---

Process of Counselling and Testing
Pre-test Group education
‘opt-out’ technique
Identifies:
Purpose of testing and processes involved
Benefits and risks of testing
Available treatment and support
Respects  Individual’s autonomy and right to confidentiality

--- SLIDE ---

Post-HIV test Counselling
This session is influenced by the result of HIV test which could either be positive or negative.

Human Sexuality and Adolescent Sexual Behaviour
Ademola J. Ajuwon, MPH, PhD
1

--- SLIDE ---

Definition of adolescence
An interface between childhood and adulthood. 

According to the World Health Organization an adolescent is someone aged 10-19 years. 

Early adolescence (between 10-14 years)

Late adolescence (between 15-19 years)

Other common terms used to describe the young population are “youth” and “young people”. 

A youth is someone aged 15-24 years while a young person is an individual aged 10-24 years.
2

--- SLIDE ---

Social definition of adolescence
In some communities, participation in some rites of passage confers adulthood to the individual regardless of his/her age. 

Thus, among the Yoruba of South West Nigeria, for example, an individual is considered an adult once he/she marries. 

Among the Zulu of South Africa, a boy is considered an adult once he becomes circumcised.
3

--- SLIDE ---

Universally Acceptable Definition of a Young Person
“Although no longer a child, the young person is not yet considered an adult”
(McCauley and Salter, 1995)
4

--- SLIDE ---

Features of adolescence
A time of self-definition  (self consciousness ) which is also full of experimentation, spontaneity in especially in sexual activity and drug use (WHO, 1998). 

He/she develops more intense relationship with peers and take major life decisions.

Growth spurt occurs, in which the size and shape of the body change markedly and bring out the differences between boys and girls. 

Boys: Increase in the size of the genital organs, growth of hair in the genital       area, and deep voice 

Girls: Menstruation, growth and development of breast in girls. 

Reproductive capacity is established.
5

--- SLIDE ---

Young people
6

--- SLIDE ---

Significance of adolescents
1.	Sheer large number of the Adolescents and Young Persons (AYP) population in the country.  For example, according to the 2006 national census, AYP aged 10-24 years constitute 31% of the Nigerian population (WHO, 2020).  

2.	A sizable proportion of AYP engage in risky sexual practices including unprotected sex with multiple partners  


3.	AYP represents the potential for the future of any community; therefore, necessary investments must be made in the growth and development of this segment of the population. 


4. 	AYP have enthusiasm, energy and optimism (UNAIDS, 2004) which must be properly channeled for positive outcomes in Nigeria.
7

--- SLIDE ---

Sexuality defined
Sexuality is a major aspect of being human throughout life (WHO, 2002). 

According to the World Health Organization (WHO) sexuality encompasses sex, gender identities and roles, sexual orientation, eroticism, pleasure, intimacy and reproduction.
8

--- SLIDE ---

Sexuality education
Sexuality education is a process of learning about how an individual can be comfortable about all aspects of being human. 

Sexuality education is the process of providing information, skills and services that enable persons adopt safe sexual behaviors 
	-abstinence 
	-non-penetrative sex such as hugging, and holding hands
	-correct and consistent use of condoms. 

Sexually healthy behaviors also include seeking care from trained health workers during incidence of any disease such as sexually transmitted infections (STI), unwanted pregnancy, and infertility.
9

--- SLIDE ---

Why sexuality education is important for AYP
Adolescents reach sexual maturity before they develop the mental / emotional maturity and acquire the skills needed to appreciate the consequences of their sexual activity 

Unmet needs of AYP in Nigeria are largely unmet 
	-lack knowledge about reproduction health (pregnancy cannot occur during first  sexual episode) 
	
	-Sexually active, do not want to become pregnant, but not using any protection 

Investment in sexuality education will pay dividend in the long run
10

Examples of adolescent risky behaviors
1. Early sexual debut

2. Sex with casual partners

GES 107 :OVERVIEW OF SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS
Olufunmilola B. MAKANJUOLA , Olubukola ADESINA, Aderemi O. KEHINDE
Department of Medical Microbiology and Parasitology, 
College of Medicine, 
University of Ibadan
1

--- SLIDE ---

Male and female reproductive system
2

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction and Definition
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) are a group of contagious diseases in which the main mode of transmission is by sexual intercourse 
Until recent times, they were traditionally referred to as Venereal Disease (VD) 
Venereal is derived from the latin word venereus
Venereus means relating to sexual intercourse or sexual desire
Originates from Venus, the Roman goddess of love
3

--- SLIDE ---

They are also often called Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STD)
However, the term Sexually transmitted infection (STI) is preferred to these other terminologies
STI has a broader range of meaning
A person may be infected, and has the potential to infect others, without showing signs of disease. 
Important particularly when transmission and control of STIs are considered
STI also includes infections that may not necessarily cause clinical disease in the genital area but are transmitted by sexual contact
4

--- SLIDE ---

Sites of infection
The principal sites of infections are moist mucous surfaces such as penis, vagina and cervix 

These are the affected sites in the usual heterosexual vaginal intercourse.
5

--- SLIDE ---

Sites of infection
Additional parts of the body, such as the lips, oropharynx (throat), anus and rectum, could be affected 
Seen in  who practice other forms of sex such as oral sex and anal sex                         
Becoming important sites of infections with increase in the practice oral and anal sex, especially among homosexuals
6

--- SLIDE ---

STIs affect both men and women, 
However, in many cases, the health problems they cause can be more severe for women. If a pregnant woman has an STI, it can cause serious health problems for the baby as well
7

--- SLIDE ---

Epidemiology of STIs
Globally sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are of significant public health importance
More than 1 million STIs are acquired worldwide every day
Resulting in over 370 infections annually   
The rate of STI acquisition is increasing in many places 
Over 30 different organisms such as bacteria, viruses and parasites can be transmitted through sexual contact
Eight of these are associated with the highest incidence of STIs
Four are curable while the other four are either incurable or difficult to manage
8

--- SLIDE ---

Common STIs
“Curable STIs”
Chlamydia,
Gonorrhoea
Trichomoniasis, 
Syphilis 
Prevalence and incidence in adults remain high- estimated 376 million new infections annually
“Incurable STIs” 
These are viral infections 
Hepatitis B
Herpes simplex virus (HSV or herpes)
HIV, 
Human papillomavirus (HPV)
9

--- SLIDE ---

STI in Nigeria
In Nigeria, STI is one of the leading causes of outpatient visits 
Average prevalence rate of 9.3%
The burden of STIs is further compounded by the advent of HIV infection
The epidemiology of STIs involves the study of sexual active reproductive age groups in the community
10

--- SLIDE ---

STI in Nigeria (2)
Studies have shown that Candidiasis, genital warts, genital ulcer disease, non-gonococcal urethritis and gonorrhea are the most common STIs in Nigeria 
According to the Nigeria National HIV/AIDS Indicator and Impact Survey (NAIIS) released March 2019 
The National HIV prevalence in Nigeria as 1.4% among adults aged 15–49 years (previous estimate was 2.8%) 
In essence, 1.9 million people are living with HIV in Nigeria
11

--- SLIDE ---

Transmission of STIs
STIs are transmitted primarily via sexual contact, which could be vaginal, anal or oral sex 
In addition to sexual transmission, some of the STI pathogens may also be transmitted by other means 
These other means are of particular importance among the viral STIs
12

S.B. Olaleye, B.Sc, M.Sc, Ph.D (Ibadan)Department of Physiology, College of Medicine, University of Ibadan Olutosin A. Awolude, MBBS, MSc, FWACS
Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, College of Medicine, University of Ibadan

--- SLIDE ---

SYNOPSIS
The aim of the section is to learn about the essential physiology of the reproductive system, issues related to reproductive system and  reproductive health  dysfunctions associated with reproductive system considered necessary for this class will be dealt with.

--- SLIDE ---

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
To understand, in a simplified manner, the structure and function of the female and male reproductive systems.

To understand basic health issues related to the reproductive system

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
The reproductive system is unique:
  only organ system that is not vital for survival of the organism because an individual can live long, health and happy life without reproducing 
major function is to ensure continuity of the species.
achieved with the contribution of other systems in the body, such as the endocrine and urinary systems. 
However, if the species is to continue to exist, at least some individuals must produce offspring.

--- SLIDE ---

Functions of Reproductive system
Production of egg and sperm cells 
Transportation and sustenance of these cells 
Nurturing the developing offspring 
Production of hormones

--- SLIDE ---

The organs of Reproduction
These can be Primary or Secondary
Primary organs are the gonads and include:
ovaries and testes for responsible for 
Production of eggs and sperms
Production of hormones for the maturation of the eggs and the sperms and development of secondary sexual characteristics
Secondary organs include:
Ducts and glands
They transport and sustain the gametes 
They nurture the developing offspring

--- SLIDE ---

The Male Reproductive Organs

--- SLIDE ---

The Testes and the duct system

--- SLIDE ---

Spermatogenesis

--- SLIDE ---

Associated Problems with the testes
Cryptorchidism -failure of the testes to descend

Vanishing testes syndrome (Bilateral anorchia) in which  the patients will present at birth with non-palpable testes and sexual immaturity later in life

Germinal cell aphasia in which there azoospermia in association with normal virilization, testes of normal consistency but slightly smaller in size, and no gynecomastia. 

Gonadotoxins induced germinal cells damage

mumps orchitis

--- SLIDE ---

The External genitalia
This consists of:
scrotum sac of cutaneous membrane that hangs outside the abdomino-pelvic cavity at the root of the penis. 
Penis functions to deliver spermatozoa into the female reproductive tract. 
It consists of an attached root and a free shaft, which ends in an enlarged tip (glans penis).

--- SLIDE ---

Problems associated with scrotum and penis
scrotal varicocele  which results from backflow of blood secondary to incompetent or absent valves in the spermatic veins.

--- SLIDE ---

Physiology of erection and ejaculation
Erection occurs when
During sexual arousal, parasympathetic nerve activity leads to dilation of penile blood vessels and subsequently allowing blood to fill the erectile bodies.
This compresses the veins draining the penis. The result is more blood into the penis and less blood out – yielding an erection.
Erection allows the penis to function as a an organ for copulation
It is a spinal reflex action but can be modulated cerebral input

Physiology of erection and ejaculation
Ejaculation occurs when:
When sexually arousing impulses reach a certain  level, a massive increase of penile sympathetic nerve activity occurs
Contraction of reproductive ducts and glands and the emptying of their contents into the urethra
Closing of the internal urethral sphincter to prevent urine expulsion or semen reflux;
 Expulsion of semen from the urethra.

LE PREMIER TEXTE
Bonjour! 
Monsieur Kunle: Bonjour madame.
Madame Abiola: Bonjour Monsieur.
Monsieur Kunle: Comment allez-vous ?.  
Madame Abiola: Je vais bien, merci Et vous ?
Monsieur Kunle: Je vais très bien, moi aussi.
Madame Abiola: Comment vous appelez-vous ?
Monsieur Kunle : Je m’appelle Monsieur Kunle et Vous ?
Madame Abiola: Je m’appelle Madame Abiola.
Monsieur Kunle: Madame Abiola ? Veuillez epeler s’il vous plaît ?
Madame Abiola : A-B-I-O-L-A. Abiola
Monsieur Kunle : Ah oui, je comprends maintenant. Madame Abiola. On a rendez-vous 			ce vendredi ?
Madame Abiola : Non, monsieur, on re revoit le mois d’octobre 
Monsieur Kunle : D’accord. Nous avons rendez-vous le mois d’octobre pendant la fête 			nationale du Nigéria.
Madame Abiola : Au revoir monsieur Kunle !
Monsieur Kunle : Au revoir madame Abiola !   
Understanding the text
Comment s’appellent les deux interlocuteurs dans le dialogue ?
Le mois d’…….est la fête nationale du Nigéria.
Lisez le passage après votre professeur et puis lisez-le indépendamment   
Vocabulary 
Veuillez…+ infinitif	-	Could you please…
Épeler			-	To spell out a word
Je comprends		-	I understand 
Maintenant		-	Now
Rendez-vous…	-	Meeting 
Pendant 		-	During
La fête nationale	-	National Day
LE DEUXIEME TEXTE
Ce que je fais pendant la semaine / What I do during the week.
Bonjour tout le monde! Je m’appelle Aanuoluwapo, je suis une fille et j’ai seize ans et je suis grande. Voici comment je passe ma semaine : de lundi à vendredi, je vais à l’école. Samedi je reste à la maison avec mes parents et dimanche nous allons à l’église.  
Se présenter / Introducing oneself
Je m’appelle…	-	My name is…
Je suis...		-	I am…
Je suis un garçon	-	I am a boy
J’ai seize ans		-	I am 16 years old 
Je suis court (e)	-	I am short
Je suis grand (e)	-	I am tall
Je suis petit(e)		-	I am small
LE TROISIEME TEXTE
L’Anniversaire de mon père/My Father’s Birthday 
Mon père s’appelle Monsieur Bayo Olusanya. Il est directeur d’une grande usine à Abuja au Nigéria, il fête son anniversaire chaque année au mois de novembre parce qu’il est né le 7 novembre. Voilà pourquoi il fête son anniversaire aujourd’hui avec ses collègues.

1.	Comment s’appelle mon père? 
2.	Quelle est la profession de mon père ?
3.	En quel mois est-ce que mon père fête son anniversaire ? 
Mon père fête son anniversaire avec qui… ?

Le directeur		-	director

Anniversaire		-	Birthday
Voilà pourquoi…	-	That is why…
Les collègues		-	Colleagues 
Les jours de la semaine 
Il y a sept jours dans une semaine. There are seven days in a week.
Please be aware that “combien” means “how much” or “how many”?
lundi		-	Monday
mardi		-	Tuesday 
mercredi		-	Wednesday
jeudi		-	Thursday
vendredi		-	Friday
samedi		-	Saturday
dimanche		-	Sunday
While Sunday is the first day of the week in English, in French it is Monday. 
Lundi est le premier jour de la semaine/ Monday is the first day of the week.
Mardi est le deuxième jour de la semaine/ Tuesday is the second day of the week.
Mercredi est le troisième jour de la semaine/ Wednesday is the third day of the week.
Jeudi est le quatrième jour de la semaine/ Thursday is the fourth day of the week.
Vendredi est le cinquième jour de la semaine/ Friday is the fifth day of the week.
Samedi est le sixième jour de la semaine/ Saturday is the sixth day of the week.
Dimanche est le septième jour de la semaine/ Sunday is the seventh day of the week.    
Combien de mois y-a-t-il dans l’année ? How many months are there in a year?
Il y a douze mois dans une année. There are twelve months in a year.

Module 10
EXPRIMER SES GOUTS
In this unit, we learn how to express our dreams and desires. This will also broaden our vocabulary knowledge.
(Two friends meet in the University cafeteria and talk about their desires)
Dialogue :
Esther: Bonjour Marie, comment vas-tu aujourd’hui?
Aina: Bonjour Esther. Je vais très bien, merci.
Esther: Quand est-ce que tu vas finir tes cours supplémentaires aujourd’hui?
Aina: Je vais en finir à dix-sept heures. 
Esther: Qu’est-ce que tu désires manger? Tu aimes du riz au gras ou des pommes frites?
Aina: Non, je n’aime ni l’un ni l’autre, je préfère du café chaud sans lait et un peu de gâteau; Je dois être toujours en bonne forme parce que je veux devenir une athlète internationale. Et toi?
Esther: Moi aussi, je dois être en bonne forme, mais je déteste du café chaud sans lait. J’aime bien du riz gras au poulet. Moi, je vais devenir une cuisinière professionnelle, je vais avoir mon propre restaurant.
Aina: Avoir un restaurant est un bon projet. Ça va aller.
Esther: Merci beaucoup mon amie distinguée.
VOCABULARY
Cours supplémentaires		-			Extra classes
Riz au gras				-			Jollof rice
Pommes frites				-			Fried potatoes
Café chaud				-			Hot coffee
Gâteau					-		           Cake
Athlète internationale			-			International athlete
Cuisinière professionnelle		-			Professional cook
Mon amie distinguée			-			My distinguished friend
QUESTIONS
Qui va finir ses cours supplémentaires à dix-sept heures?
Qu’est-ce qu’Esther déteste?
Quelle est l’ambition de Marie?
Quel est le projet d’Esther?
Que préfère Marie?
Exprimer ses goûts (Expressing one’s tastes)
The tastes or preferences of individuals are quite different. They can be expressed in positive or negative degrees. Examples of verbs that can be used in expressing one’s tastes are:
Positive expressions                                                                                                                                                    
Aimer                         (to love / like)
Aimer bien                 (to like a lot)
Aimer beaucoup         (to like very much)
Aimer mieux              (to prefer)                                                                     
Préférer                      (to prefer)
Adorer                        (to adore / to love)
Adorer le plus             (to adore most)
Negative expressions
Ne pas aimer                 (not to like)
Haïr                               (to hate / deteste)
Détester                         (to deteste)
Dégoûter                        (to disgust)
Examples:
J’aime bien des pommes rouges.                                (I like red apples a lot.)
Ma mère préfère des oranges.                                     (My mother prefers oranges.)
Les enfants adorent les joujoux.                                  (Children adore toys.)
Les bonbons dégoûtent les adultes.                             (Candy is disgusting to adults).
Mon professeur et moi détestons les motocyclettes.   (My teacher and I hate motorcycles).
Conjugation of verbs in “futur proche” 
We use “futur proche” to express events that will take place in the nearest future.
Note:
Le verbe “Aller” au présent (Verb “to go” in the present)
Je vais                -        I go / I am going
Tu vas                -        You go / You are going 
Il / Elle va          -        He / She goes / He / She is going
Nous allons        -        We go / We are going
Vous allez          -        You go / You are going
Ils / Elles vont    -        They go / They are going
Examples:
Je vais visiter le zoo.                                	(I am going to visit the zoo.)
Bode va manger fufu.                              	(Bode is going to eat fufu.)
Mon ami et moi allons finir le devoir.  	(My friend and I are going to finish the        
  	Assignment).
Le professeur va punir les étudiants.         	(The teacher is going to punish the students.)
Vous allez attendre jusqu’au soir.               	(You are going to wait till evening.)

Module 11
A l'Hôpital
Docteur:	Bonjour Monsieur
Uche :		Bonjour Docteur
Docteur :	Qu’est-ce qui ne va pas ?
Uche :		Je ne me sens pas bien. Je crois ma température s’est élevée, je suis affaibli et j’ai 			le vertige.
Docteur :	Vous avez mangé aujourd’hui ?
Uche :		Oui docteur, rassasié à plein ventre.
Docteur :	D’accord. Je vais vous poser un peu de question.
Uche :		D’accord docteur.
Docteur :	Vous avez de la grippe ?
Uche :		Non docteur
Docteur :	Vous vomissez ?
Uche :		Non docteur.
Docteur :	De la fièvre ?
Uche :		Non docteur.
Docteur :	Avancez un peu. J’ai besoin de vérifier votre rythme 						cardiaque.
Uche :		Ahh….c’est quoi ça docteur…..une opération ?
Docteur :	Je n’ai pas dit cela. Juste un stéthoscope pour vérifier le rythme					cardiaque.
Uche :		J’ai peur de la piqûre et la salle d’opération, je ne veux pas y aller. Ah...Voilà 			docteur, je crois, je me sens bien maintenant.
Docteur :	Calmez-vous monsieur. Ouvrez les yeux, je vous vérifie les yeux. Ouvrez la 			bouche, tirez la langue.
Docteur :	Vous avez froid ? Mal au ventre ?, blessure ? Inflammation ?
Uche :		Non docteur mais j’ai mal au dos. Est-ce que c’est une fracture docteur ?
Docteur :	On ne peut pas tout dire exactement. Pour cela vous allez faire la radiographie 			mais toutefois cela ne suffit pas de vous faire malade.
Docteur :	On vous fait vérifier la tension artérielle, sentir votre pouls et prendre votre 			température. 
Docteur :	Je crois vous avez une infection. Vous allez faire le dépistage en laboratoire. 			Après on vous fait un diagnostique et quand le résultat de dépistage soit sorti, je 			vous faire une 	ordonnance des médicaments, mais pour le moment je vous 			prescris des analgésiques pour vous faire soulager la douleur au dos. La 				pharmacie n’est pas loin d’ici.
Uche :		Et l’antibiotique docteur, je peux en ajouter?
Docteur :	C’est l’abus de drogue. Patientez-vous le résultat de dépistage !
Uche :		D’accord, merci docteur.
Docteur :	Vous me rendez visite quand vous avez le résultat.
Uche :		D’accord, merci docteur. Bonne journée.
Docteur :	Bonne journée.
A
Les verbes
Faire, aller, se sentir, crois, être, vérifier, prendre, avoir, visiter, patienter, soulager, pouvoir, souffrir, se calmer, avancer, dire, vomir, poser, manger, rassasier 
B
Vocabulaire
L’analgésique				-	Analgesic
Le dépistage en laboratoire		-	Lab screening
La tension artérielle			-	Blood pressure
La radiographie			-	X-ray
Le pouls				-	Pulse
La température			-	temperature
Salle d’opération			-	Theatre room
Le stéthoscope				-	Stethoscope
Le rythme cardiaque			-	Heart beat
Le vertige				-	Vertigo, dizzy
La grippe				-	Flu
La froid				-	Cold
La fièvre				-	Fever
La vomisse				-	Vomit

Module 12
Un Jour A La Ferme
Le dimanche passé, je suis allé à la ferme de mon oncle Pierre et sa femme Rose. J’y avais passé une journée carrément amusante. J'ai enfin pu voir des animaux que je n'avais pas vus depuis longtemps tels des bœufs, des vaches, des veaux, des poulets, des oies, plusieurs espèces de poissons, des moutons, aussi bien que des cerfs. J’ai vu des fermiers et des fermières.
Après un moment de repos, nous avons bien tassé la ferme pendant une heure pour planter quelques herbes comme du manioc, d’igname, du piment, des oignons, des tomates, aussi bien que les cannes à sucre. Ouf ! C’est midi déjà. Et comme le travail était réussi, nous avons ramassé nos houes et machettes pour aller au bord de la rivière.

Je m’appelle Yakubu Jacob. Je suis d’un petit village appelé Kubo. La vie dans mon village est très intéressante parce qu’on mange des produits agricoles frais. J’habite avec mes grands-parents au village. Mon grand-père vit dans une grande hutte. Mon grand-père est chasseur et ma grand-mère est fermière. Chaque jour, je vais au champ pour aider ma grand-mère, elle plante le manioc, l’igname, et le maïs. J’aime être avec mon-grand-père le soir pour écouter les bons contes. Dans mon village, il n’y a pas de bureau comme nous l’avons dans la ville. Aussi on puise de l’eau au marigot. Les moyens de transport sont le pied, le vélo, la motocyclette ou le camion. Le tribunal reste très important dans la société humaine, car il contribue au maintien de l'ordre dans la société. Ceux qui sont en désaccord au lieu de se faire justice eux-mêmes, présentent simplement leur cas devant le tribunal. Mais, malheureusement, le tribunal ne semble être créé que pour les personnes instruites et riches dans la société, car les pauvres et les non-éduqués ignorent son importance ou sont simplement frustrés car ils n'ont pas d'argent pour "acheter" un avocat. Les pauvres se confier à Dieu pour les venger des riches qui les maltraitent alors que les riches ne cessent pas de payer des avocats pour mettre les pauvres qui les « offensent » à la prison.

VISITE A L’UNIVERSITE DE MA VILLE
L’Université de ma ville se situe à trois kilomètres de chez moi. Je la voyais toujours de loin, mais je n’y suis jamais entré. J’ai donc décidé de m’y rendre un jour. C’était lundi dernier que je m’y suis rendu. J’ai pris un taxi à la station de taxi du quartier. Et, après une heure de voyage, je suis arrivé devant le portail de l’Université. Le gardien n’a pas permis à mon taxi d’entrer, car l’entrée à l’Université est interdite aux taxis. On m’a demandé de remplir le registre pour les visiteurs; après quoi, j’ai fait à pied le trajet du portail au bloc central de l’Université. 
		Le bloc central de l’université est un grand bâtiment à trois étages. Au rez-de-chaussée se trouvent les salles de classe, l’amphithéâtre, la bibliothèque, la librairie, la clinique et le restaurant qui servent tous les étudiants, quelques soient leurs collèges, leurs départements et leurs disciplines. Au premier étage se trouvent les bureaux des professeurs, du Secrétaire Général et de l’intendant de l’université. C’est au deuxième étage que se situent les bureaux du Vice-chancelier, des Doyens des Collèges et des Chefs de Départements. 
(Extract form Ade-Ojo (2012) Practical French for Anglophone Learners)

COMMUNICATING WITH « TU » OR « VOUS »
There is the right and wrong way to say “you” in French. Or rather, there are different ways to say it depending on who you are talking to. 
PERSONAL PRONOUNS 
“Vous”- Formal you
The distinction between “tu” and “vous” indicates your relationship with the person you are talking to. We use “vous” for:
People you don’t know (people in the street, sellers…).
Person older than you or occupying positions higher than you (status).
Group of people (If you talk to several persons, you always use “vous”, because “vous” is also the plural of “you”).

Veterinarians and the concept of “One Health “
Prof. Victoria O. Adetunji
Department of Veterinary Public Health and Preventive Medicine,
University of Ibadan

--- SLIDE ---

ONE HEALTH
One Health is a collaborative, multisectoral, and transdisciplinary approach — working at the local, regional, national, and global levels — with the goal of achieving optimal health outcomes recognizing the interconnection between people, animals, plants, and their shared environment.

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
Veterinarians play an important role in One Health by striving to keep animals healthy, which helps ensure the food supply's safety and reduces disease spread from animals to humans.

--- SLIDE ---

Specific areas in which veterinarians contribute to One Health include:
Disease surveillance — Veterinarians are on the front lines of zoonotic disease surveillance, reporting outbreaks and unusual cases in animals that could impact human health.
Antibiotic stewardship — Veterinarians understand how antibiotic resistance develops in people, pets, and food animals, and take steps to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.
Education — Veterinarians educate their clients, colleagues, and communities about One Health, encouraging interdisciplinary collaboration.

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
Research — Veterinarians involved with research can directly contribute to One Health by studying disease transmission, emerging pathogens, and treatments. Veterinarians can set an example by actively collaborating and sharing knowledge with other medical professionals.
Policy — Veterinary organizations with lobbying power can advocate for One Health-friendly policies, focusing on infrastructure, veterinary care access, and environmental regulations at local and large-scale levels.

--- SLIDE ---

The Scope of Veterinary Public Health

--- SLIDE ---

One Health is not a new concept, but it has become more important in recent years because many factors have changed the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment. These changes have caused the emergence and reemergence of many diseases.

--- SLIDE ---

One Health concept
The One Health concept recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal and ecosystem health. 
A One Health approach involves applying a coordinated, collaborative, multidisciplinary and cross-sectoral approach to address potential or existing risks that originate at the animal-human-ecosystems interface. 
The overarching aim of One Health is to achieve optimal health for humans, animals and the ecosystem.

--- SLIDE ---

Zoonotic Diseases
Diseases that can be passed between animals and humans



At least 61% of all human pathogens are zoonotic.

~75% of all emerging pathogens in the past decade have been zoonotic.

--- SLIDE ---

Why is this true?
We interact with animals in our daily lives.
We raise animals for food or enjoyment.
We keep them in our homes as pets.
We come into close contact with animals at fairs and zoos.
We encounter wildlife when we are outdoors or bugs that transmit disease.

Routes of Transmission
Direct contact
Bite, scratch, contact with infected tissues
Ex. Rabies, Q-fever
Indirect contact
Food/water-borne or touching infected object (fomite)
Salmonella, E. coli, Giardia

text_snippet:
VETERINARY CLINICAL SERVICES AND NIGERIAN LIVESTOCK PRODUCTION: RUMINANT PRACTICE
BY 
PROF. O.T. JEREMIAH
Dept. of Veterinary Medicine, UI
1

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
A sick animal is better dead than alive (bad attitude among Nigerians)
Government livestock services are provided by both the national and state governments.
Ministry of Agriculture and Natural Resources with Livestock or Veterinary Divisions which operate state farms and provide technical and veterinary assistance
2

--- SLIDE ---

Livestock Population in Nigeria
Based on mid-1991 market prices, total value of Nigerian livestock is about 60 billion Naira
Ruminants occupy central stage in livestock production in Nigeria.
Goats have been estimated to be about 76,300,000, while sheep are said to be 48,600,000 in number and cattle have a population of 21,200,000. FAOSTAT (2021)
In Nigeria, livestock provides about 36.5% of total protein intake
3

--- SLIDE ---

RUMINANTS
A ruminant is any hoofed animal and usually horned animal that digests its food in two steps, first by eating the raw material and regurgitating a semi-digested form known as cud, then eating the cud. 
Ruminants have a stomach with four chambers, which are rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.
4

--- SLIDE ---

EXAMPLES OF RUMINANTS
Broadly there are two classes:				(1) Domestic ruminants, such as cattle, sheep, goats (and recently camels in the NE and NW parts of Nigeria).					(2) Wild ruminants, such as buffaloes, deer, elands, elks, giraffes and antelopes.
In Nigeria (and Sub-Saharan Africa), domestic ruminants  are responsible for about 75% of the total meat supply.
5

--- SLIDE ---

Cattle (Large ruminants)
Cattle are the single most important livestock species in Nigeria, in terms of animal protein supply, value and biomass
They provide meat and milk, skin, bone, blood and horn products. They are useful for transporting people and loads, to pull ploughs, carts and ridgers and for pulling water from well.
They are found most commonly(2/3) in the northern while less than half are found in other parts of Nigeria.
6

--- SLIDE ---

Cattle Cont’d
Humped zebu cattle are by far the most common, and they include White Fulani, Red Bororo, Sokoto Gudali and their crosses

Limited numbers of Keteku, Muturu and Kuri cattle and their crosses occur in southwestern, southern and north-eastern parts of the country respectively
7

--- SLIDE ---

Small ruminants
Small domestic ruminants refer to sheep and goats.
They are almost as ubiquitous as poultry, though not so numerous.
The great majority of small ruminants are sedentary village livestock
Their patterns of distribution mirror those of human settlement.
8

--- SLIDE ---

Goats
There are three main varieties (breeds) of goat in Nigeria: the West African Dwarf, the Red Sokoto and the Sahel.
They are renowned for their hardiness and ability to survive in most environments
West African Dwarf goats are kept in the forest zones and in the Middle Belt
Red Sokoto goats are kept throughout the north
Sahel goats are restricted to a strip along the frontier with the Niger
9

--- SLIDE ---

Goats Cont’d
The most common production system is that of seasonal confinement.
Northern goats have been found to be markedly more productive than West African Dwarf goats, with lower ages at first kidding and shorter kidding intervals
There have been crosses between West African Dwarf and Red Sokoto goats
10

--- SLIDE ---

Sheep
There are four main types(breeds) of sheep native to Nigeria: the Balami, Ouda, Yankasa and West African Dwarf
Balami and Ouda are kept in the semi-arid regions
West African Dwarf sheep in the south
Yankasa breeds are kept throughout the country
Sheep are the second most numerous pastoral species, after cattle.
11

--- SLIDE ---

Sheep Cont’d
All Nigerian sheep are used for wool, but they are rarely milked
In the north, they are eaten regularly and form part of the daily protein supply
Their demand also varies with religious festivals eg Ileya, Chris

Introduction to Veterinary Medicine

Topic: Pharmacology and the Veterinarian
Dr Bisi O. Adeoye
Department of Veterinary Pharmacology and

10/09/2025
1

Introduction
Veterinary Pharmacology: The study of drug
actions and uses in animals.
To ensure effective treatment and preventing
harm to animals and humans.
2

Branches of Veterinary Pharmacology
• Pharmacokinetics: ADME.
• Pharmacodynamics: how drugs interact with body
to produce their effects.
•
Toxicology:
Studies
the
harmful
effects
of
chemicals, drugs, and toxins on living organisms and
the methods for prevention or treatment of these
effects.
• Clinical Pharmacology: Focuses on the diagnosis,
treatment, and prevention of diseases in animals
using drugs.
3

Branches of Veterinary Pharmacology…
• Regulatory
Pharmacology:
Concerns
the
approval,
regulation,
and
monitoring
of
veterinary drugs.
• Ethnopharmacology:
Investigates
the
use
of
traditional and herbal medicines in veterinary
practice. Focuses on natural remedies and their
pharmacological properties.
4

Branches of Veterinary Pharmacology…
• Comparative
Pharmacology:
Studies
the
differences in drug effects and metabolism
across
animal
species.
Essential
for
understanding species-specific responses.
• Pharmaceutical
Science:
Involves
the
development and formulation of drugs for
veterinary use.
5

Commonly Used Drugs in Veterinary 
Medicine
• Antibiotics: Amoxicillin, Enrofloxacin.
• Analgesics: NSAIDs like Meloxicam.
• Vaccines: For diseases like rabies, distemper.
• Antiparasitics: Ivermectin, Fenbendazole.
• Multivitamins.
6

Veterinary Toxicology
• Deals with the adverse effects of chemicals, drugs,
and toxins on animals.
• Also on the relationship between toxicants and
animal health and well-being.
• Sources of toxins:
- Natural: Plants, mycotoxins, venom.
- Synthetic: Pesticides, industrial chemicals.
• Routes of exposure: Oral, dermal, inhalation.
.
7

Common Toxins in Veterinary Practice
• Household Toxins: Chocolate, xylitol, cleaning
agents.
• Environmental Toxins: Lead, pesticides, antifreeze
(ethylene glycol).
• Pharmacological Toxins: Overdose of NSAIDs or
other drugs.
• Case examples of toxic effects on animals.
8

Branches of Veterinary Toxicology
• Clinical Toxicology: Focuses on the diagnosis,
treatment,
and
prevention
of
poisoning
in
animals.
• Environmental Toxicology: Studies the impact of
environmental pollutants on animal health.
• Forensic Toxicology: Concerned with the legal
aspects
of
toxicology,
such
as
investigating
animal deaths caused by poisoning.
9

Branches of Veterinary Toxicology…
• Nutritional Toxicology: Examines the effects of
contaminants or imbalances in animal feed.
• Toxicopathology: Studies the pathological effects
of toxins on animal tissues and organs.
• Food Safety Toxicology: Focuses on ensuring that
veterinary drugs and chemicals in animal products
(e.g., meat, milk, eggs) do not pose a risk to
human consumers.
10

Diagnosis and Treatment of Toxicities
• Steps in diagnosis:
- Clinical signs, history, and toxicology tests.
• Treatment protocols:
- Decontamination: Induced vomiting, activated
charcoal.
- Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen therapy.
-
Antidotes:
Pralidoxime(2-PAM)
for
organophosphates, Vitamin K for anticoagulants.
11

Regulatory Aspects
•
Drug
Approval
and
Safety:
Role
of
organizations like FDA-CVM, EMA.
• Toxicology Regulations: Testing and setting
permissible levels of toxins.
12

Challenges and Advancements
• Emerging challenges:
- Antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
- Environmental contamination by Veterinary
drugs.
• Technological advancements:
- Precision medicine.
- Nanotechnology in drug delivery.
13

Conclusion
we are to protecting animal health, welfare, and
public safety.
14

Thank you

text_snippet:
VETERINARY physiology and biochemistry: important foundation of veterinary medicine
Dr odunayo azeez
Department of veterinary physiology and biochemistry

--- SLIDE ---

Organization of the course
Veterinary Medicine and even Medicine are organized in a systematic manner.
Knowledge of normal is built first then abnormalities afterwards the treatment and control or interventions are taught.
Preclinical Section of Veterinary Medicine, which consists of Anatomy, Physiology and Biochemistry followed by Paraclinical Sciences where you learn about Pathology, Microbiology, Parasitology and enthomology. 
The final section is the Clinical section, made up of Medicine, Surgery and Theriogenology. Public Health and Preventive Medicine deals with control.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology
Physiology is the study of normal functions of the body.
It also studies the various ways by which animals respond to or adjust to various changes in the environment. 
This also involves mechanisms and strategies employed by animals to ensure survival and continuity of life irrespective of what the environment brings.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology
Physiology deals with the functions and activities of life or of living matter (such as organs, tissues, or cells) and the  physical and chemical phenomena involved. 
From historical perspectives, physiology is believed to be the basis and father of medicine, as far back as the time of Hippocrates in 420 BC.
 He coined the theory of the four humours, stating that the body contains four distinct bodily fluids: black bile, phlegm, blood, and yellow bile. 
Any disturbance in their ratios, as the theory goes, causes illnesses.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology
In physiology we take an holistic look at the organism functionally.
But looking at each system, we integrate the systems to give a general or complete overview of the entire organism.
The systems include blood and lymphatics, respiratory, excretory and cardiovascular system. Others are endocrine, reproduction and the nervous system which serves as the centre of integration and control.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology
The summary of Physiology is to evaluate homeostasis and allostasis.
Homeostasis deals with how the body maintains a stable internal environment despite the changing or unstable external environment. 
It studies how the animal maintains steady state and survive changes, harshness or limitations of the environment e.g. temperature, food supply and even survival of the generation.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology
Allostasis on the other hand deals with maintenance of steady and stable internal environment during normal physiological changes. 
This is the basis of adaptation and survival when extreme, transient or permanent change of status occurs that will require that the body redefines its normal functional parameters. 
A classical example is seen during pregnancy, lactation, hibernation or stress. During these periods, set points are changed and the new set points are maintained by homeostasis

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary physiology
We examine all the systems including:
Neurophysiology and neuroscience as the central control system, Endocrine and Cardiovascular Physiology and how they are affected by the environment (Environmental Physiology) as well as variations in responses across the various animal species including domestic and exotic species (Comparative Physiology).

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary biochemistry
Here in Veterinary Biochemisytry, we look at the molecular basis of the functions when they are optimal or during abnormalities.
It is a fundamental biological and medical science that provides an understanding of cell biology, microbiology, nutrition, pharmacology and physiology at the molecular level.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary biochemistry
In the organization of life, we have subatomic particles - Atom - Molecule - Macromolecule - Organelle - Cell - Tissue – Organ- System

FVM 101/102VETERINARY CLINICAL SERVICES AND THE NIGERIAN FISHERIES INDUSTRY
By 
Dr. G. A. Oladosu
Dept. of Veterinary Medicine, University of Ibadan, Ibadan, Nigeria.

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction
Fish are cold-blooded, gill bearing, aquatic craniates that lack limbs with digits, breath by the means of special organs called gills and move by the means of fins. They are mostly vertebrates. 

Fish is important to man as food sources or for recreational purposes (ornamental fishes). Fish provides quality animal protein low in cholesterol and high in the heart friendly omega 3 and 6 fatty acids. 

Based on the aforementioned, fisheries production has developed into an industry, contributing immensely to the economy of nations.

--- SLIDE ---

Introduction Cont’d
The total fish demand for Nigeria, based on the 2014 population estimates of 180 million is 3.32 million tons. 

However the domestic fish production from all sources for the same year is 1.123 million tons, less than half of the estimated total demand. 

The fish supply gap is augmented by importation, making Nigeria one of the largest importers of fish.

--- SLIDE ---

The Fisheries Industry
The Fisheries industry comprises 

1. Capture Fisheries which involves the hunting of fish from open waters like rivers, oceans, seas and lakes, and in turn comprise of the artisanal and the industrial fishing. The capture fisheries constitute the major source of fish supply the world over, and in not too distant past accounted for over 90% of the world production of aquatic food organisms.

--- SLIDE ---

2. Culture fishery or aquaculture which involve the farming of aquatic organisms like fish (both fin-fish and shell-fish and aquatic plants.

It is the fastest growing food producing sector in the world, with an average annual growth rate of 8.9% since 1970, compared to only 1.2% for capture fisheries and 2.8% for terrestrial farmed meat production.

 Aquaculture is a significant socio-economic activity that contributes significantly to livelihood, food security and poverty alleviation via income generation, employment and service provision, as well as domestic and international trade (in inputs and products) among many other investment opportunities.

--- SLIDE ---

Intense fishing pressure, global warming, aquatic pollution, destruction of fish breeding grounds due to human activities in the coastal regions all contributes to the dwindling yield from capture fisheries over the years, making this sector of the industry unsustainable. 

With controlled seed propagation and intensive rearing methods, culture fishery is viewed as more sustainable, but not without its challenges. 

Aquaculture production can only be sustainable when the cultured fish are healthy and free from diseases. 

However, the mass adoption of intensive rearing system in fish farming, with the accompanying stress associated with overcrowding and poor environmental conditions provide grounds for incidence of diseases.

--- SLIDE ---

Furthermore, both domestic and international trade in fish (trawled fish, frozen fish, broodstock and fingerlings/juveniles) fish products and fish feed will involve considerable fish movement.

Movement of live fish enhances the spread of disease agents. 

There is therefore the need to prevent disease occurrence and control disease incidence. 

The use of drugs and chemicals must also be controlled to avoid environmental pollution, and pathogen resistance (Anti-Microbial Resistance - AMR), and to ensure product wholesomeness.

--- SLIDE ---

Veterinary Clinical Services in the Fisheries Industry
1.	National Quarantine Service
Strict rules for fish disease reporting and movement of live fish are lacking in Nigeria. However, there is a unit of the Federal Department of Fisheries saddled with the task of fish quarantine, manning the sea and air ports of the country, to 

Limit the spread of fish diseases
Prevent the importation of exotic pathogens into the country
Ensure wholesomenes

Why surgeons think they are all that!

Clinical Veterinary Surgery
Definition of terms
Veterinary Surgeon-a person who spends a long time learning about the anatomy, physiology and behaviour of different species of animals with the end of being able to treat their illnesses and prevent transmission of their diseases to humans. 
Clinical Veterinary Practice- the practice of treatment and prevention where possible, of diseases of animals through specialized skills
Clinical Veterinary Surgery- the treatment using surgical skills, of diseases of animals and prevention of ill-health in animals and consequently humans and the effect on the environment.

--- SLIDE ---

Surgical Skills
Surgery-the use of specially acquired skills to enter the body to repair, treat and prevent diseases of a nature that requires more than medical management
Branches of Surgery- 
-Soft tissue surgery
-Anaesthesia 
-Diagnostic Imaging /Radiology
-Farm Animal Surgery  
-Orthopaedics

Veterinary Surgery
Usually ‘begins’ in the 4th year of study with introductory Surgery
Surgical Principles like asepsis are introduced.

In the 5th year, surgical diseases and how to manage them are introduced

text_snippet:
THERIOGENOLOGY IN CLINICAL PRACTICE
DR. DIDEOLU OSUNKOYA

--- SLIDE ---

INTRODUCTION
Theriogenology is a branch of veterinary medicine that focuses on animal reproduction, including the physiology and pathology of male and female reproductive systems, and the clinical practice of veterinary gynaecology and obstetrics.

--- SLIDE ---

CONT’D
The term theriogenology comes from Greek word:
thērion (beast or animal)
genesis (origin or creation)→ literally meaning “the study of animal reproduction or creation.”

--- SLIDE ---

AIMS OF THERIOGENOLOGY
To improve the fertility in animal species
To facilitate breeding of animals as a tool for genetic improvement
To investigate and solve infertility problems in animals
For conservation of endangered animal species
For development of contraceptive procedures especially in pet animals
To conduct research to use animal models to solve problems in human reproduction

--- SLIDE ---

SPECIALIZATIONS OF THERIOGENOLOGY
Veterinary Andrology: This is the study of male reproductive organs or systems with reference to reproductive diseases and their management.
Veterinary Gynaecology: This is the study of female reproductive diseases and their management.
Veterinary Obstetrics: This deals with the care of female animals before, during and after parturition.
Veterinary Neonatology: This studies the care and management of neonates.

--- SLIDE ---

CONT’D
Assisted reproductive biotechnologies (ART): This is the application of biotechnology for manipulation of reproductive processes to achieve a desired goal  in a herd.
Examples include: oestrus synchronization, artificial insemination, invitro fertilization, embryo transfer.
Reproductive toxicology: This is the study of how toxicants affect various reproductive processes.

--- SLIDE ---

Clinical applications
1. Reproductive Management and Fertility Control
Estrus detection and synchronization: Managing breeding cycles through hormonal control (e.g., prostaglandins, progesterone, GnRH protocols).
Timed artificial insemination (AI): Maximizing conception rates by synchronizing ovulation and insemination.
Fertility evaluation: Assessing breeding soundness of males (semen quality, libido) and females (ovarian function, uterine health).

--- SLIDE ---

CONT’D
2. Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART)
Artificial insemination (AI): Widespread use in cattle, horses, pigs, and dogs for genetic improvement and disease control.
Embryo transfer (ET): Collection, evaluation, and transfer of embryos to recipient females to multiply superior genetics.
In vitro fertilization (IVF) and embryo production: Generation of embryos outside the body for breeding and research purposes.

--- SLIDE ---

CONT’D
Semen collection, evaluation, and cryopreservation: For storage, transport, and long-term use of genetic material.
Oocyte retrieval and cryopreservation: Preservation of valuable female genetics.
Cloning and transgenesis (advanced ART): Experimental and commercial applications in livestock and research animals.

--- SLIDE ---

CONT’D
3. Diagnosis and Treatment of Reproductive Disorders
Female reproductive diseases:
Metritis, endometritis, cystic ovarian disease, anestrus, pyometra.
Use of ultrasonography and hormonal assays for diagnosis.
Male reproductive disorders:
Orchitis, testicular degeneration, epididymitis, prostatitis, impotence.
Evaluation via semen analysis, ultrasound, and hormonal profiling.
Infertility management: Identifying and correcting causes of subfertility or sterility in breeding animals.

--- SLIDE ---

CONT’D
4. Obstetrics and Neonatal Care
Pregnancy diagnosis: Through rectal palpation, ultrasound, or biochemical markers.
Parturition management: Monitoring and assistance during normal and dystocic births.
Dystocia correction: Manual, pharmacological, or surgical (cesarean section) interventions.
Postpartum management: Preventing or treating retained placenta, metritis, and uterine prolapse.
Neonatal care: Ensuring colostrum intake, resuscita

medicine, 
•Veterinary anatomy provides the 
foundation for understanding the 
structural organization of different 
animal species. 

Understanding Animal Structure:
•This knowledge is essential for 
veterinarians to accurately diagnose and 
treat animals.

Veterinary anatomy is the study of the structure and 
organization of animal bodies. It encompasses:
•Gross anatomy: Study of visible structures (organs, 
tissues, systems)
•Microscopic anatomy: Study of cellular and tissue 
structure
•Comparative anatomy: Study of similarities and 
differences between species
•Functional/Clinical  anatomy: Study of how structures 
function and interact and how to apply this knowledge in 
CLINICS

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
•Diagnostic Accuracy: Knowledge of anatomy enables 
veterinarians to:
•Identify normal and abnormal structures
•Localize lesions or diseases
•Interpret diagnostic images (e.g., X-rays, MRI)
•Perform surgical procedures with precision
•Minimize complications and risks
•Develop innovative surgical techniques

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
In therapeutic Interventions,anatomy informs:
•Medication administration (e.g., injection sites)
•Anesthesia and pain management
•Rehabilitation and physical therapy

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
In Preventive Medicine, knowledge of anatomy helps 
veterinarians to: 
•Identify risk factors for diseases
•Develop preventive strategies (e.g., vaccination, parasite 
control)
•Counsel clients on animal care and husbandry

Importance of Veterinary Anatomy
Anatomy provides a common language for 
veterinarians to:
•Communicate with colleagues and clients
•Document medical records accurately
•Educate students and professionals

Applications of Veterinary Anatomy 1
Clinical Practice: 
Anatomy informs daily decision-making in:
•Companion animal practice
•Livestock production
•Equine medicine
•Zoological medicine

Applications of Veterinary Anatomy 2
Research and Development: 
Anatomy drives advancements in :
•Veterinary pharmaceuticals
•Surgical innovations
•Diagnostic technologies

Education and Training: 
: Anatomy is essential for:

science undergraduate and postgraduate research

•Professional certification

Recommendations for Students:

Artificial Intelligence/ imaging, and interactive 
resources

•By embracing veterinary anatomy, you'll become 
proficient, confident, veterinarians, equipped to 
provide exceptional expertise

Veterinary anatomy is the bedrock of veterinary 
medicine. It provides the essential foundation for 
accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and 
compassionate care. 
As future veterinarians, it's crucial to:
Develop a thorough understanding of veterinary anatomy
Apply anatomical knowledge in clinical practice
Stay updated with advancements in veterinary anatomy

text_snippet:
COURSE: INTRODUCTION TO VETERINARY 
MEDICINE (FVM 101)
Topic: The Equine Veterinarian
DR. O.O. AKINNIYI
University of Ibadan,
Department of Veterinary Medicine
1

Who is an Equine Veterinarian?
• An equine veterinarian is a medical professional specializing in the care and 
treatment of horses and other members of the equine family, including 
ponies, donkeys, mules, and occasionally zebras.
• They are trained to diagnose and treat a wide range of health issues in 
equines, including performing surgeries, administering vaccinations, providing 
routine care such as dental work, and managing injuries and illnesses.
• Their role involves not only treating sick or injured animals but also advising 
on preventative health care, including parasite control, nutrition plans, 
exercise regimens, and overall wellness strategies.
• Equine veterinarians must possess strong animal handling skills, excellent 
communication abilities, and the capacity to work effectively with horse 
owners, trainers, barn managers, and other professionals in the equestrian 
industry.
2

Historical Significance of Horses in Nigeria
• Warfare and Military Strength: Historically, horses were crucial in warfare, serving as a 
symbol of military strength and power. They were used by various emirates and kingdoms 
to protect their territories and expand their influence.
• Trade and Commerce: Horses facilitated trade across the Sahara Desert, connecting Nigeria 
with other regions like Egypt, Algeria, and Morocco. This trade was vital for the economic 
development of the region.
• Status and Prestige: In pre-colonial West Africa, including Nigeria, horses were a symbol of 
wealth and status. Only the wealthy could afford to maintain horses, which were used for 
ceremonial purposes and as a display of power.
• Long-Distance Travel: Before the development of modern roads, horses were essential for 
long-distance travel, particularly in areas where other forms of transportation were not 
available. They were used by traders, travelers, and military personnel.
3

Modern Importance of Horses in Nigeria
• Cultural Festivals and Tourism: Durbar Festival is a significant cultural event that attracts 
tourists and showcases Nigeria's rich heritage. Horses are integral to preserving cultural 
traditions, particularly in the northern regions, where they are used in festivals and 
ceremonies.
• Security and Law Enforcement: (1) Mounted Police Units: Horses are actively used by 
police units in various parts of Nigeria for patrols, crowd control, and border security. These 
mounted troops provide enhanced mobility and visibility in urban centers and difficult 
terrains, such as border communities and during public events like elections. The Nigerian 
police have institutionalized mounted troop training with formal training schools, 
reaffirming horses as a valuable asset in maintaining law and order; and (2) Military Use: 
Horses in the Nigerian military serve largely ceremonial and symbolic functions rather than 
combat roles. They may participate in military parades, traditional ceremonies, and cultural 
displays that honor Nigeria's equestrian heritage. While some regions have restricted horse 
movements in active conflict zones due to security concerns, their ceremonial presence 
underscores the continued historical and cultural significance of horses within Nigeria's 
military tradition, particularly reflecting the cavalry heritage of northern Nigeria.
4

Modern Importance of Horses in Nigeria
• Economic Contributions: The breeding and sale of horses can generate income, 
both domestically and internationally, contributing to foreign exchange earnings. 
Also, the demand for veterinary care for horses supports the growth of the 
veterinary sector, creating jobs and stimulating economic activity.
• Educational and Research Opportunities: Horses provide opportunities for 
veterinary students to gain practical experience, contributing to the development of 
veterinary skills a

1 
 
LECTURE NOTE: THE ROLE OF PATHOLOGY IN VETERINARY 
PRACTICE 
DR. T.A. JARIKRE 
Department of Veterinary Pathology, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, University of 
Ibadan. 
Objective: By the end of this lecture, you will be able to define pathology, explain its critical 
subdivisions, and articulate why it serves as the indispensable "bridge" between the basic 
sciences and clinical veterinary practice. 
 
Welcome to veterinary school, and welcome to the foundation of all clinical medicine. 
This lecture note is designed specifically for fresh (pre-clinical) veterinary students. You are 
standing at the threshold of a vast and exciting field. Before you can diagnose a fracture, treat a 
cough, or perform surgery, you must first understand what disease is and how it works. That is the 
domain of pathology. 
This lecture is not about memorizing obscure disease names. It is about learning a new language—
the language of disease—which you will use every single day for the rest of your career. 
 
1. What is Pathology? (The "Study of Suffering") 
• 
Etymology: The word comes from the Greek pathos (suffering) and -logia (study of). 
• 
Definition: Pathology is the scientific study of disease. It is the discipline that asks the 
fundamental questions: What is wrong? Why did it happen? How did it develop? What will 
happen next? 

2 
 
 
Pathology provides the scientific foundation for the practice of medicine by studying the 
etiology and pathogenesis of disease at all levels. 
Veterinary pathology protects and advances both animal and human health – especially 
through the critical involvement of veterinary pathologists in evaluating the safety of drugs 
and medical devices. 
 
Veterinary Pathology is: 
• 
The study of animal disease in a variety of species, often with human implications.  
• 
Crucial in determining cause of animal disease and its risk to human health (at the 
forefront of the One Health concept). 
• 
Studies range from live animals to specific proteins involved in disease 
The Core Questions of Pathology: 
For every single disease you will encounter, pathology answers four specific questions: 
1. Etiology: What is the cause? (e.g., a virus, a toxin, a genetic defect, poor nutrition). 
2. Pathogenesis: How does the cause produce disease? (The step-by-step mechanism by 
which the body is damaged). 
3. Morphology: What are the structural changes? (What does the disease look like to the 
naked eye (gross) and under the microscope (histology)?). 
4. Clinical Significance: What are the consequences? (How do these changes lead to the 
signs you see in the live animal, and what is the likely outcome?). 
 
 

3 
 
2. The "Big Picture": Pathology is the Bridge 
As a first-year student, you are currently immersed in the basic sciences; later Anatomy, 
Physiology, Biochemistry, and Histology. There you are learning how a healthy animal 
(tissue) should work (look like). 
As a final-year student, you will be immersed in clinical sciences: Medicine, Surgery, 
Theriogenology, and Epidemiology. You will learn how to diagnose and treat a sick animal. 
Pathology is the bridge that connects these two worlds. 
• 
Anatomy tells you where the liver is. Pathology tells you what a diseased liver looks like 
(cirrhosis, fatty change, necrosis). 
• 
Physiology tells you how the kidneys filter blood. Pathology tells you why the kidneys 
fail (glomerulonephritis, tubular necrosis). 
• 
Biochemistry tells you what normal enzymes do. Pathology tells you why elevated 
enzymes in the blood indicate tissue damage (leakage from dead cells). 
Without pathology, clinical medicine is just guesswork. You cannot treat a disease effectively 
if you do not understand what is causing the signs you are observing. 
3. The Two Great Pillars of Pathology 
To understand the role of pathology, you must understand its two main subdivisions. As a 
clinician, you will rely on both. 
A. General Pathology 
• 
What it is: The study of the basic, fundamental mechanis
